Dwarpal — Zero to Hero

A book that takes you from "I have never written a line of code" to "I understand — line by line — how a real AI system that protects children online is designed, built, tested, deployed and defended."

Explain like I'm six

Imagine a door to a room that only grown-ups are allowed to enter. Next to the door stands a guard. In old Indian temples the guard who stands at the door is called a dwarpal (द्वारपाल — dwar means "door", pal means "keeper").

Our project builds a computer guard for doors on the internet. When someone tries to open a website that is only for grown-ups, the computer guard takes a quick look through the camera, makes a careful guess about whether the person is a grown-up, and then — this is the important part — forgets the face immediately. It only remembers "this person was allowed in" or "this person was not allowed in".

This book teaches you everything needed to build that guard — starting from "what is a computer?"

What this book is

This is a single, self-contained book about one project: an AI-based age estimation system for protecting minors from accessing age-restricted online content, code-named Dwarpal.

It is written for a reader who knows nothing about computers, programming, websites, servers or artificial intelligence. Every idea is introduced before it is used. Every word that might be new is explained the first time it appears, and again in the Glossary. Hover over words with a dotted underline (like API or HTTP) to see a short definition.

The book does three jobs at once:

  1. It teaches the foundations — computers, the internet, websites, databases, servers, AI — from scratch.
  2. It records the thinking — why this project is built the way it is, which alternatives were considered, and why they were rejected. In engineering, the why matters as much as the what.
  3. It explains every line of code — every single line of every file in the project, in plain language, right next to the code itself.

The 60-second version of the project

  1. A website that sells something grown-ups-only (or shows grown-ups-only content) needs to know whether a visitor is old enough. Laws in the UK, the EU, the US, Australia and India now require many websites to check this properly.
  2. Asking "Are you 18? Yes/No" doesn't work — children just click "Yes".
  3. Our system lets the website send the visitor to a verification page. The visitor looks at their camera for about three seconds and follows two or three random instructions ("turn your head left", "look up") while the screen glows softly in random colours.
  4. On our server, an AI model estimates the visitor's age as a range with a confidence level, and checks that a real, live person was in front of the camera (not a photo, a video, or a video-game character).
  5. A decision engine compares the estimate against the website's rule (for example "18+") using a carefully calculated safety margin. The answer is pass, fail, or "not sure — please use another method".
  6. The website receives a digitally signed answer — like a letter with a wax seal that cannot be forged — saying only "this person is over 18: yes". It never receives the face, the estimated age, or the person's identity.
  7. The face images are deleted from memory within about a second. They are never saved anywhere.

Throughout the book, coloured boxes mark special kinds of explanation:

Real world

A real event, law or product that shows why something matters.

Something our system cannot do, or does not do perfectly. A good engineer says this out loud.

The promise: every line explained — and how we prove it

Most explanations of software skip the "boring" lines. This book doesn't. Every source file in the project has a walkthrough: the code is shown on the left, and the explanation of each line (or small group of lines) on the right.

Promises are easy to break, so we made this one checkable by a machine. The program that builds this book:

  • counts every non-empty line of every code file in the project, and marks which lines have an explanation;
  • takes a fingerprint of each file when it is explained. If the code later changes, the fingerprint no longer matches and the book shows a red "code changed since explained" badge;
  • prints a Coverage ledger at the end of the book listing every file, how many of its lines are explained, and which files have not been explained yet.

You will learn exactly how that works — line by line — in Part X.

Part 0 — Absolute basics

This part assumes you know nothing. If you already know what a server, an API and a database are, skim it. Every later part builds on it.

0.1 What is a computer?

A computer is a machine that does exactly three things, over and over, billions of times per second:

  1. Takes in information (input) — key presses, mouse clicks, a camera picture, a message from the internet.
  2. Works on that information (processing) — adds numbers, compares them, moves them around.
  3. Gives out a result (output) — pixels on the screen, sound, a message sent back over the internet.

Explain like I'm six

A computer is like a very fast, very obedient cook who can't think for themselves. You give the cook ingredients (input), a recipe (the program), and the cook produces a dish (output). The cook will follow the recipe exactly — even if the recipe says "add 100 spoons of salt". The cook never asks "are you sure?".

The important parts inside a computer:

Part What it does Everyday comparison
CPU (Central Processing Unit) Follows instructions, one tiny step at a time, extremely fast The cook's brain and hands
GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) Does thousands of simple maths operations at the same time. Built for drawing graphics; perfect for AI A kitchen with 5,000 helpers who can each only chop, but all chop at once
RAM (memory) Holds what the computer is working on right now. Fast, but forgets everything when power is off The kitchen counter — you put things there while cooking
Storage (SSD / hard disk) Keeps files permanently, even when power is off The cupboard

The computer this project is being built on has an Intel Core i9-14900HX CPU, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Laptop GPU with 8 GB of its own memory, and 32 GB of RAM. That GPU matters: it is what will make training our AI model (Part 2) take hours instead of weeks.

Key idea — everything is numbers

Inside a computer, everything — text, photos, music, videos, programs — is stored as numbers. The smallest unit is a bit: a single 0 or 1 (think of a light switch, off or on). Eight bits make a byte, which can hold a number from 0 to 255.

  • 1 kilobyte (KB) ≈ 1,000 bytes — about a paragraph of text
  • 1 megabyte (MB) ≈ 1,000,000 bytes — about one phone photo
  • 1 gigabyte (GB) ≈ 1,000,000,000 bytes — about a film

A photo is stored as a grid of tiny dots called pixels, and each pixel is three numbers: how much Red, Green and Blue light it has (each 0–255). A 640 × 480 camera picture is therefore 640 × 480 × 3 = 921,600 numbers. When our AI "looks at a face", it is really doing arithmetic on numbers like these. Part 2 shows exactly how.

0.2 Files, folders and paths

A file is a named bundle of bytes kept in storage: a photo, a document, a program. A folder (also called a directory) is a container for files and other folders, so they form a tree.

The path of a file is its full address in that tree. On Windows a path looks like this:

C:\Users\anubh\Projects\AI_based_minor_protection\docs\zero_to_hero\build.py

Read it left to right: drive C:, then folder Users, inside it folder anubh, … and finally the file build.py. The part after the last dot, .py, is the extension. It hints at what kind of file it is (.py = Python program, .html = web page, .md = Markdown text, .json = data, .jpg = photo).

Careful — two kinds of slashes

Windows separates folders with a backslash \. Linux and macOS — and web addresses — use a forward slash /. Our code must run on both (development on Windows, servers on Linux), so it uses tools that handle either. In this book we usually write paths with /, like docs/zero_to_hero/build.py. That kind of path, measured from the project's main folder, is called a relative path.

Text files and encodings

Some files contain text (letters you can read); others contain binary data (photos, programs). But text is numbers too: each letter needs a number. The agreement that says "the number 65 means A" is called a character encoding.

The modern encoding is UTF-8. It can store every character in every language — English, हिन्दी, emoji 🧒 — and it is what every file in this project uses.

Real world — what goes wrong when encodings disagree

If a program writes a file in UTF-8 but another program reads it assuming an older encoding (such as Windows-1252), characters turn into garbage called mojibake. A long dash "—" becomes "â€”". This exact bug appears in the HTML documentation of a previous project by the same team. That is why the builder of this book reads and writes every file as UTF-8 explicitly — you will see the exact line in Part X.

0.3 What is a program?

A program is a file (or many files) of instructions for the computer. The instructions are written by people, in a programming language, as plain text. That text is called source code, or just code.

Explain like I'm six

A program is a recipe. A recipe for tea might say:

  1. Fill the kettle with water.
  2. Switch it on.
  3. If you want it sweet, add sugar.
  4. Repeat stirring 5 times.

Programs have exactly these ingredients: steps in order, decisions ("if …"), and repetition ("repeat …"). Everything else is detail.

Programs are precise. A human understands "add some sugar"; a computer needs "add 2 spoons". Most of programming is turning a fuzzy human wish into precise steps — and most bugs come from a step that wasn't quite what the programmer meant.

0.4 Programming languages

Computers really only understand machine code: long lists of numbers that mean things like "add these two" or "jump to step 7". Humans can't comfortably write that, so we write in programming languages that read almost like English. Other programs then translate them for the computer.

Language Used in this project for What it looks like
Python The servers (backend), the AI, the tools (including the one that builds this book) if age >= 18: print("welcome")
TypeScript The websites people see (frontend). It is JavaScript with extra safety checks called types if (age >= 18) { show("welcome") }
JavaScript What web browsers actually run. TypeScript is converted into it same as above, minus the types
HTML Not a programming language — a markup language that describes what's on a web page <h1>Welcome</h1>
CSS A style language: colours, sizes, layouts h1 { color: blue; }
SQL The language for asking a database questions SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE outcome = 'pass'

There are two broad ways a language gets run:

  • Interpreted (Python, JavaScript): another program — the interpreter — reads your code and does what it says, line by line, while it runs.
  • Compiled (C, Rust, Go): a compiler translates the whole program into machine code first, producing a file that runs directly.

Why Python for the backend and the AI?

Nearly every modern AI tool (PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, OpenCV, MediaPipe) is built for Python first. Using Python for both the AI and the servers means one language for the whole back half of the system — and one language for you to learn. The speed cost of an interpreted language barely matters here, because the slow part (the AI maths) runs inside highly optimised libraries written in faster languages.

0.5 The terminal

Before mouse-and-window interfaces, people used computers by typing commands. That way of working still exists and programmers use it constantly. The window you type commands into is called a terminal (on Windows: PowerShell or Command Prompt). The program that reads your commands is called a shell.

Try it yourself

Open PowerShell (press the Windows key, type PowerShell, press Enter) and type:

python --version

and press Enter. The computer answers with something like Python 3.14.6. You just asked a program a question and got an answer — that is what every command does.

Throughout this book, commands you can type are shown in boxes like this:

python build.py

0.6 How computers talk: networks and the internet

A network is computers connected so they can send each other messages. The internet is the network of all networks — billions of devices.

Messages travel in small chunks called packets. To deliver a packet, the network needs an address:

  • An IP address is a computer's address on a network, like a house address. It looks like 142.250.183.14 (IPv4) or a longer form with colons (IPv6).
  • A port is a numbered door on that computer (0–65535). One computer can run many programs that talk to the network; each listens behind its own door. Web traffic usually uses door 443 (secure) or 80 (old, insecure).

Explain like I'm six

The IP address gets the letter to the right building. The port number gets it to the right flat inside the building. Every program that wants to receive letters must sit behind a flat door with a number on it.

  • localhost (or 127.0.0.1) is a special address that always means "this same computer". When we run the project on our own laptop, we visit addresses like http://localhost:3000.
  • DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone book. Humans remember names like google.com; DNS translates them into IP addresses. When we put Dwarpal on the internet, we'll buy a name and add a DNS record pointing it at our server's IP address.

0.7 Clients and servers

Most internet programs come in pairs:

  • A client asks for something. Your web browser is a client.
  • A server answers. It is a program that starts up and then waits — forever — for clients to ask it things. Waiting for messages on a port is called listening.

Explain like I'm six — the restaurant

You sit at a table and order (you are the client). The waiter takes your order to the kitchen (the server — it waits all day for orders). The kitchen prepares the dish and sends it back. You never go into the kitchen, and the kitchen never comes to your house. The menu tells you what you're allowed to order.

The word "server" means two things — the program that answers and the computer it runs on. When people say "the website is on a server", they mean a computer, usually in a data centre, running server programs 24 hours a day.

Dwarpal has several servers. Each is a program with its own job, and each listens on its own port:

Server Its job Language
Web app Sends the pages you see in your browser TypeScript (Next.js)
API The "brain office": sessions, rules, decisions, signed answers Python (FastAPI)
Inference service The "AI room": looks at the frames and does the maths Python + ONNX Runtime
Database Remembers things long-term PostgreSQL
Valkey Remembers things short-term, very fast Valkey

0.8 HTTP — the language of the web

When a client and a server talk, they need an agreed protocol: rules for how messages are formatted. The web's protocol is HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol).

Every HTTP conversation is one request followed by one response.

A request has:

  • a method — what kind of action is wanted;
  • a path — which thing it's about;
  • headers — extra labels, like the envelope of a letter;
  • (sometimes) a body — the contents, like the letter inside.
POST /v1/verification-sessions HTTP/1.1
Host: api.dwarpal.example
Authorization: Bearer dk_test_EXAMPLEKEY000000000000
Content-Type: application/json

{"policy": "uk_osa_18", "return_url": "https://shop.example/age-check/complete"}

The common methods:

Method Means Example in Dwarpal
GET "Give me this" (never changes anything) Get the result of a verification session
POST "Create something / do something" Create a new verification session
PUT / PATCH "Replace / update this" Change a policy
DELETE "Remove this" Revoke an API key

A response has a status code (a three-digit number that summarises what happened), headers, and usually a body:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": "vs_01JA8...", "url": "https://verify.dwarpal.example/v/vs_01JA8...#cs=...", "status": "created"}
Code Name Means
200 OK Here's what you asked for
201 Created I made the thing you asked me to make
204 No Content Done; nothing to send back
301 / 302 Moved Look over there instead
400 Bad Request Your request doesn't make sense
401 Unauthorized I don't know who you are (missing or wrong key)
403 Forbidden I know who you are, but you're not allowed
404 Not Found That doesn't exist
409 Conflict That clashes with something that already happened
422 Unprocessable I understood the format, but the values are invalid
429 Too Many Requests Slow down — you're over your limit
500 Internal Server Error Something broke on my side
503 Service Unavailable I can't answer right now, try later

Key idea

The first digit tells you who is responsible: 2xx = success, 3xx = go elsewhere, 4xx = the client made a mistake, 5xx = the server made a mistake. Dwarpal follows these rules carefully, because the websites that use it will write code that reacts to these numbers.

0.9 HTTPS — the padlock

Plain HTTP travels like a postcard: anyone the message passes through can read it. HTTPS is HTTP inside a sealed, tamper-proof envelope. The sealing technology is called TLS (Transport Layer Security). The padlock icon in your browser means "this conversation is sealed".

The server proves its identity with a certificate: a digital document, signed by a trusted organisation, saying "this server really is dwarpal.example".

Key idea — why HTTPS isn't optional for us

Browsers refuse to give a web page access to your camera unless the page is served over HTTPS (or from localhost during development). This is a deliberate browser security rule. Our whole system depends on the camera, so HTTPS is built in from day one. We'll use a program called Caddy that gets and renews certificates automatically.

0.10 How a web page is made: HTML, CSS and JavaScript

When you open a website, your browser asks a server for files and turns them into the page you see. There are three kinds:

Explain like I'm six — building a puppet

  • HTML is the puppet's skeleton: what parts exist (a heading here, a button there, a picture below).
  • CSS is the puppet's clothes and paint: colours, sizes, where things sit.
  • JavaScript is the puppet's muscles: it makes things move and react when you click, type or look at the camera.
<h1>Are you old enough?</h1>
<button id="start">Start age check</button>

h1 { font-size: 32px; color: #0969da; }

document.getElementById("start").addEventListener("click", startCamera);

The frontend is everything that runs in the user's browser. The backend is everything that runs on our servers. Users never see the backend directly; they only see what the frontend shows them.

0.11 APIs and JSON

An API (Application Programming Interface) is a menu of requests that one program offers to other programs. A website shows buttons to humans. An API offers endpoints — specific paths and methods — to other programs. For example, POST /v1/verification-sessions is one endpoint on Dwarpal's API.

When programs exchange data, they need a shared format. The most common is JSON (JavaScript Object Notation). It is plain text with just six kinds of value:

Kind Looks like Means
String "hello" Text, always in double quotes
Number 42, 0.97 A number
Boolean true / false Yes or no
Null null "Nothing here"
Array [1, 2, 3] An ordered list
Object {"min_age": 18} Labelled values ("key": value) 
{
  "id": "vs_01JA8XQ2",
  "outcome": "pass",
  "age_over_18": true,
  "methods": ["face_estimation", "liveness_active"]
}

That is everything — all JSON is these six kinds nested inside each other.

0.12 Databases

Programs forget everything when they stop, like the kitchen counter being wiped clean every night. A database is a program that remembers, safely and permanently, and can quickly answer questions about what it remembers.

The most common kind is a relational database. It stores data in tables, a bit like spreadsheets:

id policy outcome created_at
vs_01JA8XQ2 uk_osa_18 pass 2026-10-15 10:02
vs_01JA8XR7 uk_osa_18 step_up 2026-10-15 10:03

Each row is one thing (here, one verification session). Each column is one property of it. You talk to it in SQL:

SELECT outcome, COUNT(*) FROM verification_sessions GROUP BY outcome;

That asks: "for each outcome, how many sessions had it?"

Why a real database instead of saving files?

Two people can't safely write to the same file at the same moment. A database handles thousands of simultaneous readers and writers without corrupting anything. It guarantees that a group of changes either all happen or none happen — this is called a transaction. It also enforces rules ("every session must belong to a project"). Dwarpal uses PostgreSQL, one of the most trusted databases in the world.

0.13 Where websites live: hosting, the cloud and domains

To be reachable by everyone, our servers must run on a computer that is always on and connected to the internet. Your laptop sleeps and moves around, so instead we rent a computer in a data centre.

  • Hosting = renting space and computing power to run your website.
  • The cloud = companies (Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Hetzner, Oracle Cloud, …) that rent out computers by the hour or month.
  • A VM (virtual machine) or VPS (virtual private server) = a slice of a big computer that behaves like your own private computer.
  • Deploying = copying your program onto that rented computer and starting it.
  • A domain = the human-friendly name (like dwarpal.example) that you rent from a registrar, then point at your server with DNS.

Explain like I'm six

Your laptop is your home kitchen. Hosting is renting a stall in a big food market that never closes. The domain name is the sign above your stall, so people can find it. Deploying is carrying your recipes and ingredients to the stall and starting to cook there.

0.14 Containers and Docker

Software that works perfectly on your laptop often breaks on a server: a different operating system, a missing library, a different version of Python. Docker solves this by packing a program together with everything it needs into one sealed box.

Word Meaning Lunchbox comparison
Image The sealed, read-only package: the operating system bits, the language version, the libraries, your code A packed lunchbox recipe — the same every time
Container A running copy of an image An actual lunchbox, opened and being eaten
Volume A folder that survives when the container is thrown away A thermos you keep and refill
Docker Compose A file that describes several containers that work together, and starts them all with one command A picnic plan: "three lunchboxes, two thermoses, start them together"

Dwarpal will start completely — web app, API, AI service, database, everything — with one command:

docker compose up

0.15 Git — a time machine for code

Git is a tool that records the history of a project.

  • Every time you reach a good point, you make a commit: a snapshot of all files plus a message saying what changed and why.
  • You can go back to any earlier snapshot, compare two snapshots, or work on an experiment in a separate branch without disturbing the main version.
  • GitHub is a website that stores Git projects online, so teams can share them and computers can automatically test every change.

Explain like I'm six

Git is a "save game" button for code. Every save has a name and a note. If you break something, you load the last good save.

0.16 Open source and licences — why "free to download" isn't "free to use"

A huge amount of software (and many AI models and datasets) is open source: the code is published for anyone to read. But publishing is not the same as permission. Every project comes with a licence — the legal rules for what you may do with it.

Licence family Examples What it allows Effect on us
Permissive MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD Use it for anything, including selling, as long as you keep the copyright notice ✅ We prefer these
Copyleft GPL, AGPL Use it, but if you distribute it (AGPL: or even just offer it over a network), you must publish your code under the same licence ⚠️ Avoided in the running system
Non-commercial CC BY-NC, "research only" Use it only for research or education — never to make money ⚠️ Fine for this academic project, but blocks commercial use

Real world — licences shaped this project's design

  • The popular YOLOv8 face detector is AGPL, so we chose YuNet (MIT licence) instead.
  • Many well-known face datasets used to train age models (IMDB-WIKI, UTKFace, …) are research-only. Our AI model can be trained on them for this project, but a company selling Dwarpal would have to retrain on properly licensed data.

That is why the system treats the AI model as a replaceable part with a version number, not as something welded in. Part 3 explains this decision.

0.17 Libraries, packages and versions

Nobody writes everything from scratch. A library (or package) is code someone else wrote and shared, so you can use it. Examples: a library that reads photos, a library that does the AI maths, a library that turns Markdown into HTML.

  • A package manager downloads libraries for you: pip or uv for Python, npm or pnpm for JavaScript.
  • Libraries have version numbers such as 3.11.1. These are usually major.minor.patch: a bigger last number means a small bug fix, a bigger middle number means new features, and a bigger first number may mean breaking changes.
  • Pinning means writing down the exact version you tested with (like pygments==2.21.0). Then the project builds the same way next month, on another computer, or on a server.
  • A lockfile (uv.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml) is an automatically generated list of the exact versions of every library, including the libraries your libraries use.

Careful

"It worked yesterday" bugs very often come from a library quietly updating itself. Pinning versions prevents that. Every library in Dwarpal is pinned.

0.18 Putting it all together — the journey of one age check

Here is everything from Part 0 in one story. Later parts explain each step in depth.

  1. Asha, 26, visits a (fictional) online shop that sells wine. Her browser (a client) asks the shop's server for a page using HTTPS.
  2. The shop must check her age. Its server sends a POST request to Dwarpal's API, authenticated with the shop's secret API key. Dwarpal's API saves a new session in the database and replies with JSON containing a link.
  3. Asha's browser opens Dwarpal's verification page (HTML, CSS, JavaScript). With her permission — only possible because the page uses HTTPS — it turns on the camera.
  4. JavaScript running in her browser helps her line up her face. Then it sends a few camera frames (photos, which are just numbers) to the API.
  5. The API passes them to the inference service. There, the AI model — running on the CPU — turns the numbers into an age estimate and a liveness check. The frames are then forgotten.
  6. The API's decision engine says pass. It creates a digitally signed answer and records "pass" (never the face) in the database.
  7. Asha's browser goes back to the shop. The shop's server checks the signature and lets her buy the wine.

All of this runs inside Docker containers on a rented VM reachable at a domain name. The code is tracked with Git, built from pinned libraries with suitable licences.

If every bold word above now makes at least a little sense, you're ready for Part 1.

Part 1 — The problem

1.1 A story

Riya is 14. She has a phone, like most of her friends. One evening a link in a group chat leads to a website showing violent videos that are made for adults. The site has a little box: "Are you 18 or older? [Yes] [No]". Riya taps Yes. Nothing stops her.

Nobody did anything illegal by building that box. Until recently, in most countries, that box was considered "enough". That has now changed. Governments around the world have decided that websites with adult content must actually check age, not just ask.

This project is about building that check properly — so that it really works, is fair to everyone, and does not turn into a surveillance machine.

1.2 What is "age-restricted content"?

Anything the law, or a website's own rules, says should only be available above a certain age:

Kind of content or service Typical minimum age (varies by country)
Pornography and sexually explicit material 18
Online gambling and betting 18 (21 in some US states)
Alcohol, tobacco and vape sales 18 (21 in the US)
Graphic violence, self-harm and suicide content 18 (or "not for children")
Social media accounts 13 in many places; 16 in Australia since December 2025
Some games and in-app purchases 12, 16 or 18 depending on rating
Processing a child's personal data at all (India) Under 18 needs a parent's verifiable consent

Key idea

The age limit is not always 18. That is why Dwarpal treats the age limit as a setting each website chooses (13, 16, 18, 21…), never as a number fixed inside the code.

1.3 Why "Are you 18? Yes / No" doesn't work

A self-declaration box checks nothing — it trusts the person it is supposed to check. Typing a date of birth is the same thing in a different costume: children simply type an earlier year. Regulators now say this plainly. The UK regulator Ofcom states that self-declaration does not count as effective age checking.

So we need something that does not depend on the person telling the truth.

1.4 What the law now says — a world tour

Explain like I'm six

Different countries have made slightly different rules, but they all say roughly the same thing to websites: "If you show grown-up stuff, you must really check who is a grown-up — and you must do it fairly, safely, and without being nosy."

Where The rule (simplified) Since
🇬🇧 United Kingdom The Online Safety Act. Adult sites and many social platforms need "highly effective age assurance". Ofcom checks four things: accurate, robust, reliable, fair. Fines up to £18 million or 10 % of worldwide turnover — and fines are already being issued July 2025
🇪🇺 European Union The Digital Services Act asks for age checks that are "accurate, reliable, robust, non-intrusive and non-discriminatory". The EU has built an official age-verification app that proves "over 18" without revealing who you are; countries are asked to roll it out by the end of 2026 2025–2026
🇺🇸 United States In June 2025 the Supreme Court allowed states to require age verification for adult sites (Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton). More than 20 states have such laws. New laws push age checks into app stores and phone operating systems 2023–2027
🇦🇺 Australia Children under 16 may not have accounts on major social media platforms. Platforms must take "reasonable steps"; fines up to AUD 49.5 million December 2025
🇮🇳 India The Digital Personal Data Protection Act and its 2025 Rules. A "child" is anyone under 18, and processing a child's data needs a parent's verifiable consent. No tracking, profiling or targeted ads aimed at children. Phased in, with full compliance expected around 2027 2025–2027

Real world

In its first six months (July–December 2025), the UK system processed around 69 million age checks across 32 large services. The two most common methods were face-based age estimation and photo-ID matching. This is not a classroom problem — it is happening at enormous scale right now.

1.5 Three ways to know someone's age

Explain like I'm six — three ways a shopkeeper can know your age

  1. Verify: you show your birth certificate or ID card. The shopkeeper reads your birth date. (Very sure — but you have shown your name, address and photo too.)
  2. Estimate: the shopkeeper just looks at you and guesses. (Quick and private — but sometimes wrong.)
  3. Infer: the shopkeeper notices clues — you drove here yourself, you are paying with a credit card. (Indirect.)
Method Official name Strength Weakness
ID card, passport, bank, digital ID app Age verification Exact date of birth Reveals identity; not everyone has ID; documents can be faked or borrowed
Looking at the face (or voice, or hand) Age estimation Fast, no documents, can reveal nothing but "over/under" It's a guess; it can be wrong, especially close to the limit
Other facts (credit card, account history, email history) Age inference Invisible to the user Indirect; needs extra data about the person

All three together are called age assurance. Dwarpal uses estimation first (fast and private). It falls back to verification only when the estimate is too close to call.

1.6 How can a computer guess age from a face?

Faces change with age in ways we all recognise: proportions change as children grow, skin texture changes, bone structure matures, and later come wrinkles and grey hair. An AI model learns these patterns by looking at hundreds of thousands of face photos whose real ages are known — the same way you learn to guess ages by meeting many people. Part 2 explains exactly how that learning works.

Honest limitation

Faces don't come with birth certificates. Some 16-year-olds look 20; some 20-year-olds look 16. Make-up, beards, lighting, camera quality, health and family genes all change how old someone looks. Even humans are often wrong by several years. No AI can remove this uncertainty completely. A good system doesn't pretend otherwise — it measures its uncertainty and acts carefully when it is unsure.

1.7 The two kinds of mistakes

Whenever a guard decides "allowed" or "not allowed", there are two ways to be wrong:

Guard says "grown-up, come in" Guard says "not sure / no"
Really a child ❌ Dangerous mistake — a child gets in ✅ correct
Really a grown-up ✅ correct ⚠️ Annoying mistake — an adult is held up

Explain like I'm six — the swimming pool

A swimming pool has a deep end only for strong swimmers. The lifeguard can make two mistakes: letting in a child who can't swim (dangerous!), or stopping a good swimmer (annoying, but nobody gets hurt). A sensible lifeguard is stricter about the dangerous mistake, and gives the stopped swimmer a fair way to prove themselves — "swim one length for me".

These two mistakes are not equally bad. Our whole design is built around that fact:

  • We measure the dangerous mistake carefully, separately for every age (13, 14, 15, 16, 17). We call it the false-adult rate.
  • We set a strict limit on it — for example "at most 2 in every 100 children near the age limit may get through" — and calculate the guard's settings to respect that limit. (The exact method is in Part 3.)
  • We give adults who were held up a fair second route (another method), instead of just saying "no".

Real world — why this matters so much

A February 2026 research benchmark tested 34 freely available AI age-guessing models. Most of the specialised ones called 39–100 % of children "adults" when the limit was 18. Even huge general-purpose AI models made that mistake 16–29 % of the time. The best commercial systems, measured by the US standards body NIST, let through roughly 5 % of minors when they use a safety margin. So "just download a model" is not safe. The gap between those numbers is what this project's engineering is for.

1.8 The safety margin: "Challenge 25"

Shops in the UK selling alcohol follow a rule called Challenge 25: the law says 18, but staff ask for ID from anyone who looks under 25. The extra seven years are a buffer. A 17-year-old might be mistaken for 19, but very rarely for 25.

Age-estimation systems use exactly the same trick, called a challenge age or buffer. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), which tests these systems, measures them this way — for example "accept only if the estimate is 25 or more, for a legal age of 18".

Explain like I'm six — the fairground ride

A ride says "you must be 120 cm tall". The measuring stick is wobbly. So the operator says: if the stick shows 130 cm or more, go straight in. If it shows less, let's measure you properly with the good tape. The extra 10 cm protects against the wobbly stick.

1.9 When the guard isn't sure: "step-up"

What happens to a 20-year-old who looks 19? With a buffer of 25, the guess "19" is not enough to let them in. But we also can't be sure they are a child. So the answer is neither "yes" nor "no", but:

"I'm not sure. Please use another method."

This is called step-up: moving to a stronger check, such as an ID document or a digital ID app. Australia's government trial called this a waterfall: try the quick, private method first; flow down to a stronger method only when needed.

Dwarpal therefore has three main answers, not two: pass, fail, and step-up. (Plus retry when the picture was too dark or blurry, and reject when it looks like someone is cheating.)

1.10 Cheaters: how people try to fool the guard

If there's a gate, someone will try to sneak past. The cheating tricks have names:

Trick Example Official name
Hold up a photo of an adult Printed photo, or a photo on another phone Presentation attack (print / screen)
Play a video of an adult A recorded video on a tablet Replay attack
Use a fake face A mask; heavy make-up; a fake beard Presentation attack (mask / disguise)
Use a computer-generated face A video-game character, a 3D avatar, a deepfake Presentation / injection attack
Skip the camera completely Software that pretends to be a camera and feeds in a fake video Injection attack
Ask a grown-up to do it An older sibling or parent looks at the camera Proxy
Try again and again Different lights and angles until it says yes Trial-and-error

Real world — the video-game trick, July 2025

Days after the UK's new rules started in July 2025, people discovered that Discord's face-based age check could be passed with a video-game character. The game Death Stranding has a "photo mode" that lets you move a very realistic character's face. Its controls could even open and close the mouth, which was exactly what Discord's "liveness" step asked for. Reports say characters from other games worked too.

Lesson for us: a simple, predictable "liveness" test (blink, open your mouth) is not enough any more. Part 3 describes our layered defence: random head-movement instructions that can't be prepared in advance, and a screen-light check — the screen glows in a secret random sequence of colours, and a real face reflects that light in a way a pre-made video or a game character cannot know ahead of time.

Honest limitation

No age check can stop a willing adult from doing the check for a child (a "proxy"). Regulators accept this. What we can do is make sure a real, live person was present at the moment of the check, keep the result short-lived, and tie it to the specific website visit.

1.11 Privacy: "look, decide, forget"

Faces are biometric data — information about your body. If a company kept millions of children's face photos, a single data leak would be a disaster.

Key idea — Dwarpal's privacy promise

  1. Look: the camera frames are used only to make the decision.
  2. Decide: the system produces "pass", "fail" or "step-up".
  3. Forget: the frames are erased from memory within about a second. They are never written to a disk, a log file or a database. There is literally no place in the system where a face could be saved.
  4. Say as little as possible: the website learns only "over 18: yes" (or no). Not the guessed age. Not a name. Not anything that could link the same person across different websites.

There is a saying in security: you can't leak what you never kept.

1.12 Fairness: the same rules for every face

AI models learn from examples. If the examples contain mostly one kind of face — say, light-skinned adult film stars — the model will be worse at guessing other faces. Research, including NIST's testing and Australia's trial, has found exactly this: some systems make more mistakes for some skin tones, for women, or for certain age groups.

An unfair age check is dangerous in both directions:

  • it can let more children through for some groups (unsafe);
  • it can block more adults from some groups (discriminatory).

Dwarpal will measure its mistakes separately for different groups, using research datasets that carry those labels. It will refuse to release a model whose groups differ too much. And it will never try to guess a person's skin colour or sex during a real check — those labels are only used offline, to test the model.

1.13 What our system must do — in plain words

  1. Let any website ask: "Is this live person over N years old?"
  2. Give the person a quick (under 15 seconds), clear, kind experience on any phone or computer.
  3. Make a careful guess, with a measured level of confidence, and be extra careful near the age limit.
  4. Detect cheating: photos, videos, masks, computer-generated faces, fake cameras, repeated tries.
  5. Answer pass, fail, step-up, retry or reject — and when something goes wrong inside the system, never answer "pass" by accident. This is called failing closed.
  6. Send the website a digitally signed answer that cannot be forged, containing as little information as possible.
  7. Never keep faces.
  8. Measure and publish how often it makes each kind of mistake, for each age and each group.
  9. Give website owners a dashboard: their settings, their keys, their statistics — never anyone's face.
  10. Be easy for websites to plug in, and easy for us to run, update and repair.

1.14 What our system will never do

  • Recognise who you are. It answers "how old do you look?", never "who are you?".
  • Store your face, even "to improve the AI".
  • Guess your race or sex during a check.
  • Promise to be perfect. It states its error rates openly instead.

1.15 How we'll know we succeeded

  • The whole system starts on a laptop with one command, and runs on the internet over HTTPS.
  • A demo shop accepts or refuses visitors using the real system.
  • We publish, for the AI model: how often children near each age limit would get through, how often adults are held up, and how this differs between groups.
  • Our own cheating tests (photos, screen videos, game characters, replayed data) are stopped.
  • Security scans are clean, and the system stays fast under load.
  • This book explains 100 % of the code, and the ledger at the end proves it.

Part 2 — AI from zero

Status of this part

This part is being written while the AI is actually built (roadmap Phase 2), so its explanations can use the project's real data, real training runs and real measured numbers, not made-up examples. Sections marked ✅ in the table are written in full below; the rest are still an outline, so you can see where the book is going.

What you will be able to do after this part: explain how a computer can learn to estimate age from a face; how we measure the mistakes it makes; why we trust some of its answers and not others; and how we make it fast and fair.

Section Question it answers
2.1 What "learning" means for a machine ✅ How can a program get better from examples instead of from rules a human wrote?
2.2 Data, labels and datasets ✅ What is a training example? Why do we split data into training, validation and test sets — and why is the test set kept locked away?
2.3 Images as numbers How does a photo become a grid of numbers (a tensor) that maths can work on?
2.4 A model is a function with knobs ✅ What are parameters, and why does a modern model have millions of them?
2.5 Loss — measuring how wrong ✅ Mean absolute error, cross-entropy, KL divergence — in pictures, not formulas first
2.6 Gradient descent — walking downhill ✅ How turning millions of knobs a tiny bit at a time makes the loss smaller
2.7 Neural networks ✅ Neurons, layers, activations — and what "deep" learning means
2.8 Convolutional networks ✅ Sliding "stencils" that find edges, then shapes, then faces
2.9 Transformers and Vision Transformers Attention: letting every patch of a face look at every other patch
2.10 Pre-training and fine-tuning ✅ Why we start from a model that has already seen millions of images
2.11 Predicting a distribution instead of a number ✅ Why "probably 22, possibly 19–26" is more useful and more honest than "22"
2.12 Measuring mistakes ✅ MAE, the confusion matrix, false-adult rate, thresholds, and why averages hide danger
2.13 Calibration ✅ Making "80 % sure" actually mean right 80 % of the time
2.14 Risk control ✅ Clopper–Pearson bounds and the conformal idea: turning test results into a guarantee
2.15 Over-fitting and domain shift ✅ Why a model can ace its exam and fail in real life (photos vs. webcams)
2.16 Measuring fairness ✅ Per-group error rates, gaps, and release gates
2.17 Faces: detection, landmarks, alignment ✅ Finding the face, finding the eyes and nose, straightening the picture
2.18 Liveness and anti-spoofing ✅ How a system tells a real, present face from a photo, a replay or an injected camera feed
2.19 Making models fast ✅ ONNX, quantisation, distillation — the same answers, in a fraction of the time

2.1 What "learning" means for a machine

An ordinary program is a list of rules a person wrote: if the password matches, let them in. Nobody can write the rules for "how old does this face look". People can do it, but can't say how: we notice skin, the shape of the jaw, the eyes, the hair, all at once, without being able to list the rules.

Machine learning turns the problem round. Instead of writing the rules, we write a program with a great many adjustable settings, show it examples together with the right answers, and let a mathematical procedure adjust the settings until the program's answers match the examples. The examples are the training data (§2.2); the program with its settings is the model; the adjusting is training.

Explain like I'm six — learning to throw at a target

Nobody can tell you exactly how hard to throw a ball so it lands in a bucket. But you can throw, see where it lands — too far, too short — and adjust a little. After a hundred throws you're good at it, though you still couldn't write down the rule. Machine learning does the same: try, measure how far off it was, adjust a little, and repeat — millions of times.

The test of whether it worked is never the examples it learned from. It is new examples it has never seen: that is what the validation and test splits are for (§2.2).

2.2 Data, labels and datasets

A program that learns is not given rules. It is given examples, and it works out the rules itself (§2.1). For age estimation, one example is a photo of a face together with the answer we want for it — the person's age. The answer is called the label. A dataset is a large collection of labelled examples, gathered and published by researchers so that others can learn from it and compare their results.

Kinds of labels

Not every dataset labels age the same way, and the difference matters a great deal for this project:

Kind Example What it can teach
Exact age "17" Everything: the model can learn to tell 17 from 18
Age band "10-19" Rough age only: a 13-year-old and a 19-year-old get the same label
Apparent age "people guessed 21" What a person looks like — which is what a camera can actually see

The first dataset this project uses, FairFace, has age bands only. It is excellent for teaching a model the broad shape of ageing, and its 97,698 faces are deliberately balanced across seven groups of people. But its band "10-19" puts children and adults together, so it can never prove anything about 15-year-olds in particular. That needs exact ages (§2.14).

Splitting the data: practice, homework, the safety check and the exam

Imagine a teacher who hands out the exam questions as homework. Every student would score full marks, and the marks would mean nothing. Machine learning has the same trap: a model tested on photos it has already learned from looks far better than it really is. So, before anything is learned, the data is divided into splits, and each split has one job:

Split Like… Its job
train the textbook the examples the model learns from
validation (val) practice tests checking progress while learning, and choosing between settings
calibration (calib) the safety inspection setting the safety lines (§2.14) — never used for learning
test the final exam measured once, at the end; nobody looks at it before

The test split is kept locked away: if people look at test results while still making choices, their choices slowly bend towards the test, and the test stops being a fair exam. This project uses FairFace's own validation set as its test set, because it was chosen by FairFace's authors — nothing we did could have influenced it.

Explain like I'm six — a fair way to pick teams

Picking teams by drawing names from a hat is fair, but if you draw again tomorrow, the teams change. We want teams that are fair and never change. So each photo's name is put through a fingerprint machine (§X.5), which turns it into a number that looks random but is always the same for the same name. Numbers 0–79 go to the textbook, 80–89 to the practice tests, and 90–99 to the safety inspection. Tomorrow, next year, on any computer: the same photo always lands in the same place.

Honest limitation — the same person twice

Splitting by photo keeps each photo in one split, but a dataset can contain the same photo twice, or two photos of the same person. If one lands in training and the other in testing, the test is slightly too easy. The project removes repeated photos across all splits (§5.2.3): FairFace had 467, of which 233 would have leaked into evaluation. Different photos of one person can't be found that way, and FairFace doesn't record who is who, so for this dataset that risk remains, and is stated.

Datasets have licences

A dataset is someone else's work, published under a licence — the rules for using it (§0.16). Some allow any use with credit; others allow research only. A model learns from its data, so the data's terms follow the model: a model trained on "research only" photos is a research-only model. That's why the project keeps a licence register (ml/datasets.toml, §5.2.1) listing every dataset, its licence, and whether the project's owner has approved it — and why nothing is downloaded until they have.

2.4 A model is a function with knobs

A function takes something in and gives something out. Our age model takes in a picture — 224 × 224 pixels × 3 colours, so 150,528 numbers (§0.1) — and gives out 101 numbers, one for each age from 0 to 100.

Between input and output is a long chain of simple calculations: multiply, add, keep only the positive part, and again. Each multiplication uses a number that isn't fixed by the design but can be adjusted. These adjustable numbers are the model's parameters (also called weights) — the knobs. The models trained in this project have 3.4 million (ConvNeXt-Atto) and 14 million (ResNet-26d). A brand-new model has its knobs set at random, so its answers are random. Training sets them.

A model's design — which calculations, in which order — is called its architecture. A well-known architecture used as the main body of a model, with a small task-specific part on top, is called a backbone. Ours come from the timm library (§5.2.4).

2.5 Loss — measuring how wrong

To improve, the model needs a single number that says how wrong it is: the loss. Small is good; zero would be perfect. Choosing the loss means choosing what "wrong" means, so it is one of the most important decisions in a project.

Simple choices first. If the model gave one age, the obvious loss would be the absolute error: answer 25 for a 22-year-old, and the loss is 3. Averaged over many faces, that is the mean absolute error (MAE), the standard score for age estimation.

But our model gives a whole distribution (§2.11), and the right answer is a distribution too: for the label "20-29", a soft hump over those years (targets.py). The standard way to compare two distributions is the Kullback–Leibler divergence: roughly, how much extra surprise you'd suffer if you expected the model's distribution but the truth was the target. It is 0 when they match, and grows the more probability the model puts in the wrong places — especially where the target says "almost impossible".

The project's loss adds the two ideas: the KL divergence, plus a tenth of how many years the predicted average age lies outside the labelled band. The first shapes the whole distribution; the second pulls its centre into place.

2.6 Gradient descent — walking downhill

Imagine every possible setting of the model's millions of knobs as a point in a vast landscape, with the loss as the height of the ground. Training means finding a low point. You can't see the landscape — it has millions of directions — but at any point you can feel which way the ground slopes. That slope is the gradient, and calculus gives a way to compute it for every knob at once, in one pass backwards through the chain of calculations (backpropagation). Then: take a small step downhill, measure again, step again. That is gradient descent.

Three practical details, all in train.py:

  • Mini-batches. Measuring the loss over all 69,000 training faces for every step would be slow. Instead each step uses a batch of 128 random faces: a slightly noisy but much cheaper estimate of the slope. One pass through the data is an epoch; our runs take 30 epochs, about 16,000 steps.
  • The step size — the learning rate — matters enormously. Too big and training overshoots and bounces around; too small and it crawls. The usual recipe, used here: start small and grow (warm-up, for the first 2 epochs, while the random knobs settle), then shrink smoothly to zero along a cosine curve, so the final steps are tiny and precise.
  • AdamW. Plain gradient descent uses one step size for every knob. Adam gives each knob its own, based on how steep and how consistent its slope has been — the standard choice today. The "W" adds weight decay: a gentle pull of every knob towards zero, so that no knob grows huge to fit a few odd examples.

Explain like I'm six — down a foggy hill

You're on a hill in thick fog and want to reach the valley. You can't see it, but you can feel the slope under your feet. So: feel the slope, take a step downhill, feel again, step again. Big steps at first, tiny careful steps at the end so you don't walk past the bottom. That's all training is — just with millions of directions instead of four.

2.7 Neural networks

A neural network is a particular kind of model, loosely inspired by brain cells. Its unit, the neuron, takes several numbers in, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up, and passes the total through a simple bend — most often "if negative, make it zero" (ReLU). Without the bend, any chain of multiply-and-add would collapse into one big multiply-and-add, which can only draw straight lines; with it, a network can bend its answers to fit almost anything.

Neurons are arranged in layers: each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs. "Deep learning" just means many layers. The first layers of a vision network learn simple things — edges, spots of colour; later layers combine them into textures, then parts (an eye, a wrinkle), then whole-face properties such as apparent age. Nobody tells it to do this: it is simply what turns out to reduce the loss.

Two more pieces appear in every modern network. Normalisation layers keep each layer's numbers in a sensible range, which makes training far more stable. Residual connections let each block of layers add a correction to its input rather than replace it, which makes very deep networks trainable.

2.8 Convolutional networks

A photo has 150,528 numbers. Connecting every one of them to every neuron of the next layer would need billions of weights, and would ignore the obvious: what matters in a picture is local patterns, and a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears.

A convolution uses this. It slides a small stencil — say 3 × 3 pixels — across the whole picture, computing the same weighted sum at every position. A stencil whose weights are learned becomes a detector: one for horizontal edges, one for a particular texture. The same few weights are reused everywhere, which makes convolutional networks small and efficient. Stack many such layers, shrinking the picture step by step, and the stencils of later layers effectively see larger and larger areas — from edges to features to a whole face.

The project compares two convolutional backbones (§5.2.4):

  • ResNet-26d — a 26-layer ResNet, the family that introduced residual connections in 2015 and became the standard workhorse of computer vision; "d" is an improved variant from the paper Bag of Tricks for Image Classification.
  • ConvNeXt-Atto — the smallest ConvNeXt (2022), a convolutional network modernised with ideas borrowed from transformers (§2.9): larger stencils, fewer bends, different normalisation.

2.10 Pre-training and fine-tuning

Teaching a network to see from nothing takes enormous amounts of data. That is why most vision models start from a backbone that was first trained on a huge general collection — usually ImageNet, 1.3 million photos of a thousand kinds of things — and then fine-tune it on the task at hand. The pretrained backbone already knows edges, textures, shapes and faces; fine-tuning only has to teach it what age looks like. With 69,000 training faces, starting from a pretrained backbone typically gives far better results than starting from random knobs.

Pretrained weights are files someone else made, and they come with their own licences — some forbid commercial use, as for the original ConvNeXt V2 weights (§5.2.4). Like datasets, they need checking and the owner's approval. For the first training runs none were approved, so the project's first models learned from FairFace alone, from scratch: a harder start, and an honest baseline. Then the owner approved one set, ConvNeXt-Tiny trained on ImageNet: after a single epoch of fine-tuning it already beat the best from-scratch model after thirty, and it finished about a fifth better (§5.2.4).

2.11 Predicting a distribution instead of a number

A model could answer with one number: "22". But a face alone often can't settle whether someone is 17 or 19, and a single number hides that doubt. Our model answers with 101 probabilities, one for each age from 0 to 100, adding up to 1: perhaps 2 % for 17, 9 % for 20, 14 % for 22, and so on.

The 101 raw outputs of the network (logits) can be any numbers. The softmax function turns them into probabilities: it raises e to the power of each (making them all positive, and exaggerating the differences), then divides by the total (making them add up to 1).

From the distribution we can read everything the system needs:

  • the expected age — each age times its probability, added up;
  • the spread — how uncertain the model is;
  • most importantly, the probability of being at least N: add up the probabilities of all ages from N to 100. This number, P(age ≥ 18), is what the safety lines of §2.14 are set on.

2.12 Measuring mistakes

A single score can hide the mistakes that matter. Dwarpal measures a model several ways, because each answers a different question.

How far off, on average? The standard score for age estimation is the mean absolute error (MAE): the average number of years between the estimate and the true age. FairFace gives age bands, not ages, so the project uses band-MAE: how many years the estimate lies outside the labelled band, 0 if it is inside. The best model so far scores 1.83 on the test split.

Which mistakes are dangerous? For an age check, errors are not equal. A 30-year-old estimated at 34 harms nobody; a 9-year-old estimated at 19 is the failure the whole system exists to prevent. So mistakes are counted separately for the cases that matter:

Truly under the limit Truly over the limit
Rated over ❌ the safety error: a child let through ✅
Rated under ✅ the convenience error: an adult sent to step-up

A table like this is called a confusion matrix. The safety error at a given threshold is what the design calls FAR-minor (false adult rate for minors).

Why averages hide danger. A model can have an excellent average and still fail a small group badly: if it is wrong about 9-year-olds 10 % of the time but 9-year-olds are 1 % of the test faces, the overall score barely notices. So every measure is also reported per age band, per group and per sex — and the gates (§2.16) look at the worst of them, not the average.

Every rate gets an interval. "18 of 1,208 children" is 1.49 %, but a different 1,208 children might have given 1.2 % or 2 %. Each rate is reported with its 95 % Clopper–Pearson interval (§2.14) — for 18 of 1,208, from 0.9 % to 2.3 % — and gates are checked against the upper end, the cautious one.

2.13 Calibration

A model that says "80 % sure" should be right about 80 % of the time. If, of all the faces it called 80 % likely to be over 18, only 60 % really were, its probabilities are overconfident — and any threshold set on them would be set on a false sense of certainty. A model whose stated probabilities match reality is well calibrated.

To measure it: put the forecasts into bins (0–10 %, 10–20 %, …), compare each bin's average forecast with how often the event really happened, and add up the gaps, weighting each bin by how many forecasts fell in it. That is the expected calibration error (ECE): 0 is perfect, and 0.05 means "off by about 5 percentage points".

FairFace can't say whether a face in the band 10–19 is over 18. But it can say, for every face, whether it is over 20, 30 or 40, because its bands never straddle those ages. So calibration is measured at each band edge. The best model's error is about 0.018 — already close to honest.

Modern networks are often a little overconfident, and there is a standard fix: temperature scaling. Dividing all the logits by one number T before the softmax spreads the probabilities out (T > 1) or sharpens them (T < 1), without changing which age is most likely. T is chosen on the validation split to make the true answers as unsurprising as possible. For our model it came out at 0.88 — slightly under-confident, so slightly sharpened — and the calibration error fell from 0.0188 to 0.0177 on the test split. Calibration matters doubly here, because the safety lines of §2.14 are set on these probabilities.

2.14 Risk control — turning test results into a guarantee

§3.3 told the story of the jar of 600 photos: 6 children got through, and "the worst the real rate could plausibly be" came out at 1.96 %. This section explains where that number comes from, and how the project uses it to set its safety lines.

The problem: a test is only a sample

Suppose we show the model 600 photos of 17-year-olds, and 6 would pass. The rate in this jar is 1 %. But another jar of 600 different 17-year-olds might give 4 passes, or 10. What we want to know is the rate for all 17-year-olds like these — and that number we can never measure directly. We can only reason about what it could be, given what we saw.

The worst plausible rate

The question is turned around: if the true rate were p, how surprising would our result be? If the true rate were 5 %, seeing only 6 passes in 600 (we would expect 30) would be wildly unlikely — so 5 % is not plausible. If the true rate were 1.5 %, seeing 6 would be quite normal. Somewhere in between is the highest rate at which our result is still not too surprising. "Not too surprising" is set by the confidence level: at 95 % confidence, we call a result too surprising if a rate p would produce it — or anything better — less than 5 % of the time.

That highest plausible rate is the Clopper–Pearson upper bound, after the two statisticians who described it in 1934. For 6 out of 600 it is 1.96 %. For 7 out of 600, 2.18 %.

For readers who like formulas: if the true rate is p, the number of passes out of n behaves like coin tosses with a coin that lands "pass" with chance p — what statisticians call a binomial distribution. The Clopper–Pearson upper bound is the value of p at which the chance of seeing k or fewer passes falls to exactly δ (5 %). There is no simple formula for it in general, but it equals a point of another well-known curve, the beta distribution, which the SciPy library computes precisely (risk.py, §5.2.2).

One case does have a simple formula, and it is a useful one. With zero passes out of n, the chance of seeing zero when the rate is p is (1 − p) multiplied by itself n times, so the bound is 1 − δ^(1/n). To prove a rate of at most 2 % with nobody getting through, you therefore need 149 people; with 148, even a perfect result can't prove it. To prove 1 % takes 299. Less evidence forces more caution.

Why this method, and not a simpler one?

The simplest-looking approach — "1 % passed, so the rate is about 1 %" — ignores luck completely. Textbook "± margin" formulas use a bell-curve shortcut that is badly wrong for rare events and small groups, which is exactly our situation: they can even promise a rate below zero. Clopper–Pearson works from the exact coin-toss maths, and errs only on the cautious side. For a safety promise, cautious is right.

From a bound to a safety line

The model gives each face a score: how likely the person is to be at least the minimum age. A pass line turns scores into decisions: at or above the line, pass. Raising the line lets fewer people through. The project chooses:

  1. The pass line: the lowest line at which, for every exact age from N−5 to N−1 and every group of people, the Clopper–Pearson bound of the pass rate is within the website's risk budget (for example, 2 %). Each age in each group is called a cell, and every cell must keep the promise — because an average hides danger: a model could let in hardly any 13-year-olds and far too many 17-year-olds, and still average under 2 %.
  2. The fail line: the highest line at which clear adults (N+3 and over) in every group are failed outright at most 1 % of the time — kept below the pass line.
  3. Between the lines, step-up: a document check instead of a guess.

A weaker model doesn't make the system less safe. It makes the lines move apart, so more people are sent to step-up. Safety stays fixed; the cost shows up as inconvenience, where it can be measured and improved.

Honest limitation — what exactly is promised

  • The promise is about photos like the calibration photos. Webcams are different (§3.3), which is why the system also refuses poor frames, trains on "webcam-style" photos, and watches its live pass rates.
  • The 95 % confidence applies to each cell on its own. With around 35 cells (5 ages × 7 groups), the chance that at least one cell's real rate is above its bound is higher than 5 %. Making the promise hold for all cells at once is possible — by giving each cell a smaller share of the 5 % — but it needs more than twice as many people per cell. That is a decision for the project's owner, and it is recorded as an open question in the Phase 2 report (docs/reports/phase-2.md).
  • Exact ages are needed. FairFace's age bands can't certify anything about a single age, so calibration waits for an exact-age dataset to be approved.

2.15 Over-fitting and domain shift

A model with millions of knobs can do something unhelpful: memorise its training faces instead of learning about ageing. Its training loss keeps falling while its answers on new faces stop improving or get worse. That is over-fitting, and it is exactly what the validation split watches for: the model is judged after every epoch on 8,625 faces it never trains on, and the version kept is the one that did best there (train.py). Our pretrained model did exactly this: its validation loss was lowest at epoch 5 and then rose for ten epochs while its training loss kept falling — the table in §5.2.4 shows it epoch by epoch.

Three defences are used in training:

  • Data augmentation: every time a face is shown, it is randomly zoomed, turned, shifted, mirrored, recoloured and roughened (data.py). The model can't memorise a picture it never sees twice in the same form.
  • Weight decay (§2.6) keeps knobs from growing large to fit a few odd faces.
  • Weight averaging (EMA): alongside the knobs being trained, a second copy keeps a slowly moving average of them. The average is smoother than any single moment of training and usually does better on new data, so it is the copy that gets evaluated and saved.

Domain shift is the same problem one level up: a model can do well on new photos from the same collection and still disappoint on a different kind of picture. FairFace's photos come from the internet; Dwarpal's come from webcams and phones — darker, blurrier, more compressed. The webcam-style damage in the augmentation is there to narrow that gap, and the quality checks at serving time refuse pictures too far outside it.

2.16 Measuring fairness

An age estimator can be accurate on average and still be worse for some people than for others: for darker skin in poor light, for women wearing makeup, for faces underrepresented in the training data. In an age check, that would mean some children are let through more often than others, or some adults sent to step-up more often. Fairness can't be assumed; it has to be measured, group by group, and published.

Dwarpal measures, for every group the test data labels (FairFace has seven ethnic groups and two sexes):

  • accuracy per group, and the ratio of the worst to the best;
  • safety per group: the share of each group's children rated more likely than not to be over 18, with its interval.

Release gates turn these into rules: limits written down before looking at a model's test results, which every model must meet before it serves anyone (ml/gates.toml). Writing them first matters: once the results are in view, it is very tempting to find reasons why a slightly worse number is fine.

Two honest difficulties come with group measurements:

  • Small groups make wide intervals. FairFace's test split has 126 Middle Eastern children under 10. With 6 of them misjudged, the true rate could plausibly be anywhere from 1.8 % to 10.1 %. Gates on groups must use the upper bound — and more data per group is the only real cure.
  • Group labels are coarse. Seven ethnic labels assigned by annotators can't describe how diverse faces really are, and skin tone, lighting and camera matter as much as any label. The labels are used because they are what the data offers, not because they are the right categories for people.

2.17 Faces: detection, landmarks, alignment

Before a model can estimate anyone's age, three questions must be answered about a picture: is there a face, where is it, and which way is it turned? The answers turn a photo of a whole scene into a small, standard picture of one face — and the age model only ever sees that.

Detection: is there a face, and where?

A face detector is itself a small neural network, trained on many thousands of photos where people had drawn boxes around faces. Shown a new picture, it answers with a box around each face it finds, a score for how sure it is (from 0 to 1), and five landmarks: the centres of both eyes, the tip of the nose, and the two corners of the mouth. The project uses YuNet (§3.3, Choice 5): it takes a few milliseconds per picture on an ordinary processor, and its licence allows any use.

When a picture holds several faces, something must decide which one counts. At serving time the rule is strict: a second clear face is a reason to ask for a new picture. In a dataset like FairFace, where every image was made by centring it on the labelled person, the face nearest the middle is the one the label describes (§5.2.3).

Alignment: the same face, the same way, every time

People tilt their heads, stand near or far, and appear anywhere in the frame. A model could learn to cope with all of that, but it learns far more easily if every face arrives the same way round. Alignment moves the picture so that the five landmarks land as close as possible to five fixed positions — a template: eyes level and at a fixed distance apart, nose in the middle, mouth below.

The movement allowed is a similarity transform: turning, resizing and shifting, but never stretching (§4.9), so a face never gets thinner or wider than it really is. The best one is found by a method that fits the five points as closely as possible while ignoring a point that is badly off (least median of squares), then applied to every pixel.

Explain like I'm six — passport photos

Imagine a pile of holiday photos: people far away, close up, tilted, off to one side. Now imagine turning them all into passport photos: same size, head straight, eyes on the same line. Comparing faces is much easier with the passport photos. Alignment makes passport photos automatically, using the eyes, nose and mouth as guides.

One recipe for training and serving

The most important rule of this whole section is simple: the faces a model learns from must be prepared exactly like the faces it will judge. If training faces were framed more tightly, or stretched differently, or had parts filled in that live faces don't, the model would be tested on pictures unlike the ones it studied — and its measured accuracy would no longer describe the real system. That is why one library, dwarpal_vision, does detection and alignment for both training and serving, and why Phase 2 replaced a dataset version whose crops were too tight for that recipe (§5.2.3).

Honest limitation

The detector can miss faces, especially very dark, very small or sharply turned ones. In FairFace it found a face in all but 53 of 97,698 photos, but those 53 are not a random sample: missed faces are more often the hard cases. A missed face at serving time asks the person to try again with better light, so nobody is silently judged on a bad picture.

2.18 Liveness and anti-spoofing

An age model answers one question: how old does this face look? It never asks whether the face belongs to a living person standing in front of the camera. A child who holds up a photo of their mother, plays a video of an older sibling, or feeds a computer-generated face into the browser could get an adult's verdict from a perfectly accurate age model. Checking that the face is real and present is called liveness detection. Attempts to fool it are called presentation attacks, or spoofing.

This is not a theoretical worry. In July 2025, people passed a large platform's age check using characters from a video game: the check asked them to open their mouth, and a game's photo mode could do that on cue (ADR-0007).

The attacks, from cheap to costly

  • Print — a photo held up to the camera. Costs nothing.
  • Screen replay — a video of someone else, played on a phone or tablet held up to the camera.
  • Masks and make-up — rare and expensive, but real.
  • Rendering — a computer-generated face, possibly moving in real time.
  • Injection — skipping the camera altogether: a virtual camera program, or a script that sends pictures straight to the server, can deliver any images at all, including a recording or a deepfake.

No single check stops all of these. So the design uses layers, each cheap to add and each defeating a different kind of attack. An attacker must get past every layer at once.

Asking for something unpredictable

The strongest idea is the challenge: ask the person to do something they couldn't have known in advance, and check that they did it. A photo can't turn its head when asked. A recording of someone turning left, then right, is useless if the server asks for right, then up, then left — chosen at random, only when the attempt begins.

Two rules make a challenge work:

  1. The server chooses it, and the server checks it. If the page chose the poses, an attacker could change the page. If the page checked them, an attacker could skip the check. So the server issues the challenge, keeps its own copy, and judges the photos against that copy — whatever the page claims.
  2. It must be measured, not believed. Each photo comes labelled "this one was taken during turn left". A label is only a claim. The server measures the head in each photo itself: the same five landmarks used for alignment (§2.17) show which way the head points.

Explain like I'm six — Simon says

If you want to know whether someone is really in the room or is just a picture on the wall, play Simon says. "Simon says: turn left! Simon says: look up!" A picture can't play. And if you change the order every time, even a recording of someone playing won't fit.

The light from the screen

A second, gentler challenge uses the screen as a lamp. For a couple of seconds it glows in a random run of colours — blue, then yellow, then teal. Skin a hand's width from a bright screen picks up a faint tint of each colour. If the tint on the face rises and falls in step with the colours, there was a real surface close to the screen. A photo or a video on another screen tends to respond differently.

How closely two series of numbers move together is measured by correlation: +1 means perfectly in step, 0 means unrelated. The page records the colours; the server measures the tint of the cheeks and forehead in each photo, removes overall brightness (which changes for many other reasons), and computes the correlation.

This signal is weak: in a bright room the screen's glow is faint, and a dim, careful replay can imitate it. So it is a soft signal — recorded and measured, but not allowed to decide anything until real-world measurements show how much it can be trusted.

Flashing colours also carry a real risk: for people with photosensitive epilepsy, flashing light can trigger seizures. The accessibility standard WCAG says nothing should flash more than three times a second. Dwarpal's colours are calm, never saturated red, and change less than twice a second — and people who have asked their device for reduced motion see no colours at all.

Passive detection, and signs of injection

Passive presentation-attack detection (PAD) uses a model trained on thousands of real faces and attacks to spot the tell-tale textures of paper, screens and masks in a single picture, without asking the person to do anything. It is a valuable layer, but it can be brittle — an attack type it never saw in training may pass. In the owner's own tests it turned out to be the decisive layer: a phone showing posed photos or a video of the owner passed the head-turn challenge — a photo of a turned head is a turned head — but the PAD networks scored the phone 0.006–0.195 and the real face 0.94–0.995 (§5.3.7).

Injection signs look for evidence that the pictures never came from a live camera: the browser reporting that a program is driving it, a camera whose name belongs to virtual-camera software, the page being hidden during the check, or frames that are too identical — a live camera always adds a little noise. These hints come partly from the browser, which an attacker controls, so they can make a check stricter but never easier.

Keeping the attacker in the dark

An attacker learns from failure. If the page said "your photo was detected as a printout", the next attempt would aim at exactly that check. So the outside world only ever hears vague reasons — "the check could not be completed" — while the full detail is stored for the people who run the system. A limit on attempts stops endless trial and error.

Honest limitation

Liveness raises the cost of cheating; it can't make cheating impossible. A determined attacker with real-time face-rendering software and a virtual camera is hard to stop, and nothing here stops a proxy attack — an adult who simply does the check for a child.
