It was new enough that Phase 1 tested whether Next.js could work with it, rather than assuming — and it could, so no fallback was needed (§5.1.4).

4.16 React: pages made of components

Writing a page as one giant file of HTML quickly becomes unmanageable. React lets you build pages from components: small functions that each draw one part of the page, and combine like building blocks.

function Greeting({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return <p className="hello">Hello, {name}!</p>;
}
// …and then, elsewhere: <Greeting name="Asha" />

The HTML-like lines are JSX: inside a .tsx file, you write tags, and React turns them into real page elements. Three differences from HTML: className instead of class; {…} to put a JavaScript value into the page; and every tag must be closed (<br />).

The values a component receives, like name above, are its props. A special prop, children, holds whatever is written between its tags — that is how <Shell>…</Shell> wraps a page.

Hooks: memory and timing for components

A component is just a function, called again every time the page must be redrawn. To remember things between calls, and to do things at the right moment, it uses hooks — functions whose names start with use:

Hook What it's for Example in this book
useState a value that, when changed, redraws the component the verify flow's current stage
useRef a box that keeps a value without redrawing the camera's stream; the <video> element
useEffect do something after drawing, and undo it later open the camera, and switch it off when the screen goes away
useCallback keep the same function between redraws the camera's error callback

An effect returns a cleanup function, which React calls when the component disappears; the effect's dependency list says when it must run again. Getting these right is what keeps a camera from staying on after its screen has gone.

Explain like I'm six — a puppet show

Each puppet (a component) knows how to act its own part. The puppeteer (React) decides when each puppet appears. When something in the story changes (state), the puppeteer redraws just the scenes that changed — and when a puppet leaves the stage, it puts its props away (cleanup) so the next scene starts tidy.

Strict Mode. In development, React deliberately runs effects twice — set up, clean up, set up again — to expose effects that misbehave when repeated. The verify page met exactly that: it reads a one-time secret from the address, and had to be written so that a second run still works (verify-flow.tsx).

4.17 Next.js: one framework for server and browser

React draws components; a real website needs much more around them — pages at addresses, data from servers, builds, security headers. Next.js is a framework that provides all of it (ADR-0012).

Folders are addresses

In Next.js's App Router, the folders inside app/ are the website's addresses, and special file names say what each file does:

File Role Example
page.tsx the page at that folder's address app/cellar/page.tsx → /cellar
layout.tsx a frame around every page below it the <html> and <body> of a whole app
[name]/ a dynamic part of the address app/v/[sessionId]/ → /v/vs_01JA…
route.ts code that answers requests directly, with no page the shop's /age-check/complete
error.tsx what to show if a page fails the shop's "couldn't start" page

Server components and client components

By default, a Next.js component is a server component: it runs on the server, and only its finished HTML is sent to the browser. It can read cookies and secrets, and costs the browser nothing.

A file that starts with "use client" holds client components: they are sent to the browser as JavaScript and run there, so they can use state, effects, and browser features such as the camera.

Server component Client component
Runs on the server in the browser
Can use secrets, cookies, databases yes never
Can use the camera, clicks, state no yes
In this book the shop's pages; the verify page's outer page the verify flow and camera screen

This split is a security tool as much as a speed tool: the shop's API key is only ever touched by server code, so no browser could ever receive it.

Server actions and route handlers

A server action — a function in a file that starts with "use server" — can be attached to a form. Pressing the button runs the function on the server. The shop's "Verify my age to enter" button works this way, which is why it can use the secret key.

A route handler (route.ts) answers requests directly — the shop's return address uses one, because it only checks things and redirects.

Building and running

next build makes an optimised production build, and reports each address as static (○, prepared in advance) or dynamic (ƒ, drawn for each request — needed for anything that reads cookies). next start serves that build; next dev serves a development version that rebuilds whenever a file changes. Next.js 16 builds with Turbopack, its fast bundler.

Settings come from environment variables. Only those whose names start with NEXT_PUBLIC_ are built into the browser's code; all others stay on the server.

Alternatives considered

React Router (formerly Remix) is excellent for server-rendered React too, with a smaller ecosystem. SvelteKit is lighter, but means leaving React's huge community of components and developers. Astro shines for mostly-static sites, and the verify page is an interactive app. Next.js's server/client split, its server actions, and its maturity fit Dwarpal best (ADR-0012).

4.18 Tailwind CSS: styling with small classes

CSS describes how a page looks (§0.10). The traditional way is to invent a class name for each element, and describe its look in a separate stylesheet. Tailwind CSS turns this around: it provides small utility classes, each doing one thing, which you write directly on the element.

<button className="rounded-2xl bg-brand-500 px-5 py-3.5 font-semibold hover:bg-brand-400">
Class Means
p-6, px-5, mt-8 padding all round / left and right; margin on top (in steps of 0.25 rem)
text-2xl, font-semibold text size; boldness
bg-white/85 a white background at 85 % opacity
rounded-3xl, border rounded corners; a thin border
flex, grid, items-center layout: rows, grids, centring
sm:p-8 only on screens at least 640 pixels wide
dark:bg-zinc-950 only in dark mode
hover:…, focus-visible:…, disabled:… only in that state
motion-safe:animate-rise only if the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion
bg-[radial-gradient(…)] an arbitrary value: anything Tailwind has no name for

Tailwind reads the code, and writes CSS for exactly the classes in use — no forgotten styles pile up. Version 4 is configured in CSS itself: an @theme block in the stylesheet defines design tokens — the brand colour, the fonts, the animations — and each token becomes a class (globals.css).

The obvious cost is long lists of classes. This project gives the most repeated ones a name in code instead — card, primaryButton — so every screen shares them (shell.tsx).

4.19 The camera in a web page

A web page can use the camera only with the person's permission, and only on a secure page: HTTPS, or localhost during development (§0.9).

  1. Ask. navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: … }) asks the browser for the camera. The browser shows its own permission prompt; the page can't fake or skip it. If the person refuses, the request fails with a NotAllowedError.
  2. Show. The answer is a MediaStream — a live flow of frames. Given to a <video> element (video.srcObject = stream), it plays as a live preview.
  3. Capture. To take a photo, the page draws the video's current frame onto a canvas — an invisible drawing surface in memory — and asks the canvas for a JPEG (canvas.toBlob(…, "image/jpeg", 0.85)).
  4. Switch off. Each stream is made of tracks; stopping every track switches the camera off, and its light with it.

The verify page adds a few habits of its own: the camera starts only after the person presses a button; the preview is mirrored (people expect a mirror) while the photos are not; and the camera is switched off the instant the burst is taken — before the upload even begins (camera.ts, camera-view.tsx).

The verify page's Permissions-Policy header allows the camera on its own pages only, and forbids the microphone and location outright (next.config.ts).

4.20 Testing JavaScript: Vitest and Playwright

The JavaScript side has the same pyramid of tests as the Python side (§4.14):

Unit tests with Vitest

Vitest runs TypeScript tests directly and fast. Its building blocks read almost like sentences:

describe("tipFor", () => {
  it("gives the tip for the first reason it knows", () => {
    expect(tipFor(["too_dark"])).toMatch(/too dark/);
  });
});

When the code under test talks to the network, the test hands it a fake: a pretend fetch that records each request and answers instantly (client.test.ts), or the global fetch swapped out with vi.stubGlobal (flow-api.test.ts). The tests then check both what was sent and what was understood.

End-to-end tests with Playwright

Playwright drives real browsers — Chromium, Firefox and WebKit — from test code: open this page, press that button, check that heading.

  • Find things like a person does: page.getByRole("button", { name: "Take photos" }). A test written this way survives redesigns, and only works if the page is properly labelled for screen readers.
  • Wait automatically: await expect(heading).toBeVisible() keeps looking until the heading appears (5 seconds by default), so tests needn't guess how long anything takes.
  • Start the system: its webServer setting starts every service the test needs and waits until each answers.
  • Record failures: a trace — a step-by-step recording with screenshots, network requests and page states — is kept for every failed test.

The camera is the hard part: there is no face in front of a CI server. Chromium can play a video file as a fake camera (--use-file-for-fake-video-capture), and the test makes that video from the project's public-domain test portrait (make_fake_camera.py). So the same "person" sits in front of the camera on every run, everywhere.

Part 5 — Building it, file by file

This is the main event: every file of the project, in the order it was built, explained line by line. Each phase of the roadmap adds a chapter here.

5.0 Phase 0 — the foundations

Phase 0 builds no features. It builds the workshop: the folder structure, the toolchains, the quality robots, the local databases and the automatic checks. Every later phase depends on them.

Here is the repository at the end of Phase 0 (design documents, ADRs, chapters and walkthroughs left out for brevity):

Explain like I'm six

Before a new school opens, someone builds the classrooms, puts up the signs, installs the fire alarms and writes the timetable. No lessons happen yet — but without that work, no lesson could happen safely. Phase 0 is the school before the first day.

5.0.1 Repository hygiene

Three tiny files make sure every computer and every editor treats the project the same way.

.editorconfig15 lines · 100% explained

EditorConfig is a standard settings file that most code editors read automatically: VS Code, all JetBrains editors, Vim, Visual Studio and more. It tells every contributor's editor the same basic rules — encoding, line endings, indentation — so files don't get silently changed just because two people use different editors.

The format is simple:

  • [pattern] lines choose which files the settings below them apply to;
  • key = value lines set a rule.
1root = true

root = true — "this is the top-level settings file; stop looking in parent folders for more". Without it, a stray .editorconfig somewhere above the project could change our rules.

2
3[*]

[*] — the rules below apply to every file (* matches any name).

4charset = utf-8

charset = utf-8 — save files as UTF-8, the encoding that can hold every character in every language (§0.2).

5end_of_line = lf

end_of_line = lf — end lines with a single line feed, the Linux/macOS convention. This matches what .gitattributes stores, so editors on Windows don't fight Git (§4.1).

6insert_final_newline = true

insert_final_newline = true — always end a file with a newline. By the classic definition, a text line ends with a newline, and many tools (and Git's diffs, which otherwise show "No newline at end of file") expect it.

7trim_trailing_whitespace = true

trim_trailing_whitespace = true — remove invisible spaces at the ends of lines. They do nothing, but they show up as noisy changes in code reviews.

8indent_style = space
9indent_size = 2

indent_style = space and indent_size = 2 — indent with spaces, two at a time, by default. Two spaces is the usual convention for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON and YAML.

10
11[*.py]
12indent_size = 4

[*.py] with indent_size = 4 — Python files use four spaces per level, the convention set by Python's official style guide (PEP 8). In Python, indentation is part of the meaning (§X.8), so consistency matters even more.

13
14[*.md]
15trim_trailing_whitespace = false

[*.md] with trim_trailing_whitespace = false — in Markdown, two spaces at the end of a line mean "line break here". Trimming them would silently change how text is displayed, so Markdown files are exempt.

.gitattributes11 lines · 100% explained

.gitattributes gives Git per-file instructions. We use it for one important job: making line endings identical on every computer (§4.1), and making sure binary files are never "corrected" as if they were text.

Each line is a file pattern followed by attributes.

1# Store every text file with Linux line endings, whatever computer it was edited on.

A comment — lines starting with # are notes for humans.

2* text=auto eol=lf

* text=auto eol=lf:

  • * — every file;
  • text=auto — let Git decide whether a file is text. It looks for bytes that only appear in binary files;
  • eol=lf — for text files, store and check out lines ending with a single line feed, even on Windows.

Without this line, a Windows checkout could turn every line into CRLF. Shell scripts copied into Linux containers would then break, and diffs would show every line as changed.

3
4# Never treat these as text.

A comment introducing the binary list.

5*.png binary
6*.jpg binary
7*.jpeg binary
8*.webp binary
9*.ico binary
10*.woff2 binary
11*.onnx binary

File types that must never be treated as text, each marked binary. This turns off line-ending conversion — which would corrupt them — and stops Git from trying to show a line-by-line diff of their bytes.

Pattern What it is
*.png, *.jpg, *.jpeg, *.webp images (logos, screenshots, test pictures)
*.ico the website's tab icon
*.woff2 web fonts
*.onnx AI model files (normally never committed, see .gitignore — but if one ever is, it must stay intact)
.gitignore45 lines · 100% explained

.gitignore lists paths that Git must pretend do not exist. It never offers them for committing, and git status never mentions them. Three kinds of things belong here (§4.1): secrets, things rebuilt automatically, and large or licence-restricted data.

Pattern rules:

  • # starts a comment;
  • a trailing / means "a folder with this name, anywhere";
  • * matches any characters;
  • [abc] matches one of the listed characters;
  • a leading ! makes an exception — "don't ignore this one after all".
1# Python

Comment: the Python section.

2__pycache__/

__pycache__/ — folders where Python stores compiled bytecode (.pyc files), so programs start faster. Python recreates them automatically.

3*.py[cod]

*.py[cod] — compiled Python files: .pyc, .pyo, .pyd. [cod] matches one character: c, o or d.

4.venv/

.venv/ — the virtual environment (§4.2): hundreds of megabytes of installed libraries, rebuilt by uv sync from uv.lock.

5.mypy_cache/
6.ruff_cache/
7.pytest_cache/
8.hypothesis/

Caches written by the type checker (.mypy_cache/), the linter (.ruff_cache/), the test runner (.pytest_cache/) and the property-testing library Hypothesis (.hypothesis/, added in Phase 1). They exist only to make re-runs faster. Hypothesis, for example, remembers any input that once broke a test, and tries it first next time.

9*.egg-info/

*.egg-info/ — metadata folders some Python build tools create when packaging. They are generated, never written by hand.

11# JavaScript

Comment: the JavaScript section.

12node_modules/

node_modules/ — installed JavaScript libraries, often hundreds of thousands of files. They are rebuilt by pnpm install from pnpm-lock.yaml.

13.next/

.next/ — the Next.js build output and cache (from Phase 1).

14.turbo/

.turbo/ — Turborepo's local task cache.

15dist/

dist/ — "distribution" folders where packages put their built output.

16coverage/

coverage/ — test-coverage reports, regenerated by each test run.

17*.tsbuildinfo

*.tsbuildinfo — files TypeScript writes to make the next compile faster.

18next-env.d.ts

next-env.d.ts — a small file of type declarations that Next.js writes into each web app every time it runs (added in Phase 1). Next.js itself recommends not committing it: it is regenerated anyway, and its contents vary between Next.js versions.

19test-results/
20playwright-report/

The output of the end-to-end tests (added in Phase 1): test-results/ holds screenshots and traces from the latest run, and playwright-report/ an HTML report, if one is asked for. Both are recreated on every run.

21e2e/.cache/

e2e/.cache/ — files the end-to-end test generates for itself, such as the fake camera's video. They can always be made again from the project's own files.

22apps/web/public/mediapipe/

apps/web/public/mediapipe/ — MediaPipe's WebAssembly engine and face model, copied into the verify page's public folder before every build (apps/web/scripts/mediapipe.mjs). They are generated from the installed package and the pinned model file, so they are never committed (added in Phase 3).

24# Machine-learning data and weights (fetched by scripts, never committed)

Comment: machine-learning data and weights are fetched by scripts and never committed.

25.datasets/

.datasets/ — the downloaded face datasets. They are huge, many of their licences restrict redistribution (§0.16), and they contain photos of real people.

26mlruns/

mlruns/ — experiment logs written by MLflow during training.

27.runs/

.runs/ — the project's own training-run records and trained weights (Phase 2, train.py).

28*.safetensors

*.safetensors — model-weight files, wherever they appear. Trained models are large, and they are published through the model registry, never through Git.

29*.onnx
30*.pt
31*.pth
32*.task

Model weight files:

  • .onnx — our serving format (ADR-0014);
  • .pt and .pth — PyTorch checkpoints;
  • .task — MediaPipe's bundled model files, such as the face landmarker the verify page uses (added in Phase 3, in place of a second, duplicate *.safetensors line).

Weights are large, and may be licence-restricted. They are fetched and verified by fingerprint, by a script.

34# Secrets and local settings

Comment: secrets and local settings.

35.env

.env — files holding passwords and keys. A secret committed once stays in Git's history forever, even if the file is deleted later. This line is the first defence.

36.env.*

.env.* — variants like .env.local or .env.production.

37!.env.example

!.env.example — the exception. Example files contain no secrets, only placeholder values, and they must be committed so people know which settings exist.

38!.env.example.*

!.env.example.* — a second exception, for files whose names merely start with .env.example: the book's walkthrough .env.example.md and its snapshot .env.example.snap. Line 28 would otherwise hide them. The book would then build on this computer but fail on any fresh copy, because the explanation would never have been committed.

Real world — a trap found by reading carefully

Nobody noticed this hazard by running the code. It was found while writing the explanation of line 28. Explaining every line is not only for the reader: it is also one of the most effective ways to review code.

40# Editors and operating systems

Comment: editors and operating systems.

41.idea/
42.vscode/

.idea/ (JetBrains editors) and .vscode/ (Visual Studio Code) — personal editor settings, different for everyone.

43.claude/

.claude/ — local settings for the AI coding assistant used to build this project. For example, .claude/launch.json tells it how to start a small local web server for previewing this book. They are personal tool settings, like the editor folders above, so they stay out of the shared history.

44.DS_Store
45Thumbs.db

Junk files that operating systems create on their own: .DS_Store (macOS Finder) and Thumbs.db (Windows thumbnail cache).

5.0.2 The Python workspace

.python-version1 lines · 100% explained

A one-line file that tells uv (and other Python tools) which Python version this project uses.

13.13

3.13 — use Python 3.13, whichever patch release is newest (we got 3.13.16).

  • The computer already has Python 3.14, but parts of the AI tool chain still lag behind the newest Python. For example, one torchvision release explicitly refused 3.14.1 (constraint C-04 in Stage 1).
  • Python 3.13 is supported by every library we need, and receives security fixes until October 2029.
  • When uv sees this file, it downloads its own private copy of Python 3.13 (§4.2), so the computer's own Python is never touched.
pyproject.toml84 lines · 100% explained

The root pyproject.toml is the control centre of the Python side of the project. It is not a package itself — Python packaging calls this a virtual workspace root. It does three jobs:

  1. names the workspace members — our five Python packages;
  2. lists the developer tools, with exact versions;
  3. holds the settings for those tools: Ruff, mypy, pytest.
1# Dwarpal — root of the Python workspace.
2# This file is not a package itself: it lists the workspace members,
3# the shared developer tools, and the settings those tools use.

Comments explaining what this file is. In TOML, # starts a comment. The first line uses a real long dash —, which is fine because the file is UTF-8.

4
5[tool.uv]

[tool.uv] — settings for uv itself. Every tool reads its own [tool.<name>] table and ignores the others.

6required-version = ">=0.13.1"

required-version = ">=0.13.1" — refuse to run with an older uv. Older versions might resolve or install things differently, so this prevents "it works with my uv" surprises.

7default-groups = ["dev", "docs"]

default-groups = ["dev", "docs"] — when uv installs the project (uv sync, or automatically before uv run), include the two dependency groups below. Without this, uv run would install only dev, and the book's tools would be missing.

8# A 7-day cooldown, as for JavaScript (pnpm-workspace.yaml): brand-new releases are where attacks and bugs show up first.
9exclude-newer = "7 days"

A 7-day cooldown (added in Phase 2): exclude-newer = "7 days" tells uv to ignore every release published in the last seven days, as the JavaScript side already does (pnpm-workspace.yaml, §5.1.4). Brand-new releases are where supply-chain attacks and fresh bugs show up first; a week gives the world time to notice. Turning it on caught six pins chosen before the rule existed — FastAPI, Hypothesis, Markdown, NumPy, Pydantic and pydantic-settings — and each was stepped back to its newest release that was at least a week old. The whole test suite passed unchanged.

10
11[tool.uv.workspace]

[tool.uv.workspace] — this file is the root of a uv workspace: several packages sharing one lockfile and one environment (§4.2).

12members = ["services/*", "libs/*", "ml"]

members = [...] — which folders are workspace packages:

  • services/* — every folder in services (api, inference);
  • libs/* — every folder in libs (contracts, vision);
  • ml.

Each member has its own pyproject.toml.

13
14[dependency-groups]

[dependency-groups] — named groups of libraries that are needed for working on the project, but are never part of any package that gets shipped. This table is a recent official Python standard (PEP 735).

15dev = [
16  "httpx==0.28.1",
17  "hypothesis==6.168.5",
18  "mypy==2.4.0",
19  "onnx==1.23.2",
20  "pytest==9.1.1",
21  "ruff==0.17.0",
22  "scipy-stubs==1.18.1.1",
23  "testcontainers==4.15.0",
24  "types-docker==7.2.0.20261006",
25]

The dev group — tools for developers, each pinned to an exact version with ==:

  • httpx 0.28.1 — an HTTP client library (added in Phase 1). Tests use it to call our services without a real network, and the model-download script uses it to fetch model files;
  • hypothesis 6.168.5 — property-based testing (added in Phase 1). Instead of a few examples picked by hand, a test states a rule that must always hold, and Hypothesis invents hundreds of inputs trying to break it (§4.14);
  • mypy 2.4.0 — the type checker;
  • onnx 1.23.2 — builds a tiny ONNX model for the inference service's tests (added in Phase 2);
  • pytest 9.1.1 — the test runner;
  • ruff 0.17.0 — the linter and formatter;
  • scipy-stubs — type stubs for SciPy, the maths library the risk-control code uses (added in Phase 2), so mypy can check every call into it;
  • testcontainers 4.15.0 — starts real, throwaway databases in Docker for the tests and removes them afterwards (added in Phase 1, §4.14);
  • types-docker — type stubs (explained in the next note) for the docker library, which the database tests use to ask whether Docker is running. mypy now checks the tests too (see files below), so it needs to know that library's types.
26docs = [
27  "markdown==3.11",
28  "pygments==2.21.0",
29  "types-markdown==3.10.2.20261007",
30  "types-pygments==2.21.0.20260819",
31]

The docs group — what the book builder needs:

  • markdown 3.11 and pygments 2.21.0 — the converter and the highlighter (Part X);
  • types-markdown and types-pygments — type stubs: files that describe the types used by a library which doesn't ship them itself, so mypy can check our calls into it. Their version numbers end with a date, which is how the typeshed project numbers its stubs.
32
33[tool.ruff]

[tool.ruff] — settings for Ruff (both the linter and the formatter).

34line-length = 120

line-length = 120 — the longest line allowed. The common default of 88 is designed for narrow screens. 120 fits a modern screen, and still fits side by side with the explanation column in this book.

35target-version = "py313"

target-version = "py313" — the oldest Python our code must run on. Ruff then only suggests syntax that Python 3.13 understands.

36include = ["*.py", "*.pyi", "**/pyproject.toml"]

include = ["*.py", "*.pyi", "**/pyproject.toml"] — which files Ruff looks at: Python code, type stubs (.pyi), and pyproject.toml files.

Real world — why this line exists

Ruff 0.17 also formats Python code inside Markdown files by default. On its first run, it quietly re-aligned the comments in a code example in a design document. In this project, Markdown holds teaching examples that must stay exactly as written, so Ruff is now limited to real Python files.

37extend-exclude = ["docs/zero_to_hero/.snapshots"]

extend-exclude = [...] — never check the book's .snapshots folder, which holds copies of code from the last stamp (§X.6). Checking copies would report every warning twice.

38src = ["services/api/src", "services/inference/src", "libs/contracts/src", "libs/vision/src", "ml/src", "docs/zero_to_hero"]

src = [...] — where our own code lives: each package's src folder, plus the book folder. Ruff's import sorter uses this list to tell first-party imports (our dwarpal_* packages) from third-party ones (FastAPI, NumPy, …), and it groups them separately. Without the line, Ruff took dwarpal_contracts for an outside library and mixed it in with FastAPI. The list mirrors mypy's mypy_path below, so both tools agree on what "ours" means.

39
40[tool.ruff.lint]

[tool.ruff.lint] — settings for the linter part.

41select = ["E", "W", "F", "I", "B", "UP", "SIM", "C4", "PTH", "S", "N", "RUF", "DTZ", "PERF", "RET"]

select = [...] — the rule families switched on: pycodestyle, Pyflakes, isort, bugbear, pyupgrade, simplify, comprehensions, pathlib, bandit security, naming, Ruff's own, datetime, performance, return. §4.3 has a table with an example for each.

42
43[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores] — specific rules switched off for specific files, each for a stated reason.

44"tasks.py" = ["S603"]

"tasks.py" = ["S603"] — rule S603 warns whenever a program starts another program (subprocess). That is risky when the command is built from untrusted text, because someone could sneak in extra commands. In tasks.py every command is a fixed list written in the file itself, and no shell is involved, so the warning is a false alarm there — and only there.

45"**/tests/**" = ["S101"]

"**/tests/**" = ["S101"] — rule S101 warns about assert, because Python can be told to skip assert statements. That makes them unsafe for checks in real code. In tests, assert is the checking mechanism, and pytest never skips it.

46
47[tool.mypy]

[tool.mypy] — settings for the type checker.

48python_version = "3.13"

python_version = "3.13" — check the code as Python 3.13 would see it.

49strict = true

strict = true — switch on every strictness option. For example: every function must have type hints, no silent Any, and every generic type such as dict must say what it holds.

50warn_unreachable = true

warn_unreachable = true — warn about code that can never run. This usually means a condition is wrong.

51explicit_package_bases = true

explicit_package_bases = true — work out each file's module name from the folders listed in mypy_path. This is needed because our packages live in separate src folders.

52exclude = ['[/\\]\.snapshots[/\\]']

exclude = [...] — a regular expression for paths mypy must skip. [/\\] means "a forward slash or a backslash", so the pattern matches .snapshots as a folder on both Linux and Windows. The single quotes make it a literal TOML string, so the backslashes reach mypy exactly as typed.

53mypy_path = "services/api/src,services/inference/src,libs/contracts/src,libs/vision/src,ml/src,docs/zero_to_hero"

mypy_path — where mypy should look for our packages' source code: each package's src folder, plus the book folder (for build.py). The comma-separated form works on every operating system.

54files = [
55  "tasks.py",
56  "infra/scripts",
57  "docs/zero_to_hero",
58  "services/api/src",
59  "services/api/tests",
60  "services/inference/src",
61  "services/inference/tests",
62  "libs/contracts/src",
63  "libs/vision/src",
64  "libs/vision/tests",
65  "ml/src",
66  "ml/tests",
67]

files = [...] — what mypy checks when you simply run mypy:

  • the task runner;
  • infra/scripts — helper scripts such as the model downloader (added in Phase 1);
  • the book builder and its tests;
  • every package's source folder (src);
  • every package's tests folder (added in Phase 1; the ML package's in Phase 2).

Why type-check tests? A test with a type mistake can pass for the wrong reason. Imagine the check outcome != "fail" where outcome is, by mistake, a whole response object instead of a piece of text. An object and a text can never be equal, so the check always passes — even when the answer really was "fail". mypy's strict mode reports comparisons between things that can never be equal.

When mypy was first pointed at the tests, it found exactly one problem: OpenCV's blur function returns a picture whose type is vaguer than the quality checker expects. It was fixed the same way as in the real code, with np.asarray(..., dtype=np.uint8) (§4.9).

68
69# timm re-exports its public names without marking them as such.
70[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
71module = ["timm.*"]
72implicit_reexport = true

A mypy exception for timm (added in Phase 2). In strict mode, mypy only accepts names a library explicitly marks as public. timm makes create_optimizer_v2 and ModelEmaV3 public in the ordinary Python way but without that marking, so mypy is told to accept them for timm only.

73
74# ONNX Runtime and ONNX ship no complete type information.
75[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
76module = ["onnxruntime.*", "onnx.*"]
77ignore_missing_imports = true

A mypy exception for ONNX (added in Phase 2): ONNX Runtime ships no type information, and the onnx library's is incomplete, so mypy is told not to demand it for these two. Our code's own types are still checked fully.

78
79[tool.pytest.ini_options]

[tool.pytest.ini_options] — settings for pytest (the name is historical: pytest settings once lived only in .ini files).

80minversion = "9.0"

minversion = "9.0" — refuse to run with a pytest older than 9.0.

81testpaths = ["docs/zero_to_hero/tests", "services", "libs", "ml"]

testpaths — where pytest looks for tests when run without arguments: the book's tests, then every package under services, libs and ml. Inside those folders pytest collects files whose names start with test_.

82pythonpath = ["docs/zero_to_hero"]

pythonpath = ["docs/zero_to_hero"] — add the book folder to Python's search path during tests, so test_build.py can simply write import build.

83addopts = ["-ra", "--strict-markers", "--strict-config", "--import-mode=importlib"]

addopts — options added to every pytest run:

  • -ra — print a short summary of every test that didn't simply pass (skipped, failed, …);
  • --strict-markers — a misspelled test label is an error, not silently ignored;
  • --strict-config — a misspelled setting in this file is an error;
  • --import-mode=importlib — import test files without modifying Python's search path, so tests in different packages can't clash by having the same file name.
84xfail_strict = true

xfail_strict = true — some tests can be marked "expected to fail" (for a known bug). If such a test unexpectedly passes, treat that as a failure, so the outdated marker gets noticed and removed.

The five packages start as skeletons: each has a pyproject.toml that names it, and an __init__.py that marks the folder as a package and describes its purpose. Real code arrives in Phase 1. Creating them now fixes the shape of the project, and proves that the workspace, the lockfile and the tools all work with five members.

services/api/pyproject.toml26 lines · 100% explained

The pyproject.toml of the API service package: its name, version, purpose, supported Python versions, libraries it needs, and how to build it. The other four packages follow exactly the same pattern, so this one is explained in the most detail.

1[project]

[project] — the standard table (defined in PEP 621) that every Python package uses to describe itself.

2name = "dwarpal-api"

name = "dwarpal-api" — the distribution name that installers use. Inside Python code, the package is imported as dwarpal_api, with an underscore, because a dash isn't allowed in a Python name (§4.2).

3version = "0.1.0"

version = "0.1.0" — semantic versioning (major.minor.patch, §0.17). A major version of 0 signals "early development; anything may still change".

4description = "Dwarpal API: relying-party, flow and console APIs, decision engine, signed age tokens."

description — one line saying what the package is for: the relying-party, flow and console APIs, the decision engine, and signed age tokens (Stage 3 §3).

5requires-python = ">=3.13,<3.14"

requires-python = ">=3.13,<3.14" — this package runs on Python 3.13 only.

Why an upper limit?

Libraries usually avoid upper limits, so their users can upgrade freely. A service is different: we test it on exactly one Python version and deploy exactly that version, so declaring anything wider would be a promise we haven't checked.

6dependencies = [
7  "alembic==1.20.0",
8  "asyncpg==0.32.0",
9  "cryptography==50.0.2",
10  "dwarpal-contracts",
11  "fastapi==0.143.0",
12  "httpx==0.28.1",
13  "joserfc==1.7.5",
14  "pydantic-settings==2.15.0",
15  "python-multipart==0.0.32",
16  "redis==8.1.0",
17  "sqlalchemy[asyncio]==2.1.4",
18  "uvicorn==0.54.0",
19]

dependencies = [...] — the libraries this package needs in order to run, added in Phase 1. Each one is pinned to an exact version with ==, for the reason given above: a service is tested and deployed with exactly one set of versions.

Library Version What the API uses it for
alembic 1.20.0 database migrations: step-by-step, versioned changes to the tables (§4.10)
asyncpg 0.32.0 the driver for PostgreSQL — the low-level code that speaks the database's own network language, without blocking while it waits (§4.8, §4.10)
cryptography 50.0.2 AES-GCM, which seals the private signing keys before they are stored (§4.12)
dwarpal-contracts — our own shared message shapes; it has no version because it lives in this repository (see below)
fastapi 0.143.0 the web framework: turns Python functions into HTTP endpoints (§4.8)
httpx 0.28.1 an HTTP client, used to call the inference service
joserfc 1.7.5 JOSE: signs age tokens (JWS/JWT) and publishes the public keys (JWK) (§4.12)
pydantic-settings 2.15.0 reads the service's settings from environment variables, with type checks
python-multipart 0.0.32 parses multipart uploads — the format a browser uses to send files such as camera frames
redis 8.1.0 the client library for Valkey, which speaks the same language as Redis (§4.11)
sqlalchemy[asyncio] 2.1.4 talks to the database through Python classes (§4.10). [asyncio] is an extra: an optional bundle of additional libraries, here the ones needed for async use
uvicorn 0.54.0 the server program that listens on a network port and hands each request to FastAPI (§4.8)

Only these direct dependencies are listed here. The libraries they need in turn are pinned in the workspace lockfile, uv.lock (§0.17).

20
21[tool.uv.sources]
22dwarpal-contracts = { workspace = true }

[tool.uv.sources] tells uv where to get a dependency when that isn't the public package index (PyPI). dwarpal-contracts = { workspace = true } means "use the workspace member of that name" — the folder libs/contracts in this repository. The curly brackets are an inline table: TOML's way of writing a small table on one line.

Because the contracts come from the same repository, the API always uses them exactly as they are in the same commit. That is why they need no version number.

23
24[build-system]

[build-system] — how to turn this folder into an installable package. Every installer, including uv and pip, reads this table first.

25requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.1,<0.14"]

requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.1,<0.14"] — the build backend needed to build it: uv_build, made by the uv team. It is small, fast, and fits the src/ layout (§4.2). The range allows bug-fix releases of 0.13 but not 0.14, which could change behaviour.

26build-backend = "uv_build"

build-backend = "uv_build" — the Python module that installers should call to perform the build.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/__init__.py1 lines · 100% explained

An __init__.py file turns a folder into a Python package (§4.2): a folder of modules that can be imported as one unit, as in import dwarpal_api. Whatever is written in it runs the first time the package is imported. This one holds only a docstring, but it is the natural place to see how the whole API service is laid out.

The API is split into four layers, each in its own sub-package. A layer may use the layers listed above it in this table, but never the ones below it:

Layer Folder What lives there Allowed to use
Domain domain/ the rules: identifiers, keys, policies, the decision engine, the session state machine nothing outside itself — no network, database, file or clock
Adapters adapters/ the code that talks to the outside world: PostgreSQL, Valkey, the inference service, signing keys the domain
Use cases app/ the steps of a verification, each written once the domain and the adapters
HTTP http/ turning web requests into use-case calls, and their results into responses the use cases

Explain like I'm six — a restaurant

The domain is the recipe book: it says what a good dish is, but never touches a stove. The adapters are the fridge, the oven and the delivery van. The use cases are the chef, who follows a recipe using the fridge and the oven. The HTTP layer is the waiter, who takes orders and brings plates but never cooks.

This shape is often called hexagonal architecture, or "ports and adapters" (Part 3, Choice 10). Its payoff is easy to see in the tests: the rules that decide whether a child gets through are plain Python, so their tests — some of which try hundreds of generated cases each — finish in about two seconds, with no database, network or clock involved.

1"""Dwarpal API service: relying-party, flow and console APIs, decision engine, signed age tokens."""

The package docstring — what the service offers. Tools such as help(dwarpal_api) and code editors show this text:

  • the relying-party API, which websites use to create verification sessions and read their results;
  • the flow API, which the hosted verify page uses while a person takes the check;
  • the console API for the admin website, which arrives in Phase 4 (the platform phase of the roadmap);
  • and inside them, the decision engine and the signer of age tokens.

Real world — the plan said modules/

The Stage 3 design sketched one sub-folder per feature, under modules/. While building Phase 1, the code turned out clearer when organised by layer instead: one verification feature runs through all four layers, and the layers are what tests and reviewers care about. The Phase 1 report records this change.

Library Why the inference service needs it

Both lists are kept sorted by Ruff, but by two different rules: the import sorter (I001) and the __all__ sorter (RUF022) compare the underscore _ with letters differently. libs/vision/pyproject.toml13 lines · 100% explained

The pyproject.toml of dwarpal-vision — the face-handling code shared by training (in ml/) and serving (in the inference service).

Key idea — one function for training and serving

An AI model learns from faces that were found, straightened and cropped in a particular way. If the live system prepared faces even slightly differently, the model would see images unlike anything it was trained on, and its accuracy would quietly drop. Engineers call this train/serve skew. Putting that code in one shared package makes skew impossible: training and serving literally call the same function.

5.0.3 One command for every check

tasks.py55 lines · 100% explained

tasks.py gives every project check a short name, and runs it the same way on Windows, macOS and Linux. uv run tasks.py check is the single command that runs everything CI runs (§4.7).

1"""Developer tasks for Dwarpal: one entry point for every check, on every operating system.
2
3uv run tasks.py check       everything CI runs: lint, types, tests, book
4uv run tasks.py lint        ruff lint + formatting check
5uv run tasks.py format      apply ruff formatting and safe automatic fixes
6uv run tasks.py typecheck   mypy in strict mode
7uv run tasks.py test        pytest: the services and libraries, then the ML package
8uv run tasks.py book        build the Zero-to-Hero book in strict mode
9"""

The docstring doubles as the help text: line 44 prints it whenever the command is used wrongly. Each line shows one task and what it does.

The usage lines start at the left edge. Ruff's formatter removed their indentation, because a docstring's common indentation is treated as layout, not content. The printed help looks the same either way.

The test line now says what the task runs: the services and libraries, then the ML package — in two separate processes (below).

10
11from __future__ import annotations

from __future__ import annotations — the same type-hint setting used in every Python file of the project.

12
13import subprocess

import subprocess — Python's tool for starting other programs and waiting for them to finish. Every task here is really another program: ruff, mypy, pytest, the book builder.

14import sys

import sys — gives access to sys.executable, sys.argv (the words typed on the command line) and sys.exit.

15from pathlib import Path

from pathlib import Path — the path object, used to find the project root.

16
17ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent — the folder this file lives in, which is the project root. Every task runs from here, wherever you start it.

18PYTHON = sys.executable

PYTHON = sys.executable — the full path of the Python interpreter running this script.

Why run tools as python -m ruff instead of just ruff?

uv run starts this script with the project's own Python, from .venv. Running each tool as "this Python, module ruff" (-m means run a module) guarantees that every task uses the exact tool versions in the project's environment, never some other copy that happens to be installed on the computer.

19
20TASKS: dict[str, list[list[str]]] = {
21    "lint": [[PYTHON, "-m", "ruff", "check", "."], [PYTHON, "-m", "ruff", "format", "--check", "."]],
22    "format": [[PYTHON, "-m", "ruff", "format", "."], [PYTHON, "-m", "ruff", "check", "--fix", "."]],
23    "typecheck": [[PYTHON, "-m", "mypy"]],
24    # Two runs: the ML tests load PyTorch, which once crashed while being imported into a process that had already
25    # loaded OpenCV's and ONNX Runtime's native libraries. Each in its own process, they can't meet.
26    "test": [
27        [PYTHON, "-m", "pytest", "docs/zero_to_hero/tests", "services", "libs"],
28        [PYTHON, "-m", "pytest", "ml"],
29    ],
30    "book": [[PYTHON, "docs/zero_to_hero/build.py", "--strict"]],
31}

TASKS — the table of tasks. The type hint dict[str, list[list[str]]] reads: "a dict from a task name to a list of commands, where each command is a list of words".

Key idea — commands as lists, not strings

["ruff", "check", "."] instead of "ruff check .". A list is handed to the operating system word by word, with no shell in between. Nothing can be misread: a space inside a path stays inside the path, and no stray character can sneak in an extra command. This is the safe way to run programs, and it is why Ruff's warning about subprocess calls (S603) is turned off for this file only (§5.0.2).

The tasks:

  • lint — Ruff's linter, then its formatter in check-only mode;
  • format — apply formatting and the safe automatic fixes;
  • typecheck — mypy (it reads its settings from pyproject.toml);
  • test — pytest, twice: first the book's, the services' and the libraries' tests, then the ML package's. The comment gives the reason. Once, in five full runs, Python crashed while importing a PyTorch library into a process that had already loaded OpenCV's and ONNX Runtime's native code — a clash between compiled libraries, not a failing test. In separate processes they never meet. (Giving pytest folders on the command line overrides the testpaths list in pyproject.toml.)
  • book — the book builder in strict mode.
32TASKS["check"] = TASKS["lint"] + TASKS["typecheck"] + TASKS["test"] + TASKS["book"]

check is built from the others by joining their command lists with +: lint, then types, then tests, then the book. Cheap checks come first, so mistakes are reported as early as possible.

33
34
35def run(name: str) -> int:

run(name) runs one task and returns its exit code: 0 means success.

36    for command in TASKS[name]:

For each command in the task, in order…

37        shown = " ".join(command[1:])

…make a readable version for display. command[1:] skips the long interpreter path, and " ".join glues the words with spaces.

38        print(f"\n> {shown}", flush=True)

Print it as > -m ruff check .. flush=True pushes the text out immediately. Otherwise Python might hold it in a buffer, and it would appear after the tool's own output, which would be confusing.

39        code = subprocess.run(command, cwd=ROOT, check=False).returncode

Run the command and wait.

  • cwd=ROOT runs it from the project root.
  • check=False means "don't raise an exception if it fails — we'll look at the result ourselves".
  • .returncode is the program's exit code.
40        if code != 0:
41            print(f"\n{name}: FAILED at '{shown}' (exit code {code})")
42            return code

Stop at the first failure. Print which task and which command failed, and pass the failing exit code on. There's no point type-checking code that doesn't even pass the linter.

43    print(f"\n{name}: OK")
44    return 0

Every command succeeded: say so, and return 0.

45
46
47def main() -> int:

main() — what happens when you run the file.

48    if len(sys.argv) != 2 or sys.argv[1] not in TASKS:
49        print(__doc__)
50        return 2

Wrong usage — no task name, too many words, or an unknown task. Print the help (the docstring) and return 2. By long convention, exit code 2 means "you used the command incorrectly", as opposed to 1, "the work failed".

51    return run(sys.argv[1])

Otherwise run the requested task. sys.argv[1] is the first word after the script name.

52
53
54if __name__ == "__main__":
55    sys.exit(main())

The entry point: run main() only when the file is executed directly, and pass its result to sys.exit, so CI sees the real exit code.

JSON has no comments, which is why the explanations live here.

  • turbo 2.11.7 — the task runner.

Real world — why turbo went down a version

Phase 0 pinned turbo 2.11.8, which had been published only two days earlier. In Phase 1 the workspace gained a release cooldown (pnpm-workspace.yaml): no package version younger than seven days may be installed. The new rule immediately refused 2.11.8, so turbo stepped back to 2.11.7, released a week before that.

@biomejs/ is a scope: a namespace on npm owned by one organisation, so nobody else can publish under that name.

22}

} — the end of the file.

pnpm-workspace.yaml6 lines · 100% explained

This file tells pnpm that this repository is a workspace: several JavaScript packages managed together, installed together and able to depend on each other (§4.4).

It is written in YAML:

  • key: followed by indented lines groups things together;
  • a line starting with - is one item of a list;
  • indentation is part of the meaning, just as in Python.
1packages:

packages: — the list of places where workspace packages live.

2  - "apps/*"

- "apps/*" — every folder directly inside apps/ is a package: the website and the demo shop (from Phase 1). * matches any folder name.

3  - "packages/*"

- "packages/*" — every folder directly inside packages/ is a package: config and, since Phase 1, the Node SDK sdk-node. Later phases add more here.

4  - "e2e"

- "e2e" — the end-to-end test is a package too (added in Phase 1). It is a single folder rather than a pattern, because there is only one.

5
6minimumReleaseAge: 10080

minimumReleaseAge: 10080 — a release cooldown: pnpm refuses to install any version of any package — including the packages our packages depend on — that was published less than 10,080 minutes (7 days) ago.

Why wait? When an attacker takes over a popular package and publishes a poisoned version, the community usually notices and removes it within hours or days. A project that installs only versions at least a week old simply never meets most of these attacks. The price is small: a bug fix reaches us a week later.

A cooldown that checks itself

pnpm also checks the cooldown when it reads an existing lockfile. On its first run it caught turbo 2.11.8, pinned in Phase 0 only two days after its release, and refused to go on until it was replaced (see package.json).

turbo.json26 lines · 100% explained

turbo.json configures Turborepo: which tasks exist, the order they must run in, and what can be cached (§4.4).

1{

{ — start of the JSON object.

2  "$schema": "https://turborepo.com/schema.json",

"$schema" — the web address of a JSON Schema: a machine-readable description of every setting this file may contain. Code editors use it to offer autocompletion and to flag mistakes as you type. Turborepo itself ignores it.

3  "ui": "stream",

"ui": "stream" — print every task's output as one continuous stream of lines. The alternative is a full-screen terminal interface; plain lines are better in CI logs and easier to copy.

4  "agentGuidance": false,

"agentGuidance": false (added in Phase 1) — when Turborepo detects that an AI coding assistant is running it, it writes a file of advice for that assistant, AGENTS.md, into the repository. That is the tool's business, not the project's: this line switches it off, so no machine-written file appears among the project's own.

5  "tasks": {

"tasks" — one entry per task name. A package takes part in a task if its own package.json has a script with the same name.

6    "build": {
7      "dependsOn": ["^build"],
8      "outputs": [".next/**", "!.next/cache/**", "dist/**"]
9    },

build:

  • "dependsOn": ["^build"] — before building a package, build every workspace package it depends on. The ^ means "my dependencies", not "myself". The design-system package must be built before the website that uses it.
  • "outputs" — which files the build produces, so Turborepo can cache them:
    • .next/** — everything under .next (the Next.js output, ** meaning any depth);
    • !.next/cache/** — except Next's own internal cache, which would bloat Turborepo's;
    • dist/** — everything under dist.

If nothing in a package changed, the next build restores these files from the cache in milliseconds instead of rebuilding.

10    "typecheck": {
11      "dependsOn": ["^build"]
12    },

typecheck also depends on ^build. Checking a package's TypeScript needs the type declarations that its dependencies produce when they are built.

13    "test": {
14      "dependsOn": ["^build"]
15    },

test depends on ^build for the same reason: tests import the built versions of dependency packages.

16    "e2e": {
17      "dependsOn": ["^build"],
18      "passThroughEnv": ["UV", "CI"],
19      "cache": false
20    },

e2e — the end-to-end test (added in Phase 1):

  • "dependsOn": ["^build"] — build the packages it depends on first: the SDK and both web apps;
  • "passThroughEnv": ["UV", "CI"] — Turborepo runs tasks in a strict environment: a task sees only the environment variables it was told about, so that no stray setting can change a result without anyone knowing. This line lets two through: UV (where the uv program is, on machines where it isn't on the PATH) and CI (set by GitHub Actions, which makes the test stricter there);
  • "cache": false — never reuse an old result: the test checks the live system, which a cached "passed" would hide.

Real world — the variable that vanished

The first run of the end-to-end test failed straight away: Playwright couldn't find uv, although UV had been set in the terminal. Turborepo's strict environment had quietly removed it. Declaring it here fixed it.

21    "dev": {
22      "cache": false,
23      "persistent": true
24    }

dev — development servers:

  • "cache": false — a running server's output is never cached; there is nothing to reuse;
  • "persistent": true — this task runs forever, until stopped. Turborepo then knows never to wait for it to finish, and never to let another task depend on it.
25  }
26}

} } — the end of the tasks object, and the end of the file.

Reformatting them by hand would break again at every export.

{ — start of the JSON object.

2  "name": "@dwarpal/config",

packages/config/tsconfig.base.json19 lines · 100% explained

The shared TypeScript configuration. Every app and package will start its own tsconfig.json with "extend @dwarpal/config/tsconfig.base.json", so all of them follow the same, strict rules.

TypeScript (§0.4) adds types to JavaScript, and its compiler checks them before the code runs. These options decide how strict that checking is and what kind of JavaScript comes out.

1{

{ — start of the JSON object.

2  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/tsconfig",

"$schema" — the community-maintained schema for tsconfig files, for editor autocompletion.

3  "compilerOptions": {

"compilerOptions" — the settings for the TypeScript compiler.

4    "target": "ES2024",

"target": "ES2024" — which version of JavaScript to produce. ECMAScript (ES) is JavaScript's official name, and a new edition comes out every year. Every browser we support understands ES2024, so modern features are kept as they are instead of being rewritten into older, longer code.

5    "lib": ["ES2024", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],

"lib": ["ES2024", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"] — which built-in features the compiler should know about:

  • the ES2024 standard library;
  • the DOM — the browser's page objects such as document and window;
  • DOM.Iterable — lets you loop over lists of page elements with for … of.
6    "module": "ESNext",

"module": "ESNext" — write imports and exports in the modern standard form (import x from "y"), as today's tools expect.

7    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",

"moduleResolution": "Bundler" — find imported files the way modern bundlers do. A bundler is a tool, such as Next.js's Turbopack, that combines many source files into a few optimised files for the browser.

8    "strict": true,

"strict": true — switch on TypeScript's whole family of strict checks. The most important one: a value that might be null or undefined must be checked before it is used.

9    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,

"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true — reading list[5] or settings[key] might find nothing, so TypeScript treats the result as "maybe undefined" until you check. This catches a very common class of crash.

10    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,

"exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true — an optional property (may be left out) is not the same as one explicitly set to undefined, and TypeScript keeps the two apart. This matters for API messages, where "missing" and "empty" can mean different things.

11    "noImplicitOverride": true,

"noImplicitOverride": true — when a class replaces a method it inherited, it must say so with the override keyword. Renaming a method in the parent class can then never silently leave a child's "replacement" pointing at nothing.

12    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,

"noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true — in a switch statement, forgetting break makes one case "fall through" into the next, which is a classic bug. This makes it an error.

13    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,

"verbatimModuleSyntax": true — imports that only bring in types must say so (import type { User } from …). Tools can then delete them safely and predictably when producing JavaScript, where types don't exist.

14    "isolatedModules": true,

"isolatedModules": true — every file must be understandable on its own. Fast tools translate files one at a time without looking at the rest of the project, and this setting guarantees that is always possible.

15    "resolveJsonModule": true,

"resolveJsonModule": true — allow importing .json files directly, with their contents typed automatically.

16    "skipLibCheck": true,

"skipLibCheck": true — don't re-check the type declarations shipped inside installed libraries. Their mistakes aren't ours to fix, and checking them makes every type check much slower.

17    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true

"forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true — import "./Button" and a file named button.tsx would work on Windows and macOS, whose file systems ignore letter case, but fail on the Linux server. This catches the mismatch on the developer's machine.

18  }
19}

} } — the end of the compiler options, and the end of the file.

5.0.5 Local infrastructure

infra/compose/compose.yaml41 lines · 100% explained

The Docker Compose file for local development. It describes two containers — the PostgreSQL database and Valkey — and how to run them, so that one command starts both, healthy and ready (§4.5). In Phase 1 it grows to include our own services too.

YAML reminder: indentation shows what belongs to what, and # starts a comment.

1# Dwarpal: local development infrastructure (the databases the services need).
2#   start:  docker compose -f infra/compose/compose.yaml up -d --wait
3#   stop:   docker compose -f infra/compose/compose.yaml down      (add -v to delete the data too)

Comments: what the file is for, and the exact commands to start and stop it.

  • -f names this file.
  • up -d starts the containers in the background (detached).
  • --wait returns only when every health check passes.
  • down -v also deletes the data volumes — a fresh start.
4
5name: dwarpal

name: dwarpal — the project name. Compose prefixes everything it creates with it (dwarpal-postgres-1, dwarpal_pgdata), so these containers never clash with another project's.

6
7services:

services: — the list of containers to run, each under its own name.

8  postgres:

postgres: — the first service, the PostgreSQL database. Inside Compose's private network, other containers will reach it simply by the name postgres.

9    image: postgres:18.6-alpine3.24

image: postgres:18.6-alpine3.24 — the official PostgreSQL image, pinned: version 18.6, built on Alpine Linux 3.24 (a tiny Linux distribution, so the image is small). Version 18 is required for the built-in uuidv7() function (ADR-0011).

10    environment:

environment: — settings passed into the container. The official image reads these on its first start.

11      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-dwarpal}
12      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-dwarpal}
13      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-dwarpal-local-only}

The database name, user and password. ${POSTGRES_DB:-dwarpal} means "use the variable POSTGRES_DB if it is set — for example in an .env file — otherwise use dwarpal". The default password is labelled local-only, as a reminder that it must never be used anywhere real.

14    ports:
15      - "127.0.0.1:${POSTGRES_PORT:-5432}:5432"

ports: — publish the container's port 5432 on the computer, so programs outside Docker (our services during development, a database viewer) can connect.

The 127.0.0.1: at the front is a security choice. It publishes the port only to this computer, not to every device on the same Wi-Fi network. The middle number can be changed through POSTGRES_PORT, in case 5432 is already in use.

16    volumes:
17      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql

volumes: — keep the database's files in a named volume called pgdata, so the data survives when the container is replaced.

The volume is mounted at /var/lib/postgresql, the location PostgreSQL 18's image expects. Older versions used /var/lib/postgresql/data; the change makes future major-version upgrades easier.

18    healthcheck:

healthcheck: — how Docker decides the database is truly ready, not just started.

19      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]

test — the check: run pg_isready inside the container, for our user and database. CMD-SHELL means "run this through the container's shell".

The doubled $$ is an escape. A single $ would be filled in by Compose on your computer; $$ becomes a literal $, so the variable is filled in inside the container, by the container's shell.

20      interval: 5s
21      timeout: 3s
22      retries: 20

Check every 5 seconds, allow each check 3 seconds, and only declare the container unhealthy after 20 failures in a row — about 100 seconds, which gives a first start plenty of time.

23    restart: unless-stopped

restart: unless-stopped — if the database crashes or the computer restarts, Docker starts it again automatically. The exception is when you stopped it yourself.

24
25  valkey:

valkey: — the second service: Valkey, the fast short-term memory (ADR-0011).

26    image: valkey/valkey:9.1.2-alpine3.24

image: valkey/valkey:9.1.2-alpine3.24 — the official Valkey image, version 9.1.2 on Alpine 3.24, pinned.

27    command: ["valkey-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]

command: — the program the container runs: valkey-server with append-only persistence switched on. Every change is also appended to a log file on disk, so the queued background jobs and other short-lived state survive a restart.

28    ports:
29      - "127.0.0.1:${VALKEY_PORT:-6379}:6379"

Publish Valkey's port 6379 to this computer only, with an optional override through VALKEY_PORT.

30    volumes:
31      - valkeydata:/data

Keep Valkey's files in the named volume valkeydata, mounted at /data, where the image stores them.

32    healthcheck:
33      test: ["CMD", "valkey-cli", "ping"]
34      interval: 5s
35      timeout: 3s
36      retries: 20

The health check: valkey-cli ping must answer (with PONG). Same timing as for PostgreSQL. CMD (instead of CMD-SHELL) runs the program directly, since no shell features are needed.

37    restart: unless-stopped

restart: unless-stopped — restart automatically, as for PostgreSQL.

38
39volumes:
40  pgdata:
41  valkeydata:

volumes: at the top level declares the two named volumes used above. Docker creates them on first use and keeps them until they are explicitly deleted (down -v).

infra/compose/.env.example6 lines · 100% explained

An example settings file. Docker Compose automatically reads a file named .env in the same folder as the Compose file, and uses its values to fill the ${…} placeholders in compose.yaml.

The real .env is never committed (see .gitignore), because in a real deployment it holds secrets. This example is committed so everyone can see which settings exist. To use it, copy it to .env and change the values.

1# Copy this file to infra/compose/.env to override the local defaults. A real .env is never committed.

A comment explaining exactly that — what to copy where, and that the real file is never committed.

2POSTGRES_DB=dwarpal

POSTGRES_DB=dwarpal — the name of the database created on first start.

3POSTGRES_USER=dwarpal

POSTGRES_USER=dwarpal — the database user created on first start.

4POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-even-for-local-use

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-even-for-local-use — a placeholder that announces it must be changed. Example files should never contain a password that looks real enough to be used as is.

5POSTGRES_PORT=5432

POSTGRES_PORT=5432 — the port PostgreSQL is published on, on this computer. Change it if another program already uses 5432.

6VALKEY_PORT=6379

VALKEY_PORT=6379 — the same for Valkey.

5.0.6 Continuous integration

.github/workflows/ci.yml81 lines · 100% explained

The continuous-integration workflow (§4.6). GitHub reads every file in .github/workflows/. Whenever this repository receives new code, GitHub starts fresh Linux machines and runs these three jobs on them. If any step fails, the change is marked with a red ✗.

1name: ci

name: ci — the workflow's name, shown on GitHub's Actions page and next to each commit.

2
3on:

on: — when the workflow runs.

4  push:
5    branches: [main]

push: to the main branch — every time new commits land on the main line of history.

6  pull_request:

pull_request: — every time someone proposes a change through a pull request. Problems are therefore found before the change is merged, not after.

7
8permissions:
9  contents: read

permissions: contents: read — the workflow may only read the repository. By default GitHub gives workflows more powers, such as writing to the repository. Following the principle of least privilege, nothing gets a power it doesn't need. Then even a compromised tool inside the workflow couldn't modify the code.

10
11concurrency:
12  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
13  cancel-in-progress: true

concurrency: — if a new commit arrives while an earlier run for the same branch is still going (group: ci-${{ github.ref }}, where github.ref is the branch name), cancel the old run (cancel-in-progress: true). Only the newest code matters, so this saves time.

14
15jobs:

jobs: — the work, divided into jobs that run at the same time on separate machines.

16  python:

python: — the first job's internal name.

17    name: Python - lint, types, tests, book

name: — the human-readable title shown on GitHub.

18    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04

runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 — a fresh virtual machine running Ubuntu Linux 24.04 LTS. It is pinned, rather than "latest", so an Ubuntu upgrade can't suddenly change our results.

19    timeout-minutes: 15

timeout-minutes: 15 — if something hangs, stop after 15 minutes instead of GitHub's default of six hours.

20    steps:

steps: — the job's steps, run in order.

21      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1

uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1 — a published action that downloads this repository's code onto the machine. Every job starts from an empty machine, so this always comes first.

The exact version tag is pinned: a newer release can only arrive through a deliberate, visible change to this file.

22      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.0
23        with:
24          version: "0.13.1"
25          enable-cache: true

astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.0 — installs uv:

  • version: "0.13.1" — the same uv version as on the developer's machine;
  • enable-cache: true — keep downloaded packages between runs, which makes later runs much faster.
26      - run: uv sync --locked

run: uv sync --locked — install Python 3.13 and every locked package. --locked means: fail if uv.lock doesn't exactly match the pyproject.toml files. Someone who changed a dependency but forgot to update the lockfile is told immediately.

27      - run: uv run infra/scripts/fetch_models.py

run: uv run infra/scripts/fetch_models.py — download the third-party model files the tests need (the YuNet face detector, §5.1) and verify each one's SHA-256 fingerprint before using it. Model files are never stored in Git (.gitignore), so every fresh machine — including CI's — fetches them this way. Added in Phase 1.

28      - run: uv run tasks.py check

run: uv run tasks.py check — the same single command developers run locally (§5.0.3): lint, types, tests and the book in strict mode. CI and developers can never disagree about what "passing" means.

29
30  javascript:

javascript: — the second job, running at the same time on its own machine.

31    name: JavaScript - lint, types, tests, builds
32    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
33    timeout-minutes: 15

Its title, the same pinned Ubuntu machine, and the same 15-minute limit. Since Phase 1 the job also builds everything, hence "builds" in its name.

34    steps:

steps: — this job's steps.

35      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1

Download the code, as in the first job.

36      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6.1.0

pnpm/action-setup@v6.1.0 — installs pnpm. No version is given here, because the action reads the packageManager field of package.json (pnpm 12.11.2), so the version lives in one place only.

37      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7.1.0
38        with:
39          node-version: 24
40          cache: pnpm

actions/setup-node@v7.1.0 — installs Node.js 24 (the LTS line in package.json). cache: pnpm keeps pnpm's package store between runs.

41      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile — install exactly what pnpm-lock.yaml says, and fail if the lockfile is out of date. This is the JavaScript twin of uv sync --locked.

42      - run: pnpm lint

run: pnpm lint — Biome's formatting and lint checks.

43      - run: pnpm typecheck

run: pnpm typecheck — TypeScript checks for every package: the SDK, both web apps and the end-to-end tests (added in Phase 1).

44      - run: pnpm test

run: pnpm test — JavaScript unit tests for every package (Vitest, §4.20).

45      - run: pnpm build

run: pnpm build — build every package with Turborepo: the SDK compiles to plain JavaScript, and both Next.js apps make their production builds. A build that only fails on a clean machine is caught here, not on deployment day.

46
47  e2e:
48    name: End to end - a real browser through every service
49    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
50    timeout-minutes: 20

The end-to-end job (added in Phase 1): the whole system, in a real browser, exactly as a person would use it — the demo shop, the verify page, the API and the inference service, with a fake camera. It gets 20 minutes, because it installs a browser and builds everything first.

51    steps:
52      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1

Its steps start, like every job, by checking out the code.

53      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.0
54        with:
55          version: "0.13.1"
56          enable-cache: true

Install uv, as in the Python job: the API and the inference service are Python programs.

57      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6.1.0
58      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7.1.0
59        with:
60          node-version: 24
61          cache: pnpm

Install pnpm and Node.js 24, as in the JavaScript job: the web apps and the test runner are JavaScript programs.

62      - run: uv sync --locked

uv sync --locked — install the Python side exactly as the lockfile says.

63      - run: uv run infra/scripts/fetch_models.py

Download the face-detection model, which the inference service needs (§5.1.1).

64      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

Install the JavaScript side exactly as its lockfile says.

65      - run: pnpm --filter @dwarpal/e2e exec playwright install --with-deps chromium

Download the Chromium browser that Playwright drives (§4.20). --with-deps also installs the system libraries a browser needs on a bare Linux machine, such as fonts.

66      - run: pnpm e2e

pnpm e2e — run the end-to-end test. Its configuration starts the databases with Docker Compose, prepares a demo project, and launches all four services itself (e2e/playwright.config.ts).

67      - if: failure()
68        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7.0.2
69        with:
70          name: e2e-results
71          path: e2e/test-results
72          retention-days: 7

Only if a step failed (if: failure()), upload the test's results — screenshots and Playwright's step-by-step trace — as an artifact: a file bundle attached to the CI run, kept for 7 days. A failure on a machine nobody can log into is then still easy to investigate.

73
74  infrastructure:

infrastructure: — the third job: proving the development databases start correctly on a completely clean machine.

75    name: Compose - databases start healthy
76    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
77    timeout-minutes: 10

Its title, machine and a 10-minute limit.

78    steps:

steps: — this job's steps.

79      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1

Download the code.

80      - run: docker compose -f infra/compose/compose.yaml up -d --wait

Start PostgreSQL and Valkey and wait until both report healthy. If either image can't be downloaded, or either health check never passes, this step fails. GitHub's Ubuntu machines come with Docker already installed.

81      - run: docker compose -f infra/compose/compose.yaml down -v

Stop the containers and delete their data volumes, leaving the machine clean. GitHub discards the machine anyway, but cleaning up after yourself is a good habit.

5.0.7 Tests for the book builder

docs/zero_to_hero/tests/test_build.py122 lines · 100% explained

These are the automatic tests for the book builder. build.py is itself a checker — it decides whether the book is complete — so if it had a bug, it could report "100 % explained" when that isn't true. Testing the checker closes that gap.

Each test is a function whose name starts with test_. pytest finds and runs every such function. Inside, each assert states something that must be true; if it isn't, pytest reports exactly which line failed and what the values were.

Explain like I'm six

Before a referee runs a real match, someone checks the referee's whistle and stopwatch. These tests check the book-builder's tools with tiny, made-up examples where we already know the right answer.

1"""Tests for the Zero-to-Hero book builder: the checker of the book must itself be checked."""

The module docstring: what this file is for, in one sentence.

2
3from __future__ import annotations

from __future__ import annotations — the same type-hint setting as in build.py, so both files behave identically.

4
5from pathlib import Path

from pathlib import Path — the Path type, used in the type hint of the last test's tmp_path folder.

6
7import pytest

import pytest — the test runner itself. These tests use it for one type name, pytest.MonkeyPatch (explained in the last test).

8
9import build
10from build import Note, Place

Import the code under test.

15    assert build.source_lines("a\nb") == ["a", "b"]

source_lines drops only the final newline.

This protects the line numbering of every walkthrough.

The fingerprint is stable and sensitive.

32def test_todo_and_empty_notes_do_not_count_as_explained() -> None:
33    assert build.is_explained(Note(1, 1, "Real text."))
34    assert not build.is_explained(Note(1, 1, "TODO"))

36    assert not build.is_explained(Note(1, 1, "  \n"))

What counts as explained. Real text counts. The skeleton placeholder TODO, the re-anchoring flag TODO(review) … and blank text do not. If any of these three lines ever broke, the coverage numbers would lie.

40    parts, problems = build.segments([Note(3, 4, "b"), Note(1, 1, "a")], total=6)
41    assert problems == []

Segments cover every line exactly once. Two notes, given in the wrong order (lines 3–4 first, then line 1), on a 6-line file. The result must be, in order:

  • line 1 (explained);
  • line 2 (a gap);
  • lines 3–4 (explained);
  • lines 5–6 (a gap at the end).

n is not None turns each note into simply True or False, which keeps the expected value readable.

50def test_line_mapping_follows_moved_lines_and_skips_deleted_ones() -> None:
51    mapping = build.line_mapping(["a", "b", "c"], ["new", "a", "c"])
52    assert mapping == {1: Place(2, 2, edited=False), 3: Place(3, 3, edited=False)}

The line mapping follows moved lines and skips deleted ones. Old file a b c; new file new a c — a line was added at the top, and b was deleted.

  • a moved from line 1 to line 2, unedited;
  • c stayed on line 3, unedited;
  • b has no entry at all, because it has no place in the new file.

55def test_line_mapping_lines_up_edited_blocks_side_by_side() -> None:
56    grown = build.line_mapping(["a", "b", "c"], ["a", "B1", "B2", "c"])
57    assert grown == {1: Place(1, 1, edited=False), 2: Place(2, 3, edited=True), 3: Place(4, 4, edited=False)}
58    shrunk = build.line_mapping(["a", "b1", "b2", "c"], ["a", "B", "c"])
59    assert shrunk[2] == shrunk[3] == Place(2, 2, edited=True)

Edited blocks are lined up side by side (the "two rows of chairs" of build.py).

  • Grown: b became two lines, B1 and B2. Old line 2 now covers new lines 2–3, marked as edited, and c moved from 3 to 4.
  • Shrunk: two lines, b1 and b2, became one line B. Both old lines now point at new line 2, marked as edited. shrunk[2] == shrunk[3] == Place(…) is a chained comparison: it is true only when all three are equal.

62def test_reanchor_moves_notes_and_flags_edited_code_for_review() -> None:
63    old = ["import os", "x = 1", "y = 2"]
64    new = ['"""Docstring."""', "import os", "x = 10", "y = 2"]
65    text = "intro\n@@ 1\nImports os.\n@@ 2\nSets x.\n@@ 3\nSets y.\n"
66    result, report = build.reanchor_text(text, build.line_mapping(old, new))

68    assert len(report) == 1

Re-anchoring moves notes and flags edited code.

  • A docstring line was added at the top, x = 1 was edited into x = 10, and the other lines are unchanged.
  • The note on import os moves from 1 to 2.
  • The note on y = 2 moves from 3 to 4.
  • The note on the edited line moves to the code that replaced it (line 3), with its text marked TODO(review).
  • The report contains exactly one message: the one about the edited line.

Notes on deleted code are dropped. Old a b c, new a c. The note on b, whose code is gone, disappears from the result, and the report says so in exactly these words. The first argument is spread over three lines by the formatter because it is long.
