54        self.detector = detector
55        self.age = age
56        self.rules = rules

FacePipeline keeps its parts: the detector, the age model, the quality rules, and — since the owner's tests — the face mesh, the hand detector and the anti-spoofing detector, each optional. They are given to it rather than created inside it. That way tests can hand it a stand-in model, or leave a part out, without changing this code. This style is called dependency injection.

The last, trust_labels (Phase 3), switches on the test mode in which liveness believes the frames' phase labels. It is off unless the service's settings turn it on — and they refuse to without the stand-in age model.

57        self.mesh = mesh
58        self.hands = hands
59        self.spoof = spoof

Keep the three optional measuring parts.

60        self.trust_labels = trust_labels

Keep the trust_labels choice.

61
62    def analyze(self, meta: FaceRequestMeta, images: list[bytes]) -> FaceAnalysis:

analyze — one burst in, one analysis out.

63        started = time.perf_counter()

Start the stopwatch. perf_counter is Python's most precise clock for measuring durations.

64        reports: list[FrameReport] = []
65        aligned: list[Image] = []
66        weights: list[float] = []

Three lists to fill: one report per frame, the aligned good faces, and a weight for each good face.

67        seen: list[Seen] = []

seen (Phase 3) — one Seen record per frame, collected for the liveness checks: the frame's description, its report, and its aligned face (if any).

68        for frame, data in zip(meta.frames, images, strict=True):

Walk through the frames and their bytes together. strict=True raises an error if the two lists differ in length, so a missing frame can never silently shift the others out of line.

69            try:
70                image = decode_image(data, max_bytes=MAX_FRAME_BYTES)
71            except DecodeError:
72                reports.append(
73                    FrameReport(
74                        index=frame.index,
75                        faces=0,
76                        detector_score=0.0,
77                        brightness=0.0,
78                        sharpness=0.0,
79                        eye_distance_px=0.0,
80                        yaw_ratio=0.0,
81                        flags=["undecodable"],
82                    )
83                )
84                seen.append(Seen(frame, reports[-1], None))
85                continue

A frame that can't be decoded doesn't stop the others. The decoder is given the contract's size limit (max_bytes=MAX_FRAME_BYTES), so the limit is defined in exactly one place. Its report carries the single flag undecodable and zeros everywhere else. It is also recorded in seen, with no face (reports[-1] is the report just added: index −1 means "the last one"). continue moves on to the next frame.

86            faces = self.detector.detect(image)
87            quality = assess(image, faces, self.rules)

Find the faces, then check the frame's quality.

88            head = self.mesh.angles(image, faces[0]) if self.mesh is not None and faces else None

The head's angles from the face mesh, for the main face — when there is a mesh and a face.

89            nearby = near_face(faces[0].box, self.hands.detect(image)) if self.hands is not None and faces else 0

How many hands are next to the main face — when there is a hand detector and a face.

90            one = quality.faces == 1
91            real = self.spoof.real(image, faces[0]) if self.spoof is not None and one else None
92            pattern = screen_pattern(image, faces[0]) if one else None

For a photo of exactly one person: the anti-spoofing networks' real-face chance (when they are loaded) and the screen-pattern measure. With nobody or several people, these would describe the wrong face, so they are left empty.

93            reports.append(
94                FrameReport(
95                    index=frame.index,
96                    faces=quality.faces,
97                    detector_score=quality.detector_score,
98                    brightness=quality.brightness,
99                    sharpness=quality.sharpness,
100                    eye_distance_px=quality.eye_distance_px,
101                    yaw_ratio=quality.yaw_ratio,
102                    pitch_ratio=quality.pitch_ratio,
103                    mesh_yaw=None if head is None else head.yaw,
104                    mesh_pitch=None if head is None else head.pitch,
105                    hands_near_face=nearby,
106                    real_score=real,
107                    screen_pattern=pattern,
108                    flags=list(quality.flags),
109                )
110            )

Record the frame's report, copying every measurement into the contract: the quality measurements, the head's angles from the five points and from the mesh, the hands, and the presentation evidence.

111            # Liveness looks at every photo of exactly one person: a turned head, or a face darkened by the screen's
112            # blue, is exactly what its checks expect. The age is estimated from flawless photos only.
113            face = align_face(image, faces[0]) if quality.faces == 1 else None
114            seen.append(Seen(frame, reports[-1], face))
115            if face is not None and not quality.flags:
116                aligned.append(face)
117                weights.append(quality.detector_score * min(1.0, quality.sharpness / 200.0))

The comment explains a change made during the owner's tests. Liveness now looks at every photo of exactly one person: a turned head, or a face darkened by the screen's blue, is exactly what its checks expect — it was these photos, set aside for their quality flags, that left the light check with nothing to measure. The age is still estimated from flawless photos only: align the face and weight it by the detector's confidence times sharpness (capped at 1 from a sharpness of 200 upwards).

118        age = self.estimate(aligned, weights) if aligned else None

Estimate age if at least one frame was good; otherwise there is no estimate (None). The decision engine turns that into a retry, never a guess.

119        challenge = meta.challenge
120        trusting = self.trust_labels

Short names for the challenge the frames are checked against (the server's stored copy; see verification.py) and for the test-mode switch.

121        liveness = Liveness(
122            pose=pose_check(seen, challenge, trusting) if challenge else None,

Build the liveness result. The pose check runs if there is a challenge to check against; otherwise None.

123            light=light_check(seen, challenge, meta.light_started_ms, meta.signals)
124            if challenge and not trusting
125            else None,

The light check runs only with a challenge and with real images: in the labels test mode the frames come from a still portrait, so measuring the light would mean nothing. The … if … else None here spans three lines; the brackets of the call allow that.

126            injection=injection_signs(seen, meta.signals, trusting),

The injection signs are always looked for.

127            presentation=median_of([r.real_score for r in reports]) if not trusting else None,
128            screen_pattern=median_of([r.screen_pattern for r in reports]) if not trusting else None,

The attempt's presentation evidence: the median real-face chance and the median screen pattern over its photos — empty in the labels test mode, whose still portrait would make them meaningless.

129            evidence="labels" if trusting else "images",
130        )

Say where the pose result came from: labels in the test mode, images otherwise. The API refuses labels for a live session.

131        elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000.0

Stop the stopwatch, in milliseconds.

132        return FaceAnalysis(
133            model_version=self.age.version,
134            frames=reports,
135            usable_frames=len(aligned),
136            age=age,
137            duration_ms=elapsed,
138            liveness=liveness,
139        )

Assemble the answer: the model version, the frame reports, the count of good frames, the age estimate, the duration — and the liveness result (Phase 3).

140
141    def estimate(self, aligned: list[Image], weights: list[float]) -> AgeEstimate:

estimate — combine the good faces into one age estimate.

142        rows = self.age.predict(aligned)

Ask the model for one 101-probability row per face, all in one batch, which is faster than one at a time.

143        share = np.asarray(weights, dtype=np.float64)
144        share = share / share.sum() if share.sum() > 0 else np.full(len(rows), 1.0 / len(rows))

Turn the weights into shares that add up to 1. If every weight were zero, fall back to equal shares instead of dividing by zero.

145        mixture = (rows * share[:, None]).sum(axis=0)

The mixture: a weighted average of the rows. share[:, None] turns the shares into a column, so each row is multiplied by its own share; then the rows are added up. The result is still a proper distribution over ages 0–100.

146        mean = float((mixture * AGES).sum())

The expected age: each age times its probability, added up.

147        std = float(np.sqrt((mixture * (AGES - mean) ** 2).sum()))

The standard deviation: how spread out the distribution is around that expected age.

148        p_over = {age: float(np.clip(mixture[age:].sum(), 0.0, 1.0)) for age in POLICY_AGES}

For each policy age N, P(age ≥ N) is the sum of the probabilities from age N upwards (mixture[age:]). It is clipped into 0–1 to absorb tiny rounding errors, because the contract insists on that range.

149        frame_means = [float((row * AGES).sum()) for row in rows]

Each frame's own expected age, so the API can check that the frames agree with each other.

150        return AgeEstimate(mean=mean, std=std, p_over=p_over, frame_means=frame_means)

Return the combined estimate.

26def build_pipeline(settings: Settings) -> FacePipeline:
27    detector = FaceDetector(settings.models_dir / settings.detector_file)
28    mesh = FaceMesh(settings.models_dir / settings.mesh_file)
29    hands = HandDetector(settings.models_dir / settings.hands_file)
30    models = [
31        SpoofModel(settings.models_dir / file, scale)
32        for file, scale in zip(settings.antispoof_files, (2.7, 4.0), strict=True)
33    ]
34    # Made from the pinned weights by `python -m dwarpal_ml.antispoof`; without them, liveness says so and decides less.
35    spoof = SpoofDetector(models) if all(model.path.is_file() for model in models) else None
36    return FacePipeline(
37        detector,
38        build_age_backend(settings),
39        mesh=mesh,
40        hands=hands,
41        spoof=spoof,
42        trust_labels=settings.liveness == "labels",
43    )

build_pipeline — load every model and return a ready pipeline: the face detector, the face mesh, the hand detector, the anti-spoofing networks and the chosen age model.

The anti-spoofing networks are the exception to "every model must be there": they are made from the pinned weights by python -m dwarpal_ml.antispoof, which needs PyTorch. As the comment says, without them the pipeline still runs — every result then has an empty presentation, and the decision has one signal fewer.

trust_labels is on only when the setting liveness is "labels" — the test mode in which liveness reads each frame's phase label instead of measuring the head (§5.3). The settings refuse that mode unless the stand-in age model is in use, so it can never reach a real deployment.

/readyz — "is it ready for work?" It answers only once the pipeline is loaded, and reports which age model is active and — as the comment says — whether the anti-spoofing networks are loaded or missing. Without them the service still analyses faces, but the API won't decide a live session (domain/decision.py); this answer lets an operator see why at a glance.

68    @app.post("/internal/v1/analyze/face")
69    async def analyze_face(request: Request) -> FaceAnalysis:

The main endpoint: POST /internal/v1/analyze/face returns a FaceAnalysis. FastAPI turns the returned model into JSON automatically.

70        if limiter.available_tokens == 0:
71            raise HTTPException(503, "inference is busy; retry shortly", headers={"Retry-After": "1"})

Back-pressure. If every worker slot is busy, refuse immediately with 503 Service Unavailable and Retry-After: 1, instead of piling up requests until the server collapses.

72        form = await request.form(max_files=MAX_FRAMES, max_fields=1)

Read the multipart form: at most MAX_FRAMES (16) files and 1 ordinary field (meta). Anything more is refused by the parser before it is stored.

73        try:
74            meta = FaceRequestMeta.model_validate_json(str(form.get("meta", "")))
75        except ValidationError as error:
76            raise HTTPException(422, "meta is missing or invalid") from error

Parse and validate meta with the contract. A missing or invalid value becomes a clear 422 Unprocessable error. from error keeps the original cause for debugging.

77        images: list[bytes] = []

Collect each frame's bytes, in order.

78        for frame in meta.frames:
79            upload = form.get(f"frame_{frame.index}")
80            if not isinstance(upload, UploadFile):
81                raise HTTPException(422, f"frame_{frame.index} is missing")

For each frame the metadata promises, the matching upload frame_<index> must exist. Otherwise the request is refused with 422, naming the missing frame.

82            data = await upload.read(MAX_FRAME_BYTES + 1)
83            if len(data) > MAX_FRAME_BYTES:
84                raise HTTPException(413, f"frame_{frame.index} is larger than {MAX_FRAME_BYTES} bytes")

Read at most one byte more than MAX_FRAME_BYTES. If that extra byte arrives, the frame is too big and is refused with 413 Content Too Large. Asking for just one extra byte means an oversized frame is never copied into memory in full.

To be precise about who checks what: by this point the form parser has already received the whole upload, keeping large files in a temporary file on disk. The size of a whole request is capped earlier — by the API, which is the only program allowed to call this service, and in production also by the web server at the front door.

85            images.append(data)

Keep the frame's bytes.

86        pipeline: FacePipeline = request.app.state.pipeline
87        return await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(pipeline.analyze, meta, images, limiter=limiter)

Run the analysis on a worker thread, within the limiter. Image work is CPU-heavy and blocking. Running it directly here would freeze the server's event loop and stall every other request, including health checks.

88
89    return app

Return the finished application.

30def burst(count: int) -> FaceRequestMeta:
31    return FaceRequestMeta(frames=[FrameMeta(index=i, t_ms=i * 120.0) for i in range(count)])

burst(count) builds request metadata for count frames, 120 milliseconds apart, as the capture page would.

34@asynccontextmanager
35async def client_for(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[httpx.AsyncClient]:
36    async with app.router.lifespan_context(app):
37        transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=app)
38        async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://inference") as client:
39            yield client

client_for(app) — run an app in memory and talk to it over HTTP, without opening any network port:

  • app.router.lifespan_context(app) runs the app's start-up code (loading the model) and, at the end, its shutdown code;
  • httpx.ASGITransport(app=app) is a "pretend network": requests go straight into the app's code;
  • the client is handed (yield) to the test, and closed automatically afterwards.

Starlette 1.8 now recommends against its older built-in test client, so this plain-httpx approach avoids that deprecated path.

115            helper.make_node("GlobalAveragePool", ["pixels"], ["pooled"]),
116            helper.make_node("Flatten", ["pooled"], ["flat"]),
117            helper.make_node("MatMul", ["flat", "weights"], ["logits"]),
118            helper.make_node("Softmax", ["logits"], ["probabilities"], axis=1),
119        ],
120        "tiny",
121        [helper.make_tensor_value_info("pixels", TensorProto.FLOAT, ["faces", 3, 224, 224])],
122        [helper.make_tensor_value_info("probabilities", TensorProto.FLOAT, ["faces", len(AGES)])],
123        [numpy_helper.from_array(weights / 255.0, "weights")],
124    )

The model's graph, node by node: average each colour over the whole picture (GlobalAveragePool, giving 3 numbers per face), lay them flat, multiply by the weights (101 scores), and turn them into probabilities (Softmax). Then its input and output, named and shaped exactly like the real model's (faces is a size left open), and the weights, scaled so that pixels of 0–255 give moderate scores.

125    model = helper.make_model(graph, opset_imports=[helper.make_opsetid("", 18)], ir_version=10)

Wrap the graph as a model for ONNX's operator set 18, in file-format version 10 — the format the real export uses. (The onnx library would otherwise write its newest format, 14, which ONNX Runtime 1.31 can't read yet: the first version of this test found that.)

126    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
127    onnx.save(model, folder / "model.onnx")
128    digest = hashlib.sha256((folder / "model.onnx").read_bytes()).hexdigest()
129    manifest = {"version": "tiny-1", "model": {"file": "model.onnx", "sha256": digest}}
130    (folder / "manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest), encoding="utf-8")
131    return folder

Save it, fingerprint it, and write a minimal manifest naming its version, file and fingerprint.

134def test_an_onnx_model_gives_one_distribution_per_face(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
135    backend = OnnxAgeBackend(tiny_model(tmp_path / "tiny"))
136    faces = [np.zeros((224, 224, 3), dtype=np.uint8), np.full((224, 224, 3), 255, dtype=np.uint8)]
137    rows = backend.predict(faces)
138    assert backend.version == "tiny-1"
139    assert rows.shape == (2, len(AGES))
140    assert rows.sum(axis=1) == pytest.approx([1.0, 1.0], abs=1e-5)
141    assert not np.allclose(rows[0], rows[1])

An ONNX model gives one distribution per face: two faces in (all black, all white), two rows of 101 probabilities out, each adding up to 1, different from each other; and the version is the manifest's.

Real world — what this step measured

All 20 tests pass.

Speed. The full face pipeline (decode, detect, check, align, estimate) was timed 20 times on this laptop's CPU (Intel i9-14900HX), using the 512 × 512 test portrait:

  • 3 frames: median 38 ms;
  • 8 frames: median 103 ms (slowest run 113 ms).

That is far inside the 1.5-second budget (NFR-05). The stand-in age model costs almost nothing, so Phase 2 re-measures with the real model.

Typing. The strict type checker found three places where OpenCV's own type descriptions were less precise than our code needed. Each was fixed with an explicit conversion, not by switching the checks off.

5.1.2 The API core — rules, memory and keys

The API is the system's brain. Websites talk to it, the verify page talks to it, and it is the only part that decides anything. This step builds everything the brain needs except its front doors: the rules, the database, the short-term memory, the signing keys, and the connection to the AI.

The code is organised in four layers — explained with the package's __init__.py in §5.0.2 — and this step builds the bottom two:

http/       problems · limits · deps · rp · flow · wellknown · health     §5.1.3
app/        verification — the steps of a check                           §5.1.3
adapters/   db · tables · migrations · store · signing · inference        this section
domain/     ids · keys · policy · decision · sessions                     this section

Each layer may only use the layers below it. The domain, at the bottom, uses nothing at all — no database, no network, no clock — which is why its rules can be tested exhaustively in seconds.

Settings and logs

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/settings.py47 lines · 100% explained

The API's settings: every value that may differ between a laptop, the test suite and production — addresses, secrets, time limits — in one checked place. It follows the same pattern as the inference service's settings.py (§5.1.1), with two additions: a secret that must never leak into logs, and a guard that refuses unsafe values in production.

Explain like I'm six — the settings card

Imagine a robot that works in many different houses. Instead of rebuilding the robot for each house, you hand it a small card: "the kitchen is through the blue door, the spare key is under the mat". The robot stays the same; only the card changes. Environment variables are that card, and this file reads it.

1"""Settings for the API service, read from environment variables that start with DWARPAL_."""

The docstring names the prefix: every setting is read from an environment variable whose name starts with DWARPAL_.

It is needed because an environment variable holds text, while the master key is 32 raw bytes, some of which aren't printable characters at all.

  • model_validator — marks a function that checks the whole settings object, after every field has been filled in.

It is readable on purpose. Anyone who meets it — in a log, in a bug report — can see at once that it is the development key, published in this repository, and therefore protects nothing.

database_url — the address of PostgreSQL, written as a URL:

  • 127.0.0.1 — the special address that always means "this same computer", also called localhost;
  • 5432 — PostgreSQL's standard port;

33    # Liveness challenges one device, and one network address, may take per project in an hour. A device is the random
34    # ID the verify page keeps; the address budget is larger, because many people can share one network.

The comment explains the two per-device budgets below: how many liveness challenges one device, and one network address, may take per project in an hour. A device is the random ID the verify page keeps (apps/web/lib/device.ts); many people can share one network, so its budget is larger.

35    device_challenges_per_hour: int = 30

38    @model_validator(mode="after")

The production guard. @model_validator(mode="after") makes Pydantic call this method after all the fields are filled in. It receives the finished settings object as self, and must either return it or raise an error. If it raises, the API refuses to start.

40        if self.environment != "production":

Outside production there is nothing more to check, so the settings are returned unchanged.

Refuse the development key in production. It is published in this repository, so with it anyone could unseal the signing keys and forge age tokens. The error names the exact variable to set.

44        for name in ("issuer", "verify_url"):

46                raise ValueError(f"DWARPAL_{name.upper()} must be an https:// address in production")

Refuse plain http:// addresses in production. Over http://, tokens and links travel unencrypted, and anyone on the network path could read or change them (§0.9).

All checks passed: return the settings.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/logs.py23 lines · 100% explained

Logs are a program's diary: short lines written as it works, such as "request received, answered 201 in 12 ms". When something goes wrong at 3 a.m., the logs are how people find out what happened.

This file decides what one diary line looks like. Every line is one JSON object (§0.11). Here is a real one, wrapped onto two lines to fit the page:

{"time": "2026-10-16T05:12:43.607+00:00", "level": "info", "logger": "dwarpal.api", "message": "request",
 "request_id": "req_0123456789abcdef", "method": "POST", "path": "/v1/verification-sessions", "status": 201, "duration_ms": 12.5}

Plain sentences are easy for people to read but hard for machines to search. JSON lines are still readable, and a log tool can answer questions such as "show every request slower than 500 ms" instantly. This style is called structured logging.

What is never logged

Request bodies, headers, query strings, API keys, client secrets and pictures. A log line names which request it is about — never what was sent. A test in test_api.py checks that neither the API key nor the client secret ever appears in the logs.

1"""Log lines as JSON — one object per line — so machines can search them and people can still read them."""

The docstring: one JSON object per line, for machines and people alike.

2
3from __future__ import annotations

The project-wide type-hint setting.

4
5import json
6import logging
7from datetime import UTC, datetime

Three modules from Python's standard library:

  • json — turns Python values into JSON text;
  • logging — Python's built-in logging system. Code calls logger.info(...), and the system routes the line to handlers (where it goes: the screen, a file) that use formatters (what it looks like);
  • datetime and UTC — dates and times, in Coordinated Universal Time. Logs from servers in different countries can only be compared if they use one clock.
8
9FIELDS = ("request_id", "method", "path", "status", "duration_ms")

FIELDS — the extra details a log line may carry: which request (request_id), what kind (method, path), how it ended (status), and how long it took (duration_ms). Only these names are copied into the output, so a careless extra={...} elsewhere can't leak anything else.

10
11
12class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):

JsonFormatter — our own formatter. It inherits from logging.Formatter: it is a Formatter in every way, except for the one method it replaces.

13    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:

format is the method the logging system calls for every line. It receives a LogRecord — everything known about one log event — and must return the text to write.

14        entry: dict[str, object] = {
15            "time": datetime.fromtimestamp(record.created, UTC).isoformat(timespec="milliseconds"),
16            "level": record.levelname.lower(),
17            "logger": record.name,
18            "message": record.getMessage(),
19        }

The four fields every line has:

  • time — when it happened. record.created is a plain number (seconds since 1 January 1970); fromtimestamp(..., UTC) turns it into a date and time in UTC, and .isoformat(timespec="milliseconds") writes it in the standard ISO 8601 form, to the thousandth of a second;
  • level — how serious: debug, info, warning, error or critical, in lowercase;
  • logger — which part of the program wrote it, such as dwarpal.api;
  • message — the text itself. getMessage() fills in any placeholders, so "unexpected %s" becomes "unexpected ValueError".

The annotation dict[str, object] tells the type checker that values of different types will be stored.

20        entry.update({name: getattr(record, name) for name in FIELDS if hasattr(record, name)})

Copy in the extra details this record carries. hasattr(record, name) asks "does the record have this detail?", and getattr reads it. The braces build a dict comprehension: a dict built from a loop, in one expression.

21        if record.exc_info:
22            entry["error"] = self.formatException(record.exc_info)

If the line describes a crash, record.exc_info holds the error. formatException turns it into the usual traceback — the list of function calls that led to the error — which is what a developer needs to find the bug. A traceback shows lines of code, not the data that was being processed.

23        return json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False)

Turn the dict into one line of JSON. ensure_ascii=False keeps characters such as — or é readable, instead of escape codes like —.

services/api/logging.json15 lines · 100% explained

The API's logging configuration: which log lines are kept, what they look like, and where they go. Uvicorn, the server program (§4.8), reads it at start-up:

uvicorn dwarpal_api.main:create_app --factory --port 8000 --log-config services/api/logging.json

Why a separate file instead of code? Where logs go is a decision for whoever runs the service, not for the code itself. In production the lines go to the screen of the container, and the platform collects them from there. The tests don't load this file at all, so they stay quiet.

The format is Python's standard dictConfig schema: a nested dict, written here as JSON.

1{

The opening brace of the JSON object.

2  "version": 1,

"version": 1 — the schema version. It is required, and 1 is the only version that exists.

3  "disable_existing_loggers": false,

"disable_existing_loggers": false — keep loggers that were created before this configuration was loaded. The default, true, would silence them, a classic surprise.

4  "formatters": {
5    "json": { "()": "dwarpal_api.logs.JsonFormatter" }
6  },

Formatters — what a line looks like. There is one, named json. The special key "()" means "build it by calling this", followed by the full import path of our class: JsonFormatter in dwarpal_api/logs.py.

7  "handlers": {
8    "stdout": { "class": "logging.StreamHandler", "formatter": "json", "stream": "ext://sys.stdout" }
9  },

Handlers — where lines go. There is one, named stdout: Python's StreamHandler, writing with the json formatter to the program's standard output. ext://sys.stdout means "the Python object sys.stdout", the normal text output of a program.

Why standard output?

A program that writes its own log files must also rotate them, clean them up and keep the disk from filling. A program that writes to standard output leaves all that to the platform running it — Docker in our case. This is one of the "12-factor app" principles (Stage 4 §9).

10  "loggers": {

Loggers — the named sources of lines, and the rules for each.

11    "dwarpal": { "handlers": ["stdout"], "level": "INFO", "propagate": false },

dwarpal — our own code. Every logger whose name starts with dwarpal., such as dwarpal.api, belongs to this family. Lines at level INFO and above go to stdout. "propagate": false stops each line from also being passed up to the root logger, which would print it a second time.

12    "uvicorn": { "handlers": ["stdout"], "level": "INFO", "propagate": false },

uvicorn — the server's own messages, such as "Application startup complete", in the same JSON format.

13    "uvicorn.access": { "handlers": [], "level": "WARNING", "propagate": false }

uvicorn.access — the server's own access log, one line per request, is switched off: no handlers, and only warnings would pass. Our own request log (http/problems.py) replaces it. Uvicorn's version includes the visitor's network address and the full address including any query string; ours records only what is needed.

14  }
15}

The closing braces.

The domain: the rules, as pure Python

The files are walked through from the simplest to the most important: identifiers, secrets, policies and their thresholds, then the decision engine and the life of a session.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/__init__.py1 lines · 100% explained

The marker file of the domain layer — the innermost ring of the API (see the package overview in dwarpal_api/__init__.py).

1"""The domain: Dwarpal's rules as pure Python. Nothing in here touches a network, a database, a file or a clock."""

The docstring states the layer's one strict rule: the domain is pure Python. It never touches a network, a database, a file or a clock.

Why be so strict? Code that only calculates is deterministic: the same inputs always give the same answer. That makes it easy to test exhaustively, and easy to trust. For example, decide() never asks "what time is it?" — whoever calls it reads the clock and passes the time in. The one place where the domain needs randomness — creating new identifiers and secrets — uses the operating system's random generator, and the tests check the shape of the results rather than exact values.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/ids.py45 lines · 100% explained

Every session, project, attempt and token needs an identifier: a name that points at exactly one thing, for ever. This file makes them, in two forms:

  • inside the system, an identifier is a UUID — a 128-bit number, so large that two randomly made ones practically never collide;
  • outside, in the API and in links, it is written as short, safe text with a type prefix: vs_01JA8XQ2MZ5BWP7C4TGN0R9K3D for a verification session, prj_… for a project.

Explain like I'm six — library books

Every book in a library gets a sticker with a number. Two rules make the stickers useful: no two books ever share a number, and the numbers tell you roughly when each book arrived — so new books sit at the end of the shelf. The prefix is like the sticker's colour: blue for books, red for DVDs. Hand the librarian a red sticker when they asked for a book, and they notice straight away.

Why UUID version 7? The newest UUID standard (RFC 9562, 2024) defines a version whose first 48 bits are the time of creation in milliseconds, followed by random bits. That brings two advantages:

  1. identifiers sort by age, which keeps database indexes tidy — new rows always land at the "end", like books on a shelf;
  2. they still can't be guessed: the 74 random bits make it hopeless to predict someone else's session ID.

Why prefixes? The same idea used by large payment APIs: a prj_ ID pasted where a vs_ ID belongs is rejected immediately, instead of quietly looking up the wrong thing.

1"""Identifiers: time-ordered UUIDv7 values, shown to the outside world with a type prefix such as vs_ or prj_."""

The docstring: time-ordered UUIDv7 values inside, prefixed text outside.

2
3from __future__ import annotations

The project-wide type-hint setting.

4
5import os

os — here for os.urandom, which asks the operating system for cryptographically secure random bytes: unpredictable even to someone who has seen millions of earlier ones.

6import uuid

uuid — Python's built-in module for UUIDs. Python 3.14 adds a ready-made uuid.uuid7(), but this project runs on 3.13, so the six lines below build one by hand, exactly to the standard's layout.

7
8CROCKFORD = "0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ"

CROCKFORD — the 32 symbols of Crockford's Base32: the digits and the capital letters except I, L, O and U. I and L look like 1, and O looks like 0, so a person reading an ID aloud or copying it by hand can't confuse them. Leaving out U makes it much less likely that an ID accidentally spells a rude word.

The symbols are in the same order as in the computer's character table, so sorting the text sorts the IDs by time, too.

9ENCODED_LENGTH = 26

ENCODED_LENGTH = 26 — each Base32 symbol carries 5 bits, and 26 × 5 = 130 bits: just enough room for 128.

10
11
12class InvalidIdError(ValueError):
13    """The text is not a well-formed identifier of the expected kind."""

InvalidIdError — the error raised for malformed text. Writing (ValueError) makes it a special kind of Python's ValueError, so code that catches ValueError catches it too. The docstring is all it needs: an empty class body would be a syntax error, and a docstring counts as a body.

14
15
16def uuid7(unix_ms: int) -> uuid.UUID:

uuid7 — make a new UUIDv7. The caller passes in the time (unix_ms: milliseconds since 1 January 1970). The domain never reads a clock itself (see domain/__init__.py).

The 128 bits are laid out like this:

 48 bits          4 bits   12 bits   2 bits   62 bits
┌────────────────┬───────┬─────────┬────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ time (ms)      │  7    │ random  │  10    │ random               │
└────────────────┴───────┴─────────┴────────┴──────────────────────┘
                  version           variant

The lines below use bit operations, which work on a number's binary digits:

Operation Meaning Example
a << n shift left by n places (multiply by 2ⁿ) 0b1 << 3 = 0b1000
a >> n shift right by n places (divide by 2ⁿ, dropping the remainder) 0b1000 >> 3 = 0b1
a & b keep only the bits that are 1 in both — a "mask" 0b1101 & 0b0110 = 0b0100

The fourth operation is written with a vertical bar, a | b: it keeps the bits that are 1 in either number, so it combines them — 0b1000 | 0b0011 = 0b1011.

0b… writes a number in binary and 0x… in hexadecimal: 0xFFF is twelve 1-bits.

17    random_bits = int.from_bytes(os.urandom(10))

Get 10 random bytes (80 bits) and read them as one big whole number.

18    rand_a = (random_bits >> 62) & 0xFFF

rand_a — 12 of those random bits: shift the number right by 62, then keep the lowest 12 bits with the mask 0xFFF.

19    rand_b = random_bits & ((1 << 62) - 1)

rand_b — the lowest 62 random bits. (1 << 62) - 1 is sixty-two 1-bits. (6 of the 80 random bits go unused.)

20    value = ((unix_ms & ((1 << 48) - 1)) << 80) | (0x7 << 76) | (rand_a << 64) | (0b10 << 62) | rand_b

Assemble the 128 bits, each piece shifted to its place and combined with |:

  • the time, cut to 48 bits, shifted up into the top 48;
  • the version number 7, in the next 4 bits;
  • rand_a, in the next 12;
  • the variant marker 0b10, in the next 2 — it says "this UUID follows RFC 9562";
  • rand_b, in the last 62.
21    return uuid.UUID(int=value)

Wrap the number in Python's UUID type, which knows how to print itself in the usual 0192a6f0-… form and how to be stored in PostgreSQL.

22
23
24def encode(prefix: str, value: uuid.UUID) -> str:

encode — UUID to prefixed text, for example encode("vs", value).

25    number = value.int
26    chars = []

Take the UUID as one whole number, and start an empty list of symbols.

27    for _ in range(ENCODED_LENGTH):
28        chars.append(CROCKFORD[number & 31])
29        number >>= 5

Repeat 26 times: take the lowest 5 bits (number & 31; 31 is five 1-bits), look up their symbol, then shift those 5 bits away (>>= 5). It is exactly how you'd write a number in base 32: peel off the last digit, again and again.

30    return f"{prefix}_{''.join(reversed(chars))}"

The digits came out last first, so reverse them, glue them together with ''.join(...), and put the prefix and an underscore in front.

31
32
33def decode(prefix: str, text: str) -> uuid.UUID:

decode — prefixed text back to a UUID, refusing anything malformed. It is the gatekeeper for every ID that arrives from outside.

34    head, separator, body = text.partition("_")

partition("_") splits the text at the first underscore into three parts: before, the underscore itself, and after. If there is no underscore, the separator comes back empty.

35    if separator != "_" or head != prefix or len(body) != ENCODED_LENGTH:
36        raise InvalidIdError(f"expected an identifier like {prefix}_…")

Refuse the text unless it has an underscore, the expected prefix, and exactly 26 symbols after it. The message shows what a good ID looks like.

37    number = 0

Start the number at zero.

38    for char in body.upper():

Go through the symbols. .upper() means lowercase IDs are accepted too — people sometimes retype them.

39        digit = CROCKFORD.find(char)
40        if digit < 0:
41            raise InvalidIdError(f"invalid character {char!r} in identifier")

CROCKFORD.find(char) gives a symbol's position, its value from 0 to 31, or -1 if it isn't one of the 32 symbols. {char!r} shows the bad character in quotes in the error message.

42        number = number * 32 + digit

The reverse of the peeling above: multiply what we have by 32 and add the new digit — exactly how you read the decimal number 472 as ((4 × 10) + 7) × 10 + 2.

43    if number >> 128:
44        raise InvalidIdError("identifier is out of range")

26 symbols can hold 130 bits, but a UUID has only 128. If anything sits above bit 128 (number >> 128 isn't zero), the text can't be a real ID, so it is refused instead of being silently cut short.

45    return uuid.UUID(int=number)

Return the UUID.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/keys.py43 lines · 100% explained

The two kinds of secret the API hands out:

Secret Looks like Who holds it What it unlocks
API key dk_test_… or dk_live_… the website's server — never a browser creating sessions and reading their results
Client secret vs_…_secret_… the person's browser, for one session only taking part in that one verification

The API never stores either secret itself. It stores only a digest — a fingerprint made by SHA-256 (§X.5, §4.12). When a secret comes back, the API makes a fresh fingerprint and compares the two. A thief who steals the database gets fingerprints, which can't be turned back into keys.

Why plain SHA-256, and not a slow password hash?

Passwords chosen by people are guessable, so they need deliberately slow hashes such as Argon2id (the console's users get exactly that in Phase 4). These secrets are different: 32 or 24 bytes from a secure random generator. Guessing a 256-bit random value is hopeless even at a billion guesses per second for the age of the universe, so a fast hash is safe — and keeps every API call fast.

Test and live keys. Following a convention from payment APIs, every key says in its prefix whether it is a test key (dk_test_) or a live key (dk_live_). Test keys work only with test sessions, which may use the stand-in age model. The prefixes also let secret-scanning tools — such as the one on GitHub — recognise a leaked key at a glance.

1"""Secrets given to relying parties: API keys (dk_test_… / dk_live_…) and one-time client secrets for sessions."""

The docstring names both kinds of secret.

2

The project-wide type-hint setting.

4
5import hashlib
6import hmac
7import secrets
8from dataclasses import dataclass

The tools:

  • hashlib — hash functions; SHA-256 lives here;
  • hmac — here only for compare_digest, explained below;
  • secrets — Python's module for secure random values (never use random for secrets: its output can be predicted);
  • dataclass — the class-writing helper (§X.8).
9
10LOOKUP_LENGTH = 12

LOOKUP_LENGTH = 12 — how many characters of a key are stored in plain text as its lookup: a label that finds the key's row in the database quickly. The rest of the key stays secret.

11
12
13@dataclass(frozen=True)
14class NewSecret:
15    plaintext: str
16    lookup: str
17    digest: bytes

NewSecret — what generating a secret produces:

  • plaintext — the secret itself, shown to its owner once and never stored;
  • lookup — the plain-text label for finding the row;
  • digest — the SHA-256 fingerprint, which is stored.

frozen=True makes it read-only once made.

18
19
20def digest(secret: str) -> bytes:
21    return hashlib.sha256(secret.encode("utf-8")).digest()

digest — encode the text as UTF-8 bytes, run SHA-256 over them, and return the 32-byte result.

22
23
24def matches(secret: str, stored_digest: bytes) -> bool:
25    return hmac.compare_digest(digest(secret), stored_digest)

matches — does a secret that just arrived match a stored digest? It fingerprints the arrival and compares with hmac.compare_digest, which takes the same time whether the first byte differs or the last.

Explain like I'm six — the slow and the careful guard

A guard checks a password letter by letter and says "wrong!" the moment a letter is wrong. A sneaky visitor times him: a quick "wrong!" means the first letter was wrong, a slower one means the first letter was right. Letter by letter, the visitor learns the password. A careful guard always checks every letter before answering, so his answer takes the same time and gives nothing away.

That trick is called a timing attack. Comparing digests instead of the secrets themselves already blunts it, and constant-time comparison closes it completely — the standard habit for anything secret.

27
28def generate_api_key(livemode: bool) -> NewSecret:

generate_api_key — make a new key; livemode chooses between test and live.

29    body = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)

32 secure random bytes, written as URL-safe Base64: 43 characters using only A–Z, a–z, 0–9, - and _, so a key can be pasted anywhere without escaping.

30    plaintext = f"dk_{'live' if livemode else 'test'}_{body}"

Put the prefix in front: dk_live_ or dk_test_. The expression 'live' if livemode else 'test' chooses one of two values in a single line.

31    return NewSecret(plaintext=plaintext, lookup=body[:LOOKUP_LENGTH], digest=digest(plaintext))

Package it all: the full key, the first 12 characters of the random part as the lookup, and the digest of the whole key. Knowing the lookup doesn't help an attacker: the other 31 characters still hold about 186 bits of randomness.

parse_api_key — read the mode and the lookup from a key that arrived, before any database work. It returns None for anything that isn't shaped like one of our keys. tuple[bool, str] | None says: either a (mode, lookup) pair, or nothing.

35    for livemode, prefix in ((False, "dk_test_"), (True, "dk_live_")):

Try each known prefix, with the mode it stands for.

36        if text.startswith(prefix) and len(text) > len(prefix) + LOOKUP_LENGTH:
37            return livemode, text[len(prefix) : len(prefix) + LOOKUP_LENGTH]

If the text starts with this prefix and is long enough to hold more than a lookup, return the mode and the 12 lookup characters. text[a : b] is a slice: the characters from position a up to (not including) b.

38    return None

No prefix matched: not one of our keys.

41def generate_client_secret(public_session_id: str) -> NewSecret:

generate_client_secret — make the one-time secret for a session. It receives the session's public ID.

The secret is vs_…_secret_ followed by 24 random bytes (32 characters). It names its session, which helps a person debugging a problem, and binds the secret to exactly one session — the digest covers the ID too.

43    return NewSecret(plaintext=plaintext, lookup=public_session_id, digest=digest(plaintext))

Package it. For client secrets the session ID itself is the lookup: the session's row is found by its ID, and then the digest is checked.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/policy.py82 lines · 100% explained

A policy is a website's rule for one age check: how old a person must be, and how strict the check is. A UK site under the Online Safety Act needs 18+; an Australian social network needs 16+. Each policy also carries a risk budget: the largest share of under-age people the system may let through, at 95 % confidence (§1.7, ADR-0006). Every preset here uses 2 %.

The second half of the file is about the age model's manifest. A model can't simply be "used" for a policy: it must first be calibrated for it — tested on labelled photos to find the exact score thresholds that keep under-age passes within the budget (Phase 2). The manifest is the model's certificate: which versions it covers, and the thresholds it earned for each (age, risk budget) pair.

The docstring: policies, and the calibrated thresholds that go with them.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/decision.py110 lines · 100% explained

The decision engine — the most important seventy lines in the project. It receives what the inference service found, and answers one of five words: pass, fail, step up, retry or reject. Everything else in the system exists to feed it good evidence, or to act on its answer.

The rules are checked in a fixed order, and the first rule that applies gives the answer (§3.7, "The decision engine, in order"):

no analysis at all? ...................... retry or step up   "analysis_unavailable"
made by the wrong model? ................. retry or step up   "model_mismatch"
fewer than 3 usable frames? .............. retry or step up   the main problem, e.g. "too_dark"
frames disagree by more than 8 years? .... retry or step up   "inconsistent_frames"
probability missing or broken? ........... retry or step up   "analysis_incomplete"
p ≥ τ (pass threshold, raised per retry) . PASS               "age_over_threshold"
p ≤ τ_fail ............................... FAIL               "age_under_threshold"
anything else ............................ STEP UP            "age_uncertain"

"Retry or step up" means: another try while the person has attempts left; on the last attempt, a stronger check instead.

Fail closed

Pass can only come from one line — the sixth rule — and only after the five checks above it found nothing wrong. Missing data, a crashed service, a broken number: each leads to retry, step up or fail, never to pass. A system built this way is said to fail closed, like a fire door that locks when the power goes out, rather than swinging open.

The engine is pure (see domain/__init__.py): no database, no network, no clock. That is why it can be tested so thoroughly — test_domain.py includes property-based tests that throw hundreds of random probabilities at it and check that its promises always hold (§4.14).

1"""The decision engine: pure rules that turn an analysis into an outcome, checked in a fixed order.
2
3The engine can only ever answer "pass" from its last rule, and only when every earlier rule is satisfied.
4Missing, broken or doubtful evidence leads to retry, step-up or fail, never to pass (it "fails closed").
5"""

The module docstring: pure rules in a fixed order; "pass" only from the last rule; doubtful evidence never passes.

68    # A live session is decided only on full evidence: measured from the images (not the labels test mode), and with
69    # the anti-spoofing networks' verdict — a service started without their files must not quietly decide without it.
70    incomplete = live is not None and (live.evidence != "images" or live.presentation is None)
71    if live is None or live.pose is None or (livemode and incomplete):
72        return Decision(try_again, ("liveness_unavailable",))

No liveness evidence we can use → try again, with liveness_unavailable. As the comment says, a live session is decided only on full evidence. The cases:

  • the report has no liveness part at all;
  • it has no pose check (no challenge was issued, or it was lost);
  • it is a live session, but the evidence is "labels" — the test mode that trusts the frames' own labels. That mode is for tests with the stand-in age model; a real session must never be decided on it, whatever the inference service was set to;
  • it is a live session, but the anti-spoofing networks gave no verdict (presentation is empty). Their files are made locally from the pinned weights, so a service could start without them; it then still works for tests, but it can't decide a real session without its strongest layer against photos and screens. The inference service's /readyz says whether they are loaded.

incomplete gathers the last two cases; they matter only when livemode is true.

73    if not live.pose.passed:
74        return Decision(Outcome.REJECT if liveness_failures >= 1 else try_again, ("liveness_check_failed",))

The pose challenge failed — the head didn't turn as asked, or not in the right order. The first time, the person may simply have been slow: try_again. If an earlier attempt already failed it too, reject the session. Two failures in a row looks like a photo or a replayed video, not a confused person.

75    looks_presented = live.presentation is not None and live.presentation < MIN_REAL
76    if any(sign not in RECORDED_ONLY for sign in live.injection) or looks_presented:
77        return Decision(Outcome.STEP_UP, ("liveness_uncertain",))

Signs of an injected camera, or of a face presented on a screen or a photo. Injection signs — browser automation, a virtual camera, a hidden page, identical frames (see liveness.py) — count unless they are only recorded. And the anti-spoofing networks' verdict counts when it was measured and fell below MIN_REAL. Either can have innocent causes, so neither rejects: the session is stepped up to a stronger method with the reason liveness_uncertain.

78    return None

No problem found: None, and the age checks may go ahead.

79
80
81def decide(
82    policy: Policy,
83    thresholds: Thresholds,
84    analysis: FaceAnalysis | None,
85    attempt_index: int,
86    model_ok: bool,
87    liveness_failures: int = 0,
88    livemode: bool = False,
89) -> Decision:

decide — the engine itself. Its inputs:

  • policy and thresholds — what is being checked, and the model's calibrated bars;
  • analysis — the report, or None if the inference service didn't deliver one;
  • attempt_index — which attempt this is, counting from 0;
  • model_ok — whether the report came from a model this manifest covers (the caller checks with serves_model).

Two inputs added in Phase 3, both with defaults so older callers keep working:

  • liveness_failures — how many earlier attempts failed the liveness check;
  • livemode — whether this is a real session.
90    try_again = Outcome.STEP_UP if attempt_index + 1 >= policy.max_face_attempts else Outcome.RETRY

First, work out what a "not good enough" answer should be: STEP_UP if this is the person's last allowed attempt, otherwise RETRY. With 3 attempts, indexes 0 and 1 give RETRY and index 2 gives STEP_UP. Computing it once keeps the checks below short.

91    if analysis is None:
92        return Decision(try_again, ("analysis_unavailable",))

Rule 1: no analysis at all — the inference service was down, too slow, or sent something malformed.

93    if not model_ok:
94        return Decision(try_again, ("model_mismatch",))

Rule 2: the report came from a model the thresholds weren't made for. Thresholds are only valid for the exact model they were calibrated on, so no decision is taken.

95    if analysis.age is None or analysis.usable_frames < MIN_USABLE_FRAMES:
96        return Decision(try_again, (dominant_problem(analysis),))

Rule 3: no age estimate, or fewer than three usable frames. The reason is the main problem, so the person can fix it.

97    if (problem := liveness_problem(analysis, liveness_failures, try_again, livemode)) is not None:
98        return problem

Liveness (Phase 3) — after the quality check, before any use of the age. The := operator (the "walrus") stores liveness_problem's answer in problem and tests it in one line: if there is a problem, that is the decision. Checking quality first matters: a dark or blurry burst should get "move to the light", not a liveness failure that counts towards a rejection.

99    means = analysis.age.frame_means
100    if len(means) > 1 and statistics.pstdev(means) > MAX_FRAME_SPREAD_YEARS:
101        return Decision(try_again, ("inconsistent_frames",))

Rule 4: the frames disagree. pstdev is the population standard deviation: roughly, the typical distance of each value from the average. For estimates 30, 31 and 29 it is about 0.8 years; for 15, 45 and 30 it is about 12 years — too much. The len(means) > 1 check comes first because a spread needs at least two values.

102    p_over = analysis.age.p_over.get(policy.min_age)

Read p: the probability that the person is at least the policy's age, from the report's p_over dict. .get(...) returns None instead of crashing if that age is missing.

103    if p_over is None or math.isnan(p_over):
104        return Decision(try_again, ("analysis_incomplete",))

Rule 5: a missing or NaN probability. NaN — "not a number" — is a special value that floating-point maths produces for undefined results such as 0 ÷ 0.

Careful — the strangest value in computing

Every comparison with NaN is false: NaN >= 0.95 is false, and NaN < 0.95 is false. Code that says "pass unless p is below the bar" would therefore pass a NaN. This explicit check catches it, and a test in test_domain.py feeds NaN to the engine to prove it never passes.

105    tau = min(0.999, thresholds.tau_pass + attempt_index * RETRY_HARDENING)

Retry hardening. The bar for this attempt is tau_pass plus 0.02 per earlier attempt — with the stub manifest: 0.95, then 0.97, then 0.99. min(0.999, …) caps it just below certainty, because no estimate can ever be 100 % sure, so a bar of 1.0 would make passing impossible.

106    if p_over >= tau:
107        return Decision(Outcome.PASS, ("age_over_threshold",), p_over, tau)

Rule 6 — the only way to pass: p is at least the bar. The decision records p and the bar used.

108    if p_over <= thresholds.tau_fail:
109        return Decision(Outcome.FAIL, ("age_under_threshold",), p_over, tau)

Rule 7: p is at or below tau_fail — the model is confident the person is too young.

110    return Decision(Outcome.STEP_UP, ("age_uncertain",), p_over, tau)

Rule 8: anything in between is genuinely uncertain — often someone close to the age limit. The fair answer is neither yes nor no but "let's check properly": step up.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/sessions.py51 lines · 100% explained

A verification session is one person's journey through one age check, from the moment a website asks for it until it ends. This file describes that journey as a state machine: a small set of states (statuses), and the list of moves allowed between them.

                ┌──────────── retry ────────────┐
                ▼                               │
 created ──► in_progress ───────────────────────┘
    │            │  └─────── step up ──────► awaiting_step_up
    │            │                                  │
    │            └──── pass / fail / reject ──► completed ◄──── (stronger check, Phase 6)
    │
    └──── (any open state) ──► expired  or  canceled

Explain like I'm six — a board game

In a board game, you can only move along the arrows: from START to square 1, from square 1 to square 2… You can't jump from FINISH back to START. A state machine is the rulebook of arrows. If the program ever tries an illegal jump — say, reopening a finished check to try again — the rulebook stops it on the spot.

Why bother with an explicit list? Without one, a status is just a text field that any line of code could set to anything. Bugs such as "a completed session went back to in-progress, and a second attempt overwrote the first result" become possible. With the list, every move goes through one function, move, which refuses anything not on it.

1"""The life of a verification session, as a small state machine that allows only legal moves."""

The docstring: the life of a session, as a state machine that only allows legal moves.

The project-wide type-hint setting.

5from datetime import datetime
6from enum import StrEnum

datetime for expiry times, and StrEnum for the statuses (see Outcome in decision.py).

8from dwarpal_api.domain.decision import Outcome

The decision outcomes, because each outcome decides the session's next status (STATUS_AFTER below).

11class Status(StrEnum):
12    CREATED = "created"
13    IN_PROGRESS = "in_progress"
14    AWAITING_STEP_UP = "awaiting_step_up"
15    COMPLETED = "completed"
16    EXPIRED = "expired"
17    CANCELED = "canceled"

Status — the six states:

  • created — the website has created the session; nobody has opened the link yet;
  • in_progress — the person has opened the verify page and is taking the check;
  • awaiting_step_up — the face check was too close to call; a stronger method is needed;
  • completed — there is a final answer: pass, fail or reject;
  • expired — the time limit ran out first;
  • canceled — stopped on purpose (by the website, in a later phase).
18
19
20ALLOWED: dict[Status, frozenset[Status]] = {

ALLOWED — the rulebook: for each status, the set of statuses it may move to. A frozenset is a set that can never be changed, so the rulebook can't be edited while the program runs.

21    Status.CREATED: frozenset({Status.IN_PROGRESS, Status.EXPIRED, Status.CANCELED}),

From created: the person starts, or the session expires or is canceled.

22    Status.IN_PROGRESS: frozenset(
23        {Status.IN_PROGRESS, Status.AWAITING_STEP_UP, Status.COMPLETED, Status.EXPIRED, Status.CANCELED}
24    ),

From in_progress: stay in progress (a retry), wait for a step-up, complete, expire or be canceled. "Stay" is listed explicitly, because a retry is a move — just to the same square.

25    Status.AWAITING_STEP_UP: frozenset({Status.COMPLETED, Status.EXPIRED, Status.CANCELED}),

From awaiting_step_up: complete (after the stronger check, Phase 6), expire, or be canceled.

26    Status.COMPLETED: frozenset(),
27    Status.EXPIRED: frozenset(),
28    Status.CANCELED: frozenset(),
29}

The three final states allow no moves at all — an empty set. A finished check stays finished for ever. The closing brace ends the rulebook.

30OPEN = frozenset({Status.CREATED, Status.IN_PROGRESS, Status.AWAITING_STEP_UP})

OPEN — the statuses in which a session is still alive, and can therefore still expire.

31STATUS_AFTER: dict[Outcome, Status] = {
32    Outcome.PASS: Status.COMPLETED,
33    Outcome.FAIL: Status.COMPLETED,
34    Outcome.REJECT: Status.COMPLETED,
35    Outcome.STEP_UP: Status.AWAITING_STEP_UP,
36    Outcome.RETRY: Status.IN_PROGRESS,
37}

STATUS_AFTER — where a face attempt's outcome sends the session:

  • pass, fail or reject → completed;
  • step up → awaiting_step_up;
  • retry → stays in_progress.

Writing it as a table, rather than a chain of if statements, puts the whole policy in one place where it can be read at a glance — and the test of move covers every row.

39
40class IllegalTransitionError(ValueError):
41    """A move the state machine does not allow, such as reopening a completed session."""

IllegalTransitionError — the error for a forbidden move. Its docstring gives the classic example.

42
43
44def move(current: Status, target: Status) -> Status:
45    if target not in ALLOWED[current]:
46        raise IllegalTransitionError(f"a session cannot go from {current} to {target}")
47    return target

move — the only way a status changes. If target isn't in the allowed set for current, raise the error, naming both. Otherwise return target, which the caller stores. Code elsewhere always writes row.status = move(old, new), never row.status = new directly.

48
49
50def is_expired(status: Status, expires_at: datetime, now: datetime) -> bool:
51    return status in OPEN and now >= expires_at

is_expired — has this session run out of time? Only if it is still open and the current time has reached its expiry time. A completed session never expires — its answer stays valid. Note that the current time is passed in as now: the domain never reads the clock itself, so a test can ask "what if it were 10 o'clock?" without waiting until 10 o'clock.

One kind of refusal

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/errors.py11 lines · 100% explained

When the API says "no" on purpose — wrong key, unknown policy, session already finished — it raises an ApiError. The HTTP layer catches it and turns it into a tidy error response (http/problems.py, §4.13).

Python exceptions are the language's way of saying "stop, something is wrong" (§X.8). Raising one jumps straight out of the current function, and out of every function that called it, until some code catches it. That makes refusals short to write: deep inside a use case, one line — raise ApiError(404, "session_not_found", "no such verification session") — ends the whole request with the right answer.

1"""The one kind of error the API's own code raises on purpose: a refusal with a status, a stable code and a reason."""

The docstring: this is the one kind of error raised on purpose, and it always carries three things.

6class ApiError(Exception):

ApiError is a kind of Exception, Python's base class for ordinary errors.

7    def __init__(self, status: int, code: str, detail: str) -> None:

Making one takes three values:

  • status — the HTTP status code (§0.8), such as 401 (who are you?), 404 (not found), 409 (conflicts with the current state) or 422 (the request makes no sense);
  • code — a short, stable name such as invalid_api_key. Programs check the code, not the human sentence, so the sentence can be improved later without breaking anyone;
  • detail — a sentence for the human reading it.
8        super().__init__(detail)

super().__init__(detail) runs Exception's own set-up, so the error prints its sentence like any other exception.

9        self.status = status
10        self.code = code
11        self.detail = detail

Store the three values on the error object, so whoever catches it can read them.

The adapters: the database

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/adapters/__init__.py1 lines · 100% explained

The marker file of the adapters layer — the API's connections to everything outside itself.

1"""Adapters: the code that talks to the outside world — the database, Valkey, the inference service, and keys."""

The docstring lists what adapters talk to:

  • the database (PostgreSQL) — db.py and tables.py;
  • Valkey, the fast short-term memory — store.py;
  • the inference service — inference.py;
  • the keys that sign age tokens — signing.py.

An adapter is like a travel plug: the domain's rules stay the same, and the adapter fits them to one particular socket. If PostgreSQL were ever swapped for another database, only the adapters would change.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/adapters/db.py18 lines · 100% explained

The API's connection to PostgreSQL, the database that remembers everything that must survive a restart: projects, keys, sessions, attempts, signing keys (§0.12, §4.10). The file is short because SQLAlchemy does the heavy lifting; these lines choose how it behaves.

Two ideas are needed:

  • an engine owns a connection pool. Opening a new database connection is slow: the two programs must greet each other and check the password. So the engine keeps a few connections open and lends them out, like a library lending books, instead of building a new one for every request;
  • a session factory makes sessions — SQLAlchemy's word for one unit of work: a conversation with the database that ends in a single commit (save everything) or rollback (save nothing).

Careful — two kinds of 'session'

This project uses the word session for two different things. A verification session is one person's age check (VerificationSession, domain/sessions.py). A database session is a unit of work with PostgreSQL. In the code, database sessions are always called session, and verification sessions are row, session_id or VerificationSession.

1"""The database connection: an async engine (a pool of connections) and a factory for units of work."""

The docstring: an async engine (a pool of connections) and a factory for units of work.

10    """Every table class inherits from this, so all tables share one catalogue: Base.metadata."""

Base — our project's own base class for tables. Every table class inherits from it, and SQLAlchemy collects them all into one catalogue, Base.metadata. Migrations and tests use that catalogue to compare the code with the real database (§4.10).

13def make_engine(url: str) -> AsyncEngine:

make_engine — create the engine for a database URL (see settings.py).

14    return create_async_engine(url, pool_pre_ping=True, pool_size=10, max_overflow=10)

create_async_engine with three choices:

  • pool_pre_ping=True — before lending out a connection, check it still works. Databases restart and networks drop idle connections; without the check, the first request after such a hiccup would fail;
  • pool_size=10 — keep up to 10 connections open;
  • max_overflow=10 — at busy moments, open up to 10 more, temporary ones. So at most 20 connections exist at once, which protects PostgreSQL from being flooded.
15
16
17def make_sessions(engine: AsyncEngine) -> async_sessionmaker[AsyncSession]:

make_sessions — create the factory that makes database sessions. Its return type, async_sessionmaker[AsyncSession], reads "a session maker that makes AsyncSessions".

18    return async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)

expire_on_commit=False — after a commit, keep the values already loaded in Python objects. By default SQLAlchemy marks them as stale, and re-reads them from the database on next use. In async code, that hidden re-read would need an await where none is written, and fail. The use cases read a few values (such as the new status) right after committing, so this setting matters.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/adapters/tables.py95 lines · 100% explained

The database tables, described as Python classes. Each class is one table; each Mapped[...] line inside it is one column. SQLAlchemy's ORM (Object-Relational Mapper, §4.10) translates between the two worlds: code works with ordinary Python objects such as row.status, and SQLAlchemy writes the SQL.

Table One row is… Lives for
projects one website using Dwarpal, with its allowed web addresses as long as the customer
api_keys one secret key of a project (only its digest) until revoked
verification_sessions one person's age check its retention period (Phase 4)
verification_attempts one face attempt within a session: outcome, reasons and numbers with its session
signing_keys one key pair for signing age tokens (the private half sealed) rotation plus overlap
issued_tokens a record that a token was issued — never the token itself with its session

What is never stored

No table has a column that could hold a picture, a face measurement or an estimated age (ADR-0013). An attempt keeps only the outcome, short reason codes, and a few numbers — such as the probability compared with the threshold — that explain the decision.

Type hints become columns. SQLAlchemy reads each Mapped[...] hint:

  • Mapped[str] — a column that must always have a value (NOT NULL in SQL);
  • Mapped[str | None] — a column that may be empty (NULL);
  • mapped_column(...) — extra details: an exact SQL type, a length limit, an index.

77    public_jwk: Mapped[dict[str, Any]] = mapped_column(JSONB)

public_jwk — the public half, in the standard JSON format for keys (JWK). It is safe to publish, and it is published.

78    private_key_sealed: Mapped[bytes] = mapped_column(LargeBinary)

private_key_sealed — the private half, encrypted under the master key before it was stored. The database never sees it in plain form.

79    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(16))

status — active (signs new tokens), retiring (still published, so tokens it already signed can still be checked) or retired.

80    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(Timestamp)

created_at — when the key was made. Key rotation — a fresh key every 30 days (ADR-0008) — uses it to tell when a key is due for replacement.

Migrations: building the tables

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/migrations/env.py31 lines · 100% explained

Alembic is the tool that changes the database's tables, step by step, in a recorded order (§4.10). Every step is a migration: a small Python file in versions/ that says how to go up to the new layout and down again. Alembic remembers, inside the database itself, which migrations have already been applied, so running "upgrade to the latest" twice does nothing the second time.

This file, env.py, is Alembic's entry point: Alembic runs it every time a migration command runs. Its job is to connect to the right database and hand over the connection.

1"""Alembic's entry point: connect to the database and apply migrations, using the API's own settings."""

The docstring: connect, and apply the migrations, using the API's own settings.

2
3from __future__ import annotations

The project-wide type-hint setting.

4
5import asyncio

asyncio — Python's built-in engine for async code (§4.8). Our database driver is async, so we need it to run anything at all.

6
7from alembic import context

context — Alembic's handle on the current run: its settings, whether it is "online" or "offline", and the methods to configure and run migrations.

8from sqlalchemy.engine import Connection
9from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

The type of a database connection, and the function that creates an async engine (db.py).

10
11from dwarpal_api.adapters.tables import METADATA
12from dwarpal_api.settings import Settings

The catalogue of our tables (tables.py) and the API's settings. Using the same Settings as the API means migrations always go to the same database the API uses — there is no second configuration to keep in step.

13
14
15def run_migrations(connection: Connection) -> None:

run_migrations — the part that actually changes tables. It receives an open connection.

16    context.configure(connection=connection, target_metadata=METADATA, compare_type=True)

Tell Alembic which connection to use, and what the tables should look like (METADATA). compare_type=True makes Alembic's comparisons also notice a column whose type changed — say, String(16) to String(40) — not just added or removed columns. The project's drift test relies on that (see test_api.py).

17    with context.begin_transaction():
18        context.run_migrations()

Run every migration that hasn't been applied yet, inside one transaction: if any step fails, PostgreSQL undoes all of them, so the database is never left half-migrated. with makes sure the transaction is finished — committed or rolled back — whatever happens.

19
20
21async def run_online() -> None:

run_online — connect to a real database, then migrate it.

22    url = context.config.get_main_option("sqlalchemy.url") or Settings().database_url

Which database? If whoever started Alembic passed an address (the tests and cli.py do), use that; otherwise use the API's normal setting. or picks the first value that isn't empty.

23    engine = create_async_engine(url)

Create an engine for that address.

24    async with engine.connect() as connection:

Open one connection. async with closes it again at the end, even after an error.

25        await connection.run_sync(run_migrations)

Alembic's own code is synchronous (ordinary, non-async functions), but our connection is async. run_sync bridges the two: it runs run_migrations with a connection that behaves like a normal one, while SQLAlchemy keeps it async underneath.

26    await engine.dispose()

Close the engine's pool. A migration is a one-off job, so nothing should be left running.

27
28
29if context.is_offline_mode():
30    raise SystemExit("offline (SQL-script) migrations are not supported; run them against a database")

Alembic also has an offline mode that writes SQL scripts for someone to run by hand, without connecting. We refuse it with a clear message: scripts made that way can't run our checks, and every migration in this project is applied by the tools, against a real database. SystemExit ends the program with that message.

31asyncio.run(run_online())

Otherwise — the normal case — run run_online to completion. asyncio.run starts the async engine, runs the function, and shuts the engine down again.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/migrations/script.py.mako27 lines · 100% explained

The blueprint for every new migration file. When a developer runs Alembic's revision command, Alembic fills in this template and saves the result in versions/. The language is Mako: ordinary text with ${...} placeholders, each replaced by the value of the Python expression inside it.

Keeping our own blueprint means every future migration starts out matching the project's rules — type hints that pass mypy --strict, and the project's import style — without anyone having to remember them.

1"""${message}

The new file's docstring begins with ${message}: the short description the developer typed, such as "add webhooks table".

2
3Revision ID: ${up_revision}

Revision ID: — this migration's own name.

4Revises: ${down_revision | comma,n}

Revises: — the migration it comes after. | comma,n passes the value through two filters: comma (provided by Alembic) joins several parents with commas, for the rare migration that merges two branches; n switches off Mako's default text filters.

5Created: ${create_date}

Created: — when the file was generated.

6"""

The docstring ends.

7
8from __future__ import annotations

The project-wide type-hint setting.

9
10from collections.abc import Sequence

Sequence — used in the type hints below, for values that may be a list of revisions.

11
12import sqlalchemy as sa
13from alembic import op

The two imports every migration needs: SQLAlchemy (as the short name sa) for column types, and Alembic's op — the operations, such as op.create_table and op.drop_table.

14${imports if imports else ""}

Any extra imports Alembic decides the migration needs — for example, PostgreSQL-only types. if imports else "" writes nothing when there are none.

15
16revision: str = ${repr(up_revision)}
17down_revision: str | Sequence[str] | None = ${repr(down_revision)}
18branch_labels: str | Sequence[str] | None = ${repr(branch_labels)}
19depends_on: str | Sequence[str] | None = ${repr(depends_on)}

Four variables that Alembic reads to place the migration in its history. repr(...) writes each value as Python source code — a text in quotes, or None. The type hints say what each may hold:

  • revision — this migration's ID;
  • down_revision — the one before it (None for the very first);
  • branch_labels — optional names for a line of history;
  • depends_on — other migrations that must run first.
20
21
22def upgrade() -> None:
23    ${upgrades if upgrades else "pass"}

upgrade — the steps that move the database forward. Alembic can generate a first draft by comparing the tables in the code with the real database; a developer always reviews it. If there are no steps, the body is pass ("do nothing"), because a Python function can't be empty.

24
25
26def downgrade() -> None:
27    ${downgrades if downgrades else "pass"}

downgrade — the steps that move the database back, undoing upgrade.

The first migration: it creates all six tables of Phase 1 in an empty database. It describes the same tables as tables.py, but as instructions ("create this table with these columns") rather than as Python classes.

Why say it twice? tables.py describes how the tables should look now. Migrations describe how to get there, one step at a time, from any older version. When Phase 4 adds a column, tables.py simply gains a line, while a new migration says "add this column to the existing table" — and every database, from a developer's laptop to production, follows exactly the same steps. A test checks that the two descriptions agree (see test_api.py).

101        "verification_sessions",
102        "api_keys",
103        "projects",

The order matters. PostgreSQL refuses to drop a table while another table still has a foreign key pointing at it, so the tables that point (the dependents) go first: tokens, signing keys, attempts, then sessions, API keys, and projects last. (Signing keys point at nothing and nothing points at them, so their place in the list doesn't matter.) The variable's name, dependents_first, says why the list is in this order.

105    for table in dependents_first:
106        op.drop_table(table)

Drop each table in that order. Dropping a table also drops its indexes.

The adapters: Valkey, the signing keys and the AI

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/adapters/store.py68 lines · 100% explained

The API's short-term memory, kept in Valkey (§4.11). Some facts only need to exist for minutes: "this browser may work on session X for the next 15 minutes", "this challenge may be used once in the next 2 minutes". Putting them in PostgreSQL would fill the database with rows that need cleaning up. Valkey stores each value with a time to live and deletes it by itself when the time runs out.

Three kinds of entry live here:

Key Value Expires after Purpose
flow:<SHA-256 of token> the session's ID 15 minutes a flow token: the browser's permission to work on one session
challenge:<challenge ID> the challenge, as JSON 2 minutes a one-time ticket for one face attempt
challenges:<session ID> a counter 30 minutes how many challenges this session has had 
1"""Short-lived state in Valkey: flow tokens and one-time challenges. Everything stored here expires on its own."""

The docstring: short-lived state that expires on its own.
