Flow tokens are stored hashed, for the same reason as API keys: someone who could read Valkey's memory would find only fingerprints, which are useless for calling the API.

37
38    async def issue_challenge(
39        self, session_id: uuid.UUID, challenge: Challenge, ttl_s: int, budget: int, budget_ttl_s: int
40    ) -> dict[str, Any] | None:

issue_challenge — store a one-time challenge for a session's next face attempt. It receives the Challenge to store (Phase 3: the poses and colours were chosen at random by domain/challenges.py), the challenge's lifetime, a budget — the most challenges this session may ever get — and how long to remember the count. It returns the issued challenge, or None when the budget is used up.

41        counter = f"challenges:{session_id}"

The counter's key, one per session.

42        await self._client.set(counter, 0, ex=budget_ttl_s, nx=True)

Create the counter at 0, with its expiry — but only if it doesn't exist yet: nx=True is Valkey's NX option, "only if Not eXists". Later calls leave the existing counter, and its expiry, alone.

43        if await self._client.incr(counter) > budget:
44            return None

INCR adds 1 and returns the new value, as a single atomic step: even if two requests arrive at the same instant, each sees a different number. Over budget? Return None.

Why a budget?

Each challenge allows one face attempt, and each attempt makes the inference service analyse up to 16 pictures. Without a limit, one session could request thousands of challenges and keep the AI busy for everyone else. The budget allows twice the policy's attempts (see issue_challenge in app/verification.py), which leaves room for a page reload or a lost connection.

45        issued = {
46            "challenge_id": secrets.token_urlsafe(16),
47            "nonce": secrets.token_urlsafe(16),
48            **challenge.model_dump(),
49            "expires_in": ttl_s,
50        }

The issued challenge:

  • challenge_id — 16 random bytes as text: the ticket's number;
  • nonce — another random value. "Nonce" means "number used once". Nothing checks it yet; it is there so that a later phase can tie the captured frames to this exact challenge;
  • **challenge.model_dump() — the challenge's own fields (poses, colours, step_ms). model_dump() turns a Pydantic model into a plain dict, and ** copies every key and value into this one;
  • expires_in — how many seconds the browser has to use it.
51        stored = json.dumps({"session_id": str(session_id), **issued})

The stored version adds the session's ID, so a challenge can't be used with a different session. **issued copies the issued challenge's keys in.

52        await self._client.set(f"challenge:{issued['challenge_id']}", stored, ex=ttl_s)

Store it under its ID, with its expiry.

53        return issued

Return the challenge, without the session ID: the browser already knows its session. The browser needs the poses and colours to show the prompts — knowing them in advance doesn't help an attacker much, because they are random and change every attempt.

54
55    async def spend_budget(self, key: str, limit: int, window_s: int) -> bool:
56        """Count one use against a budget that starts afresh every window; False once the budget is spent."""

spend_budget — count one use against a budget that starts afresh every window, as the docstring says, and answer whether there was still room. Used for the per-device and per-address budgets (app/verification.py).

57        counter = f"budget:{_hashed(key)}"

The counter's name: budget: and a fingerprint of the key. Hashing keeps device IDs and network addresses out of Valkey's key names.

58        await self._client.set(counter, 0, ex=window_s, nx=True)

Create the counter at 0 with its expiry — but only if it doesn't exist yet (nx=True): the window starts with the first use and isn't extended by later ones.

59        return await self._client.incr(counter) <= limit

Add one and compare with the limit. incr is atomic in Valkey, so two requests arriving together can't both slip through on the same count.

60
61    async def take_challenge(self, challenge_id: str, session_id: uuid.UUID) -> Challenge | None:

take_challenge — use a challenge up. It returns the stored Challenge only if it existed, hadn't expired, and belongs to this session; otherwise None.

62        stored = await self._client.getdel(f"challenge:{challenge_id}")

GETDEL reads the value and deletes it in one atomic step. If the same challenge arrives twice at the same instant, only one request can get it — the other finds nothing. Reading first and deleting later would leave a tiny gap in which both could succeed.

63        if stored is None:
64            return None
65        issued = json.loads(stored)
66        if issued["session_id"] != str(session_id):
67            return None
68        return Challenge(poses=issued["poses"], colours=issued["colours"], step_ms=issued["step_ms"])

Accept only if something was found and its session matches. The challenge is gone either way: a wrong guess burns it. Then rebuild the Challenge from what was stored — the server's copy, which is what the frames will be checked against, whatever the browser claims.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/adapters/signing.py74 lines · 100% explained

This file makes the API's answers unforgeable. When a check ends, the website receives an age token: a short text that says "session vs_… passed the 18+ check", followed by a digital signature. Anyone can check the signature with the API's public key; only the API, holding the private key, could have made it (§4.12, Choice 9 "the wax seal").

The file has two parts:

  1. MasterKey — seals (encrypts) private keys before they go into the database, and opens them again. It uses AES-256-GCM.
  2. KeyRing — loads (or, the first time, creates) the signing key, publishes the public keys, and signs tokens with Ed25519.

Explain like I'm six — the stamp and the safe

The API owns a special rubber stamp: anything stamped with it is known to come from the API, and anyone can recognise the stamp by comparing it with a picture the API hangs in the window (the public key). The stamp itself must never be stolen, so at night it goes into a safe (sealing). The code to the safe — the master key — isn't kept in the building at all: it is handed over each morning by whoever opens up (an environment variable).

1"""Signing keys and age tokens. A private key exists in plain form only in memory; the database keeps it sealed."""

The docstring states the rule: a private key exists in plain form only in memory, never in the database.

base64 (decoding the master key from text), os (random nonces), secrets (random parts of key IDs), datetime and Any.

10
11from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

AESGCM from the cryptography library — AES in GCM mode, an AEAD cipher ("Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data"). It doesn't just hide data; it also detects any change to the sealed data, and refuses to open it if a single bit was altered.

12from joserfc import jwt

jwt from joserfc — makes and checks JWTs: JSON Web Tokens (§4.12).

13from joserfc.jwk import OKPKey

OKPKey — joserfc's class for Octet Key Pair keys: the key family that includes Ed25519.

14from sqlalchemy import select, text
15from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

SQLAlchemy's select (build a query), text (raw SQL, used for the lock below) and the async session type.

16
17from dwarpal_api.adapters.tables import SigningKey

The SigningKey table (tables.py).

18
19ALG = "Ed25519"

ALG = "Ed25519" — the signature algorithm, written with its fully-specified name from RFC 9864 (ADR-0019). The older name EdDSA names a whole family of curves; Ed25519 names exactly one, so a token's header says precisely how to check it.

20JWT_TYPE = "dwarpal-age+jwt"

JWT_TYPE = "dwarpal-age+jwt" — the token's declared type. Verifiers check it, so a token made for some other purpose can never be mistaken for an age token, even if it was signed by the same key.

21KEY_CREATION_LOCK = 7_316_001

KEY_CREATION_LOCK — a number that names a database lock, explained at line 46. Any number works, as long as nothing else in the project uses the same one. The underscores in 7_316_001 are only there for readability; Python ignores them.

22
23
24class MasterKey:

MasterKey — the safe for private keys.

25    def __init__(self, encoded: str) -> None:
26        raw = base64.b64decode(encoded, validate=True)

It is given the master key as Base64 text (from DWARPAL_MASTER_KEY) and decodes it. validate=True refuses text with characters that don't belong in Base64, instead of silently skipping them.

27        if len(raw) != 32:
28            raise ValueError("the master key must be exactly 32 bytes, base64-encoded")

AES-256 needs a key of exactly 32 bytes (256 bits). Anything else stops the API at start-up, with a message saying what is expected.

29        self._aead = AESGCM(raw)

Create the cipher object once, and keep it. The leading underscore in _aead marks it as private to this class.

30
31    def seal(self, plaintext: bytes, context: bytes) -> bytes:

seal — encrypt plaintext, bound to a context.

32        nonce = os.urandom(12)

A fresh 12-byte nonce for every seal. GCM's one absolute rule: never use the same nonce twice with the same key, or its protection collapses. 96 random bits make an accidental repeat practically impossible for the handful of keys this ever seals.

33        return nonce + self._aead.encrypt(nonce, plaintext, context)

Encrypt, and store the nonce in front of the result: the nonce isn't secret, but it is needed to open the seal. The result is the nonce (12 bytes), the encrypted key, and a 16-byte authentication tag that the library adds at the end.

The context is the associated data: not encrypted, but part of the seal. We pass the key's ID. If someone swapped two sealed keys between rows in the database, opening one under the wrong ID would fail — a sealed key only opens under the name it was sealed with.

34
35    def open(self, sealed: bytes, context: bytes) -> bytes:
36        return self._aead.decrypt(sealed[:12], sealed[12:], context)

open — the reverse: split off the first 12 bytes as the nonce, and decrypt the rest with the same context. If the data, the tag or the context was changed in any way, the library raises an error instead of returning garbage.

37
38
39class KeyRing:

KeyRing — the signing keys the API currently uses.

40    def __init__(self, master: MasterKey) -> None:
41        self._master = master
42        self._signing: OKPKey | None = None
43        self._public: list[dict[str, Any]] = []

It starts with the master key, and empty slots: no signing key yet (None), and no public keys. load fills them.

44
45    async def load(self, session: AsyncSession, now: datetime) -> None:

load — run once at start-up: make sure an active signing key exists, then load it.

46        await session.execute(text("SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(:lock)"), {"lock": KEY_CREATION_LOCK})

Take a lock first. Imagine two copies of the API starting at the same moment, on an empty database: both look, both find no active key, and both create one — now there are two "active" keys. pg_advisory_xact_lock is a PostgreSQL lock with a number for a name. The second copy waits at this line until the first copy's transaction ends; by then the key exists, and the second copy simply loads it. xact means the lock is released automatically when the transaction ends.

47        query = select(SigningKey).where(SigningKey.status.in_(("active", "retiring")))
48        rows = list((await session.scalars(query)).all())

Read every key that is active or retiring — the ones whose public halves must stay published. scalars(...).all() returns the matching rows as SigningKey objects.

49        active = next((row for row in rows if row.status == "active"), None)

Find the active one, or None (the next(..., None) pattern from decision.py).

50        if active is None:
51            active = self._create(now)
52            session.add(active)
53            rows.append(active)

No active key yet — the very first start: create one, add it to the session (so the commit will save it), and add it to the list of published keys.

54        await session.commit()

Commit: save the new key if there is one, and release the lock.

55        pem = self._master.open(active.private_key_sealed, active.kid.encode())

Open the active key's seal, using its ID as the context. The result is the private key in PEM form — a standard text format for keys that starts with -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.

56        self._signing = OKPKey.import_key(pem, parameters={"kid": active.kid})

Load it as a key object for signing, labelled with its ID.

57        self._public = [row.public_jwk for row in rows]

Remember the public halves of all published keys.

58
59    def _create(self, now: datetime) -> SigningKey:

_create — make a brand-new signing key. It is private to the class.

60        kid = f"sig_{now:%Y%m%d}_{secrets.token_hex(4)}"

Its ID, such as sig_20261016_3fa9c2e1: the creation date ({now:%Y%m%d} formats the date as year, month, day) plus 4 random bytes in hexadecimal. A person reading a token's header can tell roughly how old its key is.

61        key = OKPKey.generate_key("Ed25519", parameters={"kid": kid, "use": "sig", "alg": ALG})

Generate a fresh Ed25519 key pair, labelled with three standard JWK fields: kid (its ID), use: "sig" (for signatures only, never encryption) and alg (the one algorithm it may be used with).

62        sealed = self._master.seal(key.as_pem(private=True), kid.encode())

Seal the private half, in PEM form, with the key's ID as the context.

63        return SigningKey(
64            kid=kid, public_jwk=key.as_dict(private=False), private_key_sealed=sealed, status="active", created_at=now
65        )

Return the database row: the ID, the public half as a JSON dict (as_dict(private=False) leaves the private parts out), the sealed private half, the status active, and the creation time.

66
67    def jwks(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
68        return {"keys": self._public}

jwks — the public keys in JWKS form ("JSON Web Key Set"): {"keys": [...]}. It is published at /.well-known/jwks.json, where any website can fetch it.

69
70    def sign(self, claims: dict[str, Any]) -> str:

sign — turn a set of claims (the facts in the token) into a signed token.

71        if self._signing is None:
72            raise RuntimeError("the key ring has not been loaded")

Refuse to sign before load has run. That would be a programming mistake, so it is a RuntimeError rather than an ApiError.

73        header = {"alg": ALG, "typ": JWT_TYPE, "kid": self._signing.kid}

The token's header: the algorithm, the type, and which key signed it.

74        return jwt.encode(header, claims, self._signing, algorithms=[ALG])

Sign and encode. The result is three Base64url parts joined by dots: header.claims.signature. algorithms=[ALG] is an allow-list: joserfc refuses to use anything but Ed25519, even if a header asked for something else.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/adapters/inference.py31 lines · 100% explained

The API's client for the inference service: it sends the frames over the internal network and brings back a FaceAnalysis (§5.1.1).

The whole design fits in one sentence from the docstring: any failure becomes "no analysis". The service is down? No analysis. Too slow? No analysis. It answered with nonsense? No analysis. And the decision engine turns "no analysis" into retry or step up — never pass (decision.py, rule 1). A broken AI service can make the check annoying, but it can never make it unsafe.

1"""The API's client for the inference service. Any failure becomes "no analysis", which can never become a pass."""

The docstring and its promise.

6from pydantic import ValidationError

httpx (the HTTP client) and Pydantic's ValidationError.

The shared contracts: what the API sends (FaceRequestMeta) and what it expects back (FaceAnalysis). Both services import the same classes, so they can't disagree about the shapes.

11class InferenceClient:
12    def __init__(self, client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> None:
13        self._client = client

InferenceClient keeps an httpx.AsyncClient that it is given — already configured with the service's address and a timeout (see main.py). Tests give it a client that talks to an inference app inside the same process instead (test_api.py).

14
15    async def analyze_face(self, meta: FaceRequestMeta, frames: list[bytes]) -> FaceAnalysis | None:

analyze_face — send a burst of frames; get an analysis, or None.

16        files = {
17            f"frame_{frame.index}": (f"frame_{frame.index}.jpg", data, "image/jpeg")
18            for frame, data in zip(meta.frames, frames, strict=True)
19        }

Build the uploaded files: one entry per frame, named frame_0, frame_1, … Each value is a tuple of a file name, the bytes, and the media type image/jpeg.

zip(meta.frames, frames, strict=True) walks the two lists side by side, pairing each frame's description with its bytes. strict=True raises an error if the lists have different lengths, instead of silently dropping the extras.

20        try:
21            response = await self._client.post(
22                "/internal/v1/analyze/face", data={"meta": meta.model_dump_json()}, files=files
23            )

Send it all as one multipart request (§4.13) to the inference service's internal endpoint: the frames as files, and the description as a JSON text field called meta. The path starts with /internal/ — a reminder that only the API may call it.

24        except httpx.HTTPError:
25            return None

httpx.HTTPError covers every network failure: refused connection, timeout, broken connection. Each one becomes None.

26        if response.status_code != 200:
27            return None

Any answer other than 200 OK — such as 503 "busy, retry shortly" — also becomes None.

28        try:
29            return FaceAnalysis.model_validate_json(response.content)
30        except ValidationError:
31            return None

Parse and check the answer against the FaceAnalysis contract. A malformed answer raises ValidationError and also becomes None. Only a well-formed analysis ever reaches the decision engine.

Tests for the rules

services/api/tests/test_domain.py365 lines · 100% explained

The fast tests: everything that can be checked without a database, a network or a clock — identifiers, keys, policies, the decision engine, the state machine, the production guard and the log format. All 30 finish in about two seconds.

Two styles of test appear here:

  • example tests — "for this input, expect that output", like decide(…, analysis(0.99), …) must pass;
  • property tests — "for every input, this rule must hold". The Hypothesis library invents the inputs: a hundred different ones per test by default, deliberately including awkward ones such as 0, 1, tiny fractions and huge numbers (§4.14). If any input breaks the rule, Hypothesis shrinks it to the simplest failing example and prints it.

Explain like I'm six — testing a seesaw

An example test puts one particular child on each end and checks which side goes down. A property test says: "whoever sits on the left, if a heavier child sits on the right, the right side must go down" — and then tries hundreds of children, including a feather and an elephant, to find one that breaks the rule.

61def analysis(

72@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=2**48 - 1))
73def test_uuid7_carries_version_variant_and_time(unix_ms: int) -> None:
74    value = ids.uuid7(unix_ms)
75    assert value.version == 7
76    assert value.variant == uuid.RFC_4122
77    assert value.int >> 80 == unix_ms

Property: a UUIDv7 carries its version, variant and time. For any time that fits in 48 bits (from 0 to 2⁴⁸ − 1, the limits Hypothesis explores), the made ID must say version 7, have the standard variant, and give the exact time back from its top bits (>> 80 drops the 80 lower bits).

93@pytest.mark.parametrize("text", ["prj_01ABC", "vs_" + "U" * 26, "vs_" + "0" * 25, "vs-" + "0" * 26, "vs_" + "Z" * 26])

Malformed IDs are refused. @pytest.mark.parametrize runs the same test once per value in the list:

  • prj_01ABC — the wrong prefix, and too short;
  • 26 Us — U isn't in Crockford's alphabet;
  • 25 zeros — one symbol short;
  • vs-… — a hyphen instead of the underscore;
  • 26 Zs — every symbol at its maximum is a number bigger than 128 bits.

185@given(st.floats(0.0, 1.0), st.floats(0.0, 1.0), st.integers(0, 2))

187    low, high = sorted((p, q))

193@given(st.floats(0.0, 1.0), st.integers(1, 2))
194def test_later_attempts_never_get_an_easier_bar(p: float, attempt: int) -> None:
195    earlier = decide(POLICY, THRESHOLDS, analysis(p), attempt - 1, True)
196    later = decide(POLICY, THRESHOLDS, analysis(p), attempt, True)
197    assert earlier.tau_effective is not None
198    assert later.tau_effective is not None

200    if later.outcome == Outcome.PASS:
201        assert earlier.outcome == Outcome.PASS

Property: later attempts never get an easier bar. For any probability, the threshold on a later attempt is at least the earlier one, and anything that passes later would also have passed earlier. Retrying can only make passing harder, never easier.

Property: every pass clears the calibrated threshold. Whatever the probability and attempt, if the engine says pass, the probability it used is at least tau_pass. This is the safety promise itself, stated as a test.

212def test_the_state_machine_allows_exactly_its_listed_moves() -> None:
213    for current in Status:
214        for target in Status:
215            if target in ALLOWED[current]:
216                assert move(current, target) == target
217            else:
218                with pytest.raises(IllegalTransitionError):
219                    move(current, target)

The state machine allows exactly its listed moves. Two loops try every status against every status — all 36 pairs. Listed moves must succeed; every other move must raise IllegalTransitionError.

294def test_challenges_are_random_never_repeat_a_step_and_cover_every_order() -> None:
295    rng = random.Random(7)  # noqa: S311 - reproducible test draws; real challenges use secrets.SystemRandom
296    drawn = [new_challenge(rng) for _ in range(2000)]

Challenges are random, never repeat a step, and cover every order. 2,000 challenges from a seeded random generator — random.Random(7) gives the same "random" numbers every run, so a failure can be repeated. The noqa comment tells the linter that a predictable generator is intended here: real challenges use secrets.SystemRandom, which can't be predicted.

297    for challenge in drawn:
298        assert len(challenge.poses) in POSE_STEPS
299        assert challenge.poses.count("look_up") <= MAX_LOOK_UPS
300        assert len(challenge.colours) == COLOUR_STEPS
301        assert set(challenge.colours) <= set(PALETTE)
302        for steps in (challenge.poses, challenge.colours):
303            assert all(a != b for a, b in itertools.pairwise(steps))

Every challenge has 3 or 4 poses, at most one look-up, the right number of colours, only colours from the palette (<= between sets means "is contained in"), and no step equal to the one before — itertools.pairwise gives each pair of neighbours. A repeated step would be a weaker test: holding still would satisfy it.

304    assert len({tuple(challenge.poses) for challenge in drawn}) == 24

And all 24 possible pose orders turn up: 10 with three poses and 14 with four, once the two rules are applied. If the generator favoured some orders, an attacker could prepare for those.

5.1.3 The API's endpoints — the journey of one check

This step adds the front doors. Here is one complete check, as the API sees it:

 website's server                     API                                  verify page (browser)
 ────────────────                     ───                                  ─────────────────────
 POST /v1/verification-sessions ───►  create_session
   (API key)                          ◄─── id, link …/v/vs_…#cs=secret
 sends the person to the link ───────────────────────────────────────────► opens the link
                                      start_flow  ◄─── POST …/start (client secret)
                                      ───► flow token, project name, minimum age
                                      issue_challenge  ◄─── POST …/challenge (flow token)
                                      submit_face_attempt ◄─ POST …/face-attempts (frames)
                                        → inference service → decide → record
                                      ───► pass / fail / step up / retry
                                      finish  ◄─── POST …/finish
                                      ───► back to the shop with ?session_id=vs_…
 GET /v1/verification-sessions/vs_… ► result_view + mint_token
   (API key)                          ◄─── outcome + signed age token
 checks the token's signature with the public keys from /.well-known/jwks.json

Notice what travels through the browser: only the session's ID and a one-time secret. The answer goes straight from the API to the website's server, which must use its own key to fetch it. A person can't fake a "pass" by editing a web address.

The use cases

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/app/__init__.py1 lines · 100% explained

The marker file of the use-case layer (app is short for application).

1"""Use cases: the steps of a verification, written once and called by the HTTP layer."""

The docstring: each step of a verification — create, start, challenge, attempt, finish — is written once here, as an ordinary function. The HTTP layer calls these functions. If one day the same steps had to be offered another way (a command-line tool, a message queue), the new front would call the very same functions, so the rules could never drift apart between the two.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/app/verification.py321 lines · 100% explained

The use cases: each step of a verification, written once as an ordinary function. This is where the pieces meet — the domain's rules, the database, Valkey, the inference service and the signing keys.

Here is the whole journey of one check, with the function that handles each step:

website's server ── create_session ──► session "created"; returns a link to the verify page
      ⋮  (the person opens the link)
verify page ─────── start_flow ──────► "in_progress"; returns a flow token
verify page ─────── issue_challenge ─► a one-time challenge
verify page ─────── submit_face_attempt ► decision: retry (go round again) · step up · pass · fail
verify page ─────── finish ──────────► the address to send the person back to
      ⋮  (the person returns to the website)
website's server ── result_view ─────► the outcome, plus a signed age token (mint_token)

Every function follows the same pattern: check (refuse anything wrong with an ApiError), act (inside a database transaction), answer (a plain dict that the HTTP layer sends as JSON).

1"""The use cases of a verification: create, start, challenge, attempt, finish — and the result a website reads."""

The docstring lists the steps.

Passing one "toolbox" in, instead of having each function create its own connections, is called dependency injection. Tests build a toolbox around test containers, and the use cases never know the difference.

50    parts = urlsplit(url)
51    return f"{parts.scheme}://{parts.netloc}"

origin_of — the origin of an address: its scheme, host and port, such as https://shop.example or http://localhost:3100. Browsers use exactly this unit to decide what counts as "the same website" (§4.13). urlsplit cuts the address into parts; netloc is the host with its port.

58async def load_session(session: AsyncSession, session_id: uuid.UUID, *, lock: bool = False) -> VerificationSession:

load_session — fetch a session's row by ID. The * in the parameter list makes everything after it keyword-only: callers must write lock=True, never just True, so a reader always knows what the True means.

59    query = select(VerificationSession).where(VerificationSession.id == session_id)

Build the query: SELECT … FROM verification_sessions WHERE id = ….

60    row = await session.scalar(query.with_for_update() if lock else query)

Run it. With lock=True, .with_for_update() adds FOR UPDATE: PostgreSQL locks the row until this transaction ends, and any other transaction that wants to change the same row waits its turn (§4.10). That is how two simultaneous attempts on one session are processed one after the other, never interleaved.

61    if row is None:
62        raise ApiError(404, "session_not_found", "no such verification session")

Not found? Refuse with 404. Otherwise return the row.

69    except ids.InvalidIdError:
70        raise ApiError(404, "session_not_found", "no such verification session") from None

parse_session_id — turn vs_… text into a UUID. A malformed ID gets exactly the same 404 as an ID that doesn't exist, so a stranger poking at the API learns nothing from the difference.

73def expire_if_due(row: VerificationSession, now: datetime) -> None:
74    if is_expired(Status(row.status), row.expires_at, now):
75        row.status = move(Status(row.status), Status.EXPIRED)

expire_if_due — if the session is open and past its expiry time, move it to expired. This is lazy expiry: nothing watches the clock in the background; a session's status is corrected the next time anyone looks at it. Every use case calls this before trusting a status.

80) -> tuple[VerificationSession, str]:

It receives the toolbox, the caller's project, the key's mode (live or test), the policy's name, and two optional values: where to send the person afterwards, and the website's own reference. It returns the new row and the client secret in plain form — the only moment it exists.

Find the policy, and make sure the model has thresholds for it. Each failure becomes a 422 with its own code. {policy_id!r} puts the requested name in quotes in the message.

Live sessions need a calibrated model. While the age model is only a stand-in, a live key is refused with 409 — the system must never make real decisions about real people with placeholder thresholds. Test keys keep working.

90    if return_url is not None and origin_of(return_url) not in project.allowed_origins:

The return address must belong to the project. If it didn't, someone with a stolen API key could send people to a look-alike site after the check. This kind of hole is called an open redirect.

92    now, session_id = svc.now(), svc.new_id()

Read the clock once and make the session's ID. Two names can be set in one line: a, b = x, y.

108        completed_at=None,

Build the row: every column of verification_sessions with its starting value. It starts created, with no outcome, no attempts and no model yet. It expires session_ttl_s seconds (30 minutes) from now. Only the secret's digest is stored.

Open a database session, add the row, and commit. async with closes the database session afterwards, even if an error happens.

117    async with svc.sessions() as session:

Check the secret first, before revealing anything. Without the right secret, the caller learns nothing — not even whether the session is finished.

121        expire_if_due(row, svc.now())

Correct the status if the session has expired.

122        if row.status == Status.CREATED:
123            row.status = move(Status.CREATED, Status.IN_PROGRESS)

A fresh session moves from created to in_progress. For any other status, nothing changes.

124        project = await session.get(Project, row.project_id)

Load the session's project, for its display name.

125        await session.commit()

Commit: save the status change and release the lock.

126    if row.status not in FLOW_STATUSES or project is None:

Only the statuses in FLOW_STATUSES may have a flow. An expired or canceled session gets 409, with its status in the message.

128    policy = get_policy(row.policy_id)

Open a flow token in Valkey, valid for 15 minutes. From now on, the page proves who it is with this token rather than the secret.

130    view = {

132        "status": row.status,
133        "outcome": row.outcome,
134        "project_name": project.name,
135        "min_age": policy.min_age,
136        "attempts_remaining": max(policy.max_face_attempts - row.attempts_count, 0),
137    }

The page's view of the session — exactly what the verify page needs to draw itself, and nothing more:

  • its ID, status and outcome (if any);
  • the project's name, for "Amber Cellars asks you to confirm you are 18 or over";
  • the minimum age;
  • the attempts left — max(..., 0) makes sure it never shows a negative number.

145        row = await load_session(session, session_id)

159async def spend_device_budgets(svc: Services, project_id: uuid.UUID, device: str | None, address: str | None) -> None:

spend_device_budgets — the per-device budgets.

160    """Stop endless trial and error across sessions: each device, and each network address, may take only so many
161    challenges an hour. Starting a new session doesn't reset these, unlike the per-session budget."""

The docstring gives the reason: stop endless trial and error. Someone testing photo after photo against the check could otherwise start session after session; these budgets count across all of a project's sessions.

162    settings = svc.settings
163    budgets = [
164        (f"device:{project_id}:{device}", settings.device_challenges_per_hour) if device else None,
165        (f"address:{project_id}:{address}", settings.address_challenges_per_hour) if address else None,
166    ]

The two budgets as (key, limit) pairs: one for the device ID and one for the network address, each scoped to the project. A missing ID or address gives None instead of a pair.

167    for key, limit in filter(None, budgets):
168        if not await svc.store.spend_budget(key, limit, HOUR_S):
169            raise ApiError(429, "too_many_attempts", "too many age checks from this device; try again later")

Spend one use from each budget that exists (filter(None, …) skips the Nones). If either is spent, refuse with 429 too_many_attempts; the verify page then tells the person to wait a while.

172def attempt_scores(analysis: FaceAnalysis | None, decision: Decision) -> dict[str, Any]:

attempt_scores — the numbers kept with each attempt, so any decision can be explained later. It is a plain function: no database, no waiting.

173    if analysis is None:
174        return {"analysis": "unavailable"}

No analysis at all? Record just that.

175    problems = sorted({flag for frame in analysis.frames for flag in frame.flags})

Every quality problem that occurred in any frame. The braces build a set, which drops duplicates; sorted turns it into a list in alphabetical order, so the stored value is always the same for the same problems.

176    return {
177        "model": analysis.model_version,
178        "frames": len(analysis.frames),
179        "usable_frames": analysis.usable_frames,
180        "problems": problems,
181        "p_over": decision.p_over,
182        "tau": decision.tau_effective,
183        "analysis_ms": round(analysis.duration_ms, 1),
184        # Which liveness check fired is kept here, for the people who run Dwarpal, and never shown to the user.
185        "liveness": analysis.liveness.model_dump() if analysis.liveness else None,
186    }

The scores: the model's version, how many frames were sent and how many were usable, the problems, the probability and the threshold used, and how long the analysis took (rounded to a tenth of a millisecond). No picture, and no age.

Phase 3 adds liveness: the full liveness result — which pose problems were found, the light measurements, any injection signs — turned into a plain dict by model_dump(). As the comment says, this is where the detail lives. The person sees only the vague reason; the operator can read here which check fired, and the liveness-report command (cli.py) summarises it.

189async def submit_face_attempt(
190    svc: Services, session_id: uuid.UUID, challenge_id: str, meta: FaceRequestMeta, frames: list[bytes]
191) -> tuple[Decision, int]:

submit_face_attempt — step 4, the heart of the check. It receives the session (from the flow token), the challenge's ID, the frames' description and the frames themselves. It returns the decision and the number of attempts left.

The function uses two separate transactions, with the AI call in between:

transaction 1: quick look — is the session in progress?
               use up the challenge (Valkey)
               ask the inference service (≈ 0.1 s, no database held)
transaction 2: lock the row — check again — decide — record — commit

Holding a database connection and a row lock while the AI works would make every other request for the same session wait, and could exhaust the connection pool under load.

192    async with svc.sessions() as session:
193        if (await load_session(session, session_id)).status != Status.IN_PROGRESS:
194            raise ApiError(409, "session_not_in_progress", "this session is not accepting attempts")

A quick look first, without a lock: if the session isn't accepting attempts, stop right away — before using up a challenge or the AI's time.

195    challenge = await svc.store.take_challenge(challenge_id, session_id)
196    if challenge is None:
197        raise ApiError(409, "challenge_invalid", "the challenge is unknown, expired or already used")

Use up the challenge. Unknown, expired, already used, or belonging to another session: 409. On success challenge is the server's stored copy.

198    # The frames are judged against what the server asked for, never against what the browser says it was asked.
199    analysis = await svc.inference.analyze_face(meta.model_copy(update={"challenge": challenge}), frames)

Ask the inference service. Before sending, model_copy(update=…) makes a copy of the request description with its challenge replaced by the stored one (Phase 3). Whatever challenge the browser put there — perhaps an easier one — is thrown away, as the comment says. The result may be None, which the decision engine treats safely.

200    async with svc.sessions() as session:
201        row = await load_session(session, session_id, lock=True)

Now the second transaction: load the row again, this time locked.

202        now = svc.now()
203        expire_if_due(row, now)
204        if row.status != Status.IN_PROGRESS:
205            await session.commit()
206            raise ApiError(409, "session_not_in_progress", f"this session is {row.status}")

Check again. While the AI was working, the session may have expired, or a simultaneous attempt may have finished it. If it is no longer in progress, commit (to save an expiry) and refuse.

207        policy = get_policy(row.policy_id)
208        model_ok = analysis is not None and svc.manifest.serves_model(analysis.model_version)
209        failures = await session.scalar(
210            select(func.count())
211            .select_from(VerificationAttempt)
212            .where(
213                VerificationAttempt.session_id == row.id,
214                VerificationAttempt.reasons.contains(["liveness_check_failed"]),
215            )
216        )
217        decision = decide(
218            policy,
219            svc.manifest.thresholds_for(policy),
220            analysis,
221            row.attempts_count,
222            model_ok,
223            liveness_failures=failures or 0,
224            livemode=row.livemode,
225        )

Decide. model_ok is true only if an analysis exists and came from a model the manifest covers. row.attempts_count is the index of this attempt: 0 for the first.

Phase 3 adds two inputs:

  • failures — how many of this session's earlier attempts failed the liveness check. The query counts the attempt rows whose reasons list contains liveness_check_failed (.contains([…]) becomes PostgreSQL's array operator @>). or 0 turns a missing answer into 0.
  • livemode=row.livemode — so the engine can refuse the test-only liveness evidence in a real session.
226        session.add(
227            VerificationAttempt(
228                id=svc.new_id(),
229                session_id=row.id,
230                kind="face",
231                outcome=decision.outcome,
232                reasons=list(decision.reasons),
233                scores=attempt_scores(analysis, decision),
234                created_at=now,
235            )
236        )

Record the attempt: a new row with its ID, its session, the kind (face), the outcome, the reasons (as a list, because the column is an array) and the scores.

237        row.attempts_count += 1
238        row.status = move(Status(row.status), STATUS_AFTER[decision.outcome])

Count the attempt, and move the session to the status the outcome requires (STATUS_AFTER). move refuses any illegal jump.

239        if decision.outcome != Outcome.RETRY:
240            row.outcome = decision.outcome

Store the outcome on the session — except for a retry, which isn't an outcome of the session, only of this attempt.

241        if analysis is not None:
242            row.model_version = analysis.model_version

Remember which model produced the analysis.

243        if row.status == Status.COMPLETED:
244            row.completed_at = now

If the session is now finished, record when.

245        remaining = policy.max_face_attempts - row.attempts_count

How many attempts are left. The HTTP layer never shows a negative number.

246        await session.commit()
247    return decision, remaining

Commit everything at once — the attempt, the new status, the outcome — and return.

250async def finish(svc: Services, session_id: uuid.UUID) -> str | None:

finish — step 5: where should the page send the person now?

251    async with svc.sessions() as session:
252        row = await load_session(session, session_id)

Load the session.

253    if row.status not in (Status.COMPLETED, Status.AWAITING_STEP_UP):
254        raise ApiError(409, "session_not_finished", f"this session is {row.status}")

Only a finished session (completed, or waiting for a step-up) can be left.

255    if row.return_url is None:

No return address? Return None; the page then simply shows the result.

Add session_id=vs_… to the return address, so the website knows which check just ended. If the address already has a query (?…), the new value joins it with & instead. urlencode makes sure the value is written safely. Only the session's ID travels through the browser — never the outcome, which the website must fetch itself, using its key.

261def created_view(svc: Services, row: VerificationSession, client_secret: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
262    return {
263        "id": public_id(row),
264        "object": "verification_session",
265        "status": row.status,
266        "livemode": row.livemode,
267        "policy": row.policy_id,
268        "client_secret": client_secret,
269        "url": f"{svc.settings.verify_url}/v/{public_id(row)}#cs={client_secret}",
270        "expires_at": row.expires_at.isoformat(),
271    }

created_view — what the website receives after creating a session: the ID, an object label (a convention that tells programs what kind of thing a JSON object is), the status, mode and policy, the client secret, the expiry time in standard ISO 8601 form, and the link for the person:

http://localhost:3000/v/vs_01JA8XQ2…#cs=vs_01JA8XQ2…_secret_…

The secret sits after the #, in the link's fragment. Browsers never send the fragment to any server — not to the verify page's server, and not in the Referer header to other sites. Only the page's own code, running in the browser, can read it.

result_view — step 6: the website's server asks for the result, with its API key.

275    async with svc.sessions() as session:
276        row = await load_session(session, parse_session_id(session_text))

Load the session.

277        if row.project_id != project_id or row.livemode != livemode:
278            raise ApiError(404, "session_not_found", "no such verification session")

Only the project that created a session may read it, and only with a key of the same mode. A test key can't read live sessions, and one customer can never read another's. Anything else gets the same 404 as a session that doesn't exist.

279        now = svc.now()

Correct the status if the session has expired.

281        token = mint_token(svc, session, row, now) if row.status == Status.COMPLETED else None

A completed session gets a freshly signed token. Others get none.

Commit: save any expiry, and the record of the token just issued.

The result: the session's facts, including the policy's minimum age, the number of attempts, the website's own reference, three times in ISO 8601 form (completed_at only once there is one), and the token.

299
300def mint_token(svc: Services, session: AsyncSession, row: VerificationSession, now: datetime) -> str:

mint_token — make the signed age token for a completed session.

301    policy = get_policy(row.policy_id)
302    jti, audience = svc.new_id(), ids.encode("prj", row.project_id)
303    expires = now + timedelta(seconds=policy.token_ttl_s)

Look up the policy, make a new ID for the token (jti), write the project's public ID as the audience, and work out when the token expires: 10 minutes from now.

304    session.add(IssuedToken(jti=jti, session_id=row.id, audience=audience, issued_at=now, expires_at=expires))

Record that this token was issued — its facts, not the token itself.

305    claims = {
306        "iss": svc.settings.issuer,
307        "aud": audience,
308        "iat": int(now.timestamp()),
309        "nbf": int(now.timestamp()),
310        "exp": int(expires.timestamp()),
311        "jti": str(jti),
312        "sid": public_id(row),
313        "outcome": row.outcome,
314        f"age_over_{policy.min_age}": row.outcome == Outcome.PASS,
315        "assurance": "basic",
316        "methods": ["face_estimation"],
317        "policy": row.policy_id,
318        "model": row.model_version,
319        "livemode": row.livemode,
320    }

The claims — the facts inside the token. Most names are standard JWT claims (RFC 7519):

Claim Meaning
iss the issuer: this API
aud the audience: the one project this token is for
iat, nbf, exp issued at, not valid before, expires at — whole seconds since 1970
jti the token's own unique ID
sid the session it reports on
outcome pass, fail or reject
age_over_18 true or false: the answer itself, named after the policy's age (ADR-0020)
assurance how strong the check was: basic for face estimation alone
methods which methods were used
policy, model which policy and which model version decided
livemode whether this was a live check

Line 274 builds the age claim's name from the policy: f"age_over_{policy.min_age}" gives age_over_18 for an 18+ policy and age_over_16 for a 16+ one. Its value is True only for a pass. A website checking for 18+ looks for age_over_18: true — so a token from a 13+ check simply doesn't contain the claim it needs, and can't be misused.

What is never in a token

No estimated age, no picture, no name, and nothing that could identify the person across websites. The token answers one yes-or-no question, for one website, for ten minutes.

321    return svc.keyring.sign(claims)

Sign the claims with the active key, and return the token.

The HTTP layer

The shared machinery first — errors, size limits, credentials — then the endpoints.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/http/__init__.py1 lines · 100% explained

The marker file of the HTTP layer — the outermost ring, the only part of the API that knows about web requests.

1"""The HTTP layer: it only translates between web requests and the use cases, and holds no business rules."""

The docstring states the layer's discipline: it only translates. A request arrives, its data is checked and handed to a use case, and the use case's result is turned into a response. No business rule — such as "a session may only be attempted three times" — lives here. Each rule lives in the domain or the use cases, so it can't be skipped by calling the system some other way.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/http/problems.py92 lines · 100% explained

Two jobs that every request shares:

  1. Errors in one shape. However a request fails — a wrong key, a malformed field, a bug — the answer has the same JSON shape, the standard problem details format of RFC 9457 (§4.13). Programs calling the API need to learn only one way of reading errors:

    json {"type": "/errors/invalid_api_key", "title": "invalid api key", "status": 401, "detail": "this API key is unknown or revoked", "code": "invalid_api_key", "request_id": "req_3f9a1c0be27d4e51"}

  2. A request ID and a log line for every request. Each request gets an ID, which is sent back in the X-Request-Id header, printed in every error, and written in the log. When a customer reports "it failed at 10:42", the ID leads straight to the right log line.

1"""Every error leaves the API in one shape, RFC 9457 "problem details", tagged with the request's ID."""

The docstring: one error shape, tagged with the request's ID.

Our own error class.

19SAFE_REQUEST_ID = re.compile(r"^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{8,64}$")

SAFE_REQUEST_ID — a regular expression: a pattern that text must match. It allows 8 to 64 characters, each a letter, a digit, a dot, an underscore or a hyphen. ^ and $ mean the whole text must match, not just a part of it.

A caller may send its own request ID — handy when a website wants to follow one request through its own logs and ours. But that ID ends up in our logs and headers, so it must be harmless: no spaces, no line breaks that could fake extra log lines, nothing long.

20logger = logging.getLogger("dwarpal.api")

logger — this module's logger, named dwarpal.api (see logs.py and logging.json).

23def problem(request: Request, status: int, code: str, detail: str) -> JSONResponse:

problem — build one problem-details response.

24    body = {
25        "type": f"/errors/{code}",
26        "title": code.replace("_", " "),
27        "status": status,
28        "detail": detail,
29        "code": code,
30        "request_id": request.state.request_id,
31    }

The body:

  • type — a reference that identifies the kind of problem, such as /errors/invalid_api_key. RFC 9457 asks for a URI here; a path with no host means "on this API's own address". Phase 5's documentation site can explain each code at exactly that path;
  • title — a short human name, made from the code: invalid_api_key becomes invalid api key;
  • status — the HTTP status code, repeated in the body for convenience;
  • detail — the sentence explaining this occurrence;
  • code — our stable code, which programs check (an extension member: the standard allows extra fields);
  • request_id — this request's ID.
32    return JSONResponse(body, status_code=status, media_type="application/problem+json")

Send it with the status code and the media type application/problem+json, which tells the caller "this is a problem-details document".

35async def on_unexpected(request: Request, error: Exception) -> Response:

on_unexpected — the last line of defence: any error nobody planned for — a bug, a database that vanished mid-request.

36    logger.error("unexpected %s", type(error).__name__, exc_info=error, extra={"request_id": request.state.request_id})

Log it at error level, with the error's class name, its full traceback (exc_info=error, for the developers), and the request ID.

37    return problem(request, 500, "internal_error", "something went wrong on our side; please try again")

Answer 500, with a polite, vague sentence. The real cause stays in the log: an error message shown to strangers must never reveal internal details, which could help an attacker.

40async def on_api_error(request: Request, error: Exception) -> Response:
41    if not isinstance(error, ApiError):
42        return await on_unexpected(request, error)
43    return problem(request, error.status, error.code, error.detail)

on_api_error — our own refusals become problems, carrying their status, code and sentence. The isinstance check guards against being called with the wrong kind of error: if that ever happened, the error is handled as unexpected rather than crashing the error handler itself.

46async def on_invalid_request(request: Request, error: Exception) -> Response:
47    if not isinstance(error, RequestValidationError):
48        return await on_unexpected(request, error)

on_invalid_request — when FastAPI's Pydantic checks reject a request's data, for example a JSON body with a missing field.

49    fields = sorted({".".join(str(part) for part in item["loc"][1:]) or "body" for item in error.errors()})

List which fields were wrong. Each Pydantic error has a loc ("location") such as ("body", "policy"). Skipping the first part ([1:]) and joining the rest with dots gives policy; an error about the body as a whole has nothing left, and or "body" names it instead. A set removes duplicates, and sorted fixes the order.

50    return problem(request, 422, "invalid_request", "invalid or missing: " + ", ".join(fields))

Answer 422 with one sentence naming the fields — but never echoing the values that were sent, which might be secrets typed in the wrong place.

53async def on_http_error(request: Request, error: Exception) -> Response:
54    if not isinstance(error, HTTPException):
55        return await on_unexpected(request, error)
56    return problem(request, error.status_code, "http_error", str(error.detail))

on_http_error — Starlette's own HTTP errors, such as 404 for an address that doesn't exist at all, or 405 for a wrong method. They get the generic code http_error.

57
58
59class RequestIds:

RequestIds — a middleware: code that wraps the whole app, seeing every request on its way in and every response on its way out (§4.8).

It is written in raw ASGI, the interface between a Python web server and a web app. In ASGI, an app is simply something you can call with three values:

  • scope — a dict describing the request: its type, method, path, headers…;
  • receive — a function to call to get the request's body;
  • send — a function to call to send the response, in pieces called messages.

Writing middleware at this level is a little longer than FastAPI's shortcut decorator, but it sees everything — including requests that crash — and adds no overhead.

60    def __init__(self, app: ASGIApp) -> None:
61        self.app = app

The middleware keeps the app it wraps.

62
63    async def __call__(self, scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send) -> None:

__call__ makes an object callable like a function: the server calls the middleware exactly as it would call the app.

64        if scope["type"] != "http":
65            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
66            return

Only HTTP requests get IDs. Other kinds of call — such as the lifespan messages a server sends at start-up and shutdown — pass straight through.

67        offered = Headers(scope=scope).get("x-request-id", "")
68        request_id = offered if SAFE_REQUEST_ID.match(offered) else f"req_{secrets.token_hex(8)}"

Read the caller's offered ID. Keep it if it is safe; otherwise make our own: req_ plus 8 random bytes in hexadecimal.

69        scope.setdefault("state", {})["request_id"] = request_id

Store the ID in the request's state — the place FastAPI exposes as request.state — so every later piece of code, such as problem, can find it. setdefault creates the state dict first if the server didn't.

70        started, status = time.perf_counter(), 500

Start the stopwatch, and assume the status is 500 until a response says otherwise: if the app crashes before answering, the log line will say 500.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/http/limits.py33 lines · 100% explained

A guard at the door that measures every request before letting it in. An attacker who sends a 10-gigabyte "upload" would otherwise make the API read and store it all before any check ran. This middleware refuses oversized bodies from the headers alone, before a single byte of the body has been read.

Two rules:

  1. Every body must declare its size. A request can either state its size up front, in the Content-Length header, or send its body in chunks of unknown total size (Transfer-Encoding: chunked). Browsers and normal HTTP clients state the size for the requests this API receives, so chunked bodies are simply refused with 411 Length Required.
  2. The declared size must be within the limit: 64 KiB for JSON requests, and 16 frames × 512 KiB plus 64 KiB of packaging for face uploads. Anything bigger gets 413 Content Too Large.

Once the size is declared, the server itself makes sure no more bytes than that are delivered — so a declared size really is a ceiling.

Real world — why this lives outside FastAPI

The first idea was to count bytes while FastAPI read the body. It didn't work: FastAPI catches any error raised while it reads a JSON body and replaces it with a generic 400 There was an error parsing the body. Checking the headers before the request ever reaches FastAPI avoids that, and costs nothing.

1"""Size limits on request bodies, enforced from the headers before a single byte of the body is read."""

The docstring: limits enforced from the headers, before the body is read.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/http/deps.py61 lines · 100% explained

Who is calling? Before an endpoint's own code runs, the API must know who sent the request, and refuse strangers. FastAPI handles this with dependencies: small functions that an endpoint lists among its parameters. FastAPI runs them first and passes in their results. If a dependency raises an error, the endpoint never runs.

Explain like I'm six — the ticket check

At a theme park, the ticket is checked at the gate, not on every ride. Dependencies are the gate: an endpoint written as "this ride needs a valid ticket" can be sure that, by the time it runs, someone already checked.

There are two kinds of caller, and two gates:

Caller Proves itself with Dependency
a website's server its API key: Authorization: Bearer dk_test_… rp_caller
the verify page in a person's browser a flow token: Authorization: Bearer <token> flow_session

Bearer is the standard way to send a token in HTTP: "whoever bears (carries) this token may do this".

The capture-flow API — the endpoints the hosted verify page calls from the person's browser while the check is happening:

Method and path (under /v1/flow/sessions/{id}) Proves itself with What it does
POST /start the client secret opens a flow; returns a flow token and the page's view of the session
POST /challenge the flow token issues a one-time challenge
POST /face-attempts the flow token uploads frames; returns the decision
POST /finish the flow token returns where to send the person next

Because these calls come from a browser, they are the most exposed part of the API: anyone can open the browser's developer tools and send whatever they like. So every input is checked again here, and the answers reveal as little as possible.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/http/wellknown.py34 lines · 100% explained

Two public addresses under /.well-known/ — a path prefix reserved by an Internet standard (RFC 8615) for information about a site, at places everyone can predict:

Address What it holds
/.well-known/jwks.json the public keys that check age-token signatures (§4.12)
/.well-known/dwarpal-configuration a description of this issuer: its name, where its keys are, which algorithm and token type it uses, which policies exist, and which age model is active

Neither needs a key: public keys are meant to be public. A website's SDK fetches the key set, keeps a copy for a few minutes, and from then on checks every token offline, without calling the API at all.

GET /.well-known/dwarpal-configuration — the discovery document. A program can learn everything it needs to verify our tokens from this one address. The idea is borrowed from OpenID Connect, which publishes the same kind of document for logins.

25    issuer = svc.settings.issuer

The issuer's own address, from the settings.

26    return {
27        "issuer": issuer,
28        "jwks_uri": f"{issuer}/.well-known/jwks.json",
29        "token_type": JWT_TYPE,
30        "token_signing_algorithms": [ALG],
31        "policies": sorted(PRESETS),
32        "age_model": svc.manifest.version,
33        "age_model_calibrated": svc.manifest.calibrated,
34    }

The document:

  • issuer — exactly what tokens carry in their iss claim;
  • jwks_uri — where the public keys are;
  • token_type — the typ every age token has in its header;
  • token_signing_algorithms — ["Ed25519"], the only algorithm a verifier should accept;
  • policies — the names of the preset policies, sorted;
  • age_model and age_model_calibrated — which age model decides, and whether it is calibrated. Anyone integrating can see at a glance that, today, only test sessions are possible.
services/api/src/dwarpal_api/http/health.py37 lines · 100% explained

Two health endpoints, asked by whatever runs the service (Docker, a load balancer, Kubernetes) rather than by people:

Address Question Answer
GET /livez "Is the program alive at all?" always 200, if it can answer
GET /readyz "Can it do real work right now?" 200 if PostgreSQL and Valkey both respond, otherwise 503

Why two? If /livez fails, the program is stuck, and the right fix is to restart it. If /readyz fails, the program is fine but something it needs is down — restarting won't help, but traffic should go elsewhere until it recovers. Mixing the two up leads to a classic outage: the database blinks, every copy of the API is restarted at once, and the restart storm makes everything worse. (The z at the end is an old Google naming habit, kept by Kubernetes, that makes these paths unlikely to clash with real ones.)

1"""Health endpoints: "am I alive?" and "can I do real work right now?", for whatever runs and routes the service."""

21@router.get("/readyz")
22async def readyz(response: Response, svc: Annotated[Services, Depends(services)]) -> dict[str, str]:
23    checks: dict[str, str] = {}

/readyz — it may need to change the status code, so it asks for the response. The checks are collected in a dict.

24    try:
25        async with svc.sessions() as session:
26            await session.execute(text("SELECT 1"))
27        checks["database"] = "ok"
28    except Exception:
29        checks["database"] = "unavailable"

The database check: open a database session and run SELECT 1 — the smallest possible query. Success means PostgreSQL is reachable and answering. Any error at all counts as unavailable. Catching every kind of error is usually a bad habit; here it is exactly right, because the question is simply "did it work?".

30    try:
31        await svc.store.ping()
32        checks["valkey"] = "ok"
33    except Exception:
34        checks["valkey"] = "unavailable"

The Valkey check: PING, in the same way.

35    if any(value != "ok" for value in checks.values()):
36        response.status_code = 503

If any check isn't ok, answer 503 Service Unavailable.

37    return checks

Return the checks, so a person looking at the answer sees which dependency is down, for example {"database": "ok", "valkey": "unavailable"}.

Assembling and running the API

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/main.py70 lines · 100% explained

The file that assembles the API. Every other module is a part; this one connects them in the right order when the program starts, and disconnects them when it stops. It follows the same pattern as the inference service's main.py (§5.1.1): an app factory called create_app.

What happens when the API starts, in order:

  1. Uvicorn calls create_app(), which builds the FastAPI app: its middleware, error handlers and endpoints.
  2. Before accepting any request, the app runs its lifespan start-up: it connects to PostgreSQL and Valkey, prepares the inference client, loads (or creates) the signing key, and reads the model manifest.
  3. Requests are served.
  4. On shutdown, the lifespan closes every connection it opened.

If any step of 2 fails — a wrong master key, a missing manifest, an unreachable database — the API refuses to start, loudly. A service that starts "half-working" is much harder to diagnose than one that doesn't start at all.

1"""The API application: connect every part at start-up, close them at shutdown, and route requests.
2
3Run it with:  uvicorn dwarpal_api.main:create_app --factory --port 8000 --log-config services/api/logging.json
4"""

The docstring, with the exact command to run the API: Uvicorn (§4.8), the import path of the factory, --factory (call it to get the app), the port, and the logging configuration (logging.json).

Every part, from every layer: database helpers, the inference client, the key classes, the store, the toolbox, the manifest loader, the five HTTP modules, the body-size guard, and the settings.

27
28def create_app(settings: Settings | None = None, inference_http: httpx.AsyncClient | None = None) -> FastAPI:

create_app — build and return the app. Both parameters are optional, and only tests use them: settings to point the API at test databases, and inference_http to talk to an inference app running inside the same process.

29    settings = settings or Settings()

Use the given settings, or read them from the environment.

30
31    @asynccontextmanager
32    async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:

The lifespan function. @asynccontextmanager turns a function with a single yield into a "before and after" pair: everything before yield runs at start-up, and everything after it at shutdown. Defining it inside create_app lets it use settings and inference_http directly.

33        engine = make_engine(settings.database_url)
34        sessions = make_sessions(engine)

Create the database engine (the connection pool) and the session factory (db.py).

35        valkey = Redis.from_url(settings.valkey_url)

Create the Valkey client from its URL. It connects lazily, on first use.

36        http = inference_http or httpx.AsyncClient(
37            base_url=settings.inference_url, timeout=settings.inference_timeout_s
38        )

The HTTP client for the inference service: the one a test passed in, or a new one with the service's base address and timeout from the settings.

39        keyring = KeyRing(MasterKey(settings.master_key.get_secret_value()))

Build the key ring around the master key. get_secret_value() is the only way out of a SecretStr, so this is one of very few lines in the project that ever touches the master key in plain form. A malformed key stops the start-up right here.

40        async with sessions() as session:
41            await keyring.load(session, datetime.now(UTC))

Load the signing key, creating one if the database has none (signing.py, with its lock against two copies starting at once).

42        app.state.services = Services(
43            settings=settings,
44            sessions=sessions,
45            store=FlowStore(valkey),
46            inference=InferenceClient(http),
47            keyring=keyring,
48            manifest=load_manifest(settings.models_dir / settings.age_manifest),
49        )

Fill the toolbox and store it on the app, where the services dependency finds it for every request. The model manifest is read from models_dir; a broken or missing manifest stops the start-up.

50        try:
51            yield

yield hands control to the server: the app now serves requests until shutdown begins.

52        finally:
53            if inference_http is None:
54                await http.aclose()
55            await valkey.aclose()
56            await engine.dispose()

finally runs at shutdown — even after a crash. Close the inference client only if we created it (a test closes its own; whoever creates a resource closes it), then the Valkey client, then the database pool.

57
58    app = FastAPI(title="Dwarpal API", version="0.1.0", lifespan=lifespan)

Create the FastAPI app, with a title and version for its automatic documentation, and the lifespan.

59    app.add_middleware(BodyLimit)

Add the body-size guard (limits.py).

60    app.add_middleware(
61        CORSMiddleware,
62        allow_origins=settings.cors_origins,
63        allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
64        allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type", "X-Request-Id", "X-Dwarpal-Device"],
65        expose_headers=["X-Request-Id"],
66    )

Add the CORS middleware, which tells browsers which other websites may call this API from their pages (§4.13):

  • allow_origins — only the origins in the settings: the verify page;
  • allow_methods — only GET and POST, the only methods the API uses;
  • allow_headers — the only request headers a page may send: the token, the body's type, a request ID, and the verify page's device ID (X-Dwarpal-Device, for the per-device budgets);
  • expose_headers — lets the page's code read our X-Request-Id header, so the verify page can show it in an error message.
67    problems.install(app)

Install the request IDs, request log and error handlers (problems.py). Middleware added later wraps everything added before, so the order of these lines decides the order requests flow through:

request → RequestIds → CORS → BodyLimit → error handlers → endpoint

Request IDs come first, so every later step — even a refusal by the size guard — can name the request. CORS comes before the size guard, so browsers can read even a "too large" answer.

68    for module in (rp, flow, wellknown, health):
69        app.include_router(module.router)

Add the four routers — the relying-party API, the flow API, the well-known addresses and the health checks.

70    return app

Return the finished app.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/cli.py155 lines · 100% explained

A small command-line tool for two jobs a developer needs before the API is useful:

  • migrate — bring the database's tables up to date (§4.10);
  • seed-dev — create a demo project ("Amber Cellars") with a fresh test API key, and print the key once.

The tests call the same two functions directly, so the commands developers run by hand are exactly the code the tests exercise.

Try it yourself

With the local databases running (docker compose -f infra/compose/compose.yaml up -d --wait), run:

  1. uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli migrate
  2. uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli seed-dev

The second command prints a project ID and a dk_test_… key. Keep the key: it is shown only once.

1"""Command-line helpers for the API: apply database migrations, create a demo project with a test key, and summarise
2recent liveness results.
3
4uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli migrate
5uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli seed-dev
6uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli liveness-report --since 2026-10-17T12:00
7"""

The docstring, with the three commands. python -m dwarpal_api.cli runs this module as a program; --package dwarpal-api tells uv which workspace package's environment to use. The third, liveness-report (added in Phase 3), summarises the liveness results of recent face attempts; --since says from when.

72
73def liveness_summary(attempts: list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]]) -> str:
74    """What happened to a batch of face attempts: outcomes, which liveness checks fired, and the light evidence."""

liveness_summary (Phase 3) — turn a list of face attempts into a short, readable report. Each attempt is a pair: its outcome (such as retry) and its stored scores. It is a separate, plain function — no database — so a test can call it with made-up attempts.

Its purpose is measuring the liveness checks on real people. If the owner makes, say, 30 genuine attempts, every failed pose challenge among them is a false reject: an honest person turned away. This report gives that rate, and the light measurements, from which the thresholds can be set (§5.3).

75    outcomes = Counter(outcome for outcome, _ in attempts)

Count the outcomes: how many passes, retries, rejections and so on. Counter does the counting.

76    lives = [scores["liveness"] for _, scores in attempts if scores.get("liveness")]

Pick out the liveness part of each attempt's scores, skipping attempts that have none (for example, ones whose analysis failed). scores.get("liveness") gives None instead of an error when the key is missing.

77    evidence = Counter(live["evidence"] for live in lives)

Count the kinds of evidence: images (measured) or labels (the test mode). A report on genuine attempts should show only images.

78    poses = [live["pose"] for live in lives if live["pose"] is not None]

The pose results, where there was one.

79    problems = Counter(problem for pose in poses for problem in pose["problems"])

Count every problem name over all pose results — wrong_order, not_shown:turn_left and so on. The double for reads left to right: for each pose result, for each of its problems.

80    signs = Counter(sign for live in lives for sign in live["injection"])

Count the injection signs the same way.

81    shown = sum(1 for live in lives if live["light"] is not None and live["light"].get("shown", True))

How many attempts showed the screen colours at all. .get("shown", True) treats results stored before this field existed as shown.

82    lights = [live["light"] for live in lives if live["light"] is not None and live["light"]["usable"]]

The light results that could actually be measured (usable).

83    skin = [light["r_skin"] for light in lights if light["r_skin"] is not None]

The skin correlations among them, leaving out any that are missing.

84    passed = sum(pose["passed"] for pose in poses)

How many pose challenges passed. sum of True/False values counts the Trues, because Python treats True as 1.

85    reach: dict[str, list[float]] = {}

How far each pose got, gathered by pose name: reach maps a name such as turn_left to the list of its values. dict[str, list[float]] is the type: text keys, lists of numbers as values.

86    for pose in poses:
87        for name, value in pose.get("reached", []):
88            if value is not None:
89                reach.setdefault(name, []).append(value)

For each pose result, for each [name, value] pair it recorded, add the value to its name's list — skipping None, which means there was no face to measure. pose.get("reached", []) gives an empty list for results stored before this field existed. setdefault(name, []) returns the name's list, creating an empty one first if needed.

90    reaches = [f"{name} {statistics.median(v):+.2f} / {min(v):+.2f}" for name, v in sorted(reach.items())]

One short text per pose name: the median and the lowest value, such as turn_left +0.42 / +0.29. The lowest matters most: it is the honest attempt that came closest to failing, and it shows how much room the limit leaves. sorted(…) puts the names in alphabetical order.

91    measured = Counter(pose.get("measured_by", "five_points") for pose in poses)

Which measurement each pose check used, counted.

92    real = [live["presentation"] for live in lives if live.get("presentation") is not None]
93    patterns = [live["screen_pattern"] for live in lives if live.get("screen_pattern") is not None]
94    gradual = [moved for pose in poses for _, moved in pose.get("gradual", [])]

The presentation evidence, gathered over the attempts: the real-face chances, the screen patterns, and for every pose whether it was caught mid-turn (True/False). .get(…) skips results stored before these fields existed.

95    lines = [
96        f"{len(attempts)} face attempts: " + ", ".join(f"{name} {count}" for name, count in outcomes.most_common()),

Build the report line by line. The first: the number of attempts and each outcome with its count, most common first. ", ".join(…) puts commas between the parts.

97        "evidence: " + (", ".join(f"{name} {count}" for name, count in evidence.most_common()) or "none"),

The evidence counts — or none. or "none" works because an empty text counts as false.

98        f"pose challenge passed: {passed} of {len(poses)}"
99        + (
100            f" ({passed / len(poses):.0%}); false-reject rate if all were genuine: {1 - passed / len(poses):.0%}"
101            if poses
102            else ""
103        ),

How many pose challenges passed, as a count and a percentage (:.0% formats 0.9 as 90%), and the false-reject rate if every attempt was genuine — the share that failed. The extra part is added only if there were pose results (if poses else ""), which also avoids dividing by zero.

104        "pose problems: " + (", ".join(f"{name} {count}" for name, count in problems.most_common()) or "none"),
105        "pose measured by: " + (", ".join(f"{name} {count}" for name, count in measured.most_common()) or "none"),
106        "pose reach from frontal, median / lowest: " + (", ".join(reaches) or "none"),
107        "injection signs: " + (", ".join(f"{name} {count}" for name, count in signs.most_common()) or "none"),

The pose problems, the measurement used, how far each pose got (median and lowest — the numbers from which the pose limits are set), and the injection signs, each with its count, or none.

108        "presentation: "
109        + (f"real-face chance median {statistics.median(real):.2f}, lowest {min(real):.2f}" if real else "not measured")
110        + (f"; screen pattern median {statistics.median(patterns):.2f}" if patterns else "")
111        + f"; poses caught mid-turn {sum(gradual)} of {len(gradual)}",

The presentation line: the real-face chance's median and lowest value (or not measured), the screen pattern's median, and how many poses were caught mid-turn. sum of True/False values counts the Trues.

112        f"light shown: {shown} of {len(lives)}; usable: {len(lights)} of {len(lives)}"
113        + (
114            f"; skin correlation median {statistics.median(skin):+.2f}, range {min(skin):+.2f} to {max(skin):+.2f}"
115            if skin
116            else ""
117        ),

How many attempts showed the colours and how many had a usable light measurement, and — if there were any skin correlations — their median (the middle value, which one odd attempt can't drag far) and their range. :+.2f prints a number with two decimals and always a sign, such as +0.62.

118    ]
119    return "\n".join(lines)

Close the list, and join the lines with line breaks into one text.

120
121
122async def liveness_report(settings: Settings, since: datetime) -> str:

liveness_report — read the attempts from the database and summarise them. It is async because the database code is.

123    engine = make_engine(settings.database_url)
124    async with make_sessions(engine)() as session:

Connect to the database and open a session.

125        rows = (
126            await session.execute(
127                select(VerificationAttempt.outcome, VerificationAttempt.scores).where(
128                    VerificationAttempt.kind == "face", VerificationAttempt.created_at >= since
129                )
130            )
131        ).all()

Fetch only two columns — the outcome and the scores — of every face attempt created at or after since. .all() returns the rows.

Close the connection.

133    return liveness_summary([(outcome, scores) for outcome, scores in rows])

Turn each row into an (outcome, scores) pair and summarise them.
