136def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:

main — what runs when the module is started as a program. argv lets tests pass arguments directly; normally it is None, and argparse reads the real command line.

137    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="dwarpal-api", description="Dwarpal API helpers")
138    parser.add_argument("command", choices=["migrate", "seed-dev", "liveness-report"])
139    parser.add_argument("--since", type=datetime.fromisoformat, help="liveness-report: attempts from this time on")
140    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

Describe the tool, accept exactly one command — migrate, seed-dev or liveness-report — and the optional --since, and read them. type=datetime.fromisoformat converts the text (such as 2026-10-17T12:00) into a date and time; a malformed one is refused with a message. Anything else prints a helpful usage message and stops.

141    if args.command == "migrate":
142        migrate()
143        print("database is at the latest migration")
144        return 0

migrate: apply the migrations, say so, and return 0 (success).

145    if args.command == "liveness-report":
146        since = args.since or datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=1)
147        print(asyncio.run(liveness_report(Settings(), since if since.tzinfo else since.replace(tzinfo=UTC))))
148        return 0

liveness-report: from --since, or from 24 hours ago if it was left out. A time typed without a time zone is taken as UTC (replace(tzinfo=UTC)), because the database stores times in UTC and can't compare them with a time that has none. Print the report and return 0.

149    project_id, plaintext = asyncio.run(seed_dev(Settings()))

Otherwise, seed-dev: run the async seed with the normal settings. asyncio.run starts the async engine, runs the function to the end, and returns its result.

150    print(f"project:  {project_id}\ntest key: {plaintext}\n(store the key now; it is shown only once)")

Print the project ID and the key, with a reminder to store the key now. \n inside the text starts a new line.

The message uses only plain ASCII characters. An earlier version contained a long dash —, which came out as � when the output was saved to a file on Windows: Python then writes text with Windows' older character table, which other tools don't expect.

151    return 0

Success.

154if __name__ == "__main__":
155    sys.exit(main())

Run main only when the module is started as a program, and hand its result to the operating system as the exit code: 0 means success, anything else failure (§4.6).

Try it yourself — run the API on your own computer

You need Docker running and the model files downloaded (uv run infra/scripts/fetch_models.py). Then, in four terminals from the project folder:

  1. docker compose -f infra/compose/compose.yaml up -d --wait — start PostgreSQL and Valkey;
  2. uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli migrate, then uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli seed-dev — create the tables and a test key (copy it);
  3. uv run --package dwarpal-inference uvicorn dwarpal_inference.main:create_app --factory --port 8001 — the inference service;
  4. uv run --package dwarpal-api uvicorn dwarpal_api.main:create_app --factory --port 8000 --log-config services/api/logging.json — the API.

Open http://localhost:8000/docs for FastAPI's automatic, clickable documentation, or http://localhost:8000/.well-known/dwarpal-configuration to see the discovery document. Each request you make prints one JSON log line in the API's terminal.

The integration tests

services/api/tests/test_api.py388 lines · 100% explained

The integration tests: the whole API, end to end, against the real things it depends on —

  • a real PostgreSQL and a real Valkey, each started in a throwaway Docker container by the Testcontainers library, and deleted afterwards (§4.14);
  • the real inference service, running inside the same Python process, with its stand-in age model set to whatever age a test needs;
  • the real migrations, the real signing keys, the real JWKS.

Unit tests (test_domain.py) prove that each rule is right. These tests prove that the pieces are connected right: that a pass really produces a token a website can verify, that a wrong key really gets a 401, that the migrations really build the tables the code expects.

Explain like I'm six — the dress rehearsal

Checking each actor's lines separately is the unit test. The dress rehearsal is everyone on stage together, with real costumes and real lights. Mistakes that only appear when people interact — someone walks on at the wrong moment — are only found in the rehearsal.

If Docker isn't running, these tests are skipped, with a message saying why — not failed. Everything else can still be tested.

75@dataclass
76class Harness:
77    client: httpx.AsyncClient
78    key: str
79    project: str

Harness — what each test gets to work with: an HTTP client connected to the API, the seeded project's test API key, and the project's public ID.

82@asynccontextmanager
83async def harness(
84    databases: tuple[str, str],
85    stub_age: float = 30.0,
86    livemode: bool = False,
87    liveness: Literal["images", "labels"] = "labels",
88    **overrides: Any,
89) -> AsyncIterator[Harness]:

harness — sets up a complete, fresh API for one test. Its options: the age the stand-in model should "see" (30 by default — clearly an adult), whether the seeded key is live, how liveness gets its evidence (Phase 3) — "labels" by default, because the tests' portrait is a still photo that can't turn its head — and any other API settings to change (**overrides: extra named arguments, collected into a dict), such as a smaller device budget.

90    database_url, valkey_url = databases

Unpack the two database addresses.

91    inference = create_inference(InferenceSettings(stub_age=stub_age, liveness=liveness))

Create an inference app whose stand-in model reports the chosen age, with the chosen liveness evidence.

92    inference_transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=inference)
93    async with (
94        inference.router.lifespan_context(inference),
95        httpx.AsyncClient(transport=inference_transport, base_url="http://inference") as inference_http,
96    ):

Start the inference app's lifespan (loading its face detector), and open an HTTP client wired to it through ASGITransport — httpx calls the app's Python code directly, with no network and no server. One async with with two parts, in brackets, opens both and closes both.

97        settings = Settings(environment="test", database_url=database_url, valkey_url=valkey_url, **overrides)
98        api = create_api(settings, inference_http=inference_http)

Create the API with test settings — the test databases' addresses, plus any overrides — and the in-process inference client.

99        async with api.router.lifespan_context(api):

Run the API's lifespan: connect, load the signing key, read the manifest.

100            project, key = await seed_dev(settings, livemode=livemode)

Seed a project and a key, exactly as a developer would with seed-dev.

101            transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=api)
102            async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://api") as client:
103                yield Harness(client, key, project)

Open a client wired to the API the same way, and hand the harness to the test. When the test ends, every async with closes in reverse order.

106async def create(h: Harness, **body: Any) -> httpx.Response:
107    payload = {"policy": "uk_osa_18", "return_url": RETURN_URL, **body}
108    return await h.client.post("/v1/verification-sessions", json=payload, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {h.key}"})

create — create a session as the demo shop would, with the API key. Any keyword arguments replace the defaults, so a test can write create(h, policy="anything_goes").

secret — the body for /start: the session's client secret.

115async def start(h: Harness, created: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, str]:
116    response = await h.client.post(f"/v1/flow/sessions/{created['id']}/start", json=secret(created))
117    assert response.status_code == 200, response.text
118    return {"Authorization": f"Bearer {response.json()['flow_token']}"}

start — start the flow and return the Authorization header with the flow token, ready for the next calls. The assert includes the response text, so if starting fails, the test report shows why.

120
121def following(poses: list[str], count: int) -> list[FrameMeta]:
122    """Frame labels that follow some poses: a frontal baseline, then one frame per pose, in the order given."""

following (Phase 3) — the labels for a burst whose head follows the given poses: frontal baseline frames first, then one frame per pose, in order. With 6 frames and 3 poses: baseline, baseline, baseline, then the three poses.

123    phases = ["baseline"] * (count - len(poses)) + poses

["baseline"] * n makes a list of n copies; + poses adds the poses after them.

124    return [FrameMeta(index=i, t_ms=i * 120.0, phase=phase) for i, phase in enumerate(phases)]  # type: ignore[arg-type]

One FrameMeta per phase, numbered from 0, taken 120 ms apart. enumerate gives each item with its position.

The comment at the end, # type: ignore[arg-type], silences one complaint of the type checker: it can't know that the plain texts in poses are valid Phase names. Pydantic checks them anyway when the FrameMeta is created.

127async def attempt(
128    h: Harness,
129    session: str,
130    flow: dict[str, str],
131    frames: list[bytes],
132    poses: list[str] | None = None,
133    signals: ClientSignals | None = None,
134    claimed: Challenge | None = None,
135) -> httpx.Response:

attempt — one complete face attempt, as the verify page makes it. Besides the frames, three optional inputs let a test play an attacker (Phase 3):

  • poses — label the frames with these poses instead of the ones asked for;
  • signals — report these browser signals;
  • claimed — put a challenge of the browser's own choosing into the request.
136    """One face attempt. By default the frames' labels follow the challenge the server issued; an attack may label
137    them in another order (`poses`), report other browser signals, or claim a challenge of its own."""

The docstring says the same, in short.

138    challenge = (await h.client.post(f"/v1/flow/sessions/{session}/challenge", headers=flow)).json()

Get a challenge — the server picks its random poses and colours.

139    shown = poses if poses is not None else challenge["poses"]
140    frames = frames + frames[-1:] * max(0, 3 + len(shown) - len(frames))  # at least 3 frontal frames, then the poses
141    labels = following(shown, len(frames))

Label the frames: by default they follow the challenge's own poses (an honest attempt), otherwise the poses the test gave. A challenge has 3 or 4 poses, so first make sure there are enough frames — at least 3 frontal ones, then one per pose — by repeating the last frame as many times as needed (frames[-1:] * n: a list of the last frame, n times; max(0, …) keeps n from going negative).

142    meta = FaceRequestMeta(frames=labels, signals=signals or ClientSignals(), challenge=claimed)

Describe the attempt: the frames' labels, the signals (normal ones unless given), and any claimed challenge.

143    files = {f"frame_{i}": (f"frame_{i}.jpg", data, "image/jpeg") for i, data in enumerate(frames)}
144    data = {"meta": meta.model_dump_json(), "challenge_id": challenge["challenge_id"]}
145    return await h.client.post(f"/v1/flow/sessions/{session}/face-attempts", data=data, files=files, headers=flow)

Package the frames as files frame_0, frame_1, …, add the description and the challenge's ID, and upload everything as a multipart form.

The main story: an adult passes, and the website can verify the token. @pytest.mark.anyio lets pytest run an async test function.

150    async with harness(databases) as h:
151        created = (await create(h)).json()
152        flow = await start(h, created)

156        assert finished["redirect_url"] == f"{RETURN_URL}?session_id={created['id']}"

Create, start, attempt with six portraits — the stand-in model says 30, so it passes — then finish: the redirect goes back to the shop with the session's ID.

157        reloaded = (await h.client.post(f"/v1/flow/sessions/{created['id']}/start", json=secret(created))).json()

Start the flow again, as if the person reloaded the page afterwards.

158        auth = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {h.key}"}
159        session = (await h.client.get(f"/v1/verification-sessions/{created['id']}", headers=auth)).json()
160        jwks = (await h.client.get("/.well-known/jwks.json")).json()

As the shop's server: read the result with the API key, and fetch the public keys.

161    assert reloaded["session"]["status"] == "completed"
162    assert reloaded["session"]["outcome"] == "pass"

The reloaded page sees the completed session and its outcome — no error for the person.

163    assert session["status"] == "completed"
164    assert session["outcome"] == "pass"

The result says completed, and passed.

165    token = jwt.decode(session["age_token"], KeySet.import_key_set(jwks), algorithms=["Ed25519"])

Verify the token exactly as a website would: with the published key set, accepting only Ed25519. If the signature didn't match, this line would raise an error.

166    assert token.header["typ"] == "dwarpal-age+jwt"
167    assert token.claims["outcome"] == "pass"
168    assert token.claims["age_over_18"] is True
169    assert token.claims["aud"] == h.project
170    assert token.claims["sid"] == created["id"]
171    assert token.claims["livemode"] is False

The token is an age token, says pass, says age_over_18: true (the literal True, checked with is), and is addressed to this project, about this session, in test mode.

172    assert not {"age", "mean", "estimated_age"} & set(token.claims)

No age inside. None of these names appears among the claims: the set of forbidden names and the set of claim names have nothing in common (& is set intersection; an empty set counts as false).

177    async with harness(databases, stub_age=12.0) as h:
178        created = (await create(h)).json()
179        result = (await attempt(h, created["id"], await start(h, created), [PORTRAIT] * 6)).json()
180        auth = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {h.key}"}

182        jwks = (await h.client.get("/.well-known/jwks.json")).json()
183    token = jwt.decode(session["age_token"], KeySet.import_key_set(jwks), algorithms=["Ed25519"])
184    assert result["outcome"] == "fail"
185    assert session["outcome"] == "fail"
186    assert token.claims["outcome"] == "fail"
187    assert token.claims["age_over_18"] is False

A clear child is refused, unmistakably. With the stand-in model at 12, the attempt fails, and the signed token says outcome: fail and age_over_18: false — so even a website that read only the age claim would refuse entry.

214@pytest.mark.anyio
215async def test_credentials_are_checked_and_errors_are_problem_details(databases: tuple[str, str]) -> None:
216    async with harness(databases) as h:

218        created = (await create(h)).json()

220            f"/v1/flow/sessions/{created['id']}/start", json={"client_secret": "vs_wrong_secret_0123456789"}
221        )

228    assert wrong_secret.json()["code"] == "invalid_client_secret"
229    assert no_flow.json()["code"] == "invalid_flow_token"

Credentials are checked, and errors are problem details. No API key at all: 401, with the problem-details media type, the stable code, the type reference, and a request ID that matches the response header. A wrong client secret and a missing flow token each get their own code.

335    async with harness(databases, liveness="images") as h:

Red team, from here on (Phase 3): tests that play the attacker. Red-teaming means attacking your own system on purpose, to find its weaknesses before someone else does.

The first: a printed photo. The "person" is the still test portrait, and here liveness measures the images for real (liveness="images").

336        created = (await create(h)).json()
337        flow = await start(h, created)
338        first = (await attempt(h, created["id"], flow, [PORTRAIT] * 6)).json()
339        second = (await attempt(h, created["id"], flow, [PORTRAIT] * 6)).json()

Two attempts with six identical portraits. The photo looks straight ahead throughout — it can't turn left, right or up when asked.

340    assert (first["outcome"], first["reasons"]) == ("retry", ["liveness_check_failed"])
341    assert (second["outcome"], second["reasons"]) == ("reject", ["verification_failed"])

The first attempt gets a retry, with the vague liveness_check_failed (a real person may just have been slow). The second gets rejected — and from outside the reason is only verification_failed, which doesn't even say liveness was involved.

347        created = (await create(h)).json()

349        result = (await attempt(h, created["id"], flow, [PORTRAIT] * 6, poses=["turn_right"] * 3)).json()

Poses in the wrong order. Labels mode is on, so the frames' labels are believed — but the attacker labels them turn_right three times, whatever the challenge asked. A challenge never repeats a pose twice in a row, so this can never match it.

Caught: retry, liveness_check_failed.

Automation and virtual cameras. Two fresh sessions; in each the browser honestly reports one warning sign — a program driving the browser, or a virtual camera. The frames themselves are fine and the person is a clear adult.

Both go to step up with liveness_uncertain: not passed on a face that may have been injected, but not rejected either, because these signs can have innocent causes. [x] * 2 is a list of two copies of x.

With a budget of 2 challenges an hour: three requests from the same device, each in a new session, then one from a different device.

386    assert [r.status_code for r in same] == [200, 200, 429]
387    assert same[2].json()["code"] == "too_many_attempts"
388    assert other.status_code == 200

The same device gets two challenges and then 429 too_many_attempts — new sessions don't reset its budget; the other device is unaffected.

Real world — what a careful review found

Before the walkthroughs above were written, every line of the API was read again, as a reviewer would. Writing an explanation for a beginner is a strict review in itself: a line that is hard to explain is often a line that is wrong. The review found five real problems, each now fixed and covered by a test:

  1. A token that could be misread. A token for a failed check said "outcome": "fail" — but also "age_over": 18. A website reading only the second claim would have let a child in. The claim is now "age_over_18": false (ADR-0020).
  2. Unlimited challenges. One session could ask for endless challenges, and so make the AI analyse endless pictures. Each session now gets twice its attempts.
  3. No size limit on uploads. The API would have read a body of any size before checking it. Bodies are now measured from their headers first (limits.py).
  4. A dead end after reloading. A person who reloaded the verify page after finishing got an error, with no way back to the shop. Finished sessions can now be reopened to see the result.
  5. Unsafe production settings were possible. Plain http:// addresses are now refused in production, like the development master key.

The same review moved the error documentation links from a web domain this project doesn't own to the API's own address, and fixed two bugs in the book builder itself (§X.6).

Real world — what this step measured

Tests. The API has 42 tests: 30 fast ones for the rules (about 2 seconds) and 12 integration tests against real databases (about 10 seconds, most of it starting the containers). Every one passes, along with the strict linter and type checker across all 51 Python files.

Speed. Thirty complete checks were timed through the real API, with PostgreSQL and Valkey in Docker on this laptop (median, then the slowest 10 %):

Request Median 90th percentile
create a session 11.9 ms 13.2 ms
start the flow 10.3 ms 11.3 ms
get a challenge 10.8 ms 12.2 ms
a face attempt with 4 frames, including the AI 68.6 ms 82.1 ms
read the result and sign a token 13.6 ms 14.4 ms

Where does the time go? Mostly into round trips to the databases. A typical request makes eight to ten of them — borrowing a connection, starting and ending transactions, the queries themselves — and on this laptop, through Docker Desktop's virtual network, one PostgreSQL round trip takes about 1.2 ms (Valkey: 0.6 ms). That is a property of the development machine, not of the code: on a Linux server, the same round trips are usually several times faster. Either way, the whole journey stays far inside the 1.5-second budget for an answer (NFR-05).

5.1.4 The front end — the SDK, the verify page and the demo shop

This step builds the three things people and websites actually touch:

 Amber Cellars (demo shop, port 3100)          Dwarpal verify page (port 3000)            Dwarpal API (port 8000)
 ───────────────────────────────────           ───────────────────────────────            ───────────────────────
 "Verify my age" ─ server action ─ SDK ──────────────────────────────────────────────────► create session
   remembers the session in a cookie ◄──────────────────────────────────────────────────── link with #cs=secret
 redirect ───────────────────────────────────► reads the secret, wipes it from the address
                                               start ─────────────────────────────────────► flow token
                                               camera: 5 photos ── challenge + upload ────► decide
                                               "You're all set" ── finish ────────────────► return address
 /age-check/complete ◄─────────────────────── redirect with ?session_id=
   checks the cookie · SDK: result + token ──────────────────────────────────────────────► result + signed token
   SDK: verify signature (JWKS) · age_over_18 === true
   signed pass cookie ─► /cellar

Three parts, in the order they are walked through:

  • @dwarpal/node, the SDK — what every website needs: create sessions, read results, and above all verify tokens;
  • the verify page — where a person takes the check;
  • the demo shop — a pretend customer, built exactly the way a real one should be.

The SDK: @dwarpal/node

packages/sdk-node/package.json33 lines · 100% explained

The package description of @dwarpal/node, the SDK (Software Development Kit) for websites that use Dwarpal. An SDK is a small library a service gives its customers, so that each customer doesn't have to write — and get right — the same code: calling the API with the key, and above all checking the signature of every age token.

package.json is to a JavaScript package what pyproject.toml is to a Python one (§4.4): its name, its version, how to build and test it, and what it depends on.

1{

The opening brace of the JSON object.

2  "name": "@dwarpal/node",

"name": "@dwarpal/node" — the package's name. @dwarpal/ is a scope: a family name for all of this project's packages. Apps import the SDK by exactly this name.

3  "version": "0.1.0",

"version": "0.1.0" — semantic versioning (§0.17); a major version of 0 means "early, may still change".

4  "description": "Server-side SDK for Dwarpal: create age-verification sessions and verify the signed age tokens.",

A one-line description.

5  "private": true,

"private": true — never publish this package to the public npm registry by accident. Publishing it, and under which licence, is the project owner's decision for later; until then this line makes npm publish refuse.

6  "type": "module",

"type": "module" — the package's JavaScript files are ES modules, the modern standard way JavaScript files import each other (import … from …), rather than the older CommonJS style (require(…)).

7  "exports": {
8    ".": {
9      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
10      "default": "./dist/index.js"
11    }
12  },

"exports" — what other code may import, and from which files. "." means "the package itself", as in import { verifyAgeToken } from "@dwarpal/node":

  • "types" — the file that describes the package's types, for TypeScript;
  • "default" — the JavaScript file that actually runs.

Both are in dist/, the folder the build writes. Anything not listed here can't be imported from outside, which keeps the package's insides private.

13  "files": [
14    "dist"
15  ],

"files" — when the package is packed for publishing, include only dist/: the built code, not the sources or the tests.

16  "engines": {
17    "node": ">=24.11.0"
18  },

"engines" — Node.js 24.11 or newer. The SDK uses modern built-ins such as fetch and AbortSignal.timeout.

19  "scripts": {
20    "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.build.json",
21    "typecheck": "tsc -p tsconfig.json",
22    "test": "vitest run"
23  },

The scripts (run with pnpm build, pnpm typecheck, pnpm test):

  • build — compile src/ into dist/ with the TypeScript compiler, using tsconfig.build.json;
  • typecheck — check every file, including the tests, without writing anything (tsconfig.json);
  • test — run the tests once with Vitest (§4.20). run means "once, then stop", instead of watching for changes.
24  "dependencies": {
25    "jose": "6.2.12"
26  },

"dependencies" — what the SDK needs when it runs: only jose 6.2.12, a widely used library for JWTs and JWKs that runs in Node.js, browsers and other JavaScript runtimes, and has no dependencies of its own. Every dependency is code a website must trust, so the SDK keeps the list as short as possible.

27  "devDependencies": {
28    "@dwarpal/config": "workspace:*",
29    "@types/node": "24.19.1",
30    "typescript": "7.0.2",
31    "vitest": "5.0.3"
32  }

"devDependencies" — what's needed only while developing:

  • @dwarpal/config — the shared TypeScript settings. workspace:* means "the copy in this repository", never a published one;
  • @types/node — type descriptions of Node.js's built-in modules, for the version we run (24);
  • typescript 7.0.2 — the compiler (§4.15);
  • vitest 5.0.3 — the test runner.
33}

The closing brace.

packages/sdk-node/tsconfig.json11 lines · 100% explained

The SDK's TypeScript settings for checking its code. It starts from the project's shared strict settings (packages/config/tsconfig.base.json, §5.0.4) and changes only what a library for Node.js needs differently from a web app.

1{

The opening brace.

2  "extends": "@dwarpal/config/tsconfig.base.json",

"extends" — start from the shared settings, by their package name. Everything there — strict mode, the extra safety checks — applies here unless changed below.

3  "compilerOptions": {

"compilerOptions" — the changes.

4    "lib": ["ES2024"],

"lib": ["ES2024"] — which built-in JavaScript features exist. The shared settings also include DOM, the browser's features (windows, buttons, cameras). The SDK runs on servers, where there is no DOM, so it is left out: a mistaken use of window is then caught as an error.

5    "module": "NodeNext",
6    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",

"module" and "moduleResolution": "NodeNext" — follow Node.js's own rules for modules, exactly. The web apps use a bundler that is more forgiving; a library that Node.js loads directly must follow Node.js's rules, so every import of our own files is written with its .js ending (./errors.js), as Node.js requires.

7    "types": ["node"],

"types": ["node"] — load the type descriptions of Node.js's built-ins: fetch, Response, AbortSignal, Buffer…

8    "noEmit": true

"noEmit": true — only check; never write JavaScript files. Writing is the job of tsconfig.build.json.

9  },

The closing brace of the options.

10  "include": ["src", "test"]

"include" — check both the source code (src) and the tests (test).

11}

The closing brace.

The settings for building the SDK: turning its TypeScript into the JavaScript and type files that other code uses. They extend the checking settings (tsconfig.json) and change four things.

1{

The opening brace.

2  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",

"extends": "./tsconfig.json" — start from the checking settings, so the build is held to exactly the same rules.

3  "compilerOptions": {

The changes.

4    "noEmit": false,

"noEmit": false — this time, do write files.

5    "rootDir": "src",

"rootDir": "src" — the source files live in src/…

6    "outDir": "dist",

"outDir": "dist" — …and the results go to dist/, with the same folder layout: src/token.ts becomes dist/token.js.

7    "declaration": true

"declaration": true — also write a declaration file (.d.ts) beside each JavaScript file. It contains only the types — no code — so that TypeScript users of the SDK get the same checking and autocomplete as if they had the source.

"include": ["src"] — build only the source. The tests are checked, but never shipped.

packages/sdk-node/src/errors.ts19 lines · 100% explained

The SDK's two kinds of error. A website's code can tell them apart with instanceof, and react differently: an AgeTokenError means "don't let this person in"; a DwarpalApiError carries the API's own explanation.

This is the first TypeScript file in the book walked through line by line; §4.15 explains the language.

1/** The API refused a request. `code` is stable and meant for programs; `message` is meant for people. */

A doc comment: /** … */ just before something describes it. Editors show it when you hover over a use of DwarpalApiError. It says that code is for programs and message for people — the same split as the API's problem details (§4.13).

2export class DwarpalApiError extends Error {

export class DwarpalApiError extends Error — a class (a blueprint for objects) that extends JavaScript's built-in Error: it is an error in every way, plus what's added below. export makes it importable from other files.

3  override readonly name = "DwarpalApiError";

override readonly name = "DwarpalApiError" — every error has a name, shown in error messages and logs. override says on purpose: "I am replacing the name that Error already has" — with the project's strict settings, TypeScript insists on that word, so a replacement can never happen by accident. readonly means it can't be changed after the object is made.

4  readonly status: number;
5  readonly code: string;
6  readonly requestId: string | null;

Three more fields, each with its type:

  • status — the HTTP status code, a number;
  • code — the API's stable code, a string;
  • requestId — the request's ID from the X-Request-Id header, or null if there wasn't one. string | null reads "a string or null".
7
8  constructor(status: number, code: string, message: string, requestId: string | null) {

The constructor — the function that runs when a new error is made with new DwarpalApiError(…). It takes the four values, each with its type.

9    super(message);

super(message) — first run Error's own constructor, which stores the human message. A class that extends another must call super before using this.

10    this.status = status;
11    this.code = code;
12    this.requestId = requestId;

Store the other three values on the new object. this means "the object being made".

13  }
14}

The closing braces of the constructor and the class.

15
16/** An age token failed verification: its signature, issuer, audience, type, age or session didn't check out. */

The doc comment for the second error: an age token that failed any check.

17export class AgeTokenError extends Error {
18  override readonly name = "AgeTokenError";
19}

AgeTokenError needs nothing beyond its own name: the message says what went wrong, and cause (set where it is thrown, in token.ts) holds the original error from jose, for debugging.

packages/sdk-node/src/client.ts158 lines · 100% explained

DwarpalClient — the SDK's way for a website's server to talk to the API: create a session, and read its result. It wraps the two relying-party endpoints (§5.1.3) in ordinary functions with typed inputs and outputs, so a website writes await client.createSession({ policy: "uk_osa_18" }) instead of building HTTP requests by hand.

It is careful in both directions:

  • what it sends — the key's shape is checked once, when the client is made; session IDs are checked before any request goes out;
  • what it receives — every field of every answer is checked against its expected type before the website sees it. If the API ever answered something unexpected, the SDK says so clearly instead of handing over a half-broken object.
1import { DwarpalApiError } from "./errors.js";

The SDK's error class for refusals from the API.

2
3export const STATUSES = [
4  "created",
5  "in_progress",
6  "awaiting_step_up",
7  "completed",
8  "expired",
9  "canceled",
10] as const;

STATUSES — the six session statuses, as a list. as const tells TypeScript that this list will never change, so it may remember the exact texts ("created", "in_progress", …) rather than just "some strings".

11export const OUTCOMES = ["pass", "fail", "reject", "step_up"] as const;

OUTCOMES — the outcomes a session can end with, in the same way. (step_up appears here, though not in tokens: a session waiting for a stronger check has that outcome, but no token.)

12export type SessionStatus = (typeof STATUSES)[number];
13export type SessionOutcome = (typeof OUTCOMES)[number];

Two types made from the lists. (typeof STATUSES)[number] reads: "the type of any element of STATUSES" — which, thanks to as const, is exactly "created" | "in_progress" | …. Writing each status once, in the list, gives both the runtime check (below) and the type, so the two can never disagree.

18  /** The Dwarpal API's address, such as `https://api.dwarpal.example`. */

timeoutMs? — optional: how long to wait for an answer before giving up. Default 10 seconds.

22  /** Replace the HTTP function, for tests. Default: the built-in `fetch`. */

fetch? — optional: the function used to send HTTP requests. typeof fetch means "anything shaped exactly like the built-in fetch". Tests pass a fake one that answers instantly, without a network (client.test.ts).

56type Json = Record<string, unknown>;

Json — a short name for "an object with text keys and values of unknown type": what parsed JSON looks like before it is checked. unknown is TypeScript's safest type: nothing can be done with an unknown value until its type has been checked.

58const API_KEY = /^dk_(test|live)_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}$/;

Two regular expressions (as in Python's re, §5.1.3), between slashes: the shape of an API key — dk_test_ or dk_live_ followed by at least 20 key characters — and of a session ID.

61function field<T>(data: Json, key: string, accept: (value: unknown) => value is T): T {

field — read one field from an answer, and check it. <T> makes it a generic function: T stands for whatever type the check is about, so field(data, "id", isText) returns a string, and field(data, "attempts", isCount) a number.

The third parameter, accept, is a type guard: a function returning value is T, which tells TypeScript "if I return true, this value is a T".

62  const value = data[key];
63  if (!accept(value)) {
64    throw new TypeError(`the API's answer has an unexpected "${key}"`);
65  }
66  return value;
67}

Look the field up. If the check fails, throw an error naming the field; otherwise return the value — now known to be a T.

69const isText = (value: unknown): value is string => typeof value === "string";
70const isFlag = (value: unknown): value is boolean => typeof value === "boolean";
71const isCount = (value: unknown): value is number => Number.isInteger(value);

Three simple type guards: text, a true-or-false flag, and a whole number. => defines a short arrow function.

72const oneOf =
73  <T extends string>(allowed: readonly T[]) =>
74  (value: unknown): value is T =>
75    allowed.includes(value as T);

oneOf — makes a type guard that accepts only the values in a given list. It is a function that returns a function: oneOf(STATUSES) is a guard for statuses. as T is needed only because includes expects a value of the list's own type; the check itself is exact.

76const orNull =
77  <T>(accept: (value: unknown) => value is T) =>
78  (value: unknown): value is T | null =>
79    value === null || accept(value);

orNull — turns any guard into one that also accepts null: orNull(isText) accepts text or null.

80const dateOrNull = (value: string | null): Date | null => (value === null ? null : new Date(value));

dateOrNull — turns a timestamp text into a Date, and null into null.

DwarpalClient — the class.

Four private fields. A name that starts with # is truly private in JavaScript: no code outside the class can read it, at all. Nobody can accidentally log client.#apiKey, or read it in a debugger's autocomplete list.

The constructor checks the key's shape first. A key pasted with a missing character, or a key from another service, fails right here, when the website starts — not later, when the first visitor arrives.

136    const headers: Record<string, string> = {

The headers: the key as a bearer token, and a request for JSON. Only a request with a body says what kind of body it is (Content-Type).

Send the request with the chosen fetch:

Parse the answer as JSON. If the body isn't JSON at all, .catch(() => null) turns the error into null. Then keep it only if it really is an object; otherwise use an empty one. From here on, data is safe to look into.

151    if (!response.ok) {

response.ok is true for statuses 200–299. Anything else becomes a DwarpalApiError, built from the problem details (§4.13): the stable code, the sentence, the status, and the request ID from the headers — or generic values if the answer wasn't problem details at all.

packages/sdk-node/src/token.ts85 lines · 100% explained

The most important file of the SDK: verifyAgeToken, the function a website calls before letting anyone in. It answers one question — does this token prove that this visitor passed my age check? — and it answers "yes" only when every one of these is true:

Check Why
the signature is valid, made by one of the API's published keys nobody else can make a token
the algorithm is exactly Ed25519 no algorithm tricks (§4.12)
the token's type is dwarpal-age+jwt no other kind of token can be passed off as an age token
it was issued by the expected API (iss) tokens from another issuer are refused
it is addressed to this website (aud) a token stolen from another website is useless here
it hasn't expired (exp), and is already valid (nbf) old tokens can't be replayed for ever
it describes the session this visitor just finished (sid) a token from someone else's session can't be swapped in
the outcome is pass and age_over_<the site's age> is literally true the answer is unmistakable, and only for the age the site asked about (ADR-0020)

Any failed check throws an AgeTokenError. A website's code should treat any error from this function as "no entry".

From jose:

  • jwtVerify — checks a JWT's signature and standard claims;
  • createRemoteJWKSet — fetches a key set from an address, and keeps it;
  • errors — jose's error classes;
  • JWTPayload and JWTVerifyGetKey — types: a token's claims, and "something that finds the right key for a token".

Outcome — a union type of three exact strings (§4.15): a variable of this type can only ever hold "pass", "fail" or "reject". TypeScript reports any other value as an error before the code ever runs.

12export interface VerifyAgeTokenOptions {

interface VerifyAgeTokenOptions — the shape of the second argument. An interface describes an object: which properties it has, and their types.

13  /** The API's issuer address, exactly as in its discovery document. */

issuer — the API's address, exactly as its discovery document states it.

15  /** Your project's ID (`prj_…`). Tokens addressed to anyone else are refused. */
16  audience: string;

audience — the website's own project ID.

17  /** The minimum age your site requires. Only a token stating `age_over_<minAge>: true` allows entry. */
18  minAge: number;

minAge — the age the website requires. The token must speak about exactly this age.

19  /** The session you expect, from the redirect back to your site. A token about any other session is refused. */

sessionId? — the ? makes it optional. Passing it is strongly recommended: the website knows which session the visitor just came back from (from ?session_id= in the address), and the token must be about that one.

21  /** Where the public keys come from. By default they are fetched from the issuer, cached, and refetched for a new key. */
22  keys?: JWTVerifyGetKey;

keys? — optional too: where to get public keys. Normal use leaves it out, and the keys are fetched from the issuer. Tests pass keys of their own.

23}

The interface ends.

25export interface AgeVerdict {
26  /** True only if the check passed for exactly the age you asked about. */
27  allowed: boolean;
28  outcome: Outcome;
29  sessionId: string;
30  policy: string;
31  livemode: boolean;
32  expiresAt: Date;
33}

interface AgeVerdict — what the function returns. Most important is allowed: the only field a website needs for its decision. The others are for its records: the outcome, the session, the policy, whether it was a live check, and when the token expires — as a Date object.

35const remoteKeys = new Map<string, JWTVerifyGetKey>();

remoteKeys — a Map (a dictionary that can hold any kind of key) from issuer address to its key fetcher. It lives as long as the website's server process, so the keys are fetched once and reused for every token, instead of once per visitor.

36
37function keysOf(issuer: string): JWTVerifyGetKey {

keysOf — the key fetcher for an issuer, created on first use. It isn't exported: it is the SDK's private business.

38  let keys = remoteKeys.get(issuer);
39  if (keys === undefined) {

Look in the map. If there's nothing for this issuer yet…

40    keys = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${issuer.replace(/\/+$/, "")}/.well-known/jwks.json`));

…create a fetcher for <issuer>/.well-known/jwks.json. issuer.replace(/\/+$/, "") first removes any slash at the end, so https://api.example/ and https://api.example give the same address. The text between ` backticks is a template literal: ${…} puts a value into the text.

jose's fetcher keeps the keys for up to 10 minutes. When a token names a key it doesn't know — right after the API created a new one — it fetches the set again, at most once every 30 seconds.

41    remoteKeys.set(issuer, keys);
42  }
43  return keys;
44}

Remember the fetcher, and return it.

45
46async function verifiedClaims(token: string, options: VerifyAgeTokenOptions): Promise<JWTPayload> {

verifiedClaims — check the token, and return its claims, or throw. async means it returns a Promise (§4.15): a value that arrives later, here once the keys are fetched and the signature checked.

47  try {
48    const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, options.keys ?? keysOf(options.issuer), {

await jwtVerify(…) — wait for jose's verdict. The keys: the ones passed in, or (?? means "if that is missing, use this") the issuer's published ones. const { payload } = … takes just the payload property out of the result — this is called destructuring.

49      issuer: options.issuer,
50      audience: options.audience,
51      algorithms: [ALGORITHM],
52      typ: TOKEN_TYPE,
53      requiredClaims: ["exp", "iat", "jti", "sid", "outcome"],

The rules jose must enforce, in addition to the signature:

  • issuer and audience — the iss and aud claims must match exactly;
  • algorithms: [ALGORITHM] — the allow-list: only Ed25519;
  • typ: TOKEN_TYPE — the header's type must match;
  • requiredClaims — these claims must be present at all. A token missing its expiry, its ID, its session or its outcome is refused outright, rather than read with gaps.

jose also checks exp (not expired) and nbf (not too early) automatically.

54    });
55    return payload;

The checks passed: return the claims.

56  } catch (error) {
57    if (error instanceof errors.JOSEError) {
58      throw new AgeTokenError(`the age token is not valid (${error.code})`, { cause: error });
59    }

If jose refused the token, throw our own AgeTokenError instead. The message includes jose's short error code — such as ERR_JWT_EXPIRED — and { cause: error } keeps jose's full error attached, for whoever is debugging.

60    throw error;

Any other error — say, the network failed while fetching keys — is passed on unchanged. It is still an error, so the visitor still isn't let in.

61  }
62}

The closing braces.

63
64/** Check an age token's signature and claims, and say whether it allows entry at `minAge`. Throws if it is invalid. */
65export async function verifyAgeToken(token: string, options: VerifyAgeTokenOptions): Promise<AgeVerdict> {

verifyAgeToken — the public function. It returns a Promise<AgeVerdict>: a verdict, once the checks are done.

66  if (!Number.isInteger(options.minAge) || options.minAge < 1) {
67    throw new RangeError("minAge must be a whole number of years, such as 18");
68  }

First check the website's own input: minAge must be a whole number of at least 1. A typo such as 18.5 throws a RangeError at once, instead of quietly never matching any token.

69  const claims = await verifiedClaims(token, options);

Verify the token, and get its claims.

70  const { outcome, sid, exp } = claims;

Take three claims out by destructuring: outcome, sid (the session) and exp (the expiry).

71  if (outcome !== "pass" && outcome !== "fail" && outcome !== "reject") {
72    throw new AgeTokenError("the age token has an unknown outcome");
73  }

The outcome must be one of the three known values. jose only knows standard claims; this one is ours, so we check it ourselves.

74  if (typeof sid !== "string" || (options.sessionId !== undefined && sid !== options.sessionId)) {
75    throw new AgeTokenError("the age token describes a different session");
76  }

The session must be text — and, if the website said which session it expects, exactly that one.

77  return {
78    allowed: outcome === "pass" && claims[`age_over_${options.minAge}`] === true,

The verdict. allowed is true only if the outcome is pass and the claim named after the website's age — built by a template literal, such as age_over_18 — is exactly true. === means "exactly equal, with no conversion": the text "true" or the number 1 would not count.

79    outcome,
80    sessionId: sid,
81    policy: typeof claims.policy === "string" ? claims.policy : "",
82    livemode: claims.livemode === true,
83    expiresAt: new Date((exp ?? 0) * 1000),
84  };

The record-keeping fields. typeof claims.policy === "string" ? … : "" is the conditional operator (condition ? if-true : if-false): use the policy if it is text, otherwise empty text. Token times are seconds since 1970, while JavaScript's Date counts milliseconds — hence * 1000.

85}

packages/sdk-node/src/index.ts18 lines · 100% explained

The SDK's front door — the file that package.json's exports points to (after building, as dist/index.js). It contains no code of its own: it gathers the public parts of the other files, so a website writes one import:

import { DwarpalClient, verifyAgeToken } from "@dwarpal/node";

Anything not listed here stays private to the SDK, such as the helper functions inside client.ts. This is the same idea as the Python packages' __init__.py files (§5.1.1).

From client.ts: the DwarpalClient class, and the types that describe its inputs and outputs. The word type in front of a name says "this is only a type": it exists while TypeScript checks the code, and disappears completely from the JavaScript that runs. The project's settings (verbatimModuleSyntax) require that word, so it is always clear which imports cost nothing at run time.

The .js ending in "./client.js" looks odd in a TypeScript file, but it names the file as Node.js will see it after building (see tsconfig.json).

packages/sdk-node/test/token.test.ts107 lines · 100% explained

The tests for verifyAgeToken. They don't need the real API: they make their own Ed25519 key pair, sign tokens with it exactly as the API would, and check what the SDK decides. That way each test can make precisely the token it wants — including tokens the real API would never produce, such as forgeries.

Tests run with Vitest (§4.20), whose building blocks read almost like English: describe groups tests, it("does something", …) is one test, and expect(value).toBe(expected) is one check.

From jose, the tools for making tokens:

  • generateKeyPair and exportJWK — a fresh key pair, and its public half as a JWK;
  • createLocalJWKSet — a key set held in memory, instead of fetched from an address;
  • SignJWT — builds and signs a token;
  • UnsecuredJWT — builds a token with no signature at all, for the attack test below;
  • CryptoKey and JWTPayload — types.

30    keys: createLocalJWKSet({ keys: [publicJwk] }),
31  };

The verification options every test starts from: the issuer, the audience, an 18+ requirement, the expected session, and a key set containing just the test key.

32});

The end of beforeAll.

33
34function claims(changes: JWTPayload = {}): JWTPayload {
35  const base = { iss: ISSUER, aud: AUDIENCE, jti: "0192a6f0-0000-7000-8000-000000000000", sid: SESSION };
36  return { ...base, outcome: "pass", age_over_18: true, policy: "uk_osa_18", livemode: false, ...changes };
37}

claims — the claims of a perfect "pass" token, with any changes a test asks for. Because ...changes comes last, a test's values replace the defaults: claims({ outcome: "fail" }) changes only the outcome.

38
39async function sign(
40  payload: JWTPayload,
41  typ = "dwarpal-age+jwt",
42  expires: number | string = "10m",
43): Promise<string> {

sign — make a signed token from claims. Two optional parameters with defaults: the token type (normally the right one) and the expiry (normally 10 minutes from now; "10m" is jose's short way of saying so).

44  return new SignJWT(payload)
45    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "Ed25519", typ, kid: "sig_test" })
46    .setIssuedAt()
47    .setExpirationTime(expires)
48    .sign(privateKey);

jose builds tokens step by step, each step returning the builder again — a style called method chaining: set the header (algorithm, type, key ID), stamp the issue time, set the expiry, and sign with the private key.

49}

The end of sign.

50
51describe("verifyAgeToken", () => {

All the tests below are about verifyAgeToken.

52  it("allows entry for a passed check at exactly the required age", async () => {
53    const verdict = await verifyAgeToken(await sign(claims()), options);
54    expect(verdict.allowed).toBe(true);
55    expect(verdict.outcome).toBe("pass");
56    expect(verdict.sessionId).toBe(SESSION);
57    expect(verdict.policy).toBe("uk_osa_18");
58    expect(verdict.livemode).toBe(false);
59    expect(verdict.expiresAt.getTime()).toBeGreaterThan(Date.now());
60  });

A passed check, at exactly the required age, allows entry — and every field of the verdict carries the token's facts, with an expiry in the future.

61
62  it("never allows entry for a failed check, whatever the age claim says", async () => {
63    const failed = await verifyAgeToken(await sign(claims({ outcome: "fail", age_over_18: false })), options);
64    const contradictory = await verifyAgeToken(await sign(claims({ outcome: "fail" })), options);
65    expect(failed.allowed).toBe(false);
66    expect(contradictory.allowed).toBe(false);
67  });

A failed check never allows entry, whatever the age claim says. The first token is an honest "fail". The second is contradictory: outcome: fail, but still age_over_18: true (inherited from the defaults). The real API never makes such a token, but the SDK must not be fooled by one: both must give allowed: false.

68
69  it("does not let a check for a lower age satisfy a higher requirement", async () => {
70    const teen = claims({ age_over_13: true, policy: "teen_13" });
71    delete teen.age_over_18;
72    expect((await verifyAgeToken(await sign(teen), options)).allowed).toBe(false);
73  });

A check for a lower age can't satisfy a higher requirement. The token says age_over_13: true — and delete removes its age_over_18 claim. A website requiring 18 must not let this visitor in (ADR-0020).

74
75  it("refuses tokens for someone else, of another type, or about another session", async () => {
76    const token = await sign(claims());
77    await expect(
78      verifyAgeToken(token, { ...options, audience: "prj_SOMEONEELSE000000000000000" }),
79    ).rejects.toThrow(AgeTokenError);
80    await expect(verifyAgeToken(await sign(claims(), "JWT"), options)).rejects.toThrow(AgeTokenError);
81    await expect(
82      verifyAgeToken(token, { ...options, sessionId: "vs_01M51KF05CE4GSBH7F0G43G0ZZ" }),
83    ).rejects.toThrow(/different session/);
84  });

Tokens for someone else, of another type, or about another session are refused. One valid token is checked as if by a website with a different project ID; another token is signed with the generic type JWT; and the valid token is checked against a different expected session. rejects.toThrow(…) says: "this promise must fail with this kind of error" — or with a message matching /different session/.

85
86  it("refuses expired tokens", async () => {
87    const expired = await sign(claims(), "dwarpal-age+jwt", Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 60);
88    await expect(verifyAgeToken(expired, options)).rejects.toThrow(AgeTokenError);
89  });

Expired tokens are refused: this one expired 60 seconds ago. Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) is the current time in whole seconds, as JWTs count it.

90
91  it("accepts only Ed25519 signatures: no shared secrets, and never no signature at all", async () => {
92    const shared = await new SignJWT(claims())
93      .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "HS256", typ: "dwarpal-age+jwt" })
94      .setIssuedAt()
95      .setExpirationTime("10m")
96      .sign(new TextEncoder().encode("a-shared-secret-that-anyone-could-hold"));

Only Ed25519. The first forgery is signed with HS256 — a shared-secret algorithm. A careless verifier that let the token choose its algorithm could be tricked into checking it with a secret the attacker knows. TextEncoder turns text into bytes for the secret.

97    const unsigned = new UnsecuredJWT(claims()).setIssuedAt().setExpirationTime("10m").encode();

The second forgery has no signature at all: the historic "alg": "none" attack (§4.12).

98    await expect(verifyAgeToken(shared, options)).rejects.toThrow(AgeTokenError);
99    await expect(verifyAgeToken(unsigned, options)).rejects.toThrow(AgeTokenError);
100  });

Both must be refused.

101
102  it("insists on a whole number of years", async () => {
103    await expect(verifyAgeToken(await sign(claims()), { ...options, minAge: 17.5 })).rejects.toThrow(
104      RangeError,
105    );
106  });

minAge must be a whole number: 17.5 is a mistake in the website's code, reported as a RangeError rather than silently never matching.

107});

The end of the group.

apps/web/next.config.ts37 lines · 100% explained

The verify page's Next.js configuration, and above all its security headers: instructions sent with every page that tell the browser what this page may and may not do. The verify page handles a camera, a one-time secret and a flow token, so it gets the strictest rules the app can work with.

Explain like I'm six — house rules on the door

A sign on a door says "no shoes, no dogs, no strangers upstairs". The browser is the strict babysitter who reads the sign and enforces it — even against code that somehow got into the house. Security headers are that sign.

1import type { NextConfig } from "next";

The type of a Next.js configuration, so mistakes in it are caught by the type checker. import type brings in only the type, nothing that runs.

2
3const apiUrl = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DWARPAL_API_URL ?? "http://localhost:8000";

apiUrl — the API's address, from NEXT_PUBLIC_DWARPAL_API_URL, or the local one. In Next.js, variables starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ are built into the page's code, so the browser knows where the API is.

4const development = process.env.NODE_ENV === "development";

development — true when running the development server.

5
6const contentSecurityPolicy = [
7  "default-src 'self'",
8  `connect-src 'self' ${apiUrl}`,
9  "img-src 'self' data: blob:",
10  "media-src 'self' blob:",
11  "font-src 'self'",
12  "style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'",
13  // 'wasm-unsafe-eval' lets the browser compile WebAssembly (MediaPipe) — and only that: no eval of JavaScript.
14  `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'${development ? " 'unsafe-eval'" : ""}`,
15  "object-src 'none'",
16  "base-uri 'none'",
17  "form-action 'self'",
18  "frame-ancestors 'none'",
19].join("; ");

The Content Security Policy (CSP): a list of rules about where the page may load things from and send things to. Each rule is one text, and .join("; ") puts them into one header value. 'self' means "this page's own origin".

Rule Means
default-src 'self' anything not covered below: only from this origin
connect-src 'self' <API> the page's code may talk only to itself and the API. Even injected code couldn't send a picture anywhere else
img-src 'self' data: blob: images from this origin, or made in memory
media-src 'self' blob: video only from this origin or from memory — the camera's stream is in memory
font-src 'self' fonts only from this origin
style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' styles from this origin, plus inline ones, which Next.js uses
script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' scripts from this origin, plus the inline ones Next.js writes into each page to start React
object-src 'none' no plug-ins, ever
base-uri 'none' no <base> tag may change what relative addresses mean
form-action 'self' forms may only send to this origin
frame-ancestors 'none' no other website may show this page inside a frame. That blocks clickjacking: a hostile site hiding this page under its own buttons

Line 13 adds 'unsafe-eval' only in development, where React's live reloading needs it. A production build never gets it.

Careful — honest about a gap

'unsafe-inline' for scripts weakens the policy: if an attacker ever managed to inject a <script> into the page, the browser would run it. The strict fix is a nonce — a fresh random value per page, which every allowed script must carry. It needs per-request rendering, and it is scheduled for the security-hardening phase (Phase 7). The other rules, especially connect-src, already limit what any injected code could do.

One addition in Phase 3: 'wasm-unsafe-eval' in script-src. MediaPipe's face landmarker runs as WebAssembly, a fast, compact program format browsers run beside JavaScript. A strict policy forbids compiling it; this word allows compiling WebAssembly and nothing else. Unlike 'unsafe-eval', it never lets text be run as JavaScript, so the protection against injected scripts stays intact.

20
21const securityHeaders = [
22  { key: "Content-Security-Policy", value: contentSecurityPolicy },
23  { key: "Permissions-Policy", value: "camera=(self), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()" },
24  { key: "Referrer-Policy", value: "no-referrer" },
25  { key: "X-Content-Type-Options", value: "nosniff" },
26  { key: "Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy", value: "same-origin" },
27];

The security headers, as a list of name and value pairs:

  • the CSP from above;
  • Permissions-Policy — which powerful browser features the page may use: the camera, for this page itself only (camera=(self)), and never the microphone, location or payments (() means "nobody");
  • Referrer-Policy: no-referrer — when the person leaves, don't tell the next site which address they came from. The address contains the session's ID;
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — the browser must trust the declared type of each file, and never guess. Guessing has let attackers disguise scripts as images;
  • Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin — a window opened by another site can't hold a handle on this page.
28
29const config: NextConfig = {

The configuration object, checked against NextConfig.

30  poweredByHeader: false,

poweredByHeader: false — don't announce "X-Powered-By: Next.js" in every response. Telling strangers exactly which software runs a site helps no one but attackers.

31  reactStrictMode: true,

reactStrictMode: true — in development, React runs certain parts twice on purpose, to bring hidden bugs to the surface (see verify-flow.tsx).

32  async headers() {
33    return [{ source: "/:path*", headers: securityHeaders }];
34  },

headers() — Next.js asks this function which headers to add. The answer: on every path (/:path* matches all of them), the security headers above.

35};

The end of the object.

36
37export default config;

Hand the configuration to Next.js.

Saffron is the colour of marigolds and temple doorways — the place where a dwarpal, a doorkeeper, stands.

Respecting reduced motion

Some people get dizzy or unwell from movement on screen, and ask their system to reduce it. Every animation in this app is written as motion-safe:animate-…: Tailwind applies it only when the visitor has not asked for reduced motion. Nothing needs to be switched off afterwards.

The verify page: talking to the API, and to the camera

apps/web/lib/flow-api.ts145 lines · 100% explained

The verify page's client for the flow API (§5.1.3): four methods, one per step of the check, that run in the person's browser.

start(secret)   →  flow token + what this check is about
attempt(frames) →  a fresh challenge, then the upload → pass / fail / retry / step up / reject
finish()        →  the address to return to

It is the browser's twin of the SDK's DwarpalClient, with one difference in attitude: an answer it can't read degrades to safe defaults (empty text, zero) instead of throwing. Any real problem still arrives as an error status from the API, which becomes a FlowError — and the screens show a friendly message for it (advice.ts).

1/** The verify page's client for the Dwarpal flow API. After `start`, every call carries the session's flow token. */

The doc comment: the client, and the rule that every call after start carries the flow token.

2

From challenge.ts (Phase 3): the Challenge type, readChallenge (which turns the API's answer into one), and the Signals type. The type keyword inside the braces marks which names are only types.

Keep the flow token, in a private field. It lives only in this page's memory: not in the address, not in browser storage, and gone the moment the tab closes.

The device ID is a parameter whose default is deviceId() — evaluated each time the method is called without one. Tests pass their own. Post to /challenge with no body (null), adding the X-Dwarpal-Device header when there is an ID ({} adds nothing), then check and convert the answer with readChallenge.

85  async attempt(captured: CapturedAttempt): Promise<AttemptResult> {
86    const { frames, signals } = captured;

attempt — upload one attempt. const { frames, signals } = captured; is destructuring: it takes those two fields out of captured into variables of the same names, to keep the lines below short.

87    const form = new FormData();

Build a multipart form (§4.13). FormData is the browser's own builder for one.

88    form.set("challenge_id", captured.challengeId);

The challenge's ID, as a text field.

89    form.set(
90      "meta",

93        light_started_ms: captured.lightStartedMs === null ? null : Math.round(captured.lightStartedMs),
94        signals: {
95          automation: signals.automation,

The meta field: a JSON description of the attempt, in the API's spelling (t_ms, not tMs):

  • frames — for each one, its position (index), when it was taken (t_ms, rounded to whole milliseconds) and its phase. map turns each frame into a new value; its second argument is the position in the list;
  • light_started_ms — when the colours began, rounded, or null. a === null ? x : y means "if a is null, x, otherwise y";

120    path: string,

123  ): Promise<Json> {

#post — the one private method that sends every request. Its body may be JSON text, a form, or nothing; extra holds any additional headers, none by default.

124    const headers: Record<string, string> = { Accept: "application/json", ...extra };

Only JSON text gets an explicit Content-Type. For a FormData body, the browser writes the header itself, including the random boundary that separates the parts. Setting it by hand would leave the boundary out, and the server couldn't read the form.

apps/web/lib/camera.ts182 lines · 100% explained

Everything the verify page does with the camera: open it, play a liveness challenge on it, and switch it off (§4.19). Since Phase 3 the photos are no longer a quick burst of identical shots. The page plays the server's challenge (§5.3): first a few screen colours, one photo per colour, then a head pose per prompt, three photos per pose once it is held. Each photo is labelled with the part of the challenge it belongs to.

The photos never touch the device's storage: they exist as bytes in the page's memory, travel once to the API, and are forgotten.

1/** The camera: open it, play a liveness challenge on it — screen colours, then head poses — and switch it off again. */

The doc comment: open the camera, play a challenge on it — screen colours, then head poses — and switch it off.
