3import {
4  type Challenge,
5  CUES,
6  frontalAngles,
7  type HeadAngles,
8  type Phase,
9  type Pose,
10  poseProgress,
11} from "./challenge";

From challenge.ts: the Challenge type, CUES (the instruction for each pose), frontalAngles (the person's own angles when facing the camera), the types HeadAngles, Phase and Pose, and poseProgress, which says how much of a pose the head has reached. The list is written one name per line because it is too long for one.

12
13const MAX_WIDTH = 960;

MAX_WIDTH = 960 — photos are at most 960 pixels wide. More pixels wouldn't help the AI, which works on small, aligned face crops (§5.1.1); they would only make the upload bigger and slower.

14const JPEG_QUALITY = 0.85;

JPEG_QUALITY = 0.85 — 85 % JPEG quality: visually almost perfect, and a fraction of the size of an uncompressed picture. A 960 × 540 photo then comes to well under the 512 KiB limit per frame.

15/** Frames taken without screen colours, when the person has asked their device for less motion. */
16const CALM_BASELINE = 4;
17const CALM_GAP_MS = 300;

Calm mode. Some people set their device to reduce motion — flashing colours can be uncomfortable, and for a few people with photosensitive conditions, harmful. For them the page shows no colours and instead takes CALM_BASELINE = 4 ordinary frames, CALM_GAP_MS = 300 milliseconds apart. The light check then simply has nothing to measure, which never counts against anyone (it is recorded, not decided on).

18/** How long to wait for a pose before taking the frames anyway: the server judges them either way. */
19export const POSE_TIMEOUT_MS = 6000;

POSE_TIMEOUT_MS = 6000 — wait at most 6 seconds for each pose. Then the photos are taken anyway. As the comment says, the server judges every photo itself; the page's own view of the head only decides when to take them. A page that refused to go on would lock out anyone whose face the guidance can't read. export lets the camera screen use the same number.

20/** A pose must be seen this many readings in a row, so a passing wobble doesn't count. */
21const STEADY_READINGS = 3;

STEADY_READINGS = 3 — a pose counts as reached only after 3 readings in a row show it (about a twentieth of a second). A head passing through the pose on its way somewhere else doesn't trigger the photos.

22/** Photos taken of each pose once it is held, this far apart: the server counts the best of them. */
23const FRAMES_PER_POSE = 2;

Once a pose is held, take FRAMES_PER_POSE = 2 photos of it. As the comment says, the server counts the best of them, so a blink or a small movement at the wrong moment doesn't spoil the pose.

24/** One more photo on the way, once the head is this far into the pose: a real head passes through the angles between,
25 * while swiping between photos jumps straight from one pose to the next. */
26const HALFWAY = 0.4;

HALFWAY = 0.4 — and one more photo on the way, once the meter is 40 % full. The comment gives the reason, found in the owner's red-team tests: a real head passes through the angles between, while swiping between photos of a turned head jumps straight from one pose to the next. The server records whether each pose was caught partway.

27const POSE_GAP_MS = 150;

POSE_GAP_MS = 150 — the pause between the held photos.

28
29export interface LabelledFrame {
30  image: Blob;
31  tMs: number;
32  phase: Phase;
33}

LabelledFrame — one photo: the JPEG as a Blob (a chunk of raw bytes held by the browser), when it was taken (tMs, milliseconds since the challenge began), and its phase — "baseline" for the colour photos, or the pose it was taken for.

34
35export interface ChallengeHooks {
36  /** Show this colour around the screen, or none. */
37  onColour: (colour: string | null) => void;
38  /** Show this instruction, or none. */
39  onCue: (cue: string | null) => void;
40  onProgress: (taken: number, total: number) => void;
41  /** How much of the current pose is reached, from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.05 — or `null` when it can't be measured. */
42  onReach: (share: number | null) => void;
43  /** The head's angles now, from the landmarker — or `null` when it can't see a face or isn't running. */
44  readAngles: () => HeadAngles | null;
45  /** The person asked their device for less motion: no colours are shown. */
46  calm: boolean;
47}

ChallengeHooks — how the camera code talks to the screen, without knowing anything about how the screen looks:

  • onColour — show this colour around the screen, or none (null);
  • onCue — show this instruction, such as "Turn your head to your left, eyes on the screen", or none;
  • onProgress — how many photos are taken, out of how many;
  • onReach — how much of the current pose is reached, from 0 to 1, for the on-screen meter (null hides it);
  • readAngles — a function the camera code can call at any moment to get the head's current angles from the landmarker, or null;
  • calm — whether to use calm mode.

Passing functions in like this keeps camera.ts free of React, so it is easy to test and to reason about.

48
49export interface ChallengeRun {
50  frames: LabelledFrame[];
51  /** When the colours began, on the same clock as the frames — or `null` if none were shown. */
52  lightStartedMs: number | null;
53}

ChallengeRun — what a challenge produces: the frames, and when the colours began (null if none were shown). The server needs that start time to work out which colour was on screen when each photo was taken.

54
55export async function openCamera(): Promise<MediaStream> {

openCamera — ask the browser for the camera. It returns a MediaStream: a live flow of video frames.

56  return navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({

navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(…) — the browser's standard camera-and-microphone function. The first time, the browser asks the person for permission; if they refuse, the promise fails with a NotAllowedError, which the screens turn into "We need your camera".

57    audio: false,

audio: false — never the microphone.

58    video: { facingMode: "user", width: { ideal: 1280 }, height: { ideal: 720 } },

The video wishes: facingMode: "user" — the camera facing the person (a phone's front camera), not the one on the back; and an ideal size of 1280 × 720. "Ideal" is a wish, not a demand: a camera that can't do it gives its nearest size instead of failing.

59  });
60}

The closing brackets.

61
62export function closeCamera(stream: MediaStream | null): void {

closeCamera — switch the camera off. It accepts null, so callers can pass a stream that may not exist yet.

63  for (const track of stream?.getTracks() ?? []) {
64    track.stop();
65  }
66}

A stream is made of tracks (here, one video track). Stopping every track switches the camera off — and with it the camera's indicator light — immediately. stream?.getTracks() ?? [] means: the tracks if there is a stream, otherwise an empty list.

67
68const wait = (ms: number): Promise<void> => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

wait — a promise that comes true after the given number of milliseconds, built on the browser's timer setTimeout. await wait(300) pauses the challenge without freezing the page.

69const nextPaint = (): Promise<number> => new Promise((resolve) => requestAnimationFrame(resolve));

nextPaint — a promise that comes true just before the browser next draws the screen, usually 60 times a second. requestAnimationFrame is the browser's way of saying "call me at the next frame". Waiting for it is the natural pace for checking the head: no faster than the screen changes.

70
71function toJpeg(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement): Promise<Blob> {

toJpeg — turn the picture currently on a canvas (an in-memory drawing surface) into JPEG bytes.

72  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
73    canvas.toBlob(
74      (blob) => (blob === null ? reject(new Error("a frame could not be encoded")) : resolve(blob)),
75      "image/jpeg",
76      JPEG_QUALITY,
77    );
78  });
79}

canvas.toBlob is an older-style function that reports its result by calling a function back, instead of returning a promise. Wrapping it in new Promise((resolve, reject) => …) turns it into one, so it can be awaited. It asks for a JPEG at the chosen quality; if the browser gives null instead of a blob, the promise fails with a clear error.

80
81/** Wait until the head shows `pose` steadily, measured from its frontal `baseline`, or until the timeout, reporting how
82 * far it has got on the way. */
83async function holdPose(
84  pose: Pose,
85  baseline: HeadAngles | null,
86  hooks: Pick<ChallengeHooks, "readAngles" | "onReach">,
87  onHalfway: () => void,
88): Promise<void> {

holdPose — wait until the head shows the pose steadily, measured from its frontal angles (baseline), or until the timeout, whichever comes first — reporting how far it has got on the way. It is given the pose, the frontal angles (or null), two of the hooks, and onHalfway, a function to call once when the head is partway. Pick<ChallengeHooks, "readAngles" | "onReach"> is a type with just those two hooks taken from ChallengeHooks.

89  const deadline = performance.now() + POSE_TIMEOUT_MS;
90  let steady = 0;
91  let halfway = false;

The deadline — 6 seconds from now — a counter of steady readings, starting at 0, and whether the halfway photo has been taken yet.

92  while (performance.now() < deadline && steady < STEADY_READINGS) {

Keep going while there is time left and the pose hasn't yet been held for 3 readings.

93    await nextPaint();
94    const angles = hooks.readAngles();

Wait for the next screen frame, then read the head's angles.

95    const share = angles === null || baseline === null ? null : poseProgress(pose, angles, baseline);

How much of the pose is reached: a number from 0 to 1, or null if there is no reading or no frontal angles to measure from.

96    hooks.onReach(share === null ? null : Math.round(share * 20) / 20);

Report it for the meter, rounded to steps of 0.05 (Math.round(share * 20) / 20). The screen only redraws when the value changes, so rounding spares it 60 redraws a second for invisible differences.

97    if (!halfway && share !== null && share >= HALFWAY && share < 1) {
98      halfway = true;
99      onHalfway();
100    }

The first time the head is at least 40 % of the way there (but not yet all the way), call onHalfway — the caller takes a photo — and remember that it has been taken.

101    steady = share === 1 ? steady + 1 : 0;

A full meter (exactly 1) adds one to the counter; anything less starts again from 0. That is what makes the 3 readings in a row.

102  }
103}

The closing brackets. The function simply returns: either the pose was held or time ran out, and the caller takes the photos in both cases.

104
105/** Play `challenge` on a playing video and return the labelled frames. */
106export async function runChallenge(
107  video: HTMLVideoElement,
108  challenge: Challenge,
109  hooks: ChallengeHooks,
110): Promise<ChallengeRun> {

runChallenge — play the challenge on a video element that is showing the camera, and return the labelled frames. It receives the video, the challenge from the server, and the hooks.

111  const scale = Math.min(1, MAX_WIDTH / video.videoWidth);

The scale: shrink frames wider than 960 pixels, but never enlarge smaller ones (Math.min(1, …)).

112  const width = Math.round(video.videoWidth * scale);
113  const height = Math.round(video.videoHeight * scale);

The photos' size, scaled. Math.round because pixel sizes must be whole numbers.

114  const baseline = hooks.calm ? CALM_BASELINE : challenge.colours.length;
115  const total = baseline + challenge.poses.length * (FRAMES_PER_POSE + 1);

How many photos there will be, for the progress display: the baseline ones — one per colour, or the 4 calm ones — plus 3 per pose (2 held, 1 on the way). If the head jumps straight to a pose, its halfway photo isn't taken, so the count is a little generous.

116  const started = performance.now();

Start the stopwatch. performance.now() is a precise, steadily increasing clock in milliseconds, for measuring time spans.

117  const shots: { canvas: HTMLCanvasElement; tMs: number; phase: Phase }[] = [];

shots — the pictures taken, each kept as its own canvas with its time and label, still unencoded.

118  const frontal: HeadAngles[] = [];

frontal — the landmarker's readings taken with the baseline photos, from which the person's frontal angles are worked out.

119  // Each photo is only copied here, which is instant, and stamped with that moment. Encoding to JPEG can take a
120  // second on a busy laptop, so it waits until the challenge is over: done here, it would push later photos out of
121  // their colours, and the server matches photos to colours by their times alone.

The comment explains the most important timing rule, learned in the owner's tests. Copying a picture onto a canvas is instant; encoding it to JPEG took about a second on a busy laptop. Encoding during the challenge pushed later photos out of their colours — and the server matches photos to colours by their times alone — so every photo is stamped the moment it is copied, and encoded only when the challenge is over.

122  const snap = (phase: Phase): void => {

snap — take one photo with the given label. It is defined inside runChallenge so it can use the size, the stopwatch and the lists directly. It does no waiting: it returns at once.

123    const angles = phase === "baseline" ? hooks.readAngles() : null;
124    if (angles !== null) {
125      frontal.push(angles);
126    }

For a baseline photo, also note the landmarker's reading of the head at that moment, if there is one.

127    const canvas = document.createElement("canvas");
128    canvas.width = width;
129    canvas.height = height;
130    const context = canvas.getContext("2d");
131    if (context === null) {
132      throw new Error("this browser cannot draw camera frames");
133    }

A fresh canvas for this photo, at the photos' size, and its 2D drawing context. In the rare browser that can't provide one, stop with a clear error.

134    context.drawImage(video, 0, 0, width, height);

Copy the video's current picture onto it, scaled to fit. The picture is drawn as the camera sees it — not mirrored like the preview the person sees — so a head turned to the person's left appears turned to the left in the photo too, as the server expects.

135    shots.push({ canvas, tMs: performance.now() - started, phase });

Keep it, stamped with this moment and its label.

136    hooks.onProgress(shots.length, total);
137  };

Report progress, and close snap.

138
139  let lightStartedMs: number | null = null;

When the colours began — null until they do. let, not const, because it is set later.

140  if (hooks.calm) {
141    for (let index = 0; index < CALM_BASELINE; index += 1) {
142      await wait(CALM_GAP_MS);
143      snap("baseline");
144    }

Calm mode: 4 baseline photos, each after a 300 ms pause. No colours.

145  } else {
146    // Each colour starts exactly one step after the last, by the clock, so nothing slow can shift the timetable.

Otherwise, the colours, on a fixed timetable. As the comment says, each colour starts exactly one step after the last, by the clock, so nothing slow can shift it.

147    const light = performance.now() - started;

The timetable's starting point, measured on the stopwatch.

148    const until = (ms: number): Promise<void> =>
149      wait(Math.max(0, light + ms - (performance.now() - started)));

until — wait until a given moment on the timetable: ms milliseconds after the colours began. It works out how long that is from now; if the moment has already passed, it waits 0 (Math.max(0, …)) rather than a negative time.

150    lightStartedMs = light;

Remember the start, to send to the server.

151    for (const [step, colour] of challenge.colours.entries()) {

For each colour, with its position: entries() gives pairs of [position, colour], which const [step, colour] unpacks.

152      await until(step * challenge.stepMs);
153      hooks.onColour(colour);

At the colour's moment on the timetable, show it.

154      await until((step + 0.5) * challenge.stepMs);
155      snap("baseline");

Halfway through its time on screen, take the photo — by then the screen has certainly changed, and the camera has caught up with the new light.

156    }

The end of the loop.

157    await until(challenge.colours.length * challenge.stepMs);
158    hooks.onColour(null);
159  }

When the last colour's time is up, take the colour away.

160
161  const facing = frontalAngles(frontal);

The person's frontal angles: the median of the baseline readings, or null if there were none.

162  for (const pose of challenge.poses) {

Then the poses, one at a time, in the server's order.

163    hooks.onCue(CUES[pose]);

Show the pose's instruction, from CUES.

164    await holdPose(pose, facing, hooks, () => snap(pose));

Wait until the head shows the pose — measured from the frontal angles — or 6 seconds, taking a photo on the way when the head is partway (() => snap(pose) is the function holdPose calls).

165    for (let index = 0; index < FRAMES_PER_POSE; index += 1) {
166      snap(pose);
167      await wait(index + 1 < FRAMES_PER_POSE ? POSE_GAP_MS : 0);
168    }

Take the 2 held photos, labelled with the pose, 150 ms apart (no wait after the last one).

169    hooks.onReach(null);
170  }

Hide the meter until the next pose.

171  hooks.onCue(null);

Remove the last instruction.

172  const frames = await Promise.all(
173    shots.map(
174      async (shot): Promise<LabelledFrame> => ({
175        image: await toJpeg(shot.canvas),
176        tMs: shot.tMs,
177        phase: shot.phase,
178      }),
179    ),
180  );

Now encode every photo to JPEG, all at once: shots.map(async …) starts an encoding per photo, and Promise.all waits until every one has finished, keeping their order. Each becomes a LabelledFrame with its original time and label.

181  return { frames, lightStartedMs };
182}

Return the frames and the colours' start time.

apps/web/lib/advice.ts81 lines · 100% explained

The API speaks in short codes such as too_dark or session_not_open — stable and precise, but not words to show a person. This file turns them into friendly sentences, in two kinds:

  • a tip after a "retry", saying how to take better photos;
  • a problem — a title and an explanation — when something stops the check.

Keeping every sentence in one file has two benefits: the wording can be improved without touching any logic, and when the page is translated into other languages (a later phase), this is the one file to translate.

1/** Friendly words for the API's short codes: a tip when photos weren't good enough, and a message when something stops the check. */

The doc comment.

2
3const TIPS: Record<string, string> = {
4  undecodable: "Your camera's pictures couldn't be read. Please try again.",
5  no_face: "We couldn't see a face. Look straight into the camera.",
6  multiple_faces: "We can see more than one face. Make sure only you are in view.",
7  face_too_small: "Move a little closer to the camera.",
8  too_dark: "It's too dark. Face a window or a lamp.",
9  too_bright: "There's too much light. Turn away from bright lights behind you.",
10  too_blurry: "The photos were blurry. Hold still while they are taken.",
11  not_frontal: "Look straight at the camera, not to the side.",
12  low_confidence: "We couldn't see your face clearly. Uncover your face and try again.",
13  inconsistent_frames: "Keep still and stay in view while the photos are taken.",
14  analysis_unavailable: "The checker is busy right now. Please try again in a moment.",
15  // Liveness: deliberately the same words whichever check it was, so nobody can learn which one to fool.
16  liveness_check_failed:
17    "Follow the prompts on screen: turn your head when asked, and keep your face in view.",
18  liveness_unavailable: "We couldn't complete the check. Please try again.",
19};

TIPS — one tip per reason code the decision engine can give (§5.1.2, ADVICE_ORDER), plus the two extra ones that come from the decision rules: inconsistent_frames and analysis_unavailable. Each says what to do, in plain words: "Face a window or a lamp", not "insufficient illumination".

Record<string, string> is TypeScript's type for "an object whose keys and values are all text".

Phase 3 adds two liveness tips. They are deliberately vague, the same words whichever liveness check failed (the comment on line 15): if the page said "your photo was detected", an attacker would learn exactly which check to work on next (ADR-0007). A genuine person needs only the instruction — follow the prompts, keep your face in view.

20

DEFAULT_TIP — for any reason this file doesn't know yet, such as a code added to the API later. The page never shows a raw code.

tipFor — the tip for a list of reasons.

27      return tip;
28    }
29  }

Go through the reasons in order, and return the tip for the first one known. Looking a key up in a Record may find nothing — and the project's strict settings make TypeScript insist on the !== undefined check before the tip is used.

30  return DEFAULT_TIP;
31}

None known: the general tip.

The page at /v/<session ID> — the address in every verify link. In Next.js's App Router, a folder name in square brackets is a dynamic segment: app/v/[sessionId]/page.tsx answers /v/vs_01JA8XQ2…, and Next.js hands the actual ID to the page as sessionId.

This page itself runs on the server. It only checks the ID's shape and hands over to VerifyFlow, the interactive part that runs in the browser (§4.17).

apps/web/app/v/[sessionId]/camera-view.tsx270 lines · 100% explained

The camera screen: the live preview with an oval to line the face up with, a line of guidance, and the Start button. Since Phase 3 it does three new things (§5.3):

  • live guidance — MediaPipe's face landmarker watches the preview and says, in plain words, what to fix: "Move a little closer", "Look straight at the camera";
  • the challenge — when the person presses Start, it fetches a fresh challenge and plays it: colours that light the whole screen, then prompts to turn or tilt the head;
  • signals — it notes what the browser can tell about itself (is a program driving it? is the camera a virtual one? was the page hidden?) and sends that along.

When the challenge is done, it switches the camera off at once and hands the labelled photos to the verify flow.

It is a client component (§4.17): it runs in the browser, where the camera is, and uses React's hooks — useState for values that change the screen, useRef for values that don't, and useEffect for work that must happen after the screen is drawn (§4.16).

  • onCameraError — a function to call if the camera fails.

Passing functions down like this — callbacks — keeps the camera screen simple: it doesn't need to know how the API is called or what happens with the photos.

50/** Plain words for what the landmarker sees, and whether the face is ready. */
51function guidance(reading: Reading | null): { hint: string; good: boolean } {

guidance — turn what the landmarker sees into one plain instruction, and say whether the face is ready (good). The checks go from the most basic problem to the finest, and the first one that applies wins.

52  if (reading === null || reading.faces === 0) {
53    return { hint: "We can't see your face yet. Look at the camera.", good: false };
54  }

No reading, or no face: ask the person to look at the camera.

55  if (reading.faces > 1) {
56    return { hint: "Make sure only you are in view.", good: false };
57  }

More than one face.

58  if (!reading.closeEnough) {
59    return { hint: "Move a little closer.", good: false };
60  }

The face is too small in the picture: too far away.

61  if (!reading.centred) {
62    return { hint: "Centre your face in the oval.", good: false };
63  }

The face is off to one side.

64  if (reading.angles !== null && Math.abs(reading.angles.yaw) > FRONTAL_YAW) {
65    return { hint: "Look straight at the camera.", good: false };
66  }

The head is turned: its sideways angle is more than FRONTAL_YAW either way (Math.abs ignores the direction). The challenge starts with frontal photos, so the person should begin looking straight ahead.

67  return { hint: "That's good. Press Start when you're ready.", good: true };
68}

All good: say so, and invite them to press Start.

70export function CameraView({ tip, getChallenge, onCaptured, onCameraError }: CameraViewProps) {

CameraView — the screen itself. Its props are taken out by destructuring.

71  const video = useRef<HTMLVideoElement>(null);

video — a ref to the <video> element, so the code can reach the real element in the page. useRef keeps the same box across every redraw; it starts empty (null) until React fills it.

72  const stream = useRef<MediaStream | null>(null);

stream — a ref holding the camera's stream, so it can be stopped later. A ref (rather than state) because changing it shouldn't redraw anything.

73  const landmarker = useRef<FaceLandmarker | null>(null);
74  const reading = useRef<Reading | null>(null);

landmarker — the loaded MediaPipe landmarker, once there is one. reading — what it saw most recently. Both refs: the reading changes up to 60 times a second, and redrawing the screen that often for it would be wasteful. The challenge reads it directly when it needs it.

75  const hidden = useRef({ since: null as number | null, total: 0 });

hidden — how long the page has been hidden: since (when it was last hidden, or null while it's showing) and total (milliseconds so far). null as number | null tells TypeScript that since may later hold a number.

76  const [ready, setReady] = useState(false);
77  const [guide, setGuide] = useState<{ hint: string; good: boolean } | null>(null);
78  const [graceOver, setGraceOver] = useState(false);
79  const [running, setRunning] = useState(false);
80  const [colour, setColour] = useState<string | null>(null);
81  const [cue, setCue] = useState<string | null>(null);
82  const [reach, setReach] = useState<number | null>(null);
83  const [progress, setProgress] = useState<[number, number]>([0, 0]);

The state — each piece with the function that changes it. Each time one of them changes, React draws the screen again:

  • ready — has the video started showing pictures?
  • guide — the current guidance text, and whether the face is good;
  • graceOver — has the 8-second grace period passed?
  • running — is the challenge in progress?
  • colour — the colour on screen now, or null;
  • cue — the pose instruction now, or null;
  • progress — photos taken, out of how many. [number, number] is a tuple type: a list of exactly two numbers.

Also reach (added after the owner's tests) — how much of the current pose is reached, from 0 to 1, for the meter; null hides it.

Open the camera when the screen appears. useEffect runs its function after React has drawn the screen.

86    let active = true;

active — a flag that tells whether this screen is still showing. The function returned at the end (the cleanup) sets it to false when the screen goes away.

87    openCamera().then(
88      (media) => {
89        if (!active) {
90          closeCamera(media);
91          return;
92        }

94        if (video.current !== null) {
95          video.current.srcObject = media;

97      },

98      (error: unknown) => {

100          onCameraError(error);
101        }
102      },

103    );

The end of the then.

104    return () => {
105      active = false;
106      closeCamera(stream.current);
107      stream.current = null;
108    };

109  }, [onCameraError]);

The dependency list: run this effect again only if onCameraError changes. The parent makes sure it never does (useCallback in verify-flow.tsx), so the camera opens exactly once per screen.

110
111  // Guidance: read the face on every screen refresh, for as long as the camera is open.
112  useEffect(() => {
113    if (!ready) {
114      return;
115    }

Live guidance, as the comment says. This effect depends on ready, so it runs again when the video starts; until then, it does nothing.

116    let active = true;
117    let frame = 0;
118    const grace = setTimeout(() => setGraceOver(true), GUIDANCE_GRACE_MS);

The active flag again, the number of the scheduled screen refresh (to cancel it later), and the grace timer: after 8 seconds, graceOver becomes true.

119    loadLandmarker().then((loaded) => {
120      if (!active) {
121        loaded?.close();
122        return;
123      }

124      landmarker.current = loaded;

125      const loop = () => {
126        if (!active || landmarker.current === null || video.current === null) {

128        }

134      if (loaded === null) {

139    });

165    if (video.current === null) {
166      return;

  • virtualCamera — whether the camera's name looks like virtual-camera software;
  • hiddenMs — the total hidden time;

A dishonest browser can fake every one of these, which is why they can only make the check stricter.

194      });

195    } catch (error) {

The card around the camera has a blurred background, and in CSS such an element becomes the frame of reference for fixed elements inside it. A colour drawn inside the card would cover the card only — not enough light on the face. Drawn in the body, it covers the whole screen.

213            <div
214              aria-hidden="true"

218              <p className="rounded-full bg-black/60 px-5 py-2 text-lg font-medium text-white">

In its middle, a dark rounded label: "Keep looking at the screen."

221            </div>,

The end of the layer, and the destination: document.body.

224      <div className="relative aspect-[4/3] overflow-hidden rounded-2xl bg-zinc-900 ring-1 ring-black/5 dark:ring-white/10">

The preview box: a 4 : 3 rectangle (aspect-[4/3]), hiding anything that spills out (overflow-hidden), with rounded corners, a dark background while the camera starts, and a hair-thin ring around it.

225        <video
226          ref={video}

229          muted
230          onLoadedData={() => setReady(true)}

The live preview. ref={video} connects the element to the ref. Three attributes make live video work on every browser: autoPlay (start immediately), playsInline (on iPhones, play inside the page rather than full-screen) and muted (browsers only autoplay silent video; there's no sound anyway). onLoadedData fires when the first picture arrives, which starts the guidance.

Its classes: fill the box (size-full), crop rather than squash (object-cover), and mirror it (-scale-x-100 flips it left to right). People expect a front camera to behave like a mirror, and lining up a face in a non-mirrored image feels backwards. Only the preview is mirrored; the photos sent are not (camera.ts).

233        <FaceGuide active={running} good={guide?.good ?? false} />

241            <p className="text-lg font-medium">{reach === 1 ? "That's it — hold still…" : cue}</p>

The instruction — or, once the meter is full, "That's it — hold still…" while the three photos are taken.

242            {reach === null ? null : (

The pose meter (added after the owner's first tests, in which people couldn't tell how far to turn). As the comment says, it fills as the person turns, so they can see when it is enough.

244              <div className="mt-2 h-2 overflow-hidden rounded-full bg-white/20" aria-hidden="true">

245                <div

249              </div>
250            )}
251          </div>
252        )}

The closing tags.

253      </div>

The end of the preview box.

254      <p
255        aria-live="polite"

258        {message}

What it says: message, worked out above.

259      </p>

260      <button

The Start button. type="button" makes clear it submits no form. It is disabled until the video shows pictures, while the check is running (so it can't be pressed twice), and until the guidance is satisfied or the grace period is over. Its label changes while the check runs.

268    </div>

The closing tags.

apps/web/app/v/[sessionId]/verify-flow.tsx296 lines · 100% explained

The verify flow — every screen a person sees during an age check, and the logic that moves between them. It is a state machine like the API's session (§5.1.2), but for the screen: at any moment the page is in exactly one stage, and each stage draws one screen.

loading ──► intro ──► camera ──► checking ──► finished (pass · fail · step up · reject)
   │                    ▲            │
   │                    └── retry ───┘
   └──────────► problem   (from anywhere: bad link, expired, camera refused, offline)

The whole page is one client component: it runs in the browser, because the camera, the secret in the link, and the flow token all live there (§4.17).

1"use client";

"use client" — this file runs in the browser.

2
3import { type ReactNode, useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";

From React: the ReactNode type and four hooks (§4.16).

4
5import { accentButton, card, primaryButton, Shell } from "@/components/shell";
6import { type Problem, problemFor, tipFor } from "@/lib/advice";
7import type { Challenge } from "@/lib/challenge";
8import { type CapturedAttempt, FlowClient, FlowError, type FlowSession } from "@/lib/flow-api";
9
10import { CameraView } from "./camera-view";

The shared styles and page frame, the friendly messages, the Challenge type, the flow client and its types — including CapturedAttempt, what one attempt produced — and the camera screen.

11
12type Ending = "pass" | "fail" | "step_up" | "reject";

Ending — the four ways a check can end.

13
14type Stage =
15  | { kind: "loading" }
16  | { kind: "intro"; session: FlowSession }
17  | { kind: "camera"; session: FlowSession; tip: string | null }
18  | { kind: "checking"; session: FlowSession }
19  | { kind: "finished"; session: FlowSession; ending: Ending }
20  | { kind: "problem"; problem: Problem; requestId: string | null };

Stage — every possible stage, as a discriminated union (§4.15): a list of object shapes that each carry a kind. Checking stage.kind tells TypeScript exactly which other fields exist. After if (stage.kind === "camera"), the code may use stage.tip; in any other stage, TypeScript refuses it. Impossible combinations — a "checking" screen without a session, say — can't even be written.

  • loading — waiting for the API;
  • intro — the explanation and the "Start the camera" button;
  • camera — the camera screen, with a tip after a retry;
  • checking — photos uploaded, waiting for the decision;
  • finished — an ending;
  • problem — something stopped the check, with the request ID if the API gave one.
21
22/** Read the one-time secret from the link's #fragment, then remove it from the address bar and the history. */
23function takeSecretFromLink(): string | null {

takeSecretFromLink — read the one-time secret from the link, then wipe it from the address bar.

24  const secret = new URLSearchParams(window.location.hash.slice(1)).get("cs");

window.location.hash is the address's fragment, such as #cs=vs_…_secret_…. .slice(1) drops the #, and URLSearchParams reads it as name=value pairs; .get("cs") returns the secret, or null.

25  if (secret !== null) {
26    window.history.replaceState(null, "", window.location.pathname + window.location.search);
27  }

If there was a secret, rewrite the address without its fragment, using history.replaceState. It replaces the current entry in the browser's history rather than adding one, so the secret is gone from the address bar, from the back button's history, and from any screenshot the person might take.

28  return secret;
29}

Return the secret.

30
31function problemStage(error: unknown): Stage {

problemStage — turn any error into a problem stage.

32  if (error instanceof FlowError) {
33    return { kind: "problem", problem: problemFor(error.code), requestId: error.requestId };
34  }

An error from the API: the message for its code, and its request ID.

35  if (error instanceof DOMException && error.name === "NotAllowedError") {
36    return { kind: "problem", problem: problemFor("camera_blocked"), requestId: null };
37  }
38  if (error instanceof DOMException && error.name === "NotFoundError") {
39    return { kind: "problem", problem: problemFor("camera_missing"), requestId: null };
40  }

Errors from the camera are DOMExceptions, the browser's own error type, named by kind: NotAllowedError when permission was refused, NotFoundError when there's no camera. Each gets its own message.

41  return { kind: "problem", problem: problemFor("unknown"), requestId: null };
42}

Anything else: the general message (unknown isn't in the list of codes).

44function endingOf(session: FlowSession): Ending {
45  if (session.status === "awaiting_step_up") {
46    return "step_up";
47  }

In development, React's Strict Mode deliberately runs every effect twice — set up, clean up, set up again — to expose code that breaks when that happens. The demo shop: settings and secrets

Its code is written exactly as a real website should integrate Dwarpal, so it doubles as a working example for developers.

Its setup mirrors the verify page's (apps/web/package.json), with two differences: it runs on port 3100, and it depends on the SDK.

The demo shop's Next.js configuration. A shop isn't Dwarpal's product, so its security headers are a sensible minimum rather than the verify page's strict set (apps/web/next.config.ts) — but every real website should send at least these.

1import type { NextConfig } from "next";

The Next.js configuration type.

2
3const securityHeaders = [
4  { key: "Content-Security-Policy", value: "frame-ancestors 'none'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'" },
5  { key: "Referrer-Policy", value: "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" },
6  { key: "X-Content-Type-Options", value: "nosniff" },
7];

Three security headers:

  • a small Content Security Policy: no other site may frame the shop (against clickjacking), no plug-ins, and no <base> tag may change what relative addresses mean;
  • Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin — when a visitor follows a link to another site, send only the shop's origin, never the full address. This is the browsers' default today, stated explicitly;
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — never guess a file's type.

The shop deliberately has no form-action rule: its "Verify my age" button submits a form whose answer redirects to the verify page on another origin, and a strict form-action would block that redirect.

8

10  poweredByHeader: false,
11  reactStrictMode: true,

The configuration: no "powered by" header, and React's Strict Mode in development.

12  async headers() {
13    return [{ source: "/:path*", headers: securityHeaders }];
14  },

The headers, on every path.

15};

The end of the object.

17export default config;

Hand the configuration to Next.js.

apps/demo-shop/.env.example14 lines · 100% explained

An example settings file for the demo shop. The shop reads six environment variables (lib/config.ts); this file lists them all with explanations, to copy into apps/demo-shop/.env.local, which Next.js loads automatically. The real .env.local holds a secret key and a secret, so Git ignores it (.gitignore: .env.*); only this harmless example is committed.

Careful — placeholders that fail safely

Every placeholder here is chosen to fail, never to half-work. The key dk_test_REPLACE_ME is too short for the SDK to accept; SHOP_SECRET is empty, which the shop refuses at start-up. A first version used a long placeholder secret — long enough to be accepted. Anyone who copied the file without editing it would have run a shop whose pass cookies anybody could forge, using the secret published right here.

1# Copy this file to apps/demo-shop/.env.local and fill it in. A real .env.local is never committed.

How to use the file, and the reminder that a real settings file is never committed.

16/** Read the shop's settings from the environment, and refuse to run with any of them missing. */
17export function shopConfig(env: NodeJS.ProcessEnv = process.env): ShopConfig {

shopConfig — read the settings. Its one parameter has a default: the real environment, process.env. A test could pass a made-up environment instead. NodeJS.ProcessEnv is Node.js's type for it: names mapped to text, or nothing.

18  const apiUrl = env.DWARPAL_API_URL ?? "http://localhost:8000";

The API's address, or the local default.

19  const config: ShopConfig = {
20    apiUrl,
21    issuer: env.DWARPAL_ISSUER ?? apiUrl,
22    apiKey: env.DWARPAL_API_KEY ?? "",
23    projectId: env.DWARPAL_PROJECT_ID ?? "",
24    shopUrl: (env.SHOP_URL ?? "http://localhost:3100").replace(/\/+$/, ""),
25    secret: env.SHOP_SECRET ?? "",
26  };

Build the settings: each from its variable, with a default where a safe one exists (the issuer defaults to the API's address). The key, project and secret have no safe default, so they fall back to empty text — caught just below. The shop's address loses any trailing slash.

27  const missing = [
28    config.apiKey === "" ? "DWARPAL_API_KEY" : null,
29    config.projectId === "" ? "DWARPAL_PROJECT_ID" : null,
30    config.secret.length < 32 ? "SHOP_SECRET (at least 32 characters)" : null,
31  ].filter((name) => name !== null);

List what's missing: each line gives a variable's name if its value is empty (or, for the secret, shorter than 32 characters), or null if it's fine. .filter((name) => name !== null) keeps only the names — and TypeScript understands that the result is a list of text, with the nulls gone.

32  if (missing.length > 0) {
33    throw new Error(`the demo shop is missing settings: ${missing.join(", ")}`);
34  }

Anything missing? Stop, naming every missing setting at once — not one per restart.

35  return config;
36}

All present: return the settings.

dwarpal — a new SDK client with the shop's key and the API's address. It is cheap to make, so the shop simply makes one where it needs one.

apps/demo-shop/lib/pass.ts38 lines · 100% explained

The shop's own "age checked" pass. After a successful check, the shop shouldn't ask Dwarpal again on every page; instead it gives the visitor's browser a cookie saying "this visitor passed, until 10:30". The danger is obvious: a cookie is stored by the visitor, so a visitor could try to write one. The pass is therefore signed by the shop with a secret only the shop knows, using an HMAC — a keyed fingerprint (§4.12). Change one character, and the signature no longer matches.

A pass looks like this: vs_01JA8XQ2….1792141800.Xk3f9qW… — the session's ID, the expiry time, and the signature, joined by dots.

1/** The shop's own "age checked" pass: a cookie the shop signs itself, so a visitor can't forge or extend it. */

The doc comment.

2
3import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

From Node.js's built-in crypto module: createHmac (make a keyed fingerprint) and timingSafeEqual (compare two values in constant time, §4.12). The node: prefix makes clear this is Node.js's own module, not a package from the registry.

4
5export const PASS_COOKIE = "amber_pass";

The pass cookie's name.

6export const PASS_LIFETIME_S = 30 * 60;

A pass lasts 30 minutes (30 * 60 seconds): long enough to shop, short enough that a shared computer doesn't stay "verified" all day.

7/** Remembers which check this browser started, so a return link only works in the browser that started it. */
8export const PENDING_COOKIE = "amber_pending";

The name of the second cookie, amber_pending. It remembers which check this browser started, so the return link only works in that same browser (see actions.ts and route.ts).

9
10export interface Pass {
11  sessionId: string;
12  expiresAt: Date;
13}

Pass — what a valid pass contains: the session it came from, and when it expires.

14
15function signature(body: string, secret: string): string {
16  return createHmac("sha256", secret).update(body).digest("base64url");
17}

signature — the HMAC-SHA256 of a text with the secret, written as URL-safe Base64, so it is safe to put in a cookie.

18
19/** A pass for `sessionId`, valid for `PASS_LIFETIME_S` seconds: `<session>.<expiry>.<signature>`. */
20export function issuePass(sessionId: string, secret: string, now: number = Date.now()): string {

issuePass — make a pass for a session. now defaults to the current time (Date.now(), in milliseconds); tests pass a fixed time instead.

21  const body = `${sessionId}.${Math.floor(now / 1000) + PASS_LIFETIME_S}`;

The body: the session's ID and the expiry, as whole seconds since 1970, joined by a dot.

22  return `${body}.${signature(body, secret)}`;

Append the body's signature.

23}

The closing brace.

24
25/** The pass inside a cookie, or `null` if it is missing, forged, altered or expired. */
26export function readPass(value: string | undefined, secret: string, now: number = Date.now()): Pass | null {

readPass — check a pass from a cookie. It returns the pass, or null for anything wrong. It never throws: a strange cookie simply isn't a pass.

27  const [sessionId, expiry, given, ...extra] = (value ?? "").split(".");

Split the cookie's text at the dots. Array destructuring names the first three parts, and ...extra collects any further ones. A missing cookie (undefined) is treated as empty text.

28  if (sessionId === undefined || expiry === undefined || given === undefined || extra.length > 0) {
29    return null;
30  }

Exactly three parts are required: fewer, or more, means it isn't a pass.

31  const expected = Buffer.from(signature(`${sessionId}.${expiry}`, secret));
32  const received = Buffer.from(given);

Compute the signature the body should have, and take the one that was given, both as bytes.

33  if (received.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(received, expected)) {
34    return null;
35  }

They must match, compared in constant time. timingSafeEqual only accepts two values of the same length, so the lengths are compared first (the length of a correct signature is no secret).

36  const expiresAt = new Date(Number(expiry) * 1000);
37  return expiresAt.getTime() > now ? { sessionId, expiresAt } : null;

Finally, the pass must not have expired. If all is well, return the session and the expiry.

38}

The closing brace.

What happens when a visitor presses "Verify my age to enter". It is a server action (§4.17): a function that runs on the shop's server, although it is triggered by a button in the visitor's browser. That is essential here — it uses the shop's secret API key, which must never reach a browser.

1"use server";

"use server" — every function exported from this file is a server action. Next.js turns a call to it from a page into a request to the server, and runs it there.

2
3import { cookies } from "next/headers";
4import { redirect } from "next/navigation";

From Next.js: cookies (read and write the visitor's cookies) and redirect (send the visitor elsewhere).

5
6import { dwarpal, POLICY, shopConfig } from "@/lib/config";
7import { PASS_COOKIE, PASS_LIFETIME_S, PENDING_COOKIE } from "@/lib/pass";

The shop's settings helpers, and the cookie names and lifetime — PASS_COOKIE, the pass itself, is needed by leaveCellar below.

8
9/** Ask Dwarpal for a verification session, then send the visitor to its verify page. */
10export async function startAgeCheck(): Promise<void> {

startAgeCheck — the action.

11  const config = shopConfig();

Read the settings.

12  const session = await dwarpal(config).createSession({
13    policy: POLICY,
14    returnUrl: `${config.shopUrl}/age-check/complete`,
15  });

Ask Dwarpal for a new session, through the SDK: the shop's policy, and the address to come back to afterwards.

16  (await cookies()).set(PENDING_COOKIE, session.id, {
17    httpOnly: true,
18    sameSite: "lax",
19    secure: config.shopUrl.startsWith("https://"),
20    path: "/age-check",
21    maxAge: PASS_LIFETIME_S,
22  });

Before sending the visitor away, remember which session this browser started, in the amber_pending cookie:

  • httpOnly — the page's own scripts can't read it; only the browser and the server see it;
  • sameSite: "lax" — the browser sends it back when the visitor returns to the shop by following a link or a redirect, but not with requests that other websites try to make in the background;
  • secure — sent only over HTTPS, when the shop runs on HTTPS;
  • path: "/age-check" — sent only to the return address, nowhere else in the shop;
  • maxAge — forgotten after 30 minutes, the same as an age check's own life.

Real world — why this cookie exists

Without it, the return link …/age-check/complete?session_id=vs_… would work in any browser. An adult could finish a check and send that link to a child, and the child's browser would receive the shop's pass. With the cookie, the shop only accepts a return in the browser that started the check. Websites that sign people in with another service use the same trick, which OAuth calls the state parameter.

23  redirect(session.url);

Send the visitor to the verify page, using the link from the session.

24}

The closing brace.

25

28  (await cookies()).delete(PASS_COOKIE);

Delete the pass cookie. The browser is told to forget it at once, so the next visit to the cellar needs a new age check.

29  redirect("/");
30}

apps/demo-shop/app/age-check/complete/route.ts53 lines · 100% explained

The moment of truth for the shop: the address the verify page sends the visitor back to, …/age-check/complete?session_id=vs_…. This is a route handler (§4.17) — server code that answers a request directly, with no page to draw.

The address itself proves nothing: anyone can type ?session_id= followed by anything. So the shop checks, in order:

  1. this browser started this session (the amber_pending cookie);
  2. the API, asked by the shop's server with its secret key, reports the session as completed, with a token;
  3. the token's signature and claims check out, for exactly 18+ and exactly this session.

Only then does the visitor get the shop's signed pass. Any failure leads to a polite refusal page — never to the cellar.

1import { verifyAgeToken } from "@dwarpal/node";

The SDK's token checker.

2import { type NextRequest, NextResponse } from "next/server";

From Next.js: the request type, and NextResponse for building answers.

3
4import { dwarpal, MIN_AGE, shopConfig } from "@/lib/config";
5import { issuePass, PASS_COOKIE, PASS_LIFETIME_S, PENDING_COOKIE } from "@/lib/pass";

The shop's settings helpers, and the pass functions and names.

6
7/**
8 * Dwarpal sends the visitor back here with `?session_id=vs_…`. The shop never trusts that address alone: the
9 * session must be the one this browser started, and the shop asks the API for the result with its secret key and
10 * checks the signed token before letting anyone in.
11 */

The doc comment, explaining the rule.

12export async function GET(request: NextRequest): Promise<NextResponse> {

GET — a function named after an HTTP method answers that method at this file's address. It receives the request, and returns the response.

13  const config = shopConfig();

Read the settings.

14  const sessionId = request.nextUrl.searchParams.get("session_id") ?? "";

The session's ID from the address — or empty text if there is none.

15  const go = (path: string) => {
16    const response = NextResponse.redirect(new URL(path, config.shopUrl), 303);
17    response.cookies.delete({ name: PENDING_COOKIE, path: "/age-check" });
18    return response;
19  };

go — a small helper for every possible answer: a redirect to a page of the shop, with the status 303 See Other (the standard "now go and get this page"). Every answer also deletes the pending cookie: whatever happens, a return link can be used only once.

20  if (sessionId === "" || request.cookies.get(PENDING_COOKIE)?.value !== sessionId) {
21    return go("/refused?reason=other_browser");
22  }

Check 1: was this check started in this browser? If there's no session ID, or the cookie doesn't hold exactly this ID, refuse — before even asking the API.

23  try {
24    const session = await dwarpal(config).retrieveSession(sessionId);

Check 2: ask the API for the session, with the shop's key. retrieveSession also rejects malformed IDs (§ the SDK's client.ts).

25    if (session.status === "awaiting_step_up") {
26      return go("/refused?reason=step_up");
27    }

Too close to call from photos: the visitor would need a stronger check. Explain that on the refusal page.

28    if (session.status !== "completed" || session.ageToken === null) {
29      return go("/refused?reason=unfinished");
30    }

Not finished, or no token: refuse.

31    const verdict = await verifyAgeToken(session.ageToken, {
32      issuer: config.issuer,
33      audience: config.projectId,
34      minAge: MIN_AGE,
35      sessionId,
36    });

Check 3: verify the token — its signature, issuer, audience (this shop's project), age (18) and session.

37    if (!verdict.allowed) {
38      return go("/refused?reason=not_confirmed");
39    }

The token is genuine, but doesn't allow entry: refuse, kindly.

40    const response = go("/cellar");

All checks passed: prepare the redirect into the cellar…

41    response.cookies.set(PASS_COOKIE, issuePass(sessionId, config.secret), {
42      httpOnly: true,
43      sameSite: "lax",
44      secure: config.shopUrl.startsWith("https://"),
45      path: "/",
46      maxAge: PASS_LIFETIME_S,
47    });

…and give the browser the signed pass, in a cookie that the page's scripts can't read (httpOnly), sent back on normal navigation (sameSite: "lax"), over HTTPS when available (secure), for every page of the shop (path: "/"), for 30 minutes.

48    return response;

Send it.

49  } catch (error) {
50    console.error("the age check could not be completed", error);
51    return go("/refused?reason=error");
52  }

Any error — the API unreachable, a forged or expired token, a malformed ID — is logged on the shop's server for its developers, and the visitor is sent to a polite "something went wrong" page. Errors can never lead into the cellar.

53}

Real world — what building the front end taught us

  • TypeScript 7 and Next.js. The plan kept TypeScript 6 in reserve, in case the brand-new TypeScript 7 didn't work with Next.js. It did — including Next.js's own type-checking step — so no fallback was needed. Testing a risky choice early, on real code, beats guessing.
  • A cooldown for new releases. Brand-new package versions are where supply-chain attacks and bugs show up first, so the workspace now refuses any version less than seven days old (pnpm-workspace.yaml). Its first check caught a tool pinned in Phase 0 only two days after release.
  • A return link that worked anywhere. A review of the shop found that its return link worked in any browser: an adult could pass a check and send the link to a child. The shop now remembers which check each browser started (actions.ts), and an end-to-end test proves that a link opened elsewhere is refused.
  • A placeholder that would have worked. The first example settings file had a long placeholder secret — long enough to be accepted. Placeholders are now chosen so they fail loudly instead (.env.example).

5.1.5 The end-to-end test — a real browser, a fake camera

The last step proves that everything built in Phase 1 works together, the way a person would use it: a real Chromium browser, driven by Playwright (§4.20), with the test portrait playing as its webcam.

The fake camera

infra/scripts/make_fake_camera.py39 lines · 100% explained

Makes the fake camera's video for the end-to-end test: the public-domain test portrait (the same one the vision tests use, §5.1.1), placed in a 640 × 480 picture and repeated as a two-second clip. Chromium plays it as if it were a webcam (see e2e/playwright.config.ts).

The file format is Y4M (YUV4MPEG2), the simplest video format there is: a one-line text header, then each frame's raw pixels, uncompressed. Chromium reads it directly, and Python can write it with no video library at all.

Pixels in Y4M are stored as YUV, not RGB: one channel for brightness (Y) and two for colour (U and V). The colour channels are stored at half the width and half the height — "4:2:0" — because human eyes notice detail in brightness far more than in colour. Video formats everywhere use this trick to save space.

1"""Make the fake camera's video for the end-to-end test: the public-domain test portrait as a short Y4M clip.
2
3uv run python infra/scripts/make_fake_camera.py e2e/.cache/fake-camera.y4m
4"""

The docstring, with the command that runs the script.

5
6from __future__ import annotations

The project-wide type-hint setting.

8import sys
9from pathlib import Path

sys (for the command-line argument) and Path.

10
11import cv2
12import numpy as np

OpenCV and NumPy (§4.9).

13
14WIDTH, HEIGHT, FRAMES, FPS = 640, 480, 30, 15

The clip's size: 640 × 480 pixels, 30 frames, 15 frames per second — two seconds, which Chromium plays in a loop.

15PORTRAIT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "libs" / "vision" / "tests" / "fixtures" / "astronaut.jpg"

The portrait's location, found from this script's own place: two folders up is the repository's top folder.

16
17
18def frame() -> bytes:

frame — make one frame, as Y4M's raw bytes.

19    portrait = cv2.imread(str(PORTRAIT))
20    if portrait is None:
21        raise SystemExit(f"cannot read the test portrait at {PORTRAIT}")

Read the portrait. OpenCV returns None (instead of raising an error) when a file can't be read, so the script checks, and stops with a clear message.

22    canvas = np.full((HEIGHT, WIDTH, 3), 128, dtype=np.uint8)

A 640 × 480 canvas, filled with middle grey (128).

23    left = (WIDTH - HEIGHT) // 2

Where the portrait goes: a 480 × 480 square in the middle, starting at (640 − 480) / 2 = 80 pixels from the left. // divides and drops any remainder.

24    canvas[:, left : left + HEIGHT] = cv2.resize(portrait, (HEIGHT, HEIGHT), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)

Shrink the 512 × 512 portrait to 480 × 480 (INTER_AREA is OpenCV's best method for shrinking), and paste it into the middle of the canvas. canvas[:, left : left + HEIGHT] selects every row, and the columns from 80 to 559.

25    return bytes(cv2.cvtColor(canvas, cv2.COLOR_BGR2YUV_I420).tobytes())

Convert from OpenCV's BGR colour order to YUV I420 — the 4:2:0 layout Y4M's C420jpeg expects: first the full brightness plane, then the two quarter-size colour planes. .tobytes() takes the raw bytes.

26
27
28def main(target: Path) -> None:

main — write the clip to target.

29    planes = frame()

Make the one frame; every frame of the clip is the same.

30    target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

Create the output folder if it doesn't exist.

31    with target.open("wb") as video:

Open the file for writing bytes ("wb").

32        video.write(f"YUV4MPEG2 W{WIDTH} H{HEIGHT} F{FPS}:1 Ip A1:1 C420jpeg\n".encode("ascii"))

The header line: W640 H480 (size), F15:1 (15 frames per 1 second), Ip (whole frames, not interlaced), A1:1 (square pixels) and C420jpeg (the 4:2:0 colour layout).

33        for _ in range(FRAMES):
34            video.write(b"FRAME\n" + planes)

Thirty times: the word FRAME, a line break, and the frame's bytes.

35    print(f"wrote {FRAMES} frames to {target}")

Say what was written.

50export default defineConfig({

51  testDir: "tests",

Each test may take up to 90 seconds. The main story needs about a minute: its still portrait can't turn, so the page waits out 6 seconds at each of up to four poses.

53  retries: CI ? 1 : 0,

In CI, retry a failed test once: a run that fails only sometimes — an overloaded CI machine, say — is then visible as "flaky" instead of failing the whole build. Locally, never retry: a failure should be seen at once.

One test at a time. The tests share one set of services and one database; running them side by side would make their results depend on each other.

Four Chromium switches:

  • --use-fake-ui-for-media-stream — accept camera requests without showing a prompt;
  • --disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled — don't announce that a program is driving the browser (added in Phase 3). Normally Playwright's browser sets navigator.webdriver, which the verify page reports as an injection sign — and the session would be stepped up. An attacker's tool can hide it the same way, which is the point of the comment: the server treats the page's signals as hints, never as proof;
  • --use-fake-device-for-media-stream — use a pretend camera instead of real hardware;
  • --use-file-for-fake-video-capture=… — and play this video file as its picture.

So the "person" in front of the camera is the test portrait, every time.

e2e/tests/age-check.spec.ts58 lines · 100% explained

The end-to-end tests: four short stories, acted out by Playwright in a real Chromium browser (§4.20). The first one is the whole Phase 1 slice working together — the shop, the SDK, the verify page, the camera, the API, the inference service, the decision engine, the signed token and the shop's pass:

shop: "Verify my age"  →  verify page: intro  →  camera (fake)  →  "You're all set"  →  shop: the cellar

Playwright finds things on the page the way a person would — by their role and name: "the button called Take photos", "the heading You're all set". Tests written that way keep working when the page's design changes, and they quietly check accessibility too: an element a screen reader couldn't name, the test couldn't find either.

A screenshot of the intro, for people to look at. animations: "disabled" finishes any animation first, so the picture is never caught halfway through a fade.

As the comment says, the button is enabled once the live guidance sees a well-placed face — or after a grace period, because the guidance only advises: it must never lock out someone whose face it can't read. 15 seconds allows for MediaPipe loading.

Follow the check as it happens, with a screenshot at each stage:

  • the colour phase, recognised by its instruction "Keep looking at the screen." (.first(): the text may appear in more than one place);
  • a pose prompt, up to 10 seconds later. /^(Turn your head|Lift your chin)/ is a regular expression: text that starts with (^) either phrase (| means "or") — the poses are random, so the test can't know which comes first;
  • the result, "You're all set", within 45 seconds. Meanwhile the photos travel to the API, then to the inference service: the real face detector finds the face, liveness (in the labels test mode) accepts the poses, the stand-in model reports 30, and the decision engine says pass.

Try it yourself

With Docker running and the models downloaded (uv run infra/scripts/fetch_models.py), install the browser once — pnpm --filter @dwarpal/e2e exec playwright install chromium — then run:

pnpm e2e

Turborepo builds the SDK and both apps; Playwright starts the databases and all four services, and acts out the four stories. Afterwards, the screenshots of the main story are in e2e/test-results/. (If uv isn't on your PATH, set the UV variable to its full path first.)

Real world — what this step measured

All four end-to-end stories pass, in about 15 seconds in total on this laptop — most of it starting the services. The main story, from the shop's button to the cellar, takes about 4 seconds, including starting the camera, the 0.6-second burst, the analysis, and both redirects.

Around it: 20 JavaScript unit tests (11 for the SDK, 6 for the verify page, 3 for the shop), and a clean lint, type check and production build of every package. The screenshots of every screen were also checked by eye: tests prove that the right things happen, but only a person can judge whether they look right.

The walking skeleton is complete: every layer of the system exists, connected end to end, with a stand-in where the real age model will go. Phase 2 replaces that stand-in with a trained, calibrated model.

5.2 Phase 2 — the ML core

Phase 1 left a stand-in where the age model belongs. Phase 2 builds the real one, and everything a trustworthy model needs around it: data that may lawfully be used, a fixed and fair division of that data, safety lines with a provable guarantee, and measurements of how the model treats different groups of people.

It is built in this order, and this chapter grows in the same order:

Step What Section
1 Data: the licence register, the fetch command, the unified manifest §5.2.1 ✅
2 Risk control: choosing the safety lines §5.2.2 ✅
3 Face preparation: detecting and aligning every face, finding duplicates §5.2.3 ✅
4 Training the age model §5.2.4 ✅
5 Evaluation and fairness §5.2.5 ✅
6 Exact ages and the safety lines: UTKFace, calibration §5.2.6 ✅
7 Export to ONNX, and the model's manifest §5.2.7 ✅

The ML code lives in the ml/ package, created empty in Phase 0 (§5.0.2). It now uses httpx for downloads, SciPy for statistics, the project's own vision library, so that training prepares faces exactly as serving does, and PyTorch with timm for training (its pyproject.toml walkthrough, in §5.0.2, describes them all). Data never enters the repository: downloads and manifests live in .datasets/, which Git ignores.

5.2.1 Data — the register, the fetch and the manifest

The background is in §2.2: what labels and splits are, and why datasets have licences. Three pieces of code put it into practice:

ml/datasets.toml        the licence register: which datasets, which licences, approved by whom, pinned files
        │
        ▼
dwarpal_ml.fetch        downloads an approved dataset's files; keeps a file only if its fingerprint matches
        │                 → .datasets/raw/fairface/  (578 MB of face images + 2 label files)
        ▼
dwarpal_ml.manifest     one row per image, the same columns for every dataset, with a fixed split
                          → .datasets/manifest/fairface.csv  (97,698 rows)

The project's owner approved one dataset for now: FairFace, under the CC BY 4.0 licence (use for any purpose, with credit). Three exact-age datasets are listed in the register but not approved, because their licences allow research use only (ADR-0018).

The licence register

ml/datasets.toml89 lines · 100% explained

The licence register: every dataset Dwarpal may learn from, where it comes from, who made it, how to cite it, and — above all — what its licence allows (ADR-0018). An AI model carries the terms of the data it learned from: a model trained on "non-commercial research only" photos may itself only be used for non-commercial research. Writing those terms down, per dataset, is how the project keeps track.

Two safety rules are built into the file's shape:

  • a dataset is downloaded only when the project owner has approved it (approved = true, with the date);
  • every file is pinned by its SHA-256 fingerprint (§X.5), so a download that has been tampered with, or quietly changed, is thrown away.

The design planned this register as YAML; it is written in TOML instead, because Python reads TOML with no extra library and TOML allows comments (§5.0.2).

1# The licence register: every dataset Dwarpal may train or evaluate on, where it comes from, and what its
2# licence allows. A dataset is fetched only after the project owner has approved it (`approved = true`), and every
3# file is pinned by its SHA-256 fingerprint. Models list the datasets that trained them, so their terms follow them.

The comment at the top: what the file is, and its two rules.

UTKFace (approved on 17 October 2026, Phase 2): over 24,000 photos with exact ages — exactly what teenage thresholds need — under a licence for non-commercial research only, accepted under the project's research-only first version.

  • The in-the-wild photos, not the cropped ones: alignment needs the surroundings (the lesson of FairFace's tight crops, §5.2.3).
  • age_source — the ages are exact but estimated: the DEX age estimator proposed each one and a person checked it. They are not ages from documents, and every calibration result says so.
  • subject = "only" — a photo may show other people too, and the labelled person isn't necessarily in the middle. So preparation takes the clearest face, and sets aside any photo with a second clear face rather than guess whose age the label is.

The fetch command

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/fetch.py70 lines · 100% explained

The fetch command: download an approved dataset's files, and keep each one only if its fingerprint matches the register. It works like the model downloader of Phase 1 (infra/scripts/fetch_models.py), with one more rule in front: a dataset that the owner hasn't approved is refused outright, whatever is typed.

uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.fetch fairface    →  present / fetched, file by file

2

4"""

6from __future__ import annotations

The project-wide type-hint setting.

7
8import argparse
9import hashlib
10import sys
11from pathlib import Path

argparse (the command line), hashlib (SHA-256), sys (the exit code) and Path.

13import httpx

httpx — the HTTP client, used for streaming downloads.

14
15from dwarpal_ml.register import Dataset, DatasetFile, dataset

The register's types and lookup.

16
17
18def sha256_of(path: Path) -> str:
19    digest = hashlib.sha256()
20    with path.open("rb") as handle:
21        for chunk in iter(lambda: handle.read(1 << 20), b""):
22            digest.update(chunk)
23    return digest.hexdigest()

sha256_of — a file's fingerprint, reading it 1 MiB at a time (1 << 20 bytes), so even a multi-gigabyte file never has to fit in memory at once. iter(function, b"") keeps calling function until it returns empty bytes — the end of the file.

24
25
26def fetch_file(item: DatasetFile, folder: Path) -> bool:

fetch_file — make sure one file is present and genuine. It returns True on success.

27    target = folder / item.name
28    if target.is_file() and sha256_of(target) == item.sha256:
29        print(f"present  {item.name}")
30        return True

If the file already exists and its fingerprint matches, there is nothing to do.

31    if not item.url.startswith("https://"):
32        print(f"refused  {item.name}: only https downloads are allowed")
33        return False

Only https:// addresses are allowed: an unencrypted download could be swapped by anyone on the network path.

34    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

Create the dataset's folder if needed.

35    partial = target.with_name(target.name + ".part")

Download to a temporary name ending in .part, so a half-finished download can never be mistaken for a finished one.

36    with httpx.stream("GET", item.url, follow_redirects=True, timeout=120.0) as response:
37        response.raise_for_status()
38        with partial.open("wb") as out:
39            for chunk in response.iter_bytes():
40                out.write(chunk)

Stream the download: httpx.stream reads the answer in pieces, following redirects (Google Drive redirects), giving up if the server stays silent for 120 seconds. raise_for_status() turns an HTTP error, such as 404, into an exception. Each piece is written straight to the file.

41    actual = sha256_of(partial)
42    if actual != item.sha256:
43        partial.unlink()
44        print(f"MISMATCH {item.name}: expected {item.sha256}, got {actual}; file discarded")
45        return False

Fingerprint the download. If it doesn't match the register, delete it and say so — both fingerprints are printed, so a person can investigate.

46    partial.replace(target)
47    print(f"fetched  {item.name} ({item.bytes:,} bytes)")
48    return True

It matches: rename it to its real name, and report its size. A rename is instant and atomic, so the real file appears all at once.

49
50
51def fetch(entry: Dataset) -> bool:

fetch — a whole dataset.

52    if not entry.approved:
53        print(f"refused  {entry.name}: not approved in ml/datasets.toml ({entry.licence})")
54        return False

The approval rule: refuse any dataset not approved in the register, naming its licence.

The unified manifest

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/manifest.py207 lines · 100% explained

The unified manifest: one CSV table listing every image of a dataset, one row per image, in the same columns whatever dataset it came from. Every dataset arrives in its own shape — FairFace keeps its labels in two CSV files beside a zip of images; UTKFace hides its labels inside each file's name; others use spreadsheets or folders. A small adapter per dataset turns its shape into rows of one shape, and everything later (training, testing, calibration) reads only manifests.

The manifest also fixes each image's split — which job the image may be used for (§2.2):

Split Share Used for
train 80 % of FairFace's official training set teaching the model
val 10 % checking progress while it learns, and choosing settings
calib 10 % setting the safety thresholds (risk.py) — never seen in training
test FairFace's whole official validation set the final, locked exam 
uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.manifest fairface
97,698 images
splits: calib 8,621, test 10,954, train 69,469, val 8,654
ages:   0-2 1,991, 3-9 11,764, 10-19 10,284, 20-29 28,898, …, 70+ 960
groups: Black 13,789, East Asian 13,837, …, White 18,612

The manifest holds only file names and labels — no pictures — and it is written under .datasets/, beside the images, so it is never committed either.

1"""The unified manifest: every image of every approved dataset as one row of the same shape, with a fixed split.
2
3uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.manifest fairface
4"""

The docstring, with the command.

19from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

TYPE_CHECKING — a constant that is False when the program runs, but treated as True by the type checker (mypy). Code under if TYPE_CHECKING: is read only by the checker.

21from dwarpal_ml.register import RAW, Dataset, dataset

From the register: the raw-data folder, the Dataset type, and the lookup.

22
23if TYPE_CHECKING:
24    from _typeshed import DataclassInstance

DataclassInstance — the type checker's name for "any dataclass object". It lives in _typeshed, a module that exists only for type checkers and can't be imported when the program runs — hence if TYPE_CHECKING. (Thanks to from __future__ import annotations on line 6, type hints are never evaluated at run time, so using the name in a hint is safe.)

25
26MANIFESTS = RAW.parent / "manifest"

MANIFESTS — manifests are written to .datasets/manifest/, next to .datasets/raw/.

27# FairFace writes its top band "more than 70", although its README says "70+": both mean 70 and over.
28AGE_RANGE = re.compile(r"^(?:(\d+)-(\d+)|(\d+)\+|more than (\d+))$")

AGE_RANGE — a regular expression, a pattern that text is matched against. It accepts three spellings of an age band:

  • (\d+)-(\d+) — two numbers with a dash, as in 10-19 (\d+ means "one or more digits"; each pair of brackets captures the part it matches, so the code can read it afterwards);
  • (\d+)\+ — a number and a plus sign, as in 70+ (\+ is a real plus sign: on its own, + means "one or more");
  • more than (\d+) — the words FairFace actually uses.

^ and $ mean the pattern must cover the whole text, and (?:…|…|…) means "one of these", without capturing. The comment records why the third spelling is there: FairFace's documentation says 70+, but its label file says more than 70. The first run of this code found that out by refusing the unknown spelling (see parse_age_range).

29# UTKFace keeps its labels in each file's name: age_sex_group_datetime.jpg (a few files break the pattern).
30UTKFACE_NAME = re.compile(r"^(\d+)_([01])_([0-4])_\d+\.jpg$")

UTKFACE_NAME — UTKFace keeps each photo's labels in its file name, such as 16_1_0_20170109214419099.jpg: age 16, sex 1 (female), group 0 (White), then the date and time it was collected. The pattern accepts exactly that shape: digits, 0 or 1, a digit from 0 to 4, digits, .jpg. Eight of the 24,109 files break it — 53__0_….jpg with a missing field, one ending .pg, one with a space before .jpg — and are left out rather than guessed at.

31UTKFACE_GROUPS = ("White", "Black", "Asian", "Indian", "Others")

UTKFACE_GROUPS — UTKFace's five group labels, in the order its numbers use. Its "Others" groups together Hispanic, Latino, Middle Eastern and more, so they are coarser than FairFace's seven.

32# The model answers for ages 0 to 100; the handful of faces labelled older are left out.
33AGES_SERVED = 101

AGES_SERVED = 101 — the model answers for ages 0 to 100, so the 22 faces labelled older (up to 116) are left out: there is no output to compare them with.

34# A fixed timestamp for every file written into a zip, so the same input always makes the same bytes.
35ZIP_TIME = (1980, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)

ZIP_TIME — a fixed timestamp for every file the project writes into a zip, so the same input always makes byte-for-byte the same zip. Used here for repacking UTKFace, and by face preparation.

38@dataclass(frozen=True)
39class Row:
40    image_id: str
41    dataset: str
42    archive: str
43    member: str
44    age_low: int
45    age_high: int | None
46    age_exact: int | None
47    sex: str
48    group: str
49    licence: str
50    split: str

Row — one image in the manifest:

  • image_id — a name unique across all datasets, such as fairface/train/1.jpg;
  • dataset, archive, member — where to find the image: which dataset, which zip file, and which file inside the zip;
  • age_low and age_high — the age band (age_high is None for an open band such as "70 and over");
  • age_exact — the exact age, when the dataset has one (FairFace never does);
  • sex and group — the dataset's own labels, kept so errors can be measured for each group (§2.16);
  • licence — copied from the register onto every row, so the terms travel with the data;
  • split — the image's job.

53def parse_age_range(text: str) -> tuple[int, int | None]:

parse_age_range — turn a label such as "10-19" into (10, 19), or "more than 70" into (70, None).

54    match = AGE_RANGE.match(text.strip())

Match the pattern, ignoring spaces at either end.

55    if match is None:
56        raise ValueError(f"not an age range: {text!r}")

No match: refuse loudly, rather than guess. A label nobody expected could mean anything.

57    if match[1] is not None:
58        return int(match[1]), int(match[2])

If the first capture matched, it was the dash form: return both numbers. match[1] is the first capture, match[2] the second.

59    return int(match[3] or match[4]), None

Otherwise it was one of the open forms: the number is in capture 3 (70+) or capture 4 (more than 70). a or b gives b when a is None.

60
61
62def split_for(image_id: str, official_split: str) -> str:

split_for — the split for one image.

63    if official_split == "val":
64        return "test"

FairFace's own validation set becomes our test set, untouched: it was put together by the dataset's authors, so nothing we chose can have leaked into it.

65    bucket = int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(image_id.encode("utf-8")).digest()[:4]) % 100

The rest is split by the image's fingerprint: take the SHA-256 of its image_id, read the first 4 bytes as a number, and keep the remainder after dividing by 100 — a number from 0 to 99 that looks random but is always the same for the same image. Splitting this way, rather than with a random-number generator, means the split never changes: on any computer, on any run, today or next year, an image stays in the split it started in. If a test image could ever drift into training, the test would be quietly ruined.

66    if official_split == "evaluation":
67        return "calib" if bucket < 50 else "test"

An evaluation dataset (UTKFace) is never trained on: its photos are split in half, calib for setting the safety lines and test for checking them (§5.2.6).

68    return "train" if bucket < 80 else "val" if bucket < 90 else "calib"

Numbers 0–79 are train, 80–89 val, and 90–99 calib.
