73    with zipfile.ZipFile(entry.folder / archive) as images:
74        present = set(images.namelist())

Open the zip and take the list of files it holds (namelist). Only the list is read — the zip is never unpacked.

75    for official in ("train", "val"):
76        with (entry.folder / f"fairface_label_{official}.csv").open(encoding="utf-8", newline="") as labels:

77            for record in csv.DictReader(labels):

78                member = record["file"]

81                low, high = parse_age_range(record["age"])

82                image_id = f"fairface/{member}"

89                    age_high=high,
90                    age_exact=None,

93                    licence=entry.licence,

95                )

Build the row. sex is lower-cased (Female becomes female) so all datasets spell it the same way; group keeps FairFace's own group names.

98def repack(parts: list[Path], target: Path) -> None:

repack — copy every file out of one or more .tar.gz archives into a single zip. A .tar.gz is one long compressed stream: reaching the 20,000th photo means decompressing the 19,999 before it. A zip keeps an index and can read any photo directly, which face preparation needs.

99    partial = target.with_name(target.name + ".part")
100    with zipfile.ZipFile(partial, "w", zipfile.ZIP_STORED) as out:

Write to a .part file, uncompressed (ZIP_STORED): the photos are already JPEGs.

101        for part in parts:
102            with tarfile.open(part) as tar:
103                for member in tar:
104                    handle = tar.extractfile(member) if member.isfile() else None
105                    if handle is not None:
106                        out.writestr(zipfile.ZipInfo(member.name, date_time=ZIP_TIME), handle.read())

Open each archive (tarfile.open recognises the compression by itself) and copy every regular file into the zip under the same name, with the fixed timestamp. extractfile gives a file's contents; folders and other entries give None and are skipped.

107    partial.replace(target)

Rename the finished zip to its real name.

110def utkface_rows(entry: Dataset) -> Iterator[Row]:

utkface_rows — UTKFace's adapter.

111    archive = "utkface-in-the-wild.zip"
112    if not (entry.folder / archive).is_file():
113        repack([entry.folder / item.name for item in entry.files], entry.folder / archive)

Repack the three downloaded archives into one zip, the first time only.

114    with zipfile.ZipFile(entry.folder / archive) as images:
115        members = sorted(images.namelist())

List the zip's files in sorted order, so the manifest always comes out the same.

116    for member in members:
117        label = UTKFACE_NAME.match(member.rsplit("/", 1)[-1])
118        if label is None or int(label[1]) >= AGES_SERVED:
119            continue

Read each file's labels from its name. Files that don't match the pattern, and ages beyond 100, are skipped.

120        image_id = f"utkface/{member}"
121        yield Row(
122            image_id=image_id,
123            dataset=entry.name,
124            archive=archive,
125            member=member,
126            age_low=int(label[1]),
127            age_high=int(label[1]),
128            age_exact=int(label[1]),
129            sex=("male", "female")[int(label[2])],
130            group=UTKFACE_GROUPS[int(label[3])],
131            licence=entry.licence,
132            split=split_for(image_id, "evaluation"),
133        )

One row per photo: the exact age is both ends of a one-year band and age_exact; sex and group are translated from their numbers; the split is calib or test.

ADAPTERS — the adapter for each dataset name. UTKFace was added with one function and one entry here, as planned.

139def write_table[T: DataclassInstance](kind: type[T], rows: Iterable[T], path: Path) -> list[T]:

write_table — write any list of dataclass rows to a CSV file, and return them as a list. It is used for the manifest, and for the tables that face preparation and duplicate removal write (prepare.py, dedup.py). [T: DataclassInstance] makes it generic: T stands for whichever dataclass is passed in as kind, and the type checker then knows that the list returned holds that same kind of row.

140    kept = list(rows)

Collect the rows into a list (they arrive one at a time from the adapter).

141    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

Create the folder if needed.

142    with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as out:
143        writer = csv.writer(out)

Open the file for writing, and a CSV writer on it.

144        writer.writerow([field.name for field in fields(kind)])

The header line: the names of the dataclass's fields, in order (fields(kind) lists them).

145        for row in kept:
146            writer.writerow(["" if value is None else value for value in astuple(row)])

One line per row. astuple turns a row into its values, in the same order; None (an unknown value) is written as an empty cell.

147    return kept

Return the list, for the summary.

150def write_manifest(rows: Iterable[Row], path: Path) -> list[Row]:
151    return write_table(Row, rows, path)

write_manifest — the manifest is simply a table of Rows.

154def optional_int(text: str) -> int | None:
155    return int(text) if text else None

optional_int — the reverse of writing None as an empty cell: an empty cell is read back as None, anything else as a whole number.

158def read_manifest(path: Path) -> list[Row]:
159    with path.open(encoding="utf-8", newline="") as source:
160        return [
161            Row(
162                image_id=record["image_id"],
163                dataset=record["dataset"],
164                archive=record["archive"],
165                member=record["member"],
166                age_low=int(record["age_low"]),
167                age_high=optional_int(record["age_high"]),
168                age_exact=optional_int(record["age_exact"]),
169                sex=record["sex"],
170                group=record["group"],
171                licence=record["licence"],
172                split=record["split"],
173            )
174            for record in csv.DictReader(source)
175        ]

read_manifest — read a manifest back into Rows, turning each column's text into the right type: numbers with int, possibly-empty numbers with optional_int, and everything else kept as text. Face preparation and duplicate removal both start from it.

178def age_label(row: Row) -> str:
179    return f"{row.age_low}-{row.age_high}" if row.age_high is not None else f"{row.age_low}+"

age_label — a row's age band as text: 10-19, or 70+ for an open band.

181
182def summary(rows: list[Row]) -> str:

summary — the short report printed after a manifest is written. A person should see how much data there is, and how it divides, before anything is trained on it.

183    by_split = Counter(row.split for row in rows)
184    by_age = Counter((row.age_low, age_label(row)) for row in rows)
185    by_group = Counter(row.group for row in rows)

Count the images per split, per age band, and per group. The age bands are counted by (age_low, label) pairs, so that sorting puts them in age order — 3-9 before 10-19, which plain text sorting would get wrong.

186    lines = [f"{len(rows):,} images"]

The first line: how many images. :, writes numbers with thousands separators (97,698).

187    lines.append("splits: " + ", ".join(f"{name} {count:,}" for name, count in sorted(by_split.items())))
188    lines.append("ages:   " + ", ".join(f"{label} {count:,}" for (_, label), count in sorted(by_age.items())))
189    lines.append("groups: " + ", ".join(f"{name} {count:,}" for name, count in sorted(by_group.items())))

One line each for splits, ages and groups. ", ".join(...) puts commas between the parts; for (_, label), count in … unpacks each counted pair, ignoring the number used only for sorting (_).

190    return "\n".join(lines)

Join the lines, one under another ("\n" is a line break).

And write_manifest returns both rows.

Real world — what the data showed

  • The documentation was wrong. FairFace's documentation says its oldest age band is written 70+; its label file actually says more than 70. The manifest refused the unknown spelling instead of guessing, which is how it was found. Refusing what you don't understand turns a silent mistake into a visible one.
  • The numbers. 97,698 faces: 69,469 for training, 8,654 for validation, 8,621 for calibration and 10,954 for the final test. They are spread fairly evenly across the seven groups (from 10,425 to 18,612 faces each), which is what FairFace was built for.
  • What it can't do. Only 10,284 faces fall in the band "10-19", and that band holds children and adults together. FairFace can teach a model to see age; it can't prove where the line between 17 and 18 falls. That needs exact ages, from a dataset the owner hasn't approved yet (§2.14).

5.2.2 Risk control — choosing the safety lines

The background is in §2.14: the Clopper–Pearson bound, cells, and how a bound becomes a line. This code is the calculation itself. It works on any list of (age, group, score) triples, so it was written and tested before any model exists, on made-up populations. When the trained model scores the calibration split, the same code chooses its lines.

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/risk.py158 lines · 100% explained

The safety lines — the most important calculation in the project (ADR-0006, §2.14). The age model gives each face a score p_over: how likely the person is to be at least the minimum age N, from 0 to 1. This file chooses the two lines that turn the score into a decision:

p_over:   0 ─────────────── τ_fail ════════ step-up ════════ τ_pass ─────────────── 1
               fail (clearly under N)                            pass (clearly N or over)
  • tau_pass (τ is the Greek letter tau, a traditional name for a threshold) is the lowest line at which, for every exact age from N−5 to N−1 and every group, the worst plausible share of those children who would pass is within the risk budget ε (epsilon) — with 95 % confidence.
  • tau_fail is the highest line at which the worst plausible share of clear adults (N+3 and over) who would be failed outright is within 1 %, in every group.

Everyone between the two lines gets step-up (a document check), never a rejection.

Why "every age and every group", and not just "all children together"? Because an average hides danger. A model could let in 0.5 % of 13-year-olds and 6 % of 17-year-olds and still average under 2 %. Checking every cell — one age in one group — separately means the promise holds for each of them.

1"""Risk-controlled thresholds (ADR-0006): the lowest pass bar whose under-age pass rate is provably small.
2
3For a minimum age N, the pass threshold is the lowest score bar at which, for every exact age from N-5 to N-1 and
4every group, the one-sided Clopper-Pearson upper bound of the share of those people who would pass is at most the
5risk budget, at confidence 1 - delta. The fail threshold is chosen the same way for adults aged N+3 and over, so
6that they are almost never failed outright.
7"""

The docstring: the rule above, in one paragraph.

11import bisect
12import math
13from collections import defaultdict
14from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Sequence
15from dataclasses import dataclass

bisect (fast searching in sorted lists), math, defaultdict (a dictionary that creates missing entries automatically), the types for functions and sequences, and dataclass.

16
17from scipy.stats import beta

beta — the beta distribution, from SciPy, Python's standard library of scientific maths. The Clopper–Pearson bound is a value read off this distribution (§2.14). The formula is famous and short, but computing it accurately for any input is not: SciPy's code for it has been tested for decades, so we use it rather than write our own.

18
19DELTA = 0.05

DELTA (δ, delta) — the chance we accept of the bound itself being wrong: 5 %, so the guarantee holds with 95 % confidence.

20MINOR_SPAN = 5

MINOR_SPAN — how many years under N are checked: for N = 18, ages 13 to 17. Younger children are further from the line, so they are even safer.

21ADULT_MARGIN = 3

ADULT_MARGIN — the fail line protects adults from N+3 upwards (21 and over, for N = 18). People aged 18–20 may land in step-up more often, which is the price of keeping children out.

22ADULT_FAIL_BUDGET = 0.01

ADULT_FAIL_BUDGET — at most 1 % of those adults may be failed outright, in any group.

23
24type Cells = dict[str, list[float]]

Cells — the scores sorted into cells: a cell's name (such as age 15 · Indian) mapped to its list of scores. type … = … names a type, so long types can be written once.

25type Count = Callable[[list[float]], int]

Count — a function that counts, in one cell's sorted scores, how many would pass (or fail) at some line.

26
27
28@dataclass(frozen=True)
29class Scored:
30    age: int
31    group: str
32    p_over: float

Scored — one calibration image after the model has looked at it: the person's real age, their group, and the model's score.

33
34
35@dataclass(frozen=True)
36class Thresholds:
37    min_age: int
38    risk_budget: float
39    tau_pass: float
40    tau_fail: float
41    minor_bound: float
42    adult_bound: float
43    by_group: bool = True

Thresholds — the result: the minimum age and risk budget it was made for, both lines, the worst bound each line achieved (minor_bound for children passing, adult_bound for adults failing), and whether the promise holds for every group or only for every age (by_group, below). These numbers go into the model's manifest, so anyone can see what was promised.

44
45
46class CalibrationError(ValueError):
47    """The calibration data can't support a guarantee, and saying so is safer than returning a threshold."""

CalibrationError — the data can't support the promise. The docstring states the rule: refusing, with a reason, is safer than handing back a line that only looks safe.

48
49
50def cell_name(person: Scored, by_group: bool) -> str:
51    return f"age {person.age} · {person.group}" if by_group else f"age {person.age}"

cell_name — the name of a person's cell. Normally one cell per age and group (age 15 · Indian); when the data is too thin for that, one cell per age, all groups together (age 15). The second is a weaker promise — it holds on average across groups, not for each — and the results always record which one was made.

52
53
54def clopper_pearson_upper(successes: int, trials: int, delta: float = DELTA) -> float:
55    """The one-sided upper bound, at confidence 1 - delta, of a rate observed as `successes` out of `trials`."""

clopper_pearson_upper — the bound itself. Out of trials people, successes passed; how high could the true pass rate plausibly be? (For 6 out of 600: 1.96 %.)

56    if trials <= 0 or not 0 <= successes <= trials:
57        raise ValueError(f"need 0 <= successes <= trials and trials > 0, got {successes} of {trials}")

Refuse impossible inputs — no people, or more passes than people.

58    if successes == trials:
59        return 1.0

If everyone passed, the true rate could be anything up to 100 %: the bound is 1. (The formula below would divide by zero here.)

60    return float(beta.ppf(1.0 - delta, successes + 1, trials - successes))

The Clopper–Pearson upper bound: the value below which the beta distribution with parameters successes + 1 and trials − successes holds 1 − δ of its weight (ppf reads the distribution "backwards", from a share to a value). float(...) turns SciPy's number type into an ordinary Python number.

61
62
63def minimum_cell_size(epsilon: float, delta: float = DELTA) -> int:
64    """The fewest people a cell needs before even zero passes can prove a rate of at most epsilon."""
65    return math.ceil(math.log(delta) / math.log(1.0 - epsilon))

minimum_cell_size — the fewest people a cell needs before the promise is even possible. With zero passes the bound is 1 − δ^(1/n), and requiring that to be at most ε gives n ≥ log δ ÷ log(1 − ε). For ε = 2 %: 149 people. With 148, even a perfect result can't prove 2 %. math.ceil rounds up to a whole person.

66
67
68def cells_of(labelled: Iterable[tuple[str, float]]) -> Cells:

cells_of — sort labelled scores into cells.

69    cells: dict[str, list[float]] = defaultdict(list)
70    for label, score in labelled:
71        cells[label].append(score)

Add each score to its cell's list; defaultdict(list) creates an empty list the first time a cell is seen.

72    return {label: sorted(scores) for label, scores in cells.items()}

Return each cell's scores sorted, so counting how many lie above a line becomes a fast search (passes_at, below).

73
74
75def check_size(cells: Cells, epsilon: float, delta: float, who: str) -> None:

check_size — refuse any cell too small to certify the budget.

76    needed = minimum_cell_size(epsilon, delta)
77    small = sorted(f"{label} ({len(scores)})" for label, scores in cells.items() if len(scores) < needed)

Work out the minimum, and list every cell that falls short, with its size.

78    if small:
79        raise CalibrationError(f"too few {who} to certify {epsilon:.0%} (need {needed} per cell): " + "; ".join(small))

If any do, refuse, naming them all — such as too few minors to certify 2% (need 149 per cell): age 15 · b (100). The message says exactly which data is missing.

80
81
82def worst_bound(cells: Cells, count: Count, delta: float) -> float:
83    return max(clopper_pearson_upper(count(scores), len(scores), delta) for scores in cells.values())

worst_bound — the highest bound across all cells, for a given way of counting. The promise is only as good as its weakest cell.

84
85
86def first_safe(candidates: Sequence[float], is_safe: Callable[[float], bool]) -> float:

first_safe — find the first safe value in a list, given that the list is in order: once one candidate is safe, every candidate after it is safe too. It uses binary search: the guessing game where someone thinks of a number from 1 to 100, you guess 50, they say "higher" or "lower", and each guess throws away half of what's left — so seven guesses are always enough.

87    """The first safe candidate, given that once a candidate is safe, every later one is safe too."""

The docstring states that condition, because the search is only correct when it holds. It does here: raising the pass line can only make fewer people pass.

88    low, high = 0, len(candidates) - 1

Search between the first and the last candidate.

89    while low < high:
90        middle = (low + high) // 2
91        if is_safe(candidates[middle]):
92            high = middle
93        else:
94            low = middle + 1

Look at the middle one. If it is safe, the first safe one is here or earlier: keep the left half. If not, it's later: keep the right half. Each step halves the range, so even 100,000 candidates take about 17 steps.

95    return candidates[low]

When the range has shrunk to one, that's the answer. (If no candidate were safe, this would return the last one; the callers check for that.)

96
97
98def passes_at(tau: float) -> Count:
99    return lambda scores: len(scores) - bisect.bisect_left(scores, tau)

passes_at — make a counting function for a pass line τ: how many scores are at or above τ. In a sorted list, bisect_left finds where τ would go; everything from there on is at least τ.

100
101
102def fails_at(tau: float) -> Count:
103    return lambda scores: bisect.bisect_right(scores, tau)

fails_at — the same for a fail line: how many scores are at or below τ. bisect_right finds the position just after any scores equal to τ.

104
105
106def tau_pass_for(
107    people: Sequence[Scored], min_age: int, epsilon: float, delta: float = DELTA, by_group: bool = True
108) -> tuple[float, float]:
109    """The lowest pass threshold that keeps every under-age cell's pass rate provably at most epsilon."""

tau_pass_for — the lowest safe pass line, and the bound it achieves. by_group chooses the kind of cell.

110    ages = range(min_age - MINOR_SPAN, min_age)
111    minors = [person for person in people if person.age in ages]

The ages checked (range(13, 18) is 13 to 17 — the end is not included), and the people of those ages.

112    missing = sorted(set(ages) - {person.age for person in minors})
113    if missing:
114        raise CalibrationError(f"no calibration data for ages {missing}")

If any of those ages has no data at all, refuse: a promise about 13–17-year-olds can't be made without 16-year-olds.

115    cells = cells_of((cell_name(person, by_group), person.p_over) for person in minors)

The cells: one per age and group, or one per age.

116    check_size(cells, epsilon, delta, "minors")

Refuse any cell under the minimum size.

117    scores = sorted({score for cell in cells.values() for score in cell})

Every distinct score seen, in order.

118    candidates = [0.0, *(math.nextafter(score, math.inf) for score in scores)]

The candidate lines. A line only matters where it crosses a score, so the candidates are 0 (everyone passes) and, for each score, the smallest number just above it (math.nextafter(score, math.inf) — the next number a computer can represent, heading towards infinity). A line just above a score makes that person, and everyone below them, fail. Trying only these lines covers every possible outcome, with nothing missed.

119    tau = first_safe(candidates, lambda t: worst_bound(cells, passes_at(t), delta) <= epsilon)

Find the first — so the lowest — candidate at which the worst cell's pass bound is within the budget. A lower line lets more adults pass straight away, so the lowest safe line is the best one.

120    if tau > 1.0:
121        raise CalibrationError("a minor scored 1.0: no pass threshold is safe")

If the only safe line is above 1, some child scored exactly 1.0 ("certainly an adult"), and no line on the 0–1 scale keeps them out: refuse.

122    return tau, worst_bound(cells, passes_at(tau), delta)

Return the line and its bound.

123
124
125def tau_fail_for(
126    people: Sequence[Scored],
127    min_age: int,
128    epsilon: float = ADULT_FAIL_BUDGET,
129    delta: float = DELTA,
130    below: float = math.inf,
131    by_group: bool = True,
132) -> tuple[float, float]:
133    """The highest fail threshold, under `below`, that keeps every group's rate of failed adults (N+3+) provably small.
134
135    A lower fail threshold only ever fails fewer adults, so capping it below the pass threshold keeps it safe.
136    """

tau_fail_for — the highest safe fail line for clear adults, and its bound. The extra setting below caps the line under a given value — the pass line, when calibrate calls it (math.inf, "infinity", means no cap). The docstring records why capping is always allowed: lowering a fail line can only fail fewer adults, so a safe line stays safe.

137    adults = (person for person in people if person.age >= min_age + ADULT_MARGIN)
138    cells = cells_of((person.group if by_group else "adults", person.p_over) for person in adults)

One cell per group holding everyone N+3 and over — or, without groups, a single cell of all those adults.

139    if not cells:
140        raise CalibrationError(f"no calibration data for adults aged {min_age + ADULT_MARGIN} and over")

No adults at all: refuse.

141    check_size(cells, epsilon, delta, "adults")

Refuse any group under the minimum size (299 people for 1 %).

142    scores = sorted({score for cell in cells.values() for score in cell}, reverse=True)
143    candidates = [*scores, math.nextafter(scores[-1], -math.inf)]

The candidates run the other way: every distinct score, highest first, and finally a value just below the lowest score (a line that fails no one). Lowering the fail line can only fail fewer adults, so once a candidate is safe, every later one is too — the condition first_safe needs.

144    highest = first_safe(candidates, lambda t: worst_bound(cells, fails_at(t), delta) <= epsilon)

Find the highest safe line.

145    tau = max(0.0, min(highest, math.nextafter(below, -math.inf)))

Then cap it: no higher than just below below, and no lower than 0, to stay on the 0–1 scale.

146    bound = worst_bound(cells, fails_at(tau), delta)
147    if bound > epsilon:
148        raise CalibrationError("an adult scored 0.0: no fail threshold is safe")

Measure the bound at the final line, and check it again: if an adult scored exactly 0.0, even the line at 0 fails them, so no fail line is safe — refuse.

149    return tau, bound

Return the line and its bound.

150
151
152def calibrate(
153    people: Sequence[Scored], min_age: int, epsilon: float, delta: float = DELTA, by_group: bool = True
154) -> Thresholds:
155    """Both thresholds for one minimum age and risk budget, or a CalibrationError explaining why there are none."""

calibrate — both lines for one minimum age and budget, with either kind of cell.

156    tau_pass, minor_bound = tau_pass_for(people, min_age, epsilon, delta, by_group)

First the pass line, which protects children — it is never moved to suit anything else.

157    tau_fail, adult_bound = tau_fail_for(people, min_age, delta=delta, below=tau_pass, by_group=by_group)

Then the fail line, capped just below the pass line, so the two can never cross and no score can mean both "pass" and "fail".

A first version of this function refused to answer when the highest safe fail line came out above the pass line, calling it a model that "can't separate" the ages. Writing this book's explanation of its test showed that was wrong: in that test the children all scored 0.9 and the adults 0.95 — a model that separates the ages perfectly. A fail line chosen without looking at the pass line can drift up past it, but it can always be lowered again safely. Now it is.

158    return Thresholds(min_age, epsilon, tau_pass, tau_fail, minor_bound, adult_bound, by_group)

Return the result, recording the kind of cell.

ml/tests/test_risk.py95 lines · 100% explained

Tests for the safety lines. The calculation in risk.py is the promise the whole system makes to parents and regulators, so it is tested three ways:

  • known values worked out independently — the 149-person minimum;
  • properties that must hold for every input, checked by Hypothesis on hundreds of invented ones — including the central claim, "the pass line is safe, and is the lowest safe line";
  • refusals — every way the data can be too thin, each one checked to be refused with a clear reason.

The tests use made-up populations: people with ages, groups and scores, but no faces.

83def test_a_model_that_cannot_tell_ages_apart_passes_and_fails_no_one() -> None:

89def test_a_model_that_separates_perfectly_gets_lines_that_never_cross() -> None:
90    minors = [Scored(age, "a", 0.9) for age in range(13, 18) for _ in range(800)]
91    adults = [Scored(age, "a", 0.95) for age in range(21, 40) for _ in range(800)]

A model that separates perfectly. Every child scores 0.9 and every adult 0.95.

92    thresholds = calibrate(minors + adults, 18, 0.02)
93    assert 0.9 <= thresholds.tau_fail < thresholds.tau_pass <= 0.95
94    assert thresholds.minor_bound <= 0.02
95    assert thresholds.adult_bound <= 0.01

Calibration succeeds, and puts both lines in the gap between the two groups: children are failed, adults pass, and both bounds are within budget. An earlier version of calibrate wrongly refused this model; this test, rewritten when the mistake was found, makes sure it can't come back.

Real world — a mistake the book caught

The first version of calibrate refused to answer when the highest safe fail line came out above the pass line, reporting that the model "can't separate" the ages. Its test used children who all scored 0.9 and adults who all scored 0.95, and the test passed.

Explaining that test for this book showed that the expected result was wrong. Those scores describe a model that separates the ages perfectly, and the right answer was two lines in the gap, not a refusal. Each line had been chosen without looking at the other, but a fail line can always be lowered safely, so it is now capped just below the pass line. This is exactly why the book explains every line: putting code into plain words is a review.

Try it yourself

Run the ML tests (no download needed):

uv run pytest ml/tests

Then, in Python (uv run --package dwarpal-ml python), ask the bound some questions:

python from dwarpal_ml.risk import clopper_pearson_upper, minimum_cell_size clopper_pearson_upper(6, 600) # 0.0196… — the jar from §3.3 clopper_pearson_upper(7, 600) # 0.0218… — one more child, and the line must move minimum_cell_size(0.02) # 149

5.2.3 Face preparation — the same faces the service sees

The background is in §2.17: finding a face, finding its landmarks, and straightening it. This step runs every FairFace image through the vision library built in Phase 1 — the very code that handles webcam frames — and then removes repeated photos.

manifest ──► dwarpal_ml.prepare   97,698 images → 97,645 aligned faces (53 without a face)      45 s on 24 cores
         ──► dwarpal_ml.dedup     123,774 candidate pairs → 502 confirmed → 467 copies removed    about 1 min
         ──► usable faces:        train 69,012 · val 8,625 · calib 8,600 · test 10,941

Preparing the faces

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/prepare.py171 lines · 100% explained

Face preparation: for every image in a manifest, find the face, straighten and crop it, and save the result — using exactly the code the inference service uses on webcam frames (§5.1.1). This matters more than it sounds. A model learns whatever its training pictures look like: if training faces were cropped one way and live faces another, the model would be judged on pictures unlike anything it learned from (§2.17).

.datasets/raw/fairface/…margin125….zip   ──►  for each image:  decode → detect → pick the central face
                                                                  → quality measurements → align to 256×256
                                                                  → fingerprint
                                          ──►  .datasets/processed/fairface.zip     (97,645 aligned faces, 1.7 GB)
                                          ──►  .datasets/manifest/fairface.faces.csv (one row per image: outcome,
                                                                                      measurements, fingerprint)

All 97,698 FairFace images take about 45 seconds, spread over 24 processor cores.

1"""Face preparation: find, straighten and crop every face with the code that serves, and fingerprint each one.
2
3uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.prepare fairface
4"""

29PROCESSED = RAW.parent / "processed"

30DETECTOR = ROOT / "models" / "third_party" / "face_detection_yunet_2023mar.onnx"

DETECTOR — the YuNet face-detector model, downloaded in Phase 1 (models/third_party.json).

31SIZE = 256

SIZE = 256 — faces are saved at 256×256 pixels, with exactly the framing the service uses at 224×224, only larger. Training will cut slightly smaller pieces from them at random positions (a standard way of adding variety, §2.15) and shrink them to 224.

32JPEG_QUALITY = 95

JPEG_QUALITY = 95 — saved as high-quality JPEG: about 20 KB a face, with no visible loss.

34# Dataset photos may be larger than any webcam frame: they are decoded with roomier limits, then shrunk to the
35# largest size the service accepts, so detection works on pictures like the ones it will see.
36DATASET_BYTES = 32 * 1024 * 1024
37DATASET_SIDE = 16_384

Roomier limits for dataset photos. The service refuses uploads over 512 KB or 1,920 pixels a side, and rightly: a webcam frame is never bigger. But a dataset photo can be — 254 of UTKFace's photos are over 512 KB, and one is 8,739 pixels wide. The comment states the approach: decode them with generous limits (32 MB, 16,384 pixels), then shrink them to the service's largest size, so the detector works on pictures like the ones it will meet in service.

40@dataclass(frozen=True)
41class Prepared:
42    image_id: str
43    status: str
44    faces: int = 0
45    detector_score: float = 0.0
46    eye_distance_px: float = 0.0
47    brightness: float = 0.0
48    sharpness: float = 0.0
49    yaw_ratio: float = 0.0
50    flags: str = ""
51    phash: str = ""

Prepared — what happened to one image:

  • status — ok, or why not: undecodable, no_face or unalignable;
  • faces — how many faces the detector found;
  • the quality measurements of the chosen face (detector_score, eye_distance_px, brightness, sharpness, yaw_ratio — §5.1.1) and the names of any quality rules it broke (flags);
  • phash — the face's perceptual hash (below), as 16 hexadecimal digits.

The = 0 and = "" are default values, so a failure can be recorded with just the image and its status.

52
53
54def central_face(image: Image, faces: list[Face]) -> Face:

central_face — when a photo shows several people, choose the face nearest the middle. FairFace made each image by centring it on the labelled person, so the central face is the one the age label belongs to — and the most confident face may well be someone else's, nearer the camera.

55    height, width = image.shape[:2]

The picture's height and width.

56
57    def distance(face: Face) -> float:
58        x, y, w, h = face.box
59        return math.hypot(x + w / 2 - width / 2, y + h / 2 - height / 2)

The distance from a face's centre to the picture's centre. math.hypot(a, b) is √(a² + b²): Pythagoras's theorem, the straight-line distance.

60
61    return min(faces, key=distance)

The face with the smallest distance. min(…, key=distance) compares the faces by their distance, but returns the face itself.

62
63
64def perceptual_hash(image: Image) -> int:

perceptual_hash — a 64-bit fingerprint of what a picture looks like. A SHA-256 fingerprint (§X.5) changes completely if a single pixel changes; a perceptual hash barely changes when a photo is resized, re-saved or slightly recoloured. Two copies of one photo get nearly the same hash. That makes it a quick way to shortlist possible duplicates (dedup.py).

65    gray = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
66    small = cv2.resize(gray, (32, 32), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)

Turn the picture grey and shrink it to 32×32 pixels: only the broad pattern of light and dark is kept.

67    low = cv2.dct(small)[:8, :8].flatten()

The discrete cosine transform (DCT) describes the little picture as a sum of wave patterns, from smooth (top-left of the result) to fine (bottom-right) — the same idea JPEG compression is built on. The top-left 8×8 values hold the 64 smoothest patterns: the picture's overall structure. flatten lays them out in one row.

68    bits = low > np.median(low[1:])

Each of the 64 values becomes one bit: is it above the middle value (the median)? The first value — the picture's overall brightness — is left out when finding the median, so that a brighter copy of a photo gets the same bits.

69    return int.from_bytes(np.packbits(bits).tobytes(), "big")

Pack the 64 true/false values into 8 bytes, and read them as one whole number.

70
71
72def within_frame(image: Image) -> Image:

within_frame — shrink a picture so its longer side is at most 1,920 pixels, keeping its shape.

73    height, width = image.shape[:2]
74    if max(height, width) <= MAX_SIDE:
75        return image

A picture that already fits is returned unchanged.

76    scale = MAX_SIDE / max(height, width)
77    size = (round(width * scale), round(height * scale))
78    return np.asarray(cv2.resize(image, size, interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA), dtype=np.uint8)

Otherwise, work out the scale and the new size, and shrink it (INTER_AREA averages the pixels being merged, the best method for shrinking).

79
80
81def prepare_one(detector: FaceDetector, data: bytes, image_id: str, subject: str = "central") -> tuple[Prepared, bytes]:

prepare_one — one image, from bytes to an aligned face. It returns the record and the face as JPEG bytes (empty bytes when there's no face). subject is the dataset's rule for finding the labelled person (ml/datasets.toml).

82    try:
83        image = within_frame(decode_image(data, DATASET_BYTES, DATASET_SIDE))
84    except DecodeError:
85        return Prepared(image_id, "undecodable"), b""

Decode the image with the vision library's careful decoder, which checks the file before decoding it (§5.1.1), using the roomier dataset limits, then shrink it if needed. Anything it refuses is recorded as undecodable.

86    faces = detector.detect(image)
87    if not faces:
88        return Prepared(image_id, "no_face"), b""

Find the faces. None at all: no_face.

89    face = central_face(image, faces) if subject == "central" else faces[0]

Choose the face: for a central dataset such as FairFace, the one nearest the middle; for an only dataset such as UTKFace, the clearest one (the detector lists faces most confident first).

90    quality = assess(image, [face, *(other for other in faces if other is not face)])

Measure its quality. assess judges the first face of the list, so the chosen face goes first, followed by the others (* unpacks them into the list). The quality rules are the ones for live webcam frames; here they are only recorded, never used to drop a face. Dataset photos break them often (a quarter of FairFace's faces are turned too far to one side for the live check) and a model needs to learn from such faces too. The records feed the data report.

91    if subject == "only" and "multiple_faces" in quality.flags:
92        return Prepared(image_id, "several_faces", faces=len(faces)), b""

For an only dataset, a photo with a second clear face is set aside as several_faces: the label could belong to either person, and a wrong guess would teach or test the model with someone else's age. In UTKFace, 519 photos were set aside this way.

93    try:
94        aligned = align_face(image, face, size=SIZE)
95    except ValueError:
96        return Prepared(image_id, "unalignable", faces=len(faces)), b""

Straighten and crop the face to 256×256. If its landmarks are impossible to align, record unalignable.

97    encoded = cv2.imencode(".jpg", aligned, [cv2.IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY, JPEG_QUALITY])[1]

Encode the aligned face as JPEG. imencode returns a success flag and the bytes; [1] takes the bytes.

98    prepared = Prepared(
99        image_id=image_id,
100        status="ok",
101        faces=quality.faces,
102        detector_score=round(quality.detector_score, 4),
103        eye_distance_px=round(quality.eye_distance_px, 2),
104        brightness=round(quality.brightness, 4),
105        sharpness=round(quality.sharpness, 2),
106        yaw_ratio=round(quality.yaw_ratio, 4),
107        flags="|".join(quality.flags),
108        phash=f"{perceptual_hash(aligned):016x}",
109    )

The record of a success: the measurements, each rounded to a sensible number of decimals so the table stays readable; the quality flags joined into one text such as not_frontal|too_dark; and the perceptual hash of the aligned face, written as 16 hexadecimal digits (:016x).

110    return prepared, encoded.tobytes()

Return the record and the JPEG bytes.

113def prepare_chunk(
114    folder: Path, rows: list[Row], subject: str = "central", model: Path = DETECTOR
115) -> list[tuple[Prepared, bytes]]:

prepare_chunk — prepare 500 images. This is the work one process does at a time. It is told the dataset's subject rule.

116    cv2.setNumThreads(1)

setNumThreads(1) — tell OpenCV to use a single thread. The work is already spread over one process per core; if each process also started threads of its own, they would fight over the same cores.

117    detector = FaceDetector(model)

Each chunk loads its own detector: objects like this can't be shared between processes. Loading takes a few milliseconds — nothing, next to 500 images.

118    results = []

The results so far.

119    with ExitStack() as stack:
120        archives: dict[str, zipfile.ZipFile] = {}
121        for row in rows:
122            if row.archive not in archives:
123                archives[row.archive] = stack.enter_context(zipfile.ZipFile(folder / row.archive))

Open each zip file the rows need, once. ExitStack remembers every file opened inside it and closes them all at the end, even if something fails halfway.

124            results.append(prepare_one(detector, archives[row.archive].read(row.member), row.image_id, subject))

Read the image's bytes from inside the zip, and prepare it with the subject rule.

125    return results

Return the chunk's results.

128def prepare(rows: list[Row], folder: Path, target: Path, workers: int, subject: str = "central") -> list[Prepared]:

prepare — prepare a whole manifest, using several processes, with the dataset's subject rule.

129    chunks = [rows[start : start + CHUNK] for start in range(0, len(rows), CHUNK)]

Cut the rows into chunks of 500.

130    target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
131    partial = target.with_name(target.name + ".part")

Create the output folder; write to a .part file first, as in the fetch command, so a half-finished run is never mistaken for a finished one.

132    prepared: list[Prepared] = []

The records, in manifest order.

133    with ProcessPoolExecutor(workers) as pool, zipfile.ZipFile(partial, "w", zipfile.ZIP_STORED) as out:

Start the process pool — workers copies of Python, each able to run prepare_chunk — and open the output zip. ZIP_STORED means "don't compress": JPEGs are already compressed, and compressing them again would only waste time.

134        for done, results in enumerate(pool.map(prepare_chunk, repeat(folder), chunks, repeat(subject)), 1):

pool.map sends the chunks to the workers and hands back their results in the original order, as they become ready. repeat(folder) and repeat(subject) supply the same folder and rule to every chunk. enumerate(…, 1) counts the chunks from 1.

135            for item, jpeg in results:
136                prepared.append(item)
137                if jpeg:
138                    out.writestr(zipfile.ZipInfo(item.image_id, date_time=ZIP_TIME), jpeg)

Keep every record. For each face that was prepared, add its JPEG to the zip under the image's name, with the fixed timestamp.

139            print(f"\r{len(prepared):,}/{len(rows):,} images", end="", flush=True)

Show progress on one line: \r returns to the start of the line, so each update overwrites the last; flush=True shows it immediately.

140            if done == len(chunks):
141                print()

After the last chunk, end the progress line.

142    partial.replace(target)

Rename the finished zip to its real name.

143    return prepared

Return the records.

146def summary(prepared: list[Prepared]) -> str:

summary — what to print at the end.

147    statuses = Counter(item.status for item in prepared)
148    flags = Counter(flag for item in prepared for flag in item.flags.split("|") if flag)

Count the outcomes, and every quality flag (split("|") separates them again).

149    lines = [f"{len(prepared):,} images: " + ", ".join(f"{name} {count:,}" for name, count in statuses.most_common())]
150    lines.append("quality flags (recorded, not removed): " + ", ".join(f"{n} {c:,}" for n, c in flags.most_common()))

One line for outcomes and one for flags, most common first. The second line says plainly that flagged faces are kept.

151    return "\n".join(lines)

Removing duplicates

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/dedup.py180 lines · 100% explained

Near-duplicate removal. Photo collections gathered from the internet contain the same photo more than once — re-uploaded, resized, re-compressed, turned grey. If one copy lands in training and another in the test set, the model is tested on a photo it has already studied, and looks better than it is (§2.2). If two copies land in the calibration set, they count as two people when they are one, and the safety bound (§2.14) claims more evidence than it has.

Comparing every face with every other in detail would mean 4.8 billion comparisons. So the work is done in two stages:

97,645 faces ──► 1. the sieve: perceptual hashes within 10 bits of each other ──► 123,774 candidate pairs
                                (fast: bit arithmetic on whole blocks of hashes)
             ──► 2. the check: compare the pairs' fine detail; similarity ≥ 0.6 ──► 502 confirmed pairs
             ──► 3. group copies of the same photo; keep one per group, in the most protected split
             ──► .datasets/manifest/fairface.duplicates.csv: 467 copies removed

Both limits — 10 bits and 0.6 — were chosen by looking at real pairs on either side of them; §5.2.3 tells that story.

1"""Near-duplicate removal: find faces that are the same photo, and keep one copy, in the most protected split.
2
3Two stages: perceptual hashes cheaply shortlist pairs that might be the same photo, then the fine detail of each
4shortlisted pair is compared to confirm it.
5
6uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.dedup fairface
7"""

The docstring: the job, the two stages, and the command.

26from dwarpal_ml.manifest import MANIFESTS, Row, age_label, read_manifest, write_table

31# Both limits were chosen by looking at FairFace's pairs on either side of them (docs/reports/phase-2.md).
32SIEVE_DISTANCE = 10
33MIN_SIMILARITY = 0.6

The two limits, and a comment saying where the evidence for them is written down:

  • SIEVE_DISTANCE = 10 — two hashes are a candidate pair if at most 10 of their 64 bits differ;
  • MIN_SIMILARITY = 0.6 — a candidate pair is confirmed as the same photo if its fine-detail similarity is at least 0.6.
34DETAIL_SIZE = 64
35DETAIL_BLUR = 2.0

How fine detail is measured: on a 64×64 grey version of the face, with a blur of strength 2 (below).

36BLOCK = 256

BLOCK = 256 — the sieve compares 256 hashes against the rest at a time.

37# A duplicate keeps the copy whose split is hardest to reach: the exam outranks the safety check, and so on.
38SPLIT_PRIORITY = {"test": 0, "calib": 1, "val": 2, "train": 3}

SPLIT_PRIORITY — which copy to keep. Lower numbers win: a copy in test is kept over one in calib, calib over val, and val over train. The copy that survives is always the one in the split that matters most to keep clean, and the copies that would have leaked into it are the ones removed.

39
40type Vector = NDArray[np.float32]

Vector — a name for "a list of decimal numbers in a NumPy array".

41
42
43@dataclass(frozen=True)
44class Duplicate:
45    image_id: str
46    split: str
47    kept: str
48    kept_split: str
49    similarity: float
50    same_label: bool

Duplicate — one removed copy: which image, its split, the copy that was kept and its split, how similar they were, and whether both copies had the same age label.

51
52
53def close_pairs(hashes: NDArray[np.uint64], max_distance: int = SIEVE_DISTANCE) -> Iterator[tuple[int, int]]:

close_pairs — the sieve. It yields every pair of positions (a, b), with a before b, whose hashes differ in at most max_distance bits.

54    for start in range(0, len(hashes), BLOCK):
55        block = hashes[start : start + BLOCK]
56        rest = hashes[start:]

Take the hashes 256 at a time (block), and compare each block only with itself and everything after it (rest): pairs with earlier hashes were already found by earlier blocks.

57        distances = np.bitwise_count(block[:, None] ^ rest[None, :])

The heart of the sieve, in one line. block[:, None] ^ rest[None, :] arranges the block as a column and the rest as a row, and NumPy fills in the whole table between them: each cell is the XOR of two hashes, which has a 1 exactly where the two differ. np.bitwise_count counts those 1s — the Hamming distance. For a block of 256 against 97,645 hashes, that is 25 million distances, computed by NumPy's fast built-in loops in a fraction of a second. The whole sieve, over all 97,645 faces, takes well under a minute.

58        for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(distances <= max_distance), strict=True):
59            if i < j:
60                yield start + int(i), start + int(j)

np.nonzero gives the positions of every close pair in the table. Within the block's own square of the table, each pair appears twice (and every hash is at distance 0 from itself), so only i < j is kept. The positions are turned back into positions in the full list.

61
62
63def fine_detail(jpeg: bytes) -> Vector:

fine_detail — the check's view of a face: only its fine detail.

64    gray = cv2.cvtColor(decode_image(jpeg), cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
65    pixels = cv2.resize(gray, (DETAIL_SIZE, DETAIL_SIZE), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)

Decode the aligned face, turn it grey, and shrink it to 64×64.

66    detail = (pixels - cv2.GaussianBlur(pixels, (0, 0), DETAIL_BLUR)).flatten()

Subtract a blurred copy of the face from itself. Blurring keeps only the broad shapes; taking them away leaves only the fine detail — pores, hair strands, the edges of glasses, the texture of the background. This is the trick that makes the check work. After alignment, every face has its eyes, nose and mouth in the same places, so the broad shapes of two strangers can look remarkably alike. Their fine detail never matches, but two copies of one photo share it exactly, even after resizing, re-compression or conversion to grey.

67    detail -= detail.mean()
68    return detail / max(float(np.linalg.norm(detail)), 1e-6)

Shift the numbers so they average zero, and scale them so that their length (np.linalg.norm, √ of the sum of squares) is 1. max(…, 1e-6) avoids dividing by zero for a completely flat picture.

69
70
71def similarity(a: Vector, b: Vector) -> float:
72    return float(np.dot(a, b))

similarity — multiply two such vectors number by number and add up (np.dot). Because both were shifted and scaled, the result is their correlation: 1 for identical detail, around 0 for unrelated detail.

73
74
75class Details:
76    def __init__(self, archives: dict[str, zipfile.ZipFile], rows: list[Row]) -> None:
77        self.archives = archives
78        self.rows = rows
79        self.cache: dict[int, Vector] = {}

Details — fine detail on demand, from the zips of prepared faces: one zip per dataset, since a search may span two (--against, below). Many faces take part in several candidate pairs, so each is computed once and remembered in cache.

80
81    def __getitem__(self, index: int) -> Vector:
82        if index not in self.cache:
83            row = self.rows[index]
84            self.cache[index] = fine_detail(self.archives[row.dataset].read(row.image_id))
85        return self.cache[index]

__getitem__ is what Python calls for details[index]: compute the detail — reading the face from its own dataset's zip — if it isn't remembered yet, then return it.

86
87
88def confirmed_pairs(
89    pairs: Iterable[tuple[int, int]], details: Details, min_similarity: float = MIN_SIMILARITY
90) -> Iterator[tuple[int, int, float]]:

confirmed_pairs — the check: from the candidate pairs, yield the ones whose fine detail is at least min_similarity alike, with their score.

91    for a, b in pairs:
92        score = similarity(details[a], details[b])
93        if score >= min_similarity:
94            yield a, b, score

Score each pair, and pass on the confirmed ones.

95
96
97def groups_of(count: int, pairs: Iterable[tuple[int, int, float]]) -> list[list[int]]:

groups_of — turn confirmed pairs into groups of copies. If A matches B and B matches C, then A, B and C are one group, even if A and C were never compared.

98    links = DisjointSet(range(count))

A DisjointSet starts with every face in a group of its own.

99    for a, b, _ in pairs:
100        links.merge(a, b)

Each confirmed pair merges the two groups its faces belong to.

101    return [sorted(group) for group in links.subsets() if len(group) > 1]

Return every group with more than one face, its members in order.

103
104def resolve(rows: list[Row], groups: list[list[int]], details: Details, seen: str | None = None) -> list[Duplicate]:

resolve — decide which copy of each group to keep. seen names a dataset that models have already learned from, if the search includes one.

105    duplicates = []
106    for group in groups:
107        learned = [index for index in group if rows[index].dataset == seen]

For each group, first find any copies that belong to the seen dataset.

108        if learned:
109            keep = min(learned, key=lambda index: rows[index].image_id)
110            removed = [index for index in group if rows[index].dataset != seen]

If the group has a copy a model learned from, keep that one, and remove every copy in the other dataset — whatever split it is in. A model trained on FairFace has already studied that photo; testing it on UTKFace's copy would measure its memory, not its judgement. Copies inside the seen dataset itself are never removed here: that dataset's own duplicates were handled when it was prepared, and its models are already trained.

111        else:
112            keep = min(group, key=lambda index: (SPLIT_PRIORITY[rows[index].split], rows[index].image_id))
113            removed = [index for index in group if index != keep]

Otherwise, as before: keep the copy in the highest-priority split (between copies in the same split, the one whose name sorts first, so the choice is always the same), and remove the rest.

114        for index in removed:
115            row, kept = rows[index], rows[keep]
116            duplicates.append(
117                Duplicate(
118                    image_id=row.image_id,
119                    split=row.split,
120                    kept=kept.image_id,
121                    kept_split=kept.split,
122                    similarity=round(similarity(details[index], details[keep]), 4),
123                    same_label=age_label(row) == age_label(kept),
124                )
125            )

Every removed copy is recorded as a Duplicate, with its similarity to the kept copy and whether their age labels agree.

126    return duplicates

Return the removed copies.

136def find_duplicates(
137    rows: list[Row], hashes: NDArray[np.uint64], faces: dict[str, Path], seen: str | None = None
138) -> list[Duplicate]:
139    with ExitStack() as stack:
140        archives = {name: stack.enter_context(zipfile.ZipFile(path)) for name, path in faces.items()}
141        details = Details(archives, rows)
142        pairs: Iterable[tuple[int, int]] = close_pairs(hashes)
143        if seen is not None:
144            pairs = ((a, b) for a, b in pairs if not rows[a].dataset == rows[b].dataset == seen)
145        confirmed = confirmed_pairs(pairs, details)
146        return resolve(rows, groups_of(len(rows), confirmed), details, seen)

find_duplicates — the whole process: open every dataset's prepared faces (closing them all at the end), sieve, check, group and resolve. When a seen dataset is included, pairs within it are skipped before the costly check: they aren't this search's business. The stages are chained as generators, so pairs flow through one at a time and the candidates are never all held in memory at once.

149def summary(rows: list[Row], duplicates: list[Duplicate]) -> str:

summary — what to print.

150    crossing = Counter(f"{d.split} -> {d.kept.split('/')[0]} {d.kept_split}" for d in duplicates)
151    disagree = sum(not d.same_label for d in duplicates)
152    lines = [f"{len(rows):,} faces: {len(duplicates):,} duplicates removed, {disagree:,} with a different age label"]

Count the removed copies by where they were and where the kept copy is — train -> fairface test means a training copy of a FairFace test photo was removed — and how many disagreed about the age.

153    lines.append("removed -> kept: " + ", ".join(f"{pair} {count:,}" for pair, count in sorted(crossing.items())))

List those split pairs.

154    removed = {d.image_id for d in duplicates}
155    usable = Counter(row.split for row in rows if row.image_id not in removed)
156    lines.append("usable: " + ", ".join(f"{split} {count:,}" for split, count in sorted(usable.items())))

How many usable faces remain in each split, once duplicates are taken out.

157    return "\n".join(lines)

Join the lines.

160def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
161    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="dwarpal-ml dedup", description="Find and remove near-duplicate faces")
162    parser.add_argument("name", help="a dataset prepared by dwarpal_ml.prepare")
163    parser.add_argument("--against", help="a dataset models learned from: copies of its photos are removed here")
164    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

main — the dataset's name and, optionally, --against: a dataset that models learned from.

165    entry = dataset(args.name)
166    rows, hashes = faces_with_hashes(entry.name)
167    faces = {entry.name: PROCESSED / f"{entry.name}.zip"}
168    every_row, every_hash = rows, hashes
169    if args.against:
170        other_rows, other_hashes = faces_with_hashes(args.against)
171        every_row, every_hash = rows + other_rows, np.concatenate([hashes, other_hashes])
172        faces[args.against] = PROCESSED / f"{args.against}.zip"
173    duplicates = find_duplicates(every_row, every_hash, faces, args.against)
174    write_table(Duplicate, duplicates, MANIFESTS / f"{entry.name}.duplicates.csv")
175    print(summary(rows, duplicates))
176    return 0

Look up the dataset and its faces. With --against, add the other dataset's faces and hashes to the search. Find the duplicates, write the removed copies of this dataset to .datasets/manifest/<name>.duplicates.csv, and print the summary. (Approval was checked when the faces were prepared; this step only reads what preparation wrote.)

Real world — the smeared foreheads

The first run used FairFace's tightly cropped images, and the numbers looked fine: a face in 99.8 % of them. Only looking at the aligned faces showed the problem. Our alignment frames a face with room for hair and forehead, but the tight crops had cut those off, so the missing parts were filled by stretching the edge pixels: a third of each face was smeared streaks. A model trained on those would have learned from pictures unlike any webcam frame.

FairFace also publishes a version with a much wider margin. The owner approved its download (2.1 GB, the same 97,698 photos, the same licence), it replaced the tight crops in the register, and the faces came out clean. Faces not found fell from 151 to 53.

The smears had a second effect: they made strangers' fingerprints look alike, which is how they were noticed in the first place. Measure, then look: a number can say "99.8 % fine" about pictures that are a third garbage.

Real world — choosing the duplicate limits by eye

There is no textbook value for "how similar is the same photo", so the limits were chosen from FairFace itself, by looking at pairs of faces.

  • The first check failed. Comparing small, whole grey versions of two faces gave a smooth range of scores, with no gap between copies and strangers. Faces of different people scored 0.95 out of 1, because after alignment every face has its features in the same places.
  • Fine detail separated them. Comparing only fine detail (each face minus a blurred copy of itself) split the pairs cleanly: most scored between 0 and 0.35, very few between 0.5 and 0.6, and a separate cluster sat near 1. Every pair looked at from 0.6 upwards was the same photo — including colour and grey copies. Below 0.5 they were almost all strangers.
  • The sieve was widened. Allowing 10 differing bits instead of 8 found 31 more confirmed copies (502 instead of 471) for six times as many pairs to check: still about a minute's work. The extra pairs scoring 0.5–0.6 included strangers, which is why the confirmation limit is 0.6, not 0.5.

Real world — what the duplicates revealed

467 copies were removed. 233 of them would have leaked into evaluation: 75 training copies of test photos, 65 of calibration photos, 60 of validation photos, and 33 more between the evaluation splits themselves.

The copies also measured something unexpected: how consistent FairFace's age labels are. In 189 of the 467 pairs (40 %), the two copies of the same photo carry different age bands: 175 one band apart, 14 two or more. FairFace's ages are people's estimates from looking at photos, and this shows how often such estimates disagree. It is one more reason why the safety lines must be set on data with exact, documented ages (§2.14).

Try it yourself

With FairFace fetched and its manifest built (§5.2.1), and the face-detector model downloaded:

uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.prepare fairface

uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.dedup fairface

Then open .datasets/processed/fairface.zip and look at some of the faces — every one with its eyes in the same place.

5.2.4 Training the age model

The background is in Part 2: what learning is (§2.1), models and their knobs (§2.4), the loss (§2.5), gradient descent (§2.6), neural and convolutional networks (§2.7–2.8), predicting a distribution (§2.11), and over-fitting (§2.15). This step puts them together:

usable faces ─► data.py     weighted sampling, random changes, webcam damage    ┐  14 loader processes,
                                                                                ┘  ~1,500 faces a second
             ─► model.py    pixels → timm backbone → 101 scores                 ┐  GPU, bfloat16,
             ─► targets.py  label → target distribution; KL + band distance     │  AdamW, warm-up + cosine,
             ─► train.py    30 epochs; averaged weights scored on validation    ┘  weight averaging
             ─► .runs/<time>-<backbone>/   run.json + model.safetensors

Choices made before writing any code

  • Which backbone weights may be used. The design named ConvNeXt V2 as a candidate, but its published weights are licensed for non-commercial use only (CC BY-NC 4.0), while FairFace itself allows commercial use. Apache-2.0 alternatives were found (timm's own ConvNeXt, DINOv2) and offered to the owner, who approved PyTorch but no pretrained weights for now. So these first models learn from scratch (§2.10): a harder start, and an honest baseline for pretrained models later.
  • A cooldown for Python packages. Adding PyTorch brought in new libraries, three of them only days old. uv can now refuse any release younger than a week, as pnpm already does for JavaScript, and that rule is now on (root pyproject.toml). It also caught six earlier pins, which were stepped back by a release each.
  • The right PyTorch for each computer: the CUDA build on the Windows development laptop, the small CPU build on Linux, where CI runs (ml/pyproject.toml).

The targets and the loss

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/targets.py49 lines · 100% explained

What the right answer looks like, and how wrong an answer is. The model never answers with a single age. It answers with 101 numbers, one for each age from 0 to 100, which become a probability distribution — "probably 22, possibly 19 to 26" (§2.11). So the right answer for each training face must be a distribution too, and the loss must measure how far the model's distribution is from it (§2.5).

label "20-29"  ──► target: a soft hump over 20–29, edges spilling a little into 18–19 and 30–31
model output   ──► 101 scores ──softmax──► 101 probabilities
loss           =   how different the two distributions are (KL divergence)
               +   0.1 × how far the predicted average age lies outside 20–29

1"""What the model should answer for each label, and how wrong an answer is: label distributions and the loss."""

The docstring.

5import numpy as np
6import torch
7from numpy.typing import NDArray
8from torch.nn import functional

NumPy, PyTorch (§2.6), NumPy's array type, and PyTorch's functional module of ready-made calculations.

9
10AGES = 101

AGES = 101 — one output for each age from 0 to 100.

11# FairFace's open band "70 and over" is spread over 70-89: older faces are rare, and a target reaching 100 would
12# teach the model to expect them.
13OPEN_BAND_TOP = 89

OPEN_BAND_TOP — FairFace's oldest band is "70 and over", with no upper end. The target spreads it over 70–89. The comment explains why: real faces over 90 are rare, and a target reaching all the way to 100 would teach the model that a 75-year-old might well be 98.

14MEAN_WEIGHT = 0.1

MEAN_WEIGHT = 0.1 — how much the second part of the loss counts, as the design specifies (Stage 3 §8.4).

15
16_ages = np.arange(AGES, dtype=np.float64)

All 101 ages as numbers, made once and reused. The leading _ marks it as internal to this file.

17
18
19def spread(age: float) -> float:
20    return 1.0 + 0.04 * age

spread — how uncertain an age label is, growing with age: 1 year for a baby, 1.6 at 15, 3 at 50. A face changes much faster at 5 than at 50, so a label of "5" is sharper than a label of "50". The formula comes from the design.

21
22
23def label_distribution(age_low: int, age_high: int | None, age_exact: int | None) -> NDArray[np.float32]:

label_distribution — turn a label into the target distribution.

24    if age_exact is not None:
25        low, high = age_exact, age_exact
26    else:
27        low, high = age_low, age_high if age_high is not None else OPEN_BAND_TOP

An exact age is treated as a band one year wide. An open band ends at OPEN_BAND_TOP.

28    target = np.zeros(AGES, dtype=np.float64)
29    for age in range(low, min(high, AGES - 1) + 1):
30        target += np.exp(-0.5 * ((_ages - age) / spread(age)) ** 2) / spread(age)

For each age in the band, add a bell curve (a Gaussian) centred on it, with that age's spread; dividing by the spread keeps each curve's total the same, so wide and narrow ones count equally. A band becomes a smooth hump whose edges spill gently past the band's limits. That is deliberate: FairFace's bands are people's estimates, and the duplicate photos showed that people often disagree by one band (§5.2.3). For a real FairFace band, 72–88 % of the target lies inside the band.

31    return (target / target.sum()).astype(np.float32)

Scale the hump so it adds up to 1, as a probability distribution must, and store it in the compact float32 type.

32
33
34def distance_to_band(age: torch.Tensor, low: torch.Tensor, high: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
35    return torch.clamp(low - age, min=0) + torch.clamp(age - high, min=0)

distance_to_band — how many years an age lies outside a band: 0 inside it, otherwise the distance to the nearer end. torch.clamp(…, min=0) turns negative numbers into 0. This is the yardstick for every age-band measurement: it is the band version of the mean absolute error (MAE), the standard measure of age estimators (§2.12).

36
37
38def expected_age(logits: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
39    ages = torch.arange(logits.shape[-1], device=logits.device, dtype=torch.float32)
40    return (logits.float().softmax(dim=-1) * ages).sum(dim=-1)

expected_age — the average age of a predicted distribution. softmax turns the model's 101 raw scores (logits) into probabilities that are positive and add up to 1; each age is multiplied by its probability, and the results added. float() does this sum at full precision even when the model computes in reduced precision (train.py).

41
42
43def age_loss(
44    logits: torch.Tensor, target: torch.Tensor, low: torch.Tensor, high: torch.Tensor, mean_weight: float = MEAN_WEIGHT
45) -> torch.Tensor:

age_loss — one number saying how wrong a batch of answers is. Training is the search for model settings that make this number small (§2.6).

46    log_probabilities = functional.log_softmax(logits.float(), dim=-1)
47    divergence = functional.kl_div(log_probabilities, target, reduction="batchmean")

The main part: the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the target and the predicted distribution — a standard measure of how badly one distribution stands in for another, which is 0 only when they are identical (§2.5). PyTorch's kl_div expects the prediction as log-probabilities (log_softmax computes them accurately in one step) and averages over the batch (batchmean).

48    miss = distance_to_band(expected_age(logits), low, high).mean()

The second part: how far, on average, each predicted average age lies outside its band. The KL part cares about the whole shape of the distribution; this part pulls its centre directly into the right band.

49    return divergence + mean_weight * miss

The loss: the KL part, plus a tenth of the distance part.

The data

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/data.py178 lines · 100% explained

Feeding the model. Training shows the model its faces in batches of 128, over and over: one pass through all of them is an epoch. This file decides which faces are usable, how often each is shown, what random changes are made to it each time, and how it becomes numbers for PyTorch.

usable faces (manifest − no face − duplicates)
     │  sampling_weights: rare bands, and the years around the age limits, shown more often
     ▼
for each face:  decode (256×256) → Augment: zoom/turn/shift/flip → colour → webcam damage → 224×224
                                  (validation: just shrink to 224×224, no randomness)
     ▼
(pixels, target distribution, band low, band high)  → a batch of 128 → the GPU

38def band_of(row: Row) -> tuple[int, int]:
39    if row.age_exact is not None:
40        return row.age_exact, row.age_exact
41    return row.age_low, row.age_high if row.age_high is not None else AGES - 1

band_of — a row's age band as two numbers. An exact age is a one-year band; the open band "70 and over" ends at 100.

43
44def sampling_weights(rows: list[Row]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:

sampling_weights — how likely each face is to be picked when a batch is drawn. FairFace's training split has 20,392 faces in their twenties but only 684 aged 70 and over; drawn evenly, the model would hardly ever see old faces and could do well by mostly guessing "twenties".

45    bands = [band_of(row) for row in rows]
46    counts = Counter(bands)
47    weights = np.array([counts[band] ** -0.5 for band in bands])

Count the faces in each band, and give each face a weight of 1 ÷ √(its band's size). Dividing by the size itself would show every band equally often — but then each of the 684 older faces would be seen 30 times as often as each face in its twenties, and the model would start memorising those few. The square root is a common middle way: rare bands are shown more, but not so much that their few faces wear out.

48    focus = np.array([low <= FOCUS[1] and high >= FOCUS[0] for low, high in bands])
49    weights[focus] *= FOCUS_BOOST

Double the weight of faces whose band touches ages 10–25.

50    return np.asarray(weights / weights.sum(), dtype=np.float64)

Scale the weights to add up to 1.

53def fit(image: Image, size: int = INPUT_SIZE) -> Image:

56
57class Augment:
58    """Random changes that keep a face recognisably the same face, then webcam-like damage."""

Augment — random changes for training (data augmentation, §2.15). Each time a face is shown it looks slightly different, so the model can't simply memorise 69,000 particular pictures; it has to learn what ageing looks like. The changes are ones a real face really goes through — a slightly different pose, other light, another camera — never ones that would change how old someone looks.

59
60    def __init__(self, size: int = INPUT_SIZE, seed: int | None = None) -> None:
61        self.size = size
62        self.seed = seed
63        self.generator: np.random.Generator | None = None

The output size, an optional fixed seed (for tests), and the random-number generator, created later.

64
65    @property
66    def rng(self) -> np.random.Generator:
67        # Created on first use, inside each loader process, from that process's own seed: copies made before the
68        # processes start would otherwise all make the same "random" changes.
69        if self.generator is None:
70            self.generator = np.random.default_rng(self.seed if self.seed is not None else torch.initial_seed())
71        return self.generator

rng — the generator, created on first use. The comment explains why: the loader starts several processes, each with a copy of this object. A generator made beforehand would be copied too, and every process would then make the same random changes. Created inside each process from PyTorch's per-process seed (torch.initial_seed()), each gets its own.

72
73    def chance(self, probability: float) -> bool:
74        return bool(self.rng.random() < probability)

chance — true with the given probability: chance(0.3) is true about 3 times in 10.

75
76    def __call__(self, image: Image) -> Image:
77        return self.webcam(self.colour(self.geometry(image)))

The full change: geometry, then colour, then webcam damage.

78
79    def geometry(self, image: Image) -> Image:

geometry — zoom, turn, shift and maybe mirror, all at once.

80        height, width = image.shape[:2]
81        zoom = self.rng.uniform(0.92, 1.08) * self.size / width
82        angle = self.rng.uniform(-10.0, 10.0)

Zoom between 92 % and 108 % (while shrinking 256 to 224), and turn up to 10° either way.

83        matrix = np.asarray(cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((width / 2, height / 2), angle, zoom), dtype=np.float64)

getRotationMatrix2D builds the affine matrix (§4.9) that turns and zooms about the picture's centre.

84        centre = np.array([self.size - width, self.size - height], dtype=np.float64) / 2
85        matrix[:, 2] += centre + self.rng.uniform(-0.04, 0.04, 2) * self.size

Shift the result so the centre of the face lands at the centre of the 224×224 output, plus a random nudge of up to 4 % in each direction.

86        out = cv2.warpAffine(
87            image, matrix, (self.size, self.size), flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR, borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101
88        )

Apply all of it in one step. Doing the zoom, turn and shift as a single warp is much faster than doing them one after another — the first version used separate steps and spent most of its time there (§5.2.4). Where the turn uncovers a corner, BORDER_REFLECT_101 fills it with a mirror image of the nearby pixels.

89        if self.chance(0.5):
90            out = out[:, ::-1]
91        return np.ascontiguousarray(out, dtype=np.uint8)

Half the time, mirror the face left to right: a mirrored face is just as old.

92
93    def colour(self, image: Image) -> Image:

colour — different light and cameras.

94        pixels = image.astype(np.float32)
95        grey = pixels @ np.array([0.114, 0.587, 0.299], dtype=np.float32)

Work in decimals, and compute the grey version of each pixel (the standard weights for blue, green and red: the eye is most sensitive to green).

96        pixels = grey[..., None] + (pixels - grey[..., None]) * self.rng.uniform(0.7, 1.3)

Saturation: move each pixel towards or away from its own grey, by 70 % to 130 %: from washed-out to vivid colour.

97        pixels = (pixels - grey.mean()) * self.rng.uniform(0.7, 1.3) + grey.mean()

Contrast: stretch or squash all values around the average brightness.

98        pixels *= self.rng.uniform(0.7, 1.3)

Brightness: scale everything by 70 % to 130 %.

99        return np.clip(pixels, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

Keep the values within 0–255, and return to whole numbers.

100
101    def webcam(self, image: Image) -> Image:

webcam — damage a webcam does, each kind with its own probability. Training on such damage is how the model is prepared for the gap between dataset photos and live frames (§3.3).

102        out = image
103        if self.chance(0.5):
104            gamma = self.rng.uniform(0.6, 1.4)
105            table = (np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 256) ** gamma * 255.0).astype(np.uint8)
106            out = np.asarray(cv2.LUT(out, table), dtype=np.uint8)

Half the time, change the gamma — the curve from dark to light — between 0.6 and 1.4: like a camera that brightens shadows or a dim room. A lookup table (LUT) maps each of the 256 possible values to its new value at once.

107        if self.chance(0.3):
108            out = np.asarray(cv2.GaussianBlur(out, (0, 0), self.rng.uniform(0.3, 1.5)), dtype=np.uint8)

A third of the time, blur slightly, like a camera slightly out of focus.

109        if self.chance(0.2):
110            out = self.motion_blur(out)

One time in five, motion blur, like a hand moving the phone.

111        if self.chance(0.3):
112            out = self.downscale(out)

A third of the time, shrink and enlarge again, like a low-resolution camera.

113        if self.chance(0.3):
114            noise = self.rng.normal(0.0, self.rng.uniform(2.0, 10.0), out.shape)
115            out = np.clip(out.astype(np.float64) + noise, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

A third of the time, add sensor noise: random speckle of strength 2 to 10, like a camera in poor light.

116        if self.chance(0.5):
117            quality = int(self.rng.integers(30, 91))
118            out = decode_image(cv2.imencode(".jpg", out, [cv2.IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY, quality])[1].tobytes())

Half the time, save as JPEG at a quality between 30 and 90 and decode again, like a frame compressed for upload.

119        return np.ascontiguousarray(out, dtype=np.uint8)

Return the result as a tidy block of whole numbers.

120
121    def motion_blur(self, image: Image) -> Image:

motion_blur — smear the picture along a line.

122        length = int(self.rng.integers(3, 10))
123        kernel = np.zeros((length, length), dtype=np.float32)
124        kernel[length // 2, :] = 1.0

A kernel: a small square grid of 3 to 9 pixels with a single horizontal line of ones across its middle.

125        turn = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(((length - 1) / 2, (length - 1) / 2), float(self.rng.uniform(0, 180)), 1.0)
126        turned = np.asarray(cv2.warpAffine(kernel, turn, (length, length)), dtype=np.float32)

Turn that line to a random angle.

127        return np.asarray(cv2.filter2D(image, -1, turned / max(float(turned.sum()), 1e-6)), dtype=np.uint8)

filter2D slides the kernel over the picture, replacing each pixel by the average of the pixels along the line — a smear in that direction. Dividing by the kernel's total keeps the overall brightness unchanged.

128
129    def downscale(self, image: Image) -> Image:
130        height, width = image.shape[:2]
131        factor = self.rng.uniform(0.25, 0.6)
132        size = (max(8, int(width * factor)), max(8, int(height * factor)))
133        small = cv2.resize(image, size, interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
134        return np.asarray(cv2.resize(small, (width, height), interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR), dtype=np.uint8)

downscale — shrink to between a quarter and 60 % of the size (never below 8 pixels), then enlarge back: the fine detail is lost, as with a cheap camera.

137def to_tensor(image: Image) -> torch.Tensor:
138    rgb = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
139    return torch.from_numpy(np.ascontiguousarray(rgb)).permute(2, 0, 1)

to_tensor — turn OpenCV's blue-green-red picture into red-green-blue, and rearrange it from height, width, colour into PyTorch's colour, height, width (permute). The pixels stay whole numbers from 0 to 255; the model scales them itself (model.py).
