142@dataclass
143class FaceDataset(Dataset[Sample]):
144    """The faces of one split. Each loader process is sent only this short description and reads the rows itself:
145    on Windows, the next process can't start until the previous one has taken everything it was sent."""

FaceDataset — the faces of one split, in the shape PyTorch's loader expects. The docstring records a lesson from the first full training run (§5.2.4). The loader starts its helper processes one after another, and on Windows each must receive everything it is sent before the next can start. When each was sent the full list of 69,000 rows, the next process waited until the previous one had finished loading PyTorch: 14 processes took over a minute to start. Now each is sent only a short description, reads the rows itself, and all start together in about 11 seconds.

The model

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/model.py71 lines · 100% explained

The age model itself: a backbone — a ready-designed neural network from the timm library (§2.7–2.8) — with 101 outputs, one per age. The wrapper adds two things.

  1. It takes plain pixels and prepares them itself. Most vision models expect their input scaled in a particular way, and if training scales pictures one way and the service another, the model quietly sees the wrong numbers — a classic and hard-to-spot mistake. With the scaling inside the model, it travels with the model into the exported file (Phase 2, step 6), and the service only has to hand over a face's pixels.
  2. It can start from pretrained weights (§2.10) — but only from weights in the project's model register (models/third_party.json): pinned to an exact file, with a recorded licence, approved by the owner, downloaded by the project's own fetcher, and checked against their fingerprint before use. Nothing is ever downloaded from inside training.

MEAN and STD — the average and the spread of the red, green and blue values in ImageNet, the 1.3-million-photo collection most vision models are first trained on. Scaling pixels by them gives numbers centred around 0, which networks learn from most easily, and a pretrained backbone expects exactly these numbers, because it learned with them.

50class AgeModel(nn.Module):
51    """Pixels in (RGB, 0-255, shaped batch, 3, height, width), one score per age from 0 to 100 out."""

AgeModel — a PyTorch module, the base type for every network. The docstring states the contract: pixels in, as numbers 0–255 in red-green-blue order, arranged as batch, colour, height, width; 101 scores out.

52
53    mean: torch.Tensor
54    std: torch.Tensor

Type declarations for the two stored constants (below), so the type checker knows they are tensors.

55
56    def __init__(self, backbone: str, weights: Weights | None = None, drop_path: float = 0.0) -> None:
57        super().__init__()

Build the model: from a backbone name, optional approved weights, and optional stochastic depth (drop_path, below). super().__init__() sets up PyTorch's own bookkeeping first.

58        self.backbone = timm.create_model(
59            backbone,
60            pretrained=weights is not None,
61            pretrained_cfg_overlay={"file": str(weights.file)} if weights is not None else None,
62            num_classes=AGES,
63            drop_path_rate=drop_path,
64        )

Create the backbone by name, such as resnet26d or convnext_tiny.in12k_ft_in1k:

  • pretrained — whether to start from weights; pretrained_cfg_overlay={"file": …} tells timm to load them from our local, checked file instead of fetching them from the internet;
  • num_classes=AGES — 101 outputs. The pretrained file has 1,000 outputs (for ImageNet's 1,000 kinds of things); timm notices the difference and gives the new model a fresh, untrained final layer, keeping everything else. Of the file's 182 tensors, the 180 that make up the backbone are loaded exactly; the 2 of the old final layer are replaced;
  • drop_path_rate — stochastic depth: during training, each block of layers is skipped at random now and then, so the network can't rely too much on any single block. ConvNeXt was designed to be trained with it. During evaluation nothing is skipped.
65        self.register_buffer("mean", torch.tensor(MEAN).view(1, 3, 1, 1) * 255.0)
66        self.register_buffer("std", torch.tensor(STD).view(1, 3, 1, 1) * 255.0)

Store the averages and spreads, scaled from the 0–1 range to the 0–255 range of pixels, and shaped (1, 3, 1, 1) so that PyTorch applies each colour's value to every pixel of that colour (broadcasting, as in §5.2.3). register_buffer makes them part of the model — saved with it and moved to the GPU with it — without being settings that training changes.

67
68    def forward(self, pixels: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:

forward — what the model does with a batch of pixels. PyTorch calls it when the model is used like a function: model(pixels).

69        scaled = (pixels.float() - self.mean) / self.std

Convert the pixels to decimal numbers and scale them.

70        logits: torch.Tensor = self.backbone(scaled.contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last))

Run the backbone. channels_last rearranges the numbers in memory so that each pixel's three colours sit side by side, the layout the GPU's matrix units process fastest; it changes nothing about the result.

71        return logits

Return the 101 scores for each face.

The training loop

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/train.py227 lines · 100% explained

Training: gradient descent (§2.6), run on the GPU, with a written record of every run. Each run gets its own folder in .runs/ (which Git ignores) holding two files:

  • model.safetensors — the knobs of the best version so far;
  • run.json — everything needed to understand or repeat the run: the settings, the exact code version, fingerprints of the data, the software and hardware, and the scores after every epoch.
uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.train --backbone convnext_atto --epochs 30 --workers 14

epoch   1/30  loss 2.7053  val band-MAE 8.637  in band 26.0%  672 img/s
…
epoch  30/30  loss 0.8867  val band-MAE 2.605  in band 49.3%  1106 img/s
run 20261016-231806-convnext_atto: best val band-MAE 2.605 at epoch 30

The design planned to track runs with MLflow, a popular tracking server. A plain JSON file per run does the same job at this stage, with nothing extra to install or run; MLflow can be added if runs ever need comparing by the hundred.

timm, PyTorch, save_file from safetensors, timm's optimiser builder and weight averager, PyTorch's network building blocks, and its data loader and weighted sampler.

safetensors is a file format for model weights, created by Hugging Face. PyTorch's own format (.pt) is built on Python's pickle, which can run arbitrary code when a file is loaded — a real risk with model files from elsewhere. A .safetensors file holds only numbers, so loading one can never run code.

40@dataclass(frozen=True)
41class Config:
42    dataset: str = "fairface"
43    backbone: str = "resnet26d"
44    pretrained: bool = False
45    drop_path: float = 0.0
46    epochs: int = 30
47    batch_size: int = 128
48    learning_rate: float = 2e-3
49    weight_decay: float = 0.05
50    warmup_epochs: int = 2
51    ema_decay: float = 0.999
52    image_size: int = INPUT_SIZE
53    workers: int = 12
54    seed: int = 0
55    limit: int = 0

Config — every setting of a run, with its default. Each one can be changed from the command line (parse, below), and all of them are written into the run record.

  • backbone — which network design (§2.8);
  • pretrained — start from the approved pretrained weights for that backbone (§2.10), or from random knobs;
  • drop_path — the strength of stochastic depth (model.py); 0 switches it off;
  • epochs — how many passes through the training faces;
  • batch_size — 128 faces per step;
  • learning_rate, weight_decay, warmup_epochs — the step size, the pull towards zero, and the gentle start (§2.6);
  • ema_decay — how slowly the averaged copy follows the trained one (§2.15): each step it moves 0.1 % of the way;
  • image_size, workers — the input size and the number of loader processes;
  • seed — the starting point of the random numbers, so a run can be repeated;
  • limit — use only this many faces per split (0 means all), for quick trials.
56
57
58def learning_rate_factor(step: int, total: int, warmup: int) -> float:

learning_rate_factor — how much of the full learning rate to use at a given step.

59    if step < warmup:
60        return (step + 1) / warmup

During warm-up, rise in a straight line from almost nothing to the full rate.

61    progress = (step - warmup) / max(1, total - warmup)
62    return 0.5 * (1.0 + math.cos(math.pi * min(1.0, progress)))

After it, glide down to zero along half a cosine wave: slowly at first, faster in the middle, gently at the end.

63
64
65@torch.no_grad()
66def evaluate(model: nn.Module, loader: DataLoader[Any], device: torch.device) -> dict[str, float]:

evaluate — score a model on the validation faces. @torch.no_grad() tells PyTorch not to prepare for a backward pass (§2.6), which saves memory and time.

67    model.eval()

eval() switches the model to evaluation behaviour (some layers, such as normalisation, behave differently while training).

68    loss = miss = hits = count = 0.0

Running totals.

69    for images, targets, low, high in loader:
70        images, targets = images.to(device, non_blocking=True), targets.to(device, non_blocking=True)
71        low, high = low.to(device), high.to(device)

For each batch: move the pixels, targets and bands to the GPU. non_blocking=True lets the copy overlap with other work.

72        with torch.autocast(device.type, dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=device.type == "cuda"):
73            logits = model(images)

Run the model under autocast: on the GPU, most calculations are done in bfloat16, a 16-bit number format with the same range as normal 32-bit numbers but less precision. Modern GPUs process it two to four times faster, and for neural networks the lost precision makes no measurable difference. On a computer without a GPU (as in CI), everything stays at full precision.

74        distance = distance_to_band(expected_age(logits), low, high)

How far each predicted average age lies outside its band.

75        loss += float(age_loss(logits, targets, low, high)) * len(images)
76        miss += float(distance.sum())
77        hits += float((distance == 0).sum())
78        count += len(images)

Add up the loss, the distances, the number of faces whose predicted age lands inside their band, and the number of faces.

79    return {"loss": loss / count, "band_mae": miss / count, "band_accuracy": hits / count}

Return three scores: the average loss, the band-MAE (average years outside the band; 0 is perfect) and the in-band share.

82def gpu_memory_share(device: torch.device) -> float:
83    if device.type != "cuda":
84        return 0.0
85    return torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved(device) / torch.cuda.get_device_properties(device).total_memory

gpu_memory_share — the largest share of the GPU's memory PyTorch has held since training began (max_memory_reserved), as a fraction of the card's total. Without a GPU, 0.

86
87
88def sha256_of(path: Path) -> str:
89    return hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()

sha256_of — a file's fingerprint (§X.5), for the run record.

92def git_state() -> dict[str, Any]:
93    def git(*args: str) -> str:
94        return subprocess.run(["git", *args], capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=ROOT, check=False).stdout.strip()  # noqa: S603, S607 - fixed git commands
95
96    return {"commit": git("rev-parse", "HEAD"), "uncommitted_changes": bool(git("status", "--porcelain"))}

git_state — which version of the code is running (git rev-parse HEAD) and whether it had uncommitted changes. A run made from uncommitted code can't be exactly reproduced, and the record says so. The noqa note tells the security linter that these are fixed commands, not built from outside input.

97
98
99def loader(
100    dataset: FaceDataset, config: Config, workers: int, sampler: WeightedRandomSampler | None = None
101) -> DataLoader[Any]:

loader — PyTorch's DataLoader: it asks the dataset for examples in several processes at once and stacks them into batches.

102    return DataLoader(
103        dataset,
104        batch_size=config.batch_size,
105        sampler=sampler,
106        num_workers=workers,
107        persistent_workers=workers > 0,
108        pin_memory=torch.cuda.is_available(),
109        drop_last=sampler is not None,
110    )

The settings: 128 per batch; the sampler that picks faces with the right weights (training only); how many processes; keep the processes running between epochs (persistent_workers), since starting them is slow; put batches in memory the GPU can copy from directly (pin_memory); and in training, drop the last, incomplete batch, so every step sees a full 128.

111
112
113def train(config: Config, run: Path) -> dict[str, Any]:

train — one complete run.

114    torch.manual_seed(config.seed)
115    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True
116    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

Fix the random seed; let cuDNN, NVIDIA's library of network calculations, try several methods at the start and keep the fastest (benchmark); and use the GPU if there is one.

117    faces = PROCESSED / f"{config.dataset}.zip"
118    train_set = FaceDataset(config.dataset, "train", faces, Augment(config.image_size), config.image_size, config.limit)
119    val_set = FaceDataset(config.dataset, "val", faces, None, config.image_size, config.limit)
120    train_rows, val_rows = train_set.rows, val_set.rows

The training faces with random changes, the validation faces without, and their rows.

121    sampler = WeightedRandomSampler(
122        sampling_weights(train_rows).tolist(),
123        num_samples=len(train_rows),
124        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(config.seed),
125    )

The weighted sampler: each epoch draws as many faces as there are, picking each with the probability from sampling_weights (§5.2.4). Drawing with replacement means some faces appear twice in an epoch and others not at all; over many epochs it evens out. It has its own seeded generator, so the order can be repeated.

126    # Each loader process takes a while to start on Windows (it loads PyTorch); validation needs far fewer.
127    train_loader = loader(train_set, config, config.workers, sampler)
128    val_loader = loader(val_set, config, config.workers // 4)

The two loaders. The comment explains the split of processes: validation, without random changes, needs only a quarter as many.

129
130    weights = pretrained_weights(config.backbone) if config.pretrained else None
131    model = AgeModel(config.backbone, weights, config.drop_path).to(device)

If asked, look up the backbone's approved, fingerprint-checked weights — or stop with an error saying why there are none. Then build the model and move it to the GPU.

132    ema = ModelEmaV3(model, decay=config.ema_decay, use_warmup=True)

The weight average (§2.15), from timm. use_warmup=True lets it follow quickly at first, while the knobs are still far from good, and slowly later.

133    optimizer = create_optimizer_v2(model, "adamw", lr=config.learning_rate, weight_decay=config.weight_decay)

The AdamW optimiser (§2.6). timm's builder applies weight decay only to the knobs that should have it: the multiplying weights, not the small "add a constant" ones or the normalisation layers.

134    steps = config.epochs * len(train_loader)
135    warmup = config.warmup_epochs * len(train_loader)
136    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(optimizer, lambda step: learning_rate_factor(step, steps, warmup))

The total number of steps and of warm-up steps, and the scheduler, which sets the learning rate before every step using learning_rate_factor.

137
138    record: dict[str, Any] = {
139        "config": asdict(config),
140        "started": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
141        "git": git_state(),
142        "data": {
143            "train": len(train_rows),
144            "val": len(val_rows),
145            "fingerprints": {path.name: sha256_of(path) for path in sorted(MANIFESTS.glob(f"{config.dataset}*.csv"))},
146        },
147        "environment": {
148            "python": platform.python_version(),
149            "torch": torch.__version__,
150            "timm": timm.__version__,
151            "device": torch.cuda.get_device_name(device) if device.type == "cuda" else platform.processor(),
152        },
153        "pretrained": {"name": weights.name, "sha256": weights.sha256, "licence": weights.licence} if weights else None,
154        "parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()),
155        "epochs": [],
156    }

The run record, started before training: the settings, the start time, the code version, how many faces were used and the fingerprints of every data table they came from, the software and the device, which pretrained weights were used (name, fingerprint and licence, so a model's licence terms can always be traced), and the number of knobs (numel counts the numbers in each tensor).

157    run.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
158    best = math.inf
159    step = 0

Create the run's folder; no best score yet (math.inf, infinity, is worse than anything); no steps yet.

160    for epoch in range(1, config.epochs + 1):
161        model.train()
162        started, total, seen = time.perf_counter(), 0.0, 0

The epochs. Switch the model to training behaviour, and start the clock and the running totals.

163        for images, targets, low, high in train_loader:
164            images = images.to(device, non_blocking=True)
165            targets, low, high = (t.to(device, non_blocking=True) for t in (targets, low, high))

For each batch: move everything to the GPU.

166            with torch.autocast(device.type, dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=device.type == "cuda"):
167                logits = model(images)
168            loss = age_loss(logits, targets, low, high)

Forward pass: the model's answers, under autocast, and the loss.

169            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
170            torch.autograd.backward(loss)

Backward pass: clear the previous step's gradients, then compute new ones for every knob (backpropagation, §2.6).

171            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)

Gradient clipping: if the gradients are unusually large all together, scale them down, so that one strange batch can't throw the knobs far off course.

172            optimizer.step()
173            scheduler.step()

Take the step, and move the learning rate on.

174            step += 1
175            ema.update(model, step)

Count the step, and update the weight average.

176            total += float(loss.detach()) * len(images)
177            seen += len(images)

Add to the running loss. detach() takes the plain number, without the record PyTorch keeps for the backward pass.

178        seconds = time.perf_counter() - started
179        peak = gpu_memory_share(device)
180        if peak > MEMORY_WARNING:
181            print(f"warning: {peak:.0%} of GPU memory used; on Windows the rest spills to system memory, very slowly")
182        metrics = evaluate(ema.module, val_loader, device)

The epoch's duration, and the largest share of the GPU's memory used so far. Above 92 %, print a warning. This guard comes from experience (§5.2.4): when a Windows GPU runs out of memory, the driver doesn't stop with an error but quietly borrows ordinary memory, and training slows to a crawl. Then score the averaged model on validation.

183        record["epochs"].append(
184            {
185                "epoch": epoch,
186                "train_loss": round(total / seen, 4),
187                **{name: round(value, 4) for name, value in metrics.items()},
188                "seconds": round(seconds, 1),
189                "images_per_second": round(seen / seconds, 1),
190                "gpu_memory_share": round(peak, 3),
191            }
192        )

Record the epoch: training loss, validation scores (rounded to four decimals), seconds, speed, and the memory share.

193        if metrics["band_mae"] < best:
194            best = metrics["band_mae"]
195            save_file({k: v.contiguous() for k, v in ema.module.state_dict().items()}, str(run / "model.safetensors"))
196            record["best"] = record["epochs"][-1]

If this is the best validation band-MAE so far, save the averaged model's knobs (state_dict, every tensor by name) as model.safetensors, and note which epoch it was. Choosing the version by its validation score is what the validation split is for (§2.2); the test split is never used to choose.

197        (run / "run.json").write_text(json.dumps(record, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

Rewrite run.json after every epoch, so a run that stops halfway still leaves a full record of what it did.

198        latest = record["epochs"][-1]
199        print(
200            f"epoch {epoch:>3}/{config.epochs}  loss {latest['train_loss']:.4f}  val band-MAE {latest['band_mae']:.3f}"
201            f"  in band {latest['band_accuracy']:.1%}  {latest['images_per_second']:.0f} img/s",
202            flush=True,
203        )

Print one progress line.

204    return record

Return the record.

206
207def parse(argv: list[str] | None) -> Config:
208    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="dwarpal-ml train", description="Train an age model")
209    for field in fields(Config):
210        option = f"--{field.name.replace('_', '-')}"
211        if isinstance(field.default, bool):
212            parser.add_argument(option, action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction, default=field.default)
213        else:
214            parser.add_argument(option, type=type(field.default), default=field.default)
215    return Config(**vars(parser.parse_args(argv)))

parse — read the settings from the command line. Instead of listing each setting by hand, it goes through Config's fields and adds an option for each: epochs becomes --epochs, warmup_epochs becomes --warmup-epochs, with the default's type (type(field.default)). A new setting needs only a new line in Config.

Yes-or-no settings need different handling, because bool("False") is True in Python — any non-empty text counts as true. So for those, BooleanOptionalAction creates a pair of switches instead: --pretrained and --no-pretrained.

216
217
218def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
219    config = parse(argv)
220    name = f"{datetime.now(UTC):%Y%m%d-%H%M%S}-{config.backbone}"
221    record = train(config, RUNS / name)
222    print(f"run {name}: best val band-MAE {record['best']['band_mae']:.3f} at epoch {record['best']['epoch']}")
223    return 0

main — name the run after the time (in UTC) and the backbone, train, and report the best epoch.

226if __name__ == "__main__":
227    sys.exit(main())

Run main when the module is started as a program. On Windows this guard is essential (see prepare.py).

The tests

ml/tests/test_train.py176 lines · 100% explained

Tests for training. A real run takes most of an hour on a GPU, so these test the pieces separately, and finish with one tiny run: 16 faces, a very small network (resnet10t), 64×64 pixels, two epochs, on the processor. It proves the whole loop works — loading, training, scoring, recording, saving — in seconds, on any computer, including CI's, which has no GPU.

40@given(st.integers(0, 90), st.integers(0, 10))
41def test_a_band_becomes_a_distribution_that_sums_to_one_and_peaks_in_the_band(low: int, width: int) -> None:
42    target = label_distribution(low, low + width, None)

48@pytest.mark.parametrize(("low", "high"), [(0, 2), (3, 9), (10, 19), (20, 29), (60, 69)])
49def test_most_of_a_real_band_stays_inside_it_with_soft_edges(low: int, high: int) -> None:

51    assert 0.7 < inside < 0.95

FairFace's real bands keep most of their weight inside, between 70 % and 95 %: mostly inside, with soft edges. The first version of this test demanded 90 %, and failed; measuring showed 72–88 %, exactly as designed — wider labels for older ages spill further (§5.2.4).

66def test_the_loss_prefers_the_right_answer_to_a_wrong_one() -> None:
67    target = torch.from_numpy(label_distribution(20, 29, None))[None]
68    low, high = torch.tensor([20.0]), torch.tensor([29.0])
69    right = torch.log(target + 1e-6)
70    wrong = torch.log(torch.from_numpy(label_distribution(60, 69, None))[None] + 1e-6)
71    assert float(age_loss(right, target, low, high)) < 0.01 < float(age_loss(wrong, target, low, high))
72    assert float(expected_age(right)) == pytest.approx(24.5, abs=1.0)

The loss prefers the right answer. A model output equal to the target (as log-probabilities) gives a loss near 0; one that says "60s" for a face labelled "20s" gives a large loss. And the expected age of "20s" is about 24.5, the middle of the band.

Sampling. Nine faces in their thirties, one in its sixties, one teenager. The weights add up to 1; the rare sixties face is shown more often than each thirties face; and the teenager, equally rare but in the focus years, twice as often as the sixties face.

Real world — making the GPU wait less

The first trial runs managed 261 faces a second, with the GPU mostly idle. Two fixes, each found by measuring rather than guessing:

  • Slow random changes. Timing every step of preparing one face showed torchvision's colour change taking 17 milliseconds — mostly its hue adjustment — and its rotation another 4. All the changes were rewritten with OpenCV: zoom, turn and shift as one warp, and colour as simple arithmetic, dropping hue shifts, which don't occur in real faces anyway. From 27 to 7.5 milliseconds a face.
  • Slow start-up. The first epoch of every run took minutes. The loader's 14 processes were starting one at a time, 17 seconds apart: on Windows each had to receive the full list of 69,000 faces before the next could start, and couldn't receive it until it had finished loading PyTorch. Sending each only "FairFace, training split" let all 14 start at once: from 78 seconds to 11.

Now the loader prepares about 1,500 faces a second, more than the GPU can use, which is how it should be.

Real world — the first model

ConvNeXt-Atto, 3.4 million knobs, trained from scratch for 30 epochs (32 minutes):

Measure (validation, 8,625 faces) Guessing "29" for everyone ConvNeXt-Atto
Band-MAE (years outside the band) 8.55 2.61
Predicted age inside the band 29 % 49 %

It is best for faces in their twenties (1.5 years outside the band, on average) and worst for older faces (4–5 years), which are rare in the training data. Between groups, band-MAE ranges from 2.35 to 3.05; the largest gap, for faces labelled Black, is a fairness finding for step 5 to measure properly.

The number that matters most for Dwarpal: children under 10 were given at least a 50 % chance of being 18 or over in 4.5 % of cases. That is why nothing in the system ever passes someone at 50 %: the safety lines are set by risk control (§2.14), on calibration data with exact ages.

Real world — the second model, and the baseline

ResNet-26d, 14.2 million knobs, trained the same way (63 minutes, at half the speed):

Measure (validation) Constant guess ConvNeXt-Atto ResNet-26d
Band-MAE 8.55 2.61 2.28
Predicted age inside the band 29 % 49 % 52 %
Ages 3–9 given P(18+) ≥ 50 % — 4.5 % 3.5 %
Band-MAE, best to worst group — 2.35–3.05 2.05–2.63

ResNet-26d is better on every measure, and becomes the baseline that pretrained models will have to beat. Both models were still improving slowly at their last epoch, and their training loss sat only a little below their validation loss: neither had begun to over-fit (§2.15), so longer training might squeeze out a little more. A pretrained backbone (§2.10) is the likelier big step.

Each run's run.json records that it was made from uncommitted code — true, since this step was still being written. Runs for a release will be made from a commit.

Real world — starting from pretrained weights

The owner then approved one set of pretrained weights: timm's ConvNeXt-Tiny, trained on ImageNet-12k and ImageNet-1k (Apache-2.0, 114 MB, 28 million knobs). They were pinned in the model register with their fingerprint and licence, and fetched by the project's own downloader (fetch_models.py --training). Fine-tuning used the gentler recipe for pretrained models: a learning rate eight times lower, a one-epoch warm-up, stochastic depth, and 15 epochs.

The first attempt crawled. ConvNeXt-Tiny at 128 faces a batch needed more than the laptop GPU's 8 GB, and on Windows the driver doesn't fail with "out of memory": it quietly borrows ordinary memory, which is many times slower. The GPU showed 100 % busy but drew a third of its usual power, waiting on memory. At 64 faces a batch (with the learning rate halved to match), it used 59 % of the memory and ran at full speed. Training now records each epoch's memory use, and warns above 92 % (train.py).

Measure (validation) ResNet-26d, from scratch ConvNeXt-Tiny, pretrained
Band-MAE 2.28 1.84
Predicted age inside the band 52 % 55 %
Ages 3–9 given P(18+) ≥ 50 % 3.5 % 1.7 %
Ages 0–2 given P(18+) ≥ 50 % 1.1 % 0.6 %
Band-MAE, best to worst group 2.05–2.63 1.72–2.02
Best epoch, training time 30 of 30, 63 min 6 of 15, 54 min

After one epoch it was already better than the from-scratch model after thirty — the value of starting from a backbone that already knows how to see (§2.10). It is now the best model, and the one the next steps evaluate.

Real world — over-fitting, caught in the act

The pretrained model shows what §2.15 describes, epoch by epoch:

Epoch 1 3 5 6 8 10 12 15
Training loss 1.41 0.93 0.78 0.72 0.58 0.45 0.35 0.29
Validation loss 0.95 0.88 0.86 0.86 0.89 0.94 1.02 1.08
Validation band-MAE 2.15 1.91 1.86 1.84 1.87 1.92 2.00 2.04

Up to epoch 5 or 6, both losses fall together: the model is learning about ageing. After that, the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss rises: the model is memorising its 69,000 training faces, and getting worse at new ones. Because training keeps the version with the best validation score, the saved model is the one from epoch 6, before the memorising set in. The next run of this recipe can stop at about 8 epochs — half the time, and half the heat.

5.2.5 Evaluation and fairness

The background is in Part 2: measuring mistakes (§2.12), calibration (§2.13) and fairness (§2.16). This step builds one evaluation protocol for every model, writes the release gates down before the test results are seen, and opens the test split for the first time — once.

model + validation faces ─► logits ─► temperature fitted (validation only)
model + test faces       ─► logits ─► accuracy · clear minors/adults at 13, 16, 18, 21 · calibration · fairness
                                    ─► evaluation-test.json  ─► every gate in ml/gates.toml: PASS / FAIL

The release gates

ml/gates.toml37 lines · 100% explained

The release gates: the minimum a model must achieve before it may serve real people. They turn "is this model good enough?" from a judgement made while looking at the results — when it's tempting to be generous — into rules written down beforehand (§2.16).

The design calls this file gates.yaml; it is TOML for the same reasons as the licence register (ml/datasets.toml).

1# Release gates: what a model must achieve before it may serve. `uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.evaluate`
2# checks every gate against the evaluation's results; `metric` is a path into evaluation.json, and a gate fails if
3# the value is above `max` or below `min`.

What the file is, and how a gate works: metric is a path into a model's evaluation results (dwarpal_ml/evaluate.py), checked against a max or a min.

4#
5# PROVISIONAL. These gates fit what FairFace can measure (age bands, no exact ages). The final gates of NFR-01 and
6# NFR-04 (rates per exact age 13-17 under the risk-controlled thresholds) need an exact-age dataset, and every value
7# here is for the project owner to confirm.

Provisional, and why. The design's real gates (NFR-01 and NFR-04 in the problem analysis) are about children of each exact age from 13 to 17, under the final risk-controlled thresholds. FairFace's age bands can't measure that, so these gates measure what it can. Every value is the project owner's decision; these are proposals.

8
9[[gate]]
10name = "accuracy"
11metric = "overall.band_mae"
12max = 2.0
13why = "On average, a predicted age at most 2 years outside the labelled band"

Accuracy: overall band-MAE at most 2.0 years. Each gate has a name, a metric, its limit, and a why in plain words.

14
15[[gate]]
16name = "children-rated-adult"
17metric = "limits.18.minor_rate_upper"
18max = 0.05
19why = "Children under 10 rated more likely than not 18+: at most 5 %, with 95 % confidence (the NFR-01 gate level)"

Children rated adult: of the children under 10, the share rated more likely than not 18 or over, with 95 % confidence, at most 5 % — the release-gate level of NFR-01. It uses the upper end of the interval, so the gate holds even with bad luck in the sample.

20
21[[gate]]
22name = "children-rated-adult-every-group"
23metric = "fairness.worst_minor_rate_upper_18"
24max = 0.10
25why = "The same, in every group; looser only because each group has a few hundred children"

The same in every group, at most 10 %. It is looser only because each group has a few hundred children, and a small sample's upper bound is wide: with zero mistakes in 160 children, the upper end is still 2.3 %.

26
27[[gate]]
28name = "accuracy-gap"
29metric = "fairness.band_mae_ratio"
30max = 1.25
31why = "The worst group's band-MAE at most 25 % above the best group's"

Accuracy gap: the worst group's band-MAE at most 25 % above the best group's.

32
33[[gate]]
34name = "calibration"
35metric = "calibration.after.ece_mean"
36max = 0.05
37why = "Stated probabilities of being over an age match observed frequencies to within 5 points, on average"

Calibration: the probabilities of being over an age match reality to within 5 percentage points, on average (§2.13).

The protocol

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/evaluate.py239 lines · 100% explained

Evaluation: one fixed set of measurements for every model (§2.12, §2.13, §2.16), so that models can be compared fairly and nobody can pick, after the fact, the numbers that flatter one. It answers four questions:

Question Measured as
How accurate? band-MAE and in-band share — overall, per age band, per group, per sex
How often would it get a clear case dangerously wrong? for each age limit (13, 16, 18, 21): clear minors rated more likely than not over the limit, and clear adults rated under it, each with a 95 % interval
Can its probabilities be trusted? calibration error of "at least b years old", for every band edge b, before and after a temperature correction
Is it fair? the worst group against the best

The results go to evaluation-<split>.json in the run's folder and are checked against the release gates (ml/gates.toml).

The test split is opened once. While developing, everything is measured on validation. The test split is evaluated a single time per model, and a second attempt is refused: if people could look at test results, change something and look again, the test would slowly turn into one more validation set, and stop being an honest exam (§2.2).

1"""Evaluation: one fixed protocol for every model, on validation while developing and on the test split once.
2
3uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.evaluate .runs/<run>                 validation
4uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.evaluate .runs/<run> --split test    the locked exam, once
5"""

The docstring, with the two commands.

32
33GATES = ROOT / "ml" / "gates.toml"

GATES — the release gates file.

34LIMITS = (13, 16, 18, 21)

LIMITS — the age limits websites use, which every model is measured at.

35# FairFace's band edges: for each of these ages, every face is known to be entirely above or entirely below it.
36EDGES = (10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70)

EDGES — FairFace's band edges. The comment gives the reason they matter: "is this person at least 20?" has a known answer for every face, because no FairFace band straddles 20. At these ages, calibration can be measured exactly, even without exact ages.

37BINS = 10

BINS = 10 — calibration groups forecasts into ten bins: 0–10 %, 10–20 %, …

38
39type Floats = NDArray[np.float64]

Floats — a name for "an array of decimal numbers".

40
41
42def softmax(logits: Floats, temperature: float = 1.0) -> Floats:

softmax — turn logits into probabilities (§2.11), with a temperature.

43    scaled = logits / temperature

Divide the logits by the temperature. Above 1, the differences shrink and the probabilities spread out (less confident); below 1, they sharpen (more confident).

44    scaled = scaled - scaled.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)

Subtract each row's largest logit first. It changes nothing about the result, but keeps exp from overflowing on large numbers — a standard precaution.

45    weights = np.exp(scaled)
46    return np.asarray(weights / weights.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True), dtype=np.float64)

Raise e to each, and divide by the row's total.

47
48
49def bands(rows: list[Row]) -> tuple[Floats, Floats]:
50    pairs = np.array([band_of(row) for row in rows], dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1, 2)
51    return pairs[:, 0], pairs[:, 1]

bands — every row's band as two arrays: lower ends and upper ends. reshape(-1, 2) keeps the shape right even for an empty list.

52
53
54def band_probability(probabilities: Floats, low: Floats, high: Floats) -> Floats:
55    ages = np.arange(probabilities.shape[1])
56    inside = (ages >= low[:, None]) & (ages <= high[:, None])
57    return np.asarray((probabilities * inside).sum(axis=1), dtype=np.float64)

band_probability — how much probability the model gave to the labelled band: for each row, add up the probabilities of the ages inside it. low[:, None] turns the list of lower ends into a column, so that comparing it with the row of 101 ages gives a table: one row per face, one column per age, true inside the band.

58
59
60def fit_temperature(logits: Floats, low: Floats, high: Floats) -> float:

fit_temperature — find the temperature that makes the model's probabilities most honest (§2.13).

61    def surprise(temperature: float) -> float:
62        likelihood = band_probability(softmax(logits, temperature), low, high)
63        return float(-np.log(np.clip(likelihood, 1e-12, None)).mean())

For a candidate temperature: the average surprise, −log(probability given to the true band). A model that gives the true band 90 % is barely surprised (0.1); one that gave it 1 % is very surprised (4.6). The smallest average surprise is the most honest temperature. clip avoids log(0).

64
65    return float(minimize_scalar(surprise, bounds=(0.25, 4.0), method="bounded").x)

Search temperatures between 0.25 and 4 for the smallest surprise. It is fitted on validation only, never on test.

66
67
68def interval(successes: int, trials: int, delta: float = DELTA) -> tuple[float, float]:
69    lower = 0.0 if successes == 0 else float(beta.ppf(delta / 2, successes, trials - successes + 1))
70    upper = 1.0 if successes == trials else float(beta.ppf(1 - delta / 2, successes + 1, trials - successes))
71    return lower, upper

interval — the two-sided Clopper–Pearson 95 % interval for a rate (§2.14): the range the true rate plausibly lies in, given k out of n. The lower end uses δ/2, the upper end 1 − δ/2, so that each end is wrong at most 2.5 % of the time. At 0 out of n the lower end is exactly 0, and at n out of n the upper end is exactly 1.

72
73
74def rate(flags: NDArray[np.bool_]) -> dict[str, Any]:
75    count, trials = int(flags.sum()), len(flags)
76    if trials == 0:
77        return {"rate": None, "count": 0, "of": 0, "lower": None, "upper": None}
78    lower, upper = interval(count, trials)
79    return {"rate": count / trials, "count": count, "of": trials, "lower": lower, "upper": upper}

rate — a share of yes-or-no flags with its interval, how many, and out of how many. With no faces at all, every number is None ("not measurable"), never a misleading 0.

80
81
82def accuracy(mean_age: Floats, low: Floats, high: Floats) -> dict[str, float]:
83    miss = np.clip(low - mean_age, 0, None) + np.clip(mean_age - high, 0, None)
84    return {"faces": len(miss), "band_mae": float(miss.mean()), "in_band": float((miss == 0).mean())}

accuracy — band-MAE (average years outside the band) and the share inside the band (§2.12).

85
86
87def calibration_error(probability: Floats, truth: NDArray[np.bool_], bins: int = BINS) -> float:

calibration_error — the expected calibration error (ECE): how far stated probabilities are from what actually happens (§2.13).

88    which = np.minimum((probability * bins).astype(int), bins - 1)

Put each forecast into one of ten bins by its probability: 0.37 goes into bin 3. minimum(…, 9) puts a forecast of exactly 1.0 into the last bin.

89    error = 0.0
90    for b in range(bins):
91        members = which == b
92        if members.any():
93            error += abs(float(probability[members].mean()) - float(truth[members].mean())) * members.mean()
94    return error

For each bin: the gap between the average forecast and the share that actually came true, weighted by the share of forecasts in that bin. If the model says "about 35 %" for some faces and 35 % of them really are over the age, that bin adds nothing.

95
96
97def calibration(probabilities: Floats, low: Floats, high: Floats) -> dict[str, Any]:

calibration — the calibration error of "at least edge", for every band edge.

98    errors = {}
99    for edge in EDGES:
100        known = (low >= edge) | (high < edge)
101        over = probabilities[known, edge:].sum(axis=1)
102        errors[str(edge)] = calibration_error(over, low[known] >= edge)
103    return {"ece": errors, "ece_mean": float(np.mean(list(errors.values())))}

For each edge: the faces whose answer is known (all of them, for FairFace); the model's probability of being at least that age (the sum of the probabilities from edge upwards); and whether they truly are (low >= edge). Then the average over all edges.

104
105
106def limit_view(probabilities: Floats, low: Floats, high: Floats, limit: int) -> dict[str, Any]:

limit_view — the dangerous mistakes at one age limit.

107    over = probabilities[:, limit:].sum(axis=1)

Each face's probability of being at least the limit.

108    minors = rate(over[high < limit] >= 0.5)

Clear minors: faces whose whole band lies below the limit (for 18, the bands 0–2 and 3–9; FairFace's 10–19 can't be called either way). How many were rated more likely than not to be over it.

109    adults = rate(over[low >= limit + ADULT_MARGIN] < 0.5)

Clear adults: faces whose whole band starts at least 3 years above the limit (for 18, bands from 30 up). How many were rated more likely than not to be under it.

110    return {"clear_minors_rated_over": minors, "clear_adults_rated_under": adults, "minor_rate_upper": minors["upper"]}

Both rates, and the minors' upper bound on its own, for the gates. These are measured at the plain 50 % line. The system's real decisions use the risk-controlled lines of §2.14, set on exact-age data, which will be stricter; these numbers describe the model, not the final system.

111
112
113def gap(values: list[float]) -> float | None:
114    worst, best = max(values), min(values)
115    if best == 0:
116        return 1.0 if worst == 0 else None
117    return worst / best

gap — the worst value divided by the best. If the best is perfectly 0, the ratio is 1 when everything is 0, and otherwise undefined (None), which fails any gate. The tests found the first version dividing by zero here.

118
119
120def order(view: str, name: str) -> tuple[int, str]:
121    return (int(name.split("-")[0]), name) if view == "bands" else (0, name)

order — the order to list a view's entries in: age bands by their lower age (so "3-9" comes before "10-19"), everything else alphabetically.

122
123
124def evaluate(logits: Floats, rows: list[Row], temperature: float) -> dict[str, Any]:

evaluate — the whole protocol, on one model's logits for one split.

125    probabilities = softmax(logits, temperature)

137    results: dict[str, Any] = {"faces": len(rows), "temperature": temperature}

For every entry in every view: its accuracy, and how many of its clear minors were rated 18 or over. partial(order, view) makes a one-argument version of order with the view filled in, as sorted requires.

149    results["limits"] = {str(limit): limit_view(probabilities, low, high, limit) for limit in LIMITS}

The dangerous-mistake rates at every limit.

150    results["calibration"] = {
151        "before": calibration(softmax(logits), low, high),

171def check(results: dict[str, Any], gates: Path = GATES) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
172    outcomes = []
173    for gate in tomllib.loads(gates.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["gate"]:
174        value = lookup(results, gate["metric"])
175        passed = value is not None and value <= gate.get("max", np.inf) and value >= gate.get("min", -np.inf)
176        outcomes.append({"name": gate["name"], "metric": gate["metric"], "value": value, "passed": bool(passed)})
177    return outcomes

check — read every gate from ml/gates.toml, look up its value, and pass it only if the value exists and is within its max and min (a missing limit is infinitely far away).

21def peaked(ages: list[int], sharpness: float = 4.0) -> np.ndarray:
22    logits = np.zeros((len(ages), AGES))
23    for i, age in enumerate(ages):
24        logits[i] = -sharpness * np.abs(np.arange(AGES) - age) / 5
25    return logits

peaked — made-up logits that peak at chosen ages: each age's score falls in a straight line with its distance from the peak, so after softmax most of the probability sits near it. sharpness sets how confident the "model" is.

Real world — the first exam

ConvNeXt-Tiny, pretrained and fine-tuned (§5.2.4), evaluated on the locked test split: 10,941 faces it had never seen, and nobody had looked at.

Measure Validation Test
Band-MAE 1.86 1.83
Inside the band 55.6 % 55.7 %
Children under 10 rated 18+ (more likely than not) 1.49 % (18 of 1,208) 1.74 % (27 of 1,553), up to 2.52 %
Adults 30+ rated under 18 0.66 % 0.65 %
Calibration error (after temperature 0.88) 0.017 0.018
Worst-to-best group band-MAE 1.17 1.21

Validation and test agree closely: choosing the best epoch and the temperature on validation did not flatter the model.

Four of the five gates pass. One fails. Of 126 Middle Eastern children under 10 in the test split, 6 (4.8 %) were rated more likely than not to be 18 or over. With so few children, the true rate could plausibly be as high as 10.1 %, just over the provisional 10 % gate. On validation, the same group had 1 of 81. Two other patterns stand out: girls were misjudged more often than boys (2.5 % against 1.2 %), and the age limit 13 is the model's weak point — 10.6 % of children under 10 were rated 13 or over, because FairFace's single 10–19 band can't teach the difference between 10 and 13.

This result stays exactly as measured. The test split has now been used for this model, and the code refuses to evaluate it again: changing something and re-taking the exam until it passes would make the exam meaningless. The next model must do better on its own first attempt — through more and better data (exact ages, more children of every group), and through the risk-controlled thresholds of §2.14, which are stricter than the plain 50 % line used here.

Try it yourself

Evaluate any trained run on validation as often as you like:

uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.evaluate .runs/<run>

The results are in evaluation-val.json in the run's folder. Then, once you are sure, the exam: add --split test. Try it a second time to see the lock.

5.2.6 Exact ages and the safety lines

Everything so far was measured with FairFace's age bands, which can't tell a 15-year-old from a 19-year-old. Setting the safety lines (§2.14) needs exact ages. The owner approved UTKFace for this, under the project's research-only first version: over 24,000 photos, each labelled with an exact age. It is used only to measure, never to train: half of it for setting the lines, half for checking them.

UTKFace ─► fetch (3 files, 1.39 GB) ─► manifest (repack to one zip; labels from file names; calib/test halves)
        ─► prepare (clearest face; photos with a second clear face set aside)
        ─► dedup --against fairface (copies within UTKFace, and of photos the model learned from)
        ─► calibrate: lines certified on the calib half ─► decisions checked on the test half, once

Three things about UTKFace shaped the code:

  • The labels are estimated. UTKFace's ages were proposed by an age-estimation algorithm (DEX) and checked by a person. They are not ages from documents. The register records this (age_source), and every calibration result carries the note.
  • The labelled person isn't always alone, or in the middle. FairFace centred each photo on its subject; UTKFace's in-the-wild photos don't. So the register gained a subject rule: for UTKFace, take the clearest face, and set the photo aside if a second clear face appears (519 photos).
  • Some photos are bigger than any webcam frame. The vision library refuses uploads over 512 KB or 1,920 pixels, rightly for a service. Dataset preparation now decodes with roomier limits, then shrinks each photo to the service's largest size.

Changes to files walked through earlier are explained in their walkthroughs (ml/datasets.toml, register.py, manifest.py, prepare.py, dedup.py, risk.py, evaluate.py, the vision library's decode.py, and their tests).

Calibration

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/calibrate.py165 lines · 100% explained

Exact-age calibration: where the safety lines of §2.14 are finally set, on real faces with exact ages, and then checked on faces nobody has looked at.

UTKFace calib half (11,301 faces) ─► model ─► P(age ≥ N) for every face
                                  ─► for N = 13, 16, 18, 21: try budgets 2 %, 3 %, 5 %, … with cells per age and group,
                                     then per age; keep the strictest that the data can certify     ─► calibration-utkface.json
UTKFace test half (11,637 faces)  ─► the same model and lines ─► pass / step-up / fail for every face
                                  ─► children passed at each exact age; adults' outcomes; per group  ─► evaluation-utkface-test.json

Two rules make it honest:

  • The lines are certified on one half and checked on the other. Clopper–Pearson already gives a guarantee on the calibration half; the test half shows whether it holds on faces that played no part in choosing the lines.
  • The strictest budget the data supports is used, and every stricter one that failed is recorded with the reason. Nobody can quietly pick a comfortable number.

54def decide(p_over: Floats, tau_pass: float, tau_fail: float) -> NDArray[np.str_]:
55    return np.where(p_over >= tau_pass, "pass", np.where(p_over <= tau_fail, "fail", "step_up"))

The refusals: FairFace, which has no exact ages, is refused; and a run that has already been checked on UTKFace's test half is refused a second time.

Real world — what UTKFace showed before any model looked at it

  • Teenagers are scarce. UTKFace has 82 faces aged 13, 164 aged 14, 180 aged 15, 253 aged 16 and 159 aged 17 — and only 4 Asian 13-year-olds. Risk control needs 149 people per age-and-group cell to certify 2 % (§2.14). Only one cell in the whole dataset reaches that. So the promise can be certified per age, but not per group, and only at a looser budget than 2 %.
  • Repeated photos disagree about age. Duplicate removal found 533 extra copies of photos within UTKFace, and 324 of them (61 %) carry a different age from the copy that was kept — the same photo, labelled with two ages. Estimated labels are noisy, even when checked.
  • Age heaping. 2,206 faces are labelled exactly 26, but only 616 are labelled 27: a sign of estimated, rounded labels.
  • Only 6 UTKFace photos were copies of FairFace photos — removed, so the model is never tested on a face it learned from.

Real world — the safety lines, on exact ages

ConvNeXt-Tiny (§5.2.4), trained on FairFace only, calibrated on UTKFace's calibration half (11,301 faces) and checked on its test half (11,637 faces, opened once). Exact-age error on these new faces: 4.96 years on average (1.6 for children under 13, 3.3 for teenagers, 9.6 over 60).

Limit Strictest budget the data certifies Pass line τ Teenagers passed on the test half (ages N−5 to N−1)
18 7.5 %, per age 0.964 2.9 % (12 of 416; up to 5.0 %) — by age: 13: 0 %, 14: 0 %, 15: 3.7 %, 16: 2.7 %, 17: 6.4 %
21 7.5 %, per age 0.927 1.3 % (7 of 520)
16 15 %, per age 0.761 7.6 % (25 of 327)
13 15 %, per age 0.809 4.1 % (16 of 392)

On faces that played no part in choosing the lines, every age's pass rate stayed inside its certified budget: the guarantee held. At 18, children under 13 passed 0.4 % of the time (7 of 1,741).

The price is paid by adults. At the 18 line, only 13 % of 18–20-year-olds and 30 % of 21–24-year-olds pass straight away; most are sent to step-up. From 30 upwards, 94 % pass. That is exactly the trade risk control is built to make: with a model this uncertain about teenagers, it keeps children out by sending more adults to a document check — never by letting more children through.

What these lines are not. They are not yet good enough to serve: the design's target is 2 % per age and group (NFR-01), and the data supports only 7.5 % per age; the ages are estimates; and the per-group pass rates are measurements on a few dozen teenagers each (3 of 50 Black teenagers passed at 18, for example), not guarantees. More exact-age data of every group — and a better model — are what will move all three.

Try it yourself

With UTKFace fetched, its manifest built and its faces prepared and deduplicated, calibrate any trained run:

uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.calibrate .runs/<run> utkface

Read calibration-utkface.json in the run's folder to see every budget that was refused, and why.

5.2.7 From trained model to served model

The last step turns the trained, calibrated model into what the inference service runs (§2.19), proves that nothing changed on the way, and gives the model a manifest in the registry.

.runs/<run>/ ─► export.py ─► models/registry/age/age-convnext-tiny-2026.10.17/model.onnx      (110 MB, not in Git)
                         ─►                                           …/manifest.json   (thresholds, provenance, checks)
inference service ─► DWARPAL_INFERENCE_AGE_BACKEND=onnx ─► OnnxAgeBackend: fingerprint check ─► ONNX Runtime
API               ─► DWARPAL_AGE_MANIFEST=registry/age/age-convnext-tiny-2026.10.17/manifest.json

Both services still default to the stand-in model. Switching to the trained one is two settings, and only for test mode: the manifest says calibrated: false, because the thresholds don't yet meet the release standard (§5.2.6), and the API refuses live sessions with such a model.

One conversion for training's checks and for serving

libs/vision/src/dwarpal_vision/batch.py18 lines · 100% explained

Faces in, the age model's input out. It is three lines of code, and it lives in the shared vision library because it is exactly the kind of step that drifts apart when written twice: the inference service uses it before every prediction, and the export checks use it to prove the exported model matches (ml/src/dwarpal_ml/export.py). If training's checks and serving ever prepared the numbers differently — another colour order, another layout — the model would quietly be fed the wrong numbers.

16    (faces, 3, height, width), with pixel values still 0-255: the model scales them itself."""

The export

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/export.py245 lines · 100% explained

Export: turn a trained, calibrated model into the file the service runs, prove that file gives the same answers, and write the model's manifest — its passport in the model registry.

run folder (.runs/…) ─► model + temperature + softmax ─► ONNX file ─► models/registry/age/<version>/model.onnx
                                                     ─► checks:  parity (PyTorch vs ONNX, same faces)
                                                                 serving path (faces aligned the service's way)
                                                                 CPU speed (one burst of 5 faces)
                                                     ─► models/registry/age/<version>/manifest.json

ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open file format for trained models: the network's layers and all its knobs, written down in a standard way that many engines can run. The service runs it with ONNX Runtime (§2.19), which is small, fast on ordinary processors, and doesn't need PyTorch — a 2 GB library the service would otherwise have to carry.

In batches of 64: convert the faces with the shared conversion, run PyTorch and ONNX Runtime on the very same numbers, and keep each face's largest difference across its 101 probabilities.

105        "tolerance": TOLERANCE,
106        "passed": largest <= TOLERANCE,
107    }

The largest difference over all faces, the tolerance, and whether it passed. On the first model: 0.0000008 — about a hundred times inside the tolerance.

Both use the same alignment, so they should give nearly the same face — this measures how nearly.

131    return {

How far apart the two answers are: the expected age (average, and the gap that 95 % of faces stay within) and the probability of being 18 or over. On the first model: 0.16 years on average, 0.45 for 95 % of faces, and 0.003 in probability — training and serving see practically the same face.

latency — the third check: how long one burst takes on the processor.

The typical time (p50, the median: half the runs were faster) and the slow-case time (p95: 95 % were faster). Services are judged by their slow cases, because every user waits for their own request, not the average one. On one thread: 668 ms typical, 697 ms at p95, inside the design's budget of 1.5 s for a whole submission on 4 virtual CPUs (NFR-05).

The API reads its first fields and its thresholds (§5.1.2); everything else is there so that anyone can see, years later, exactly what this model is, where it came from, what it promises and under which terms it may be used.

The inference service's changes — the ONNX backend, its settings, and its tests — are explained in their walkthroughs (services/inference/src/dwarpal_inference/backends.py, settings.py, main.py, tests/test_inference.py), alongside the vision library's new export and test.

Real world — the served model

  • Parity: the ONNX file and PyTorch agree to within 0.0000008 on every probability of 512 validation faces.
  • The service's way of aligning (straight from the photo, at 224 pixels) against training's (at 256, then shrunk): 0.16 years apart on average, and 0.003 in the probability of being 18 or over.
  • Speed on the processor: a burst of 5 faces in 0.67 s typical, 0.70 s slow case, on a single thread. Through the whole service pipeline — decode, detect, check quality, align, estimate — a 5-frame burst took 239 ms with 4 threads.
  • The export crashed once, on an emoji. PyTorch's exporter prints progress messages containing ✅, which the Windows console's old character set can't display. Turned off; the lesson is that tools are tested on someone else's computer.
  • A real verdict. Through the service, the test portrait — an astronaut photographed in her forties — was estimated at 25.4 years, with P(18 or over) = 0.937. At the 18 line of 0.964, the system would send her to step-up: not a pass, not a refusal. That is the strict line doing its job while the model is uncertain.

Try it yourself

With the model exported, start the inference service with it:

DWARPAL_INFERENCE_AGE_BACKEND=onnx uv run --package dwarpal-inference uvicorn dwarpal_inference.main:create_app --factory --port 8001

and the API with its manifest (DWARPAL_AGE_MANIFEST=registry/age/age-convnext-tiny-2026.10.17/manifest.json), then use a test key in the demo shop (§5.1.5). A live key is refused: the model isn't calibrated to the release standard yet.

5.3 Phase 3 — liveness and anti-spoofing

Phase 2 gave the system a real age model. But an age model only answers how old does this face look? — never is this a living person, here, now? Phase 3 adds that second question, with the layered design of ADR-0007 and the ideas of §2.18: a random challenge chosen by the server, evidence measured from the photos, and a decision that tells an attacker as little as possible.

Layer (ADR-0007) What Status
L1 Capture quality gate ✅ since Phase 1
L2 Passive PAD — MiniFASNet, two networks that spot faces shown on paper or screens ✅ decides (§5.3.3, §5.3.7)
L3 Random head-pose challenge, checked on the server with a 478-point face mesh ✅ turns decide; look-up and mid-turn photos are recorded
L4 Screen-light challenge — colours reflected on the skin ✅ measured and recorded; too variable to decide
L5 Injection signs — automation, virtual cameras, hidden page, frozen frames; hands beside the face ✅ hands recorded only
— Decision, vague outward reasons, per-session and per-device attempt limits ✅ §5.3.4

The journey of one attempt, with liveness:

verify page ── POST …/challenge ──► API: new_challenge() → random poses + colours, stored in Valkey (one use)
     │  ◄── { challenge_id, poses: [turn_right, look_up, turn_left, turn_right], colours: [4 × #rrggbb], step_ms: 600 }
     │
     │  MediaPipe guidance: "Move a little closer" … "That's good. Press Start"
     │  Start ► the screen glows in 4 colours, one baseline photo each   (none in calm mode)
     │        ► "Turn your head to your right, eyes on the screen"  [████░░░░░░] photo … [██████████] 2 photos (≤ 6 s)
     │        ► "Lift your chin up, eyes on the screen" … ► "Turn your head to your left, …" … ► …
     │
     └─ POST …/face-attempts  (up to 16 labelled photos + timings + browser signals)
            │
            ▼
API: take_challenge() — the server's own copy replaces whatever the page claimed
            │
            ▼
inference service: per photo — quality and people, face-mesh angles, hands, MiniFASNet real-face chance, screen pattern
            pose_check: frontal start? poses in order? each turn really shown, from the person's own frontal angles?
            light_check: did the cheeks follow the screen's colours?          (recorded only)
            injection_signs: automation, virtual camera, hidden page, frozen frames, hands (recorded only)
            │
            ▼
API: decide() — quality, then liveness, then age
            pose failed      → retry "liveness_check_failed"; the second time → reject "verification_failed"
            injection signs, or a real-face chance below 0.5 → step up "liveness_uncertain"
            otherwise        → the age decision of Phase 1–2

5.3.1 The challenge — chosen and kept by the server

Every attempt gets a fresh challenge: three or four head poses, never the same twice in a row and at most one look-up (24 possible orders), and four screen colours from a calm palette. It is drawn with the operating system's unpredictable random numbers, stored once, and destroyed when used. The page receives it so it can show the prompts — knowing the order a moment in advance doesn't help a prepared recording.

services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/challenges.py48 lines · 100% explained

Liveness challenges — what the person will be asked to do in their next face attempt (§5.3). Each challenge is a random order of three or four head poses and a random run of four screen colours, made fresh for every attempt.

Why random? A replay attack plays a recording of someone — a video of an adult turning their head — to the camera. If the challenge were always "turn left, then right", one recording would work every time. With 24 possible pose orders and hundreds of colour runs, chosen only when the attempt begins, an attacker can't prepare the right recording in advance.

1"""Liveness challenges: a random order of head poses and a random run of screen colours, new for every attempt."""

The module docstring: a random order of poses and a random run of colours, new for every attempt.

2
3from __future__ import annotations

from __future__ import annotations — the project-wide type-hint setting.

4
5import random

random — Python's random-number tools. Only its type random.Random is used here, so a test can pass in a generator of its own.

6import secrets

secrets — random numbers that are safe for security: they come from the operating system and can't be predicted from earlier ones. The plain random module is fast but predictable — someone who sees enough of its output can work out what comes next.

7from collections.abc import Sequence

Sequence — the type for "anything that can be indexed and counted", such as a tuple or a list.

8
9from dwarpal_contracts import POSES, Challenge, Pose

POSES (the three head poses), the Challenge contract, and the Pose type.

10
11# Calm, clearly different colours. None is a saturated red, and each is shown for STEP_MS, so the screen changes
12# fewer than two times a second: well below the three flashes a second that WCAG 2.3.1 warns about.

The comment explains how the colours were chosen, with people with photosensitive epilepsy in mind. Flashing light can trigger seizures; the accessibility standard WCAG (rule 2.3.1) says nothing should flash more than three times a second. So: calm colours, no saturated red (the most dangerous colour for this), and each shown for 600 ms — fewer than two changes a second. People who have asked their device for reduced motion see no colours at all (camera.ts).

13PALETTE = ("#3c78ff", "#20c8a0", "#ffd23c", "#c060ff", "#f0f0f0")

PALETTE — the five colours, written as web colours: blue, teal, yellow, violet, and near-white. They are far apart from each other, so the change in the light reflected from a face is as clear as possible.

14# Three or four poses. Turns are the strong proof (a flat picture can't turn); looking up is hard to measure from five
15# landmarks, so it appears at most once, and every challenge still holds at least two turns.

The comment explains the pose rules, which came out of the owner's genuine tests (§5.3.6). A turn is the strong proof: a flat picture can't turn its head, and every genuine turn was measured clearly. Looking up is hard to measure from five landmarks, so it appears at most once — and every challenge still holds at least two turns.

16POSE_STEPS = (3, 4)
17MAX_LOOK_UPS = 1
18COLOUR_STEPS = 4
19STEP_MS = 600

The challenge's size: 3 or 4 poses (POSE_STEPS = (3, 4), a tuple to choose from), at most MAX_LOOK_UPS = 1 look-up, COLOUR_STEPS = 4 colours, and STEP_MS = 600 milliseconds per colour. The colours take 2.4 seconds in all.

20
21_unpredictable = secrets.SystemRandom()

_unpredictable — the one secure random generator the module uses by default. SystemRandom has the same methods as random.Random, but draws on secrets' source. The leading _ marks it as private to this module.

22
23
24def sequence[T](options: Sequence[T], length: int, rng: random.Random) -> list[T]:

sequence — pick length items from options, at random, never the same item twice in a row. Used for the colours. [T] after the name makes it generic: it works for any type T, and the type checker knows the result is a list of the same type as the options.

25    chosen = [rng.choice(options)]

The first item: any of the options. rng.choice picks one at random.

26    while len(chosen) < length:
27        chosen.append(rng.choice([option for option in options if option != chosen[-1]]))

While the list is too short, add a random item from the options other than the last one picked (chosen[-1]). A repeated step would be a weak one: "turn left" twice in a row can be passed by simply staying turned, and the same colour twice doesn't change the light.

28    return chosen

Return the list.

29
30
31def pose_sequence(length: int, rng: random.Random) -> list[Pose]:

pose_sequence — pick length poses at random, with two rules: never the same pose twice in a row, and at most one look-up.

32    chosen: list[Pose] = []

The poses chosen so far: none yet.

33    while len(chosen) < length:

Until there are enough:

34        allowed = [
35            pose
36            for pose in POSES
37            if (not chosen or pose != chosen[-1]) and (pose != "look_up" or chosen.count("look_up") < MAX_LOOK_UPS)
38        ]

List the poses allowed next. A pose is allowed if it is not the one just chosen (or nothing is chosen yet), and it is not a look-up — or not enough look-ups have been chosen yet. chosen.count("look_up") counts them.

39        chosen.append(rng.choice(allowed))
40    return chosen

Pick one of the allowed poses at random, add it, and finally return the list.

41
42
43def new_challenge(rng: random.Random = _unpredictable) -> Challenge:

new_challenge — make one challenge. Normally it uses the secure generator; a test can pass a seeded one to get the same "random" challenges every run.

44    return Challenge(
45        poses=pose_sequence(rng.choice(POSE_STEPS), rng),
46        colours=sequence(PALETTE, COLOUR_STEPS, rng),
47        step_ms=STEP_MS,
48    )

The challenge: 3 or 4 poses (rng.choice(POSE_STEPS) picks the number), four colours, each colour shown for 600 ms. Pydantic checks it against the contract's limits as it is created.

The rest of the server side changed in existing files, each explained in its own walkthrough: the contracts gained Challenge, ClientSignals and Liveness (libs/contracts/src/dwarpal_contracts/face.py); the store saves the challenge and hands it back (adapters/store.py); and app/verification.py puts the server's copy into the request before the inference service sees it.

5.3.2 The verify page plays it

The page does three things. It guides: MediaPipe's face landmarker, running inside the browser, turns what it sees into plain instructions before the check begins. It plays the challenge: the colours, on a fixed timetable so the server can tell which colour lit which photo, then each pose, with a meter that fills as the head turns, taking one photo on the way and two once the head has held it for three readings — or after six seconds anyway. Every photo is only copied while the challenge runs; encoding them to JPEG waits until the end, so nothing slow can shift the colours' timetable. It reports: the browser's own signals, which can only make the check stricter.

The guidance never decides anything. After 8 seconds Start can be pressed regardless, and if MediaPipe can't run at all the page simply works without it: a person whose face the landmarker reads badly must never be locked out by the page.

apps/web/lib/challenge.ts110 lines · 100% explained

The verify page's side of the liveness challenge (§5.3): the shape of a challenge, the browser's signals, how a head pose is read from the face, and how the server's answer is checked before the page plays it.

Two numbers describe the head here, exactly as on the server: yaw (how far it is turned sideways) and pitch (how far it is tilted up). Using the same formulas on both sides means the page and the server agree on what a pose is — the page only decides when to take a photo, and the server checks the photo itself.

Pose — the three head poses, as a TypeScript union type: a value of this type must be exactly one of these three texts.

Phase — what a photo is labelled with: "baseline" (looking straight ahead, during the colours) or one of the poses. | Pose adds all three of them.

7  id: string;
8  poses: Pose[];

16  virtualCamera: boolean;

23  /** Sideways turn: positive when the person turns to their left (the nose moves to the right of the picture). */
24  yaw: number;
25  /** Up and down: smaller when the head tilts back. About 0.55 when looking straight ahead. */

HeadAngles — the two numbers, with what they mean:

  • yaw — the sideways turn. Positive when the person turns to their left. Photos are not mirrored, so a person turning to their left moves their nose towards the right of the picture;
  • pitch — where the nose sits between the eyes and the mouth. About 0.55 looking straight ahead; smaller when the head tilts back, because the nose appears to rise towards the eyes.

29/** The page's targets, as shifts from the person's own frontal angles. The page's landmarks read a head a little further

The comment explains the page's targets: shifts from the person's own frontal angles, set well above the server's limits (0.18 for a turn, 0.03 for looking up). In the owner's tests, the page's landmarks (MediaPipe's mesh) read a head as more turned than the server's (YuNet's five points) did. Aiming higher on the page means that when its meter is full, the photos pass on the server too.

33export const RAISE_SHIFT = 0.12;

36export const CUES: Record<Pose, string> = {
37  turn_left: "Turn your head to your left, eyes on the screen",
38  turn_right: "Turn your head to your right, eyes on the screen",
39  look_up: "Lift your chin up, eyes on the screen",
40};

CUES — the instruction shown for each pose. "Eyes on the screen" matters: people tend to follow their own head with their eyes and lose sight of the prompts and the meter. "Lift your chin up" says plainly what "look up" means. Record<Pose, string> makes TypeScript check that every pose has exactly one instruction.

The three poses as a list, for checking the server's answer. readonly — it can't be changed.

45const VIRTUAL_CAMERA =

VIRTUAL_CAMERA — names that virtual-camera programs give their pretend cameras: OBS, ManyCam, XSplit, Snap Camera and others. Such a program can feed any video — including a recording or a deepfake — to the page as if it were a camera. In the pattern:

  • \b — a word boundary, so ndi matches the word "NDI" but not the inside of another word;
  • ( … | … ) — any one of the names;
  • i at the end — ignore upper and lower case.

As the comment says, the page only reports a match. Some people use these programs for ordinary video calls; the server weighs it with everything else.

48export const isVirtualCamera = (label: string): boolean => VIRTUAL_CAMERA.test(label);

50/** How much of the pose's target the head has reached, from its frontal `baseline`: 0 (not at all, or the wrong way)

poseProgress — how much of the pose's target the head has reached, from its frontal angles: 0 (not at all, or the wrong way) to 1 (enough). It drives the on-screen meter, and a full meter (1) is what the page waits for.

52export function poseProgress(pose: Pose, angles: HeadAngles, baseline: HeadAngles): number {

Its inputs: the pose, the head's angles now, and the frontal angles to measure from.

53  const moved =
54    pose === "turn_left"
55      ? (angles.yaw - baseline.yaw) / TURN_SHIFT
56      : pose === "turn_right"
57        ? (baseline.yaw - angles.yaw) / TURN_SHIFT
58        : (baseline.pitch - angles.pitch) / RAISE_SHIFT;

How far the head has moved in the pose's direction, as a share of the target: for a left turn, the rise in yaw divided by TURN_SHIFT; for a right turn, the fall in yaw; for looking up, the fall in pitch divided by RAISE_SHIFT. a ? b : c ? d : e is a chain of choices: "if a, b; otherwise if c, d; otherwise e".

59  return Math.min(1, Math.max(0, moved));
60}

Keep it between 0 and 1: a turn the wrong way gives a negative share, shown as 0; a turn past the target, as 1.

61
62const median = (values: number[]): number => {

median — the middle value of a list of numbers.

63  const sorted = [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b);

Sort a copy ([...values] copies the list, so the caller's list isn't reordered), smallest first. (a, b) => a - b tells sort to compare numbers by size; without it, JavaScript would sort them as text.

64  const half = Math.floor(sorted.length / 2);

The position of the middle.

65  return sorted.length % 2 === 1 ? (sorted[half] ?? 0) : ((sorted[half - 1] ?? 0) + (sorted[half] ?? 0)) / 2;
66};

With an odd number of values, the one in the middle; with an even number, the average of the two middle ones. The ?? 0 parts only satisfy TypeScript, which can't know those positions exist.
