frontalAngles — the person's angles when facing the camera: the median of the landmarker readings taken with the baseline photos, as on the server. readonly promises the list isn't changed.

70  if (readings.length === 0) {
71    return null;
72  }

No readings — the landmarker couldn't see a face, or isn't running: null. The page can't measure poses then, so it simply waits out each pose's time.

73  return { yaw: median(readings.map((r) => r.yaw)), pitch: median(readings.map((r) => r.pitch)) };
74}

The median yaw and the median pitch.

75
76export interface Point {
77  x: number;
78  y: number;
79}

Point — a position in the picture: x across, y down. MediaPipe gives positions as fractions of the picture's width and height, from 0 to 1.

80
81const middle = (a: Point, b: Point): Point => ({ x: (a.x + b.x) / 2, y: (a.y + b.y) / 2 });

middle — the point halfway between two points.

82
83/** Head angles from five points of the face, in picture coordinates: the same formulas as the server's. */
84export function anglesFrom(rightEye: Point, leftEye: Point, nose: Point, mouth: Point): HeadAngles {

anglesFrom — the head's angles from four points of the face: the two eyes, the nose tip and the middle of the mouth. As the comment says, the formulas are the server's (quality.py).

85  const eyes = middle(rightEye, leftEye);

The point between the eyes.

86  const eyeDistance = Math.max(Math.hypot(leftEye.x - rightEye.x, leftEye.y - rightEye.y), 1e-6);

The distance between the eyes — Math.hypot is Pythagoras: the length of the line from one eye to the other. Math.max(…, 1e-6) (one millionth) keeps it from ever being zero, so the division below can't fail.

87  const drop = Math.max(mouth.y - eyes.y, 1e-6);

How far the mouth is below the eyes, also never zero.

88  return { yaw: (nose.x - eyes.x) / eyeDistance, pitch: (nose.y - eyes.y) / drop };
89}

Yaw: how far the nose is to the side of the eyes' midpoint, measured in eye distances. Pitch: how far down from the eyes the nose sits, as a fraction of the way to the mouth. Dividing makes both independent of how big the face is in the picture.

90
91/** Read a challenge from the server's answer, refusing anything that isn't exactly what the page can play. */
92export function readChallenge(data: Record<string, unknown>): Challenge {

readChallenge — check and convert the server's answer. The page treats the answer as untrusted data (Record<string, unknown>: an object whose values could be anything) and refuses anything it can't play exactly.

93  const { challenge_id: id, poses, colours, step_ms: stepMs } = data;

Take the four fields out, renaming challenge_id to id and step_ms to stepMs as they come (challenge_id: id means "the field challenge_id, into a variable named id").

94  const valid =
95    typeof id === "string" &&
96    id.length > 0 &&
97    Array.isArray(poses) &&
98    poses.length > 0 &&
99    poses.every((pose) => POSES.includes(pose as Pose)) &&
100    Array.isArray(colours) &&
101    colours.length >= 2 &&
102    colours.every((colour) => typeof colour === "string" && COLOUR.test(colour)) &&
103    typeof stepMs === "number" &&
104    stepMs >= 400 &&
105    stepMs <= 2000;

Every check at once, joined with && ("and"): the ID is a non-empty text; poses is a non-empty list (Array.isArray) whose every item (every) is a known pose; colours is a list of at least two items, each a well-formed colour; stepMs is a number from 400 to 2000. pose as Pose only tells TypeScript to allow the comparison; includes does the real check.

106  if (!valid) {
107    throw new Error("the server sent a challenge this page cannot play");
108  }

If anything is wrong, stop with an error — the camera screen shows it like a camera error.

109  return { id, poses: poses as Pose[], colours: colours as string[], stepMs };
110}

Return the challenge in the page's own shape. Thanks to the checks, the type assertions (as Pose[]) are safe.

apps/web/lib/landmarker.ts75 lines · 100% explained

Live guidance for the camera screen, using Google's MediaPipe Face Landmarker (§5.3). It runs entirely inside the browser: the picture never leaves the device for it. From each picture of the preview it finds the face and 478 points on it — the eyes' corners, the nose tip, the lips and so on, called a face mesh — fast enough to keep up with live video.

From a few of those points the page works out where the face is, how big it is and which way the head points, and turns that into plain instructions ("Move a little closer"). It also tells the challenge when the head has reached each pose, so the photo is taken at the right moment.

As the first line says: it guides; it decides nothing. Every decision is made on the server, from the photos, by our own checks. If the landmarker can't run at all, the page still works — just without live guidance.

1/** MediaPipe Face Landmarker, loaded only when the camera starts. It guides the person; it decides nothing. */

The doc comment: loaded only when the camera starts — a few megabytes that nobody else needs — and it decides nothing.

2

Two MediaPipe types (only types: nothing is loaded by this line): the landmarker itself, and NormalizedLandmark — one point of the mesh, with x and y as fractions of the picture's width and height (0 to 1).

4
5import { anglesFrom, type HeadAngles } from "./challenge";

From challenge.ts: anglesFrom, which turns face points into head angles, and the HeadAngles type.

9

17}

  • faces — how many faces;
  • angles — the head's angles, or null with no face;
  • centred — whether the face is near the middle of the picture;
  • closeEnough — whether the face is wide enough: at least a fifth of the picture's width.

MESH — which of the 478 points to use, by their numbers in MediaPipe's mesh: both corners of each eye (33 and 133 for the person's right eye, 362 and 263 for the left), the nose tip (1), and the two mouth corners (61 and 291). Averaging two corners gives an eye's centre, matching the five points the server's YuNet detector finds. as const tells TypeScript these lists never change.

22function centre(points: NormalizedLandmark[], indices: readonly number[]): { x: number; y: number } {

centre — the average position of some of the points, chosen by their numbers.

23  const chosen = indices.map((index) => points[index] ?? { x: 0, y: 0 });

Look up each point. ?? { x: 0, y: 0 } stands in for a point that is missing — it shouldn't happen, but the type system can't know that.

24  return {
25    x: chosen.reduce((sum, point) => sum + point.x, 0) / chosen.length,
26    y: chosen.reduce((sum, point) => sum + point.y, 0) / chosen.length,
27  };
28}

The average: add up the x values and divide by how many there are, then the same for y. reduce walks through a list carrying a running total, starting from 0.

Load MediaPipe's code now, not when the page first opens. await import(…) is a dynamic import: the code is downloaded only when this line runs. People who never reach the camera never download it.

Point MediaPipe at its WebAssembly files, in our own /mediapipe/wasm folder.

  • faces — how many were found;

A small build step that puts MediaPipe's files where the browser can load them. It runs before the verify page's development server starts and before every production build (package.json).

Next.js serves everything in a project's public/ folder as it is, at the site's own address. The page also keeps a random device ID for the API's per-device budgets (§5.3.4) — a random number, not a fingerprint:

apps/web/lib/device.ts33 lines · 100% explained

A device ID for the per-device budgets: a random ID that this browser keeps for the verify page, so the API can limit how many age checks one device tries in an hour, across all the sessions it starts.

It is deliberately not a fingerprint. Fingerprinting would compute an ID from the device's features (screen, fonts, graphics card…) so that it can't be escaped — and it would follow people around. This ID is just a random number in the site's own storage: it says nothing about the device or the person, and clearing the site's data resets it. A determined attacker can reset it too; the API's per-address budget is the backstop for that.

1/** A random ID this browser keeps for the verify page, so the API can limit how many age checks one device tries.
2 * It is not a fingerprint: it says nothing about the device or the person, and clearing the site's data resets it. */

The camera code was rewritten around the challenge (apps/web/lib/camera.ts), and so was the camera screen (apps/web/app/v/[sessionId]/camera-view.tsx), with the full-screen colour layer, the guidance and the signals. Smaller changes: the flow client sends the labels and signals (lib/flow-api.ts), the page's security policy allows WebAssembly (next.config.ts), and package.json runs mediapipe.mjs before every start and build. The MediaPipe face model is pinned, like every other model, in models/third_party.json.

5.3.3 The evidence — measured from the photos

The inference service measures every photo: the sideways turn (yaw) it already measured, and now the up-down tilt (pitch, libs/vision/src/dwarpal_vision/quality.py). Each pose is judged against the person's own frontal angles, taken from their opening photos. The quality check also learned to count people rather than detections: a second box inside the same face, or a small face-like shape in the background, is no longer a second person (§5.3.6). From those numbers, the colours and the browser's signals, liveness.py gathers the three kinds of evidence. It decides nothing itself.

services/inference/src/dwarpal_inference/liveness.py204 lines · 100% explained

The liveness checks (§5.3, ADR-0007): evidence that a real, present person stood in front of the camera — not a photo, a screen replaying a video, or a fake camera feeding in pictures. There are three:

  1. The pose check — did the head turn as the challenge asked, in the right order? A printed photo can't turn its head when asked; a pre-recorded video doesn't know which way it will be asked to turn.
  2. The light check — while the screen showed its colours, did the skin pick up their glow? Real skin a hand's width from a bright screen reflects its colour. This one is only recorded for now: on its own it is weak (in a bright room the glow is faint), and its limits must first be measured on genuine attempts.
  3. Injection signs — anything suggesting the pictures didn't come from a live camera: the browser's own warnings, and frames that are too identical.

As the docstring says, this file only gathers evidence. The decision — retry, reject, step up — belongs to the API's decision engine (decision.py).

1"""Liveness evidence from one attempt: did the head turn as asked, did the skin reflect the screen, and does anything
2suggest the frames came from somewhere other than a live camera. Evidence only: the API decides (ADR-0007)."""

The module docstring: the three questions, and the rule that this is evidence only.

17# Provisional limits, set from the owner's genuine attempts. A turned head moves its nose sideways against its eyes; a
18# raised head moves its nose towards its eyes. Each pose is measured from the person's own frontal frames, so camera
19# height and face shape cancel out. From YuNet's five points, genuine turns moved the nose 0.23-0.69 eye-widths, but
20# lifted chins anywhere from -0.03 to 0.12 of the eyes-to-mouth distance. The 478-point face mesh measures far better:
21# genuine turns 0.42-0.70 and lifted chins 0.11-0.38 (2026-10-19/20). Turns carry the proof; looking up is recorded
22# but doesn't decide. A flat photo, turned or tilted, moves neither.

The comment explains the limits below, which were set from the owner's genuine attempts (§5.3.6), and how the head is measured: a turned head moves the nose sideways against the eyes; a raised one moves it towards the eyes. Each pose is measured against the person's own frontal angles, so camera height and face shape cancel out.

The measurements behind the numbers: from YuNet's five points, genuine turns moved the nose 0.23–0.69 eye-widths, but lifted chins anywhere from −0.03 to 0.12 — five points can't measure looking up. The 478-point face mesh does far better: turns 0.42–0.70, lifted chins 0.11–0.38. Turns carry the proof; looking up is recorded but doesn't decide. A flat photo, turned or tilted, moves neither.

23FRONTAL_YAW = 0.2

FRONTAL_YAW = 0.2 — a baseline frame must be facing the camera: sideways turn no more than 0.2 either way (five-point measure).

24TURN_SHIFT = 0.18
25RAISE_SHIFT = 0.03

The five-point limits: a turn counts from a shift of 0.18 eye-widths (about 18 degrees); a look-up from 0.03, though it is only recorded.

26MESH_TURN_SHIFT = 0.18
27MESH_RAISE_SHIFT = 0.08

The face mesh's limits: 0.18 for a turn, 0.08 for a look-up — below every genuine attempt measured (0.42 and 0.11 at the lowest).

29MIN_BASELINE = 3

MIN_BASELINE = 3 — at least three frontal frames are needed.

31STILL_FRAMES = 0.75

STILL_FRAMES = 0.75 — as the comment says, two frames from a live camera are never quite the same: even with a perfectly still person, the sensor adds a little noise. If every pair of frames differs by less than 0.75 grey levels on average (out of 255), they were probably copies of one picture.

32HAND_FRAMES = 2

HAND_FRAMES = 2 — a hand next to the face must show in at least two photos to count as a sign.

34# and the top corners, beyond the hair line.
35SKIN = ((slice(120, 150), slice(50, 80)), (slice(120, 150), slice(144, 174)), (slice(40, 60), slice(92, 132)))
36BACKGROUND = ((slice(0, 16), slice(0, 16)), (slice(0, 16), slice(208, 224)))

Where to sample on the 224 × 224 aligned face (align_face puts every face in the same place). Each slice(a, b) is a range of rows or columns.

  • SKIN — three small patches: the right cheek, the left cheek and the forehead;

149def chromaticity(image: Image, patches: tuple[tuple[slice, slice], ...]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:

chromaticity — the colour of some patches of a picture, without its brightness. Brightness changes for many reasons (the person moves, the camera adjusts itself); the balance of red, green and blue is what the screen's colour changes.

150    pixels = np.concatenate([image[rows, cols].reshape(-1, 3) for rows, cols in patches]).astype(np.float64)

Take every patch's pixels, lay them out as one long list of (blue, green, red) values (reshape(-1, 3): −1 means "as many rows as needed"), join the patches together, and switch to decimals.

151    blue, green, red = pixels.mean(axis=0)

The average of each colour. OpenCV stores pixels as Blue, Green, Red — in that order.

152    total = max(red + green + blue, 1.0)
153    return np.array([red / total, blue / total])

Divide by the total, so only the balance remains: the share of red and the share of blue. (The share of green is whatever is left, so it adds nothing.) max(…, 1.0) avoids dividing by zero on a black patch.

154
155
156def emitted(colour: str) -> NDArray[np.float64]:

emitted — the same two shares for a colour the screen showed, from its web code.

157    red, green, blue = (int(colour[i : i + 2], 16) for i in (1, 3, 5))

Read the code's three pairs of hexadecimal digits — characters 1–2, 3–4 and 5–6 of #3c78ff — as numbers from 0 to 255. int(…, 16) reads a number written in base 16.

158    total = max(red + green + blue, 1)
159    return np.array([red / total, blue / total])

The shares of red and blue, as for the skin.

160
161
162def correlation(measured: list[NDArray[np.float64]], shown: list[NDArray[np.float64]]) -> float | None:

correlation — how closely the measured colours followed the shown ones, from −1 to +1. This is Pearson's correlation: +1 means they rose and fell exactly together, 0 means no relation.

163    a = np.array(measured) - np.mean(measured, axis=0)
164    b = np.array(shown) - np.mean(shown, axis=0)

Subtract each list's average, so only the changes remain.

165    spread = float(np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

The size of each list of changes — np.linalg.norm is the length of the whole list taken as one long arrow — multiplied together.

166    return None if spread == 0 else float(np.clip((a * b).sum() / spread, -1.0, 1.0))

Correlation is the sum of the changes multiplied together, divided by that product. If either list never changed at all (spread is 0), there is nothing to compare: None. np.clip guards against rounding taking it a hair past ±1.

167
168
169def light_check(
170    frames: list[Seen], challenge: Challenge, started_ms: float | None, signals: ClientSignals
171) -> LightCheck:

light_check — did the skin follow the screen's colours? It needs the frames, the challenge (for its colours and timing), when the colours started, and the browser's signals.

172    if started_ms is None or not signals.light_shown:
173        return LightCheck(usable=False, shown=False)

No colours were shown — calm mode, or an older page: nothing to measure, and the result says so (shown=False). This never counts against anyone.

174    skin, background, shown = [], [], []

Three lists: the skin's colour in each frame, the background's, and what the screen showed.

175    for frame in frames:
176        step = int((frame.meta.t_ms - started_ms) // challenge.step_ms)

For each frame, work out which colour was on screen when it was taken: the time since the colours started, divided by the step length, rounded down (//).

177        if frame.meta.phase != "baseline" or frame.aligned is None or not 0 <= step < len(challenge.colours):
178            continue

Skip frames that aren't baseline frames, that have no usable face, or that fall outside the colours' time.

179        skin.append(chromaticity(frame.aligned, SKIN))
180        background.append(chromaticity(frame.aligned, BACKGROUND))
181        shown.append(emitted(challenge.colours[step]))

Measure the skin and the background, and note the colour shown.

182    if len(shown) < MIN_BASELINE or len({tuple(colour) for colour in shown}) < 2:
183        return LightCheck(usable=False)

At least three measured frames are needed, under at least two different colours ({…} makes a set, which keeps each colour once). Otherwise: not usable.

184    return LightCheck(usable=True, r_skin=correlation(skin, shown), r_background=correlation(background, shown))

The result: how well the skin followed the screen, and how well the background did. A real face close to the screen should follow it clearly; the background, further away, much less. A photo or a screen held up to the camera tends to behave differently — but how differently, in real rooms, is what the owner's tests will measure.

185
186
187def injection_signs(frames: list[Seen], signals: ClientSignals, trust_labels: bool = False) -> list[str]:

injection_signs — signs that the pictures didn't come from a live camera.

188    signs = []

The signs found.

189    if signals.automation:
190        signs.append("automation")
191    if signals.virtual_camera:
192        signs.append("virtual_camera")
193    if signals.hidden_ms > 0:
194        signs.append("page_hidden")

The browser's own reports: a program driving the browser (automation), a virtual camera (virtual_camera), and the page being hidden during the check (page_hidden). These come from the browser and can be faked — but only an honest browser reports them, and then they are worth knowing.

195    faces = [frame.aligned for frame in sorted(frames, key=lambda f: f.meta.t_ms) if frame.aligned is not None]

The usable faces, in time order.

196    grey = [cv2.cvtColor(face, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY).astype(np.float64) for face in faces]

Each converted to greyscale, as decimals.

197    changes = [float(np.abs(a - b).mean()) for a, b in itertools.pairwise(grey)]

How much each frame differs from the next: the average difference between their pixels.

198    if not trust_labels and len(changes) >= 2 and max(changes) < STILL_FRAMES:
199        signs.append("identical_frames")

identical_frames — if there are at least two such differences and even the largest is below 0.75 grey levels, the frames are near-copies: one picture sent several times, as a fake camera might. Not in the test mode, where the frames are copies of one test photo on purpose.

200    # A hand beside the face in more than one photo: a phone or a photo held up to the camera. One photo alone could
201    # be a passing gesture, or a false find.
202    if not trust_labels and sum(1 for frame in frames if frame.report.hands_near_face > 0) >= HAND_FRAMES:
203        signs.append("hand_near_face")

hand_near_face — a hand next to the face in at least two photos: someone may be holding a phone or a photo up to the camera. As the comment says, one photo alone could be a passing gesture, or a false find. (The API records this sign but doesn't yet let it decide: in the owner's tests the hand detector missed the holding hands and once saw one that wasn't there.)

204    return signs

Return the signs.

services/inference/tests/test_liveness.py219 lines · 100% explained

Unit tests for the liveness checks (liveness.py). They build frames by hand — a report with chosen head angles, or a synthetic "face" lit by a chosen colour — so each check can be tested on exactly the situation it is meant for, with no camera and no detector.

The real images are tested elsewhere: the red-team tests in services/api/tests/test_api.py send a real portrait through the whole system.

68def test_each_pose_is_measured_from_the_persons_own_frontal_angles() -> None:
69    front = (0.0, 0.55)

Each pose is measured from the person's own frontal angles. Here those are straight ahead: yaw 0, pitch 0.55.

70    assert shows("turn_left", report(0, yaw=TURN_SHIFT), front)
71    assert not shows("turn_left", report(0, yaw=-TURN_SHIFT), front)
72    assert shows("turn_right", report(0, yaw=-0.3), front)
73    assert shows("look_up", report(0, pitch=0.55 - 2 * RAISE_SHIFT), front)
74    assert not shows("look_up", report(0, pitch=0.55), front)
75    assert not shows("turn_left", report(0, yaw=0.6, faces=2), front)

Exactly the turn limit to the left counts as turned left; the same amount the other way doesn't. A strong right turn counts as right. A pitch twice the limit below the frontal one is looking up; the frontal pitch itself isn't. And a strong left turn with two people in the picture counts for nothing.

76    # A camera below the face: frontal pitch 0.7. Lifting the chin to 0.6 counts, though it would not from 0.55.
77    assert shows("look_up", report(0, pitch=0.6), (0.0, 0.7))
78    assert not shows("look_up", report(0, pitch=0.6), front)

Why measure from the person's own angles: with a camera below the face, the frontal pitch might be 0.7. Lifting the chin to 0.6 is then a real look-up — though from a frontal 0.55, the same 0.6 would be a head tilted down.

155def face_lit_by(colour: str, strength: float, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:

face_lit_by — a synthetic 224 × 224 "face" lit by a screen colour. strength says how much the screen's colour mixes into the skin's: 0 means not at all.

156    blue, green, red = (int(colour[i : i + 2], 16) for i in (5, 3, 1))

Read the colour's red, green and blue, in OpenCV's blue-green-red order (characters 5–6 first).

157    skin = np.array([110.0, 140.0, 190.0]) * (1 - strength) + np.array([blue, green, red]) * strength

Mix an ordinary skin tone (in blue-green-red: 110, 140, 190) with the screen's colour, in the given proportion.

158    return np.clip(skin + rng.normal(0, 2, (224, 224, 3)), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

Fill the picture with that colour, plus a little random noise, like a real camera's (rng.normal(0, 2, …): random values around 0, typically within ±2). Keep values in 0–255 and store them as image bytes.

A photo on the way into a pose shows the movement was gradual. Add a frame to the genuine attempt, labelled turn_left, turned 0.2 — partway to the full 0.5. That pose is recorded as gradual; the others, with a single photo each at their full angle, aren't.

After the owner's tests (§5.3.6–5.3.7) the service measures far more in each photo, with three components added to the vision library — all run by OpenCV from pinned files, no new libraries:

  • the face mesh, MediaPipe's 478 points, which measure the head's angles much better than YuNet's five, above all a lifted chin;
  • the hand detector, MediaPipe's palm detector, looking for a hand held next to the face (recorded only: in the tests it didn't work well enough to trust);
  • the anti-spoofing networks, MiniFASNet, filling layer L2, with a hand-made screen-pattern measure beside them.
libs/vision/src/dwarpal_vision/mesh.py80 lines · 100% explained

Head angles from a face mesh, on the server (§5.3.6). YuNet's five points — two eyes, the nose tip, two mouth corners — measure a sideways turn well, but in the owner's tests they measured a lifted chin anywhere from −0.03 to 0.12, too unreliable to judge. MediaPipe's face mesh places 478 points on the face, and in particular the eye corners, nose tip and mouth corners far more precisely: with it, the same lifted chins measured 0.11–0.38.

The mesh model was already pinned for the verify page (models/third_party.json). Here OpenCV runs it, from the same bundle — no new download, and no new library. The angles use exactly the page's formulas (apps/web/lib/challenge.ts), so the page's meter and the server measure the same thing.

40def angles_from(points: NDArray[np.float32]) -> HeadAngles:
41    right, left = centre(points, RIGHT_EYE), centre(points, LEFT_EYE)
42    nose, mouth = centre(points, NOSE), centre(points, MOUTH)

43    eyes = (right + left) / 2

The distance between the eyes — np.linalg.norm is the length of the line from one to the other. max(…, 1e-6) keeps it from ever being zero, so the division below can't fail.

45    drop = max(float(mouth[1] - eyes[1]), 1e-6)

Yaw: how far the nose is to the side of the eyes' midpoint, in eye distances. Pitch: how far down from the eyes the nose sits, as a fraction of the way to the mouth. Lifting the chin moves the nose up towards the eyes, so pitch falls.

64        x, y, w, h = face.box

91def overlap(a: Box, b: Box) -> float:
92    """How much two boxes overlap: the shared area over the combined area (0 = apart, 1 = the same box)."""

overlap — how much two boxes overlap: the shared area over the area they cover together. 0 means apart; 1 means the same box. This measure is called intersection over union.

libs/vision/src/dwarpal_vision/antispoof.py86 lines · 100% explained

Telling a real face from a face presented to the camera — a printed photo, or a phone screen showing a photo or a video. This is the empty layer L2 of ADR-0007, passive presentation-attack detection, filled after the owner's red-team tests showed that a phone carousel of their own posed selfies could pass every other check (§5.3.6).

It uses MiniFASNet: two small networks from the Silent-Face-Anti-Spoofing project (Apache-2.0), trained on thousands of real faces and attacks to spot the tell-tale look of paper and screens. Each looks at a differently sized crop around the face — one 2.7 face-sizes across, one 4 — and their answers are averaged. In the owner's tests their verdict separated real from presented faces by a wide margin: real 0.94–0.995, phone 0.006–0.195.

The file also holds a simpler, hand-made measure: the screen pattern, a sign of a screen's pixel grid in the face.

1"""Tell a real face from a photo or a screen held up to the camera: MiniFASNet (Apache-2.0), two small networks trained
2to spot presentation attacks, each looking at a differently sized crop around the face. Run by OpenCV from ONNX files
3made by `dwarpal_ml.antispoof`.
4"""

The crop can't be larger than the picture: shrink the scale if scale face-sizes wouldn't fit. max(…, 1.0) avoids dividing by zero.

45def screen_pattern(image: Image, face: Face) -> float:
46    """How strongly a regular fine pattern stands out in the middle of the face: the brightest spot of its fine-detail
47    spectrum against the typical one. Re-filming a screen leaves a grid of pixels and moiré stripes there; skin doesn't.
48    Measured on the picture as it came, never resized, which would smooth the pattern away."""

screen_pattern — how strongly a regular fine pattern stands out in the middle of the face. As the docstring says, re-filming a screen leaves its grid of pixels and moiré stripes (the wavy bands two fine grids make together) in the picture; skin has nothing so regular. It is measured on the picture as it came: resizing would smooth the pattern away.

49    x, y, w, h = face.box
50    height, width = image.shape[:2]
51    left, top = max(0, int(x + 0.2 * w)), max(0, int(y + 0.2 * h))
52    right, bottom = min(width, int(x + 0.8 * w)), min(height, int(y + 0.8 * h))

The middle of the face: the inner 60 % of its box, kept inside the picture.

53    grey = cv2.cvtColor(image[top:bottom, left:right], cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY).astype(np.float64)

In grey, as decimals.

54    if min(grey.shape) < 32:
55        return 0.0

Too small to measure (under 32 pixels across): 0.

56    grey -= grey.mean()

Subtract the average, so the overall brightness doesn't dominate what follows.

57    window = np.outer(np.hanning(grey.shape[0]), np.hanning(grey.shape[1]))

A Hanning window: a smooth weighting that fades to 0 at the edges. Without it, the crop's hard edges would themselves look like fine detail.

58    spectrum = np.abs(np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft2(grey * window)))

The Fourier transform (fft2) splits the picture into regular waves of every size and direction, and tells how strong each is — its spectrum. fftshift puts the slow waves in the middle and the fine ones at the edges; np.abs takes each wave's strength.

59    rows, cols = np.indices(spectrum.shape)
60    radius = np.hypot(
61        (rows - spectrum.shape[0] / 2) / spectrum.shape[0], (cols - spectrum.shape[1] / 2) / spectrum.shape[1]
62    )

For each point of the spectrum, how fine its wave is: its distance from the middle, as a fraction (0 = smooth, 0.5 = the finest the picture can hold). np.indices gives every point's row and column numbers; np.hypot is Pythagoras.

63    fine = spectrum[(radius > 0.15) & (radius < 0.5)]

Keep the fine waves only: between 0.15 and 0.5.

64    return float(np.log10(np.percentile(fine, 99.9) / max(float(np.median(fine)), 1e-9)))

The answer: how far the strongest fine waves (the top 0.1 %) stand above the typical one (the median), on a logarithmic scale (log10: 1 means ten times stronger). A screen's regular grid makes a few very strong peaks; skin's fine detail is spread out. In the owner's tests real faces measured 0.99–1.14 and phones 1.16–1.31 — a real but narrow gap, so it is recorded, not decided on.

MiniFASNet was published as PyTorch weights. One script turns them into the ONNX files the service runs, proving on the way that nothing changed:

ml/src/dwarpal_ml/antispoof.py178 lines · 100% explained

Converting the anti-spoofing networks for serving. The two MiniFASNet networks were published as PyTorch weight files (.pth). The inference service doesn't use PyTorch — it is 2 GB, and serving needs none of it — so this script turns them into ONNX files, the format the service already runs (§2.19), and proves the answers didn't change.

Two things make it unusual. First, the original project's model code isn't used: the network is rebuilt from the shapes stored in the weight files, and loading every weight with strict=True proves the rebuild matches — a single missing or misshapen layer would make loading fail. Second, safety: a .pth file is a Python pickle, a format that can carry code that runs when the file is opened. With weights_only=True, PyTorch reads plain numbers only and refuses anything else.

1"""Convert the pinned MiniFASNet anti-spoofing weights (PyTorch) to ONNX for serving, proving the answers don't change.
2
3uv run --package dwarpal-ml python -m dwarpal_ml.antispoof
4
5The repository's own model code isn't needed: the network is rebuilt from the shapes stored in the weight files, and
6loading every weight strictly proves the rebuild matches. The files are read as plain tensors only (`weights_only`), so
7nothing inside them can run.
8"""

The module docstring: what it does, the command that runs it, and the two points above — the rebuild proved by strict loading, and reading the files as plain tensors only.

31HALVING = {"conv1", "conv_23.conv_dw", "conv_34.conv_dw", "conv_45.conv_dw"}

HALVING — the layers that halve the picture's size, as the comment shows: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5. The weights don't record a layer's stride (how far its filter steps), so the rebuild must know it.

32TOLERANCE = 1e-4

TOLERANCE — the largest difference allowed between PyTorch's and ONNX Runtime's probabilities.

33
34type State = dict[str, torch.Tensor]

State — a name for the weights: a dict from layer names to tensors.

35
36
37class ConvBlock(nn.Module):
38    """A convolution, batch normalisation and (except in projections) a PReLU, sized from its stored weight."""

ConvBlock — a convolution, batch normalisation, and (except in projections) a PReLU: an activation like ReLU whose slope for negative values is itself learned. Its size comes from the stored weight.

39
40    def __init__(self, weight: torch.Tensor, stride: int, prelu: bool) -> None:
41        super().__init__()
42        out_c, per_group, k, _ = weight.shape

The weight's shape gives the block's size: output channels, input channels per group, and the filter's size.

43        groups = out_c if per_group == 1 and k > 1 else 1

A depthwise convolution filters each channel on its own: its weight has one input channel per group, and as many groups as channels. Otherwise one group.

44        # 1 x 1 and the final 5 x 5 (which shrinks 5 x 5 to 1 x 1) use no padding; 3 x 3 keeps the size.
45        padding = 1 if k == 3 else 0

Padding, as the comment says: 3 × 3 filters get a 1-pixel border to keep the size; 1 × 1 filters need none; the final 5 × 5 filter takes none, shrinking 5 × 5 to 1 × 1.

46        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(per_group * groups, out_c, k, stride, padding, groups=groups, bias=False)
47        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_c)
48        self.prelu = nn.PReLU(out_c) if prelu else None

The three parts. bias=False: these convolutions have no bias in the weights, since batch normalisation adds its own.

49
50    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
51        x = self.bn(self.conv(x))
52        return self.prelu(x) if self.prelu is not None else x

Run them in order; the PReLU only if there is one.

53
54
55class Squeeze(nn.Module):
56    """Squeeze-and-excitation: reweigh the channels by a summary of the whole picture (MiniFASNetV1SE only)."""

Squeeze — squeeze-and-excitation, used only in MiniFASNetV1SE: summarise each channel over the whole picture, and use the summary to strengthen or weaken that channel.

57
58    def __init__(self, state: State, prefix: str) -> None:
59        super().__init__()
60        channels, reduced = state[prefix + "fc2.weight"].shape[0], state[prefix + "fc1.weight"].shape[0]
61        self.fc1, self.bn1 = nn.Conv2d(channels, reduced, 1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(reduced)
62        self.fc2, self.bn2 = nn.Conv2d(reduced, channels, 1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(channels)

Its size comes from the weights: the number of channels, and the smaller number it squeezes them through. Two 1 × 1 convolutions, each with batch normalisation.

63
64    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
65        summary = x.mean(dim=(2, 3), keepdim=True)
66        return x * torch.sigmoid(self.bn2(self.fc2(torch.relu(self.bn1(self.fc1(summary))))))

The summary: each channel's average over the picture (mean over height and width). Squeeze it, relu, expand it, and turn it into weights from 0 to 1 (sigmoid); multiply each channel by its weight.

67
68
69class DepthWise(nn.Module):
70    """Expand (1 x 1), filter each channel on its own (3 x 3), project back (1 x 1); optionally add the input back."""

DepthWise — the network's main building block, as the docstring says: expand with a 1 × 1 convolution, filter each channel on its own with a 3 × 3, project back with a 1 × 1, and optionally add the input back on (a residual connection).

71
72    def __init__(self, state: State, prefix: str, residual: bool) -> None:
73        super().__init__()
74        self.conv = ConvBlock(state[prefix + "conv.conv.weight"], 1, True)
75        stride = 2 if prefix + "conv_dw" in HALVING else 1
76        self.conv_dw = ConvBlock(state[prefix + "conv_dw.conv.weight"], stride, True)
77        self.project = ConvBlock(state[prefix + "project.conv.weight"], 1, False)

The three convolutions, sized from their weights; the filtering one halves the picture if its layer is in HALVING.

78        has_se = prefix + "se_module.fc1.weight" in state
79        self.se_module = Squeeze(state, prefix + "se_module.") if has_se else None

A squeeze-and-excitation part, only where the weights have one.

80        self.residual = residual

Whether to add the input back.

81
82    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
83        y = self.project(self.conv_dw(self.conv(x)))
84        if self.se_module is not None:
85            y = self.se_module(y)
86        result: torch.Tensor = x + y if self.residual else y
87        return result

Run the three, the squeeze-and-excitation if any, and add the input back when residual. (result: torch.Tensor gives the type checker the type that PyTorch leaves open.)

88
89
90class Stage(nn.Module):
91    """A run of residual blocks, as many as the weights hold."""

Stage — a run of residual blocks, as many as the weights hold.

92
93    def __init__(self, state: State, prefix: str) -> None:
94        super().__init__()
95        count = len({key.split(".")[2] for key in state if key.startswith(prefix + "model.")})
96        self.model = nn.Sequential(*[DepthWise(state, f"{prefix}model.{i}.", True) for i in range(count)])

Count the blocks: the distinct numbers in names like conv_3.model.2.…. Then build that many residual DepthWise blocks, in order, as one nn.Sequential.

97
98    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
99        result: torch.Tensor = self.model(x)
100        return result

Run them in turn.

101
102
103class MiniFASNet(nn.Module):
104    """Pixels (blue-green-red, 0-255, 80 x 80) in; probabilities of the three classes out (index 1: a real face)."""

MiniFASNet — the whole network, as the docstring says: pixels in (blue-green-red, 0–255, 80 × 80); the three classes' probabilities out, index 1 being a real face.

105
106    def __init__(self, state: State) -> None:
107        super().__init__()
108        self.conv1 = ConvBlock(state["conv1.conv.weight"], 2, True)
109        self.conv2_dw = ConvBlock(state["conv2_dw.conv.weight"], 1, True)
110        self.conv_23 = DepthWise(state, "conv_23.", False)
111        self.conv_3 = Stage(state, "conv_3.")
112        self.conv_34 = DepthWise(state, "conv_34.", False)
113        self.conv_4 = Stage(state, "conv_4.")
114        self.conv_45 = DepthWise(state, "conv_45.", False)
115        self.conv_5 = Stage(state, "conv_5.")
116        self.conv_6_sep = ConvBlock(state["conv_6_sep.conv.weight"], 1, True)
117        self.conv_6_dw = ConvBlock(state["conv_6_dw.conv.weight"], 1, False)

Its layers, in order, each built from its stored weights: a halving convolution, a depthwise one, then halving blocks and stages taking the picture down to 5 × 5, and a final pair that turns it into 512 numbers.

118        embedding, features = state["linear.weight"].shape
119        self.linear = nn.Linear(features, embedding, bias=False)
120        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(embedding)
121        self.prob = nn.Linear(embedding, state["prob.weight"].shape[0], bias=False)

Then a linear layer down to an embedding (128 numbers), batch normalisation, and the final linear layer to the three classes. Their sizes come from the weights' shapes.

122
123    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
124        for stage in (self.conv1, self.conv2_dw, self.conv_23, self.conv_3, self.conv_34, self.conv_4, self.conv_45):
125            x = stage(x)
126        x = self.conv_6_dw(self.conv_6_sep(self.conv_5(x)))
127        return torch.softmax(self.prob(self.bn(self.linear(x.flatten(1)))), dim=1)

Run everything in order; flatten the 512 × 1 × 1 result into a row; and turn the three scores into probabilities with softmax — the probabilities are built into the model, so the ONNX file returns them directly.

128
129
130def load(path: Path) -> MiniFASNet:
131    raw = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)

load — read a weights file as plain tensors only (weights_only=True), on the processor.

132    # The weights were saved from a multi-GPU wrapper, which prefixes every name with "module.".
133    state = {name.removeprefix("module."): tensor for name, tensor in raw.items()}

As the comment says, the weights were saved from a multi-GPU wrapper that prefixes every name with module.; remove it.

134    model = MiniFASNet(state)
135    model.load_state_dict(state, strict=True)
136    return model.eval()

Build the network from the weights' shapes, load every weight strictly — the proof that the rebuild is exact — and switch to evaluation mode (eval), which fixes batch normalisation to its learned averages.

137
138
139def convert(model: MiniFASNet, target: Path) -> None:
140    example = torch.zeros(1, 3, SIZE, SIZE)
141    program = torch.onnx.export(
142        model, (example,), input_names=["pixels"], output_names=["probabilities"], dynamo=True, verbose=False
143    )
144    if program is None:
145        raise RuntimeError("the ONNX exporter returned nothing")
146    program.save(str(target), external_data=False)

convert — export to ONNX, as in Phase 2's export (export.py): one example input of the right shape, named input and output, the newer exporter (dynamo=True), and everything saved in one file.

147
148
149def parity(model: MiniFASNet, target: Path, patches: list[np.ndarray]) -> float:
150    session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(str(target), providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])

parity — run the ONNX file with ONNX Runtime on some crops, and compare with PyTorch.

151    gaps = []
152    for patch in patches:
153        pixels = np.ascontiguousarray(patch.astype(np.float32).transpose(2, 0, 1)[None])
154        with torch.no_grad():
155            reference = model(torch.from_numpy(pixels)).numpy()
156        gaps.append(float(np.abs(reference - session.run(None, {"pixels": pixels})[0]).max()))

For each crop: the same pixels for both, as the networks expect them; the largest difference between the two answers.

157    return max(gaps)

The largest difference over all crops.

158
159
160def main() -> int:
161    image = decode_image((ROOT / "libs" / "vision" / "tests" / "fixtures" / "astronaut.jpg").read_bytes())
162    face = FaceDetector(THIRD_PARTY / "face_detection_yunet_2023mar.onnx").detect(image)[0]

main — a real crop to compare on: the test portrait's face.

163    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
164    ok = True

A seeded random generator for extra test crops, and whether everything passed so far.

165    for weights, onnx_file, scale in MODELS:
166        model = load(THIRD_PARTY / weights)
167        convert(model, THIRD_PARTY / onnx_file)

For each network: load it strictly and convert it.

168        patches = [crop(image, face.box, scale)] + [
169            rng.integers(0, 256, (SIZE, SIZE, 3), dtype=np.uint8) for _ in range(8)
170        ]

The comparison crops: the portrait's face at the network's crop size, and eight crops of random noise — the answers must agree on anything, not just faces.

171        gap = parity(model, THIRD_PARTY / onnx_file, patches)
172        ok = ok and gap <= TOLERANCE
173        print(f"{onnx_file}: largest probability gap {gap:.2e} (tolerance {TOLERANCE:.0e})")

Compare, remember whether it passed, and print the result. On the first conversion the gaps were 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ and 5.6 × 10⁻⁸: the same answers.

174    return 0 if ok else 1

Exit with 1 if either comparison failed.

175
176
177if __name__ == "__main__":
178    sys.exit(main())

Run main when the file is run as a program.

pipeline.py collects what was seen in each photo and runs the checks; main.py and settings.py load the new models and add the labels test mode (§5.3.5).

5.3.4 The decision, and the red team

The decision engine (services/api/src/dwarpal_api/domain/decision.py) now checks liveness after quality and before age: a dark photo should be told to find light, not be counted as a liveness failure. A failed pose challenge gets one retry, then the session is rejected; signs of injection — or an anti-spoofing verdict below 0.5 — send even a clear adult to a stronger check. A live session is decided only on full evidence: never on the labels test mode, and never without the anti-spoofing networks' verdict. Their files are made locally from pinned weights, so a service could start without them; it then reports antispoof: missing on /readyz, and the API retries live attempts with liveness_unavailable rather than decide without its strongest layer. Outward reasons never say which check fired (the domain tests prove it). The detail is stored with the attempt, for the operator, and liveness-report summarises it (cli.py).

Per-device budgets stop endless trial and error. Each session already had a budget of challenges; a person testing photo after photo could simply start new sessions. Now each device (the page's random ID) may take 30 challenges per project an hour, and each network address 120, counted in Valkey whatever the session (app/verification.py, adapters/store.py). Past that, the page asks the person to wait a while.

The red-team tests (services/api/tests/test_api.py) attack the running system through its real API:

Attack Result
A printed photo (the still test portrait, measured from the images) retry, then reject
Poses labelled in the wrong order retry liveness_check_failed
A browser claiming an easier challenge of its own ignored: judged against the issued one
A reused challenge (Phase 1) refused, 409 challenge_invalid
Automation, and a virtual camera step up liveness_uncertain

5.3.5 The labels test mode

The end-to-end test's fake camera plays a still portrait (§5.1.5). It can't turn its head — so, measured honestly, it fails every pose challenge, as a photo should. To keep testing the whole journey, the inference service has a test mode, DWARPAL_INFERENCE_LIVENESS=labels, in which the pose check believes the photos' labels instead of measuring them.

Three locks keep it out of real use: the inference service refuses to start in that mode unless it uses the stand-in age model; every result says where its evidence came from (evidence: "labels"); and the API refuses that evidence for any live session. Labels mode still catches a wrong order, a missing baseline and a claimed challenge — the red-team tests above run in it, except the printed photo, which uses real measurement.

Real world — what Phase 3 found

  • A synthetic head turn doesn't fool the detector. To test turns without a person, we warped the test portrait in 2-D and in a simple 3-D projection to look turned. YuNet's sideways ratio never rose above 0.16 — far short of the 0.35 a turn needs. Good news for security (a flat picture, bent, doesn't look like a turned head); for testing, it meant the labels mode, and a real person.
  • The colour layer lit only the card at first. The card's blurred background made it the frame of reference for the full-screen layer. Drawing the layer straight into the page's body fixed it (see the comment above the portal in camera-view.tsx).
  • The end-to-end journey still passes, now with the colours, three or four pose prompts that each wait out their 6 seconds (a still portrait never turns), a pass for the 30-year-old stand-in, and leaving the cellar again: about a minute for the whole story.

5.3.6 Measuring on genuine attempts

Every liveness check turns away some honest people, so the roadmap's exit asks for that false-reject rate to be measured. The project's owner — a 21-year-old adult — made genuine attempts on the local stack with real measurement (DWARPAL_INFERENCE_LIVENESS=images) and the stand-in age model, so that only liveness was under test. Nothing was stored but numbers; liveness-report summarised each round, and the design changed after each one:

Round What the check did Result What the numbers showed
1 Fixed limits: turn yaw 0.35, look-up pitch 0.38 0 of 11 passed Turns reached about 0.25–0.35; the prompt said "a little"
2 Poses measured from the person's own frontal angles (turn 0.18, look-up 0.06); reach recorded 1 of 6 Turns 0.16–0.28; look-up often about 0 — the photo was taken before or after the chin was up
3 A meter on the page and three photos per pose 0 of 6 measurable Every photo held a "second face": a small, steady face-like shape beside the owner, about a seventh of the real face's size
4 Count people, not detections (quality.py) 8 of 12 Turns 0.23–0.66, every time; all four failures were look-up
5 3 or 4 poses, at most one look-up; look-up limit 0.03 5 of 8 Turns 22 of 22, lowest 0.29; look-up still failed 3 of 8 (−0.03 to 0.02)
6 Look-up recorded only; the turns decide not re-tested live On round 5's numbers, all 8 attempts pass

Two lessons came out of it. First, a turn is a strong, measurable proof: genuine turns cleared the limit by a wide margin every time, while a flat photo — turned or tilted — barely moves the nose against the eyes. Looking up is measured poorly by five landmarks, so it stays in the challenge (it makes the order harder to predict, and its reach is recorded for later), but it no longer decides. Second, a detector sees faces where people don't: something in the owner's room scored 0.85 as a face in every photo, and every attempt failed until the quality check learned to ignore detections that are small, faint or inside the main face.

For repeated testing, the demo shop gained a Leave the cellar button that forgets the pass — otherwise the shop's 30-minute pass lets the tester straight back in, and no new check is made.

Try it yourself

After a series of attempts, summarise everything since a given time:

uv run --package dwarpal-api python -m dwarpal_api.cli liveness-report --since 2026-10-17T12:00

It prints the outcomes, how many pose challenges passed — and so the false-reject rate, if every attempt was genuine — the most common problems, which measurement judged the poses, how far each pose got (median and lowest), the injection signs, the presentation evidence (real-face chance, screen pattern, poses caught mid-turn), and the light correlations.

5.3.7 The red team — the owner attacks their own system

With the genuine false-reject rate under control, the owner turned attacker, and a server-side face mesh had made looking up measurable (genuine chins now measured 0.11–0.38). Two findings came first, both about the page:

  • Photos darkened by the screen's blue were set aside by the quality check, leaving the light check with nothing to measure. Liveness now looks at every photo of one person; only the age needs flawless ones.
  • Encoding a photo took about a second on a busy laptop, and the page stamped each photo's time after encoding: photos landed in the wrong colours, and later colours slid out of their timetable. Photos are now copied instantly, stamped at that moment, and encoded after the challenge.

Then the attacks. The owner held their phone up to the webcam, showing selfies of themselves posed in each direction, swiping to whichever one the prompt asked for — and later a video of themselves turning, paused and skipped to match the prompts:

Defences in place Genuine attempts Attacks that reached the cellar What the numbers showed
Poses, light recorded passed posed selfies: 5 of 10 attempts A photo of a turned head is a turned head: the pose check alone can't tell
+ light decides (≥ 0.5), a large or central second face counts, hands decide 0 of 3 passed 0 of 5 Light stopped 3 attacks but also 2 genuine attempts (r 0.34, 0.38); the owner peeking from behind the phone was caught as a second face; the hand detector missed the holding hands and once saw a hand that wasn't there
+ MiniFASNet decides (≥ 0.5), light and hands record only 5 of 6 (one stepped up by light, before it was demoted) 0 of 7 (3 selfie, 4 video) Real faces 0.94–0.995; phone photos and videos 0.006–0.195

The anti-spoofing networks are the layer that finally separated the two — by a margin wide enough to trust, where light (real faces −0.25 to 0.99) never could. Two more measures point the same way and are recorded for later: the screen pattern (real faces 0.99–1.14, phone 1.16–1.31) and whether each pose was caught mid-turn (real heads 19 of 19, attacks 5 of 23).

Honest limitation

Phase 3 is not finished against its exit criteria. Every number here comes from one person, one laptop camera and one room, over a few dozen attempts: the false-reject rate and the anti-spoofing margin need more people, cameras, rooms and attack media before they can be trusted. MiniFASNet was trained by someone else on data we haven't seen, so its behaviour on other faces and skin tones is unmeasured — the fairness questions of §2.16 apply to it too. The light, the screen pattern, the mid-turn photos, the hand detector and looking up are recorded but not used. An attacker who drives a fake camera directly (no phone, no screen in the picture) or uses a convincing real-time deepfake was not tested. And the design can't stop an adult who does the check for a child.

Part X — How this book is built

This part is placed near the end, but you can read it any time. It shows the line-by-line format used for the whole project. And it is the first real code in the project, so it is explained exactly like everything else will be.

X.1 Why a program builds this book

The book you are reading is a single HTML file. We could have typed that HTML by hand, but three problems would appear quickly:

  1. It would be huge and painful to edit. Thousands of lines of HTML tags around every sentence.
  2. It would drift away from the code. When a code file changes, nothing would tell us that its explanation is now wrong.
  3. "Every line is explained" would be a promise nobody could check.

So the book is generated. We write chapters in a simple text format (Markdown) and explanations in small walkthrough files. A Python program, build.py, then assembles them into the HTML file. While doing so it checks the coverage and freshness of every explanation.

Explain like I'm six

Instead of hand-copying a whole book every time one page changes, you keep each page separately and let a machine bind them into a book. The machine also checks each page against the thing it describes and puts a red sticker on any page that's out of date.

X.2 The pieces

All of these live in docs/zero_to_hero/:

File or folder What it is
book.toml The settings: the book's title, the order of the chapters, and which project files must be explained
chapters/*.md The chapters, written in Markdown
walkthroughs/…/*.md One explanation file per code file, mirroring the project's folders. The explanation of docs/zero_to_hero/build.py lives at walkthroughs/docs/zero_to_hero/build.py.md
abbreviations.md Short definitions that appear when you hover over words like API
template.html The empty "shell" of the page — styles, sidebar, buttons — with blanks for the content
build.py The program that puts it all together
tests/test_build.py Automatic tests for build.py (the checker is itself checked)
.snapshots/… A copy of each source file as it was when its walkthrough was last stamped. Used to move notes when code changes (§X.6)
zero_to_hero.html The result — the book you are reading

The two libraries the builder needs (Python-Markdown and Pygments) are pinned in the project's root pyproject.toml, in a group called docs (§5.0.2). In the very first version of the book they were listed in a separate requirements.txt. That file was removed when the project gained its uv workspace, so the versions are written in exactly one place.

X.3 Markdown in sixty seconds

Markdown is a way of writing formatted text using ordinary symbols. A converter turns it into HTML.

You write You get
# Title A big heading (## smaller, ### smaller still)
**bold** and *italic* bold and italic
`code` code
- item on separate lines A bulleted list
1. step on separate lines A numbered list
[text](https://example.com) A link
Lines with vertical bars (|) between cells A table (like this one)
Three back-ticks, a language name, the code, three back-ticks A highlighted code block
!!! kid "Title" followed by indented lines One of the coloured boxes (an admonition)

X.4 How a walkthrough file works

A walkthrough file has three parts.

1. A header between two lines of three dashes, recording the code file's fingerprint at the moment it was explained:

---
fingerprint: 3f9a1c0be27d4e51
---

2. An introduction — ordinary Markdown describing the whole file.

3. Notes. Each note starts with a line containing two @ signs and a line number (like @@ 12) or a range (like @@ 12-14). The explanation of those lines follows in Markdown:

@@ 1
This line ...

@@ 2-4
These three lines ...

Inside a chapter, a line that contains only the word !walk followed by a file path tells the builder: "put the line-by-line walkthrough of this file here". A line containing only !ledger inserts the coverage table.

X.5 Fingerprints

How can a program notice that a file changed since it was explained? It can't keep a copy of every old version. Instead it keeps a fingerprint.

Explain like I'm six — the magic blender

Imagine a magic blender. You drop in any amount of text — one word or a whole book — and it always pours out a short code like 3f9a1c0be27d4e51. Two magic rules:

  • the same text always gives the same code;
  • change even one letter, and the code comes out completely different.

So to know whether a file changed, you don't need the old file — only the old code.

The blender is a real algorithm called SHA-256, a cryptographic hash function used everywhere in computer security, including in Git and HTTPS certificates. SHA-256 produces 64 hexadecimal characters (digits 0–9 and letters a–f). We keep the first 16. That is still 2⁶⁴ ≈ 18 quintillion possibilities — far more than enough to notice an edit.

X.6 Coverage and the ledger

For each code file the builder:

  1. counts the non-blank lines (blank lines have nothing to explain);
  2. marks the lines covered by a note that has real text — a note that is empty, or still says TODO, does not count;
  3. shows any uncovered line in the book with a red bar and the words "Not explained yet";
  4. compares the recorded fingerprint with a fresh one, and shows a red "code changed since explained" badge if they differ.

Then it walks the whole project folder, finds every code file, and prints the Coverage ledger. Files with no walkthrough at all appear there as not explained. Nothing can hide.

When code changes: re-anchoring

Notes are pinned to line numbers. Add one line at the top of a file and every note below it now points one line too high. In the first days of this book, fixing that meant renumbering notes by hand — slow and error-prone.

So the builder learned a trick. Whenever a walkthrough is stamped or re-anchored, the builder also saves a snapshot: a copy of the source file exactly as the walkthrough's line numbers describe it. Later, --reanchor compares the snapshot with the current file, works out where every line has gone, and then moves the snapshot forward:

  • a note whose lines are all unchanged simply moves with them — no human needed;
  • a note whose lines were edited moves to the new code that replaced them, and its text is prefixed with TODO(review). It then counts as not explained until someone re-reads it and removes the prefix;
  • a note whose lines were deleted is dropped, and the command prints what was dropped.

Explain like I'm six — seats in a theatre

Imagine a theatre where every seat has a name card. The theatre adds two new rows at the front. Every old seat now has a new number, but the people haven't changed — so you move each name card to its person's new seat number. If someone swapped seats with a stranger, you put a sticky note on their card: "please check this one".

How does the builder know which lines are "the same"? Python's built-in difflib module finds the longest runs of lines that appear in both versions, in the same order — the same idea behind the "diff" view of any code-review tool. It describes the change as a list of operations: these lines are equal, these were replaced, these deleted, these inserted. Inside a replaced block, the old and new lines are lined up side by side, so an edit that keeps the number of lines keeps every note exactly in place.

Key idea

Moving notes is automatic. Approving them is not: only a person can confirm that an explanation still matches the code. That is why --reanchor never stamps, and why changed notes are marked TODO(review).

The two records kept for each file have different jobs. The snapshot says which version of the code the line numbers refer to. The fingerprint says which version a person last approved.

Real world — the checker had a bug, and its tests caught the fix

During Phase 1, re-anchoring the same file twice without stamping in between scrambled its notes. The snapshot was only saved by --stamp, so the second run compared the wrong two versions. The fix: --reanchor now moves the snapshot forward too. A new test in tests/test_build.py re-anchors twice in a row, so the bug can't quietly return.

X.7 Building the book yourself

Try it yourself

With uv installed (§4.2), open a terminal in the project folder and run:

  1. uv sync — installs Python 3.13 and every tool the project needs (only needed once).
  2. uv run tasks.py book — builds the book in strict mode and prints a one-line summary.

Then open docs/zero_to_hero/zero_to_hero.html in any browser.

Strict mode makes the builder fail if anything is unexplained or stale. The project's automatic checks (CI, §4.6) run exactly this on every change, so the book can never fall behind the code.

Three helper commands keep walkthroughs in step with the code:

  • build.py --new path/to/file.py creates a walkthrough skeleton with an empty TODO note for every non-blank line, and a first snapshot;
  • build.py --reanchor path/to/file.py moves the notes to follow edits made since the last snapshot (§X.6);
  • build.py --stamp path/to/file.py records the file's current fingerprint and snapshot, after its explanations have been reviewed.

X.8 Python words you'll meet in build.py

build.py is the first Python program in this project. Its walkthrough explains every line, but a few words come up again and again, so here they are first.

Word Meaning Tiny example
variable A name that refers to a value title = "Dwarpal"
string (str) Text, in quotes "hello"
integer (int), float Whole numbers; numbers with a decimal point 42, 98.5
boolean (bool) True or False stale = False
None "Nothing here" result = None
list An ordered, changeable collection ["a", "b"]
tuple An ordered collection that can't be changed (3, 7)
dict Labelled values, looked up by key {"title": "Dwarpal"}
set A collection with no duplicates and no order; fast "is it in here?" checks {1, 2, 3}
function (def) A named, reusable recipe. It takes inputs (parameters) and gives back an output (return) def double(x): return x * 2
class A blueprint for making objects that bundle data and functions together. Functions inside a class are called methods class Book: ...
object / instance One thing made from a class book = Book(config)
self Inside a method, "the object this method belongs to" self.title
module / import A file of Python code; import brings another module's tools into this file import re
if / elif / else Decisions if age >= 18: ...
for loop Repeat something for each item in a collection for line in lines: ...
comprehension A one-line way to build a list, set or dict from a loop [x * 2 for x in numbers]
f-string A string with values slotted in, marked by f before the quote f"{count} lines"
type hint A label saying what kind of value is expected. Python itself ignores it; tools and humans use it def read_text(path: Path) -> str:
exception An error signal that stops the normal flow; try/except catches it try: ... except ClassNotFound: ...
decorator A line starting with @ that wraps or modifies the function or class below it @dataclass
indentation Python uses spaces at the start of a line to show what belongs inside what. Four spaces = one level (everywhere)

Careful — indentation is not decoration in Python

In many languages spacing is just for looks. In Python, indentation is part of the meaning: the lines indented under an if are the lines that run only when the condition is true. Get it wrong and the program means something different, or refuses to run.

X.9 The code, line by line

X.9.1 book.toml — the settings

docs/zero_to_hero/book.toml32 lines · 100% explained

book.toml holds the book's settings. Keeping settings in a separate file, rather than inside build.py, means you can add a chapter or change the title without touching any program code. "Separate the what from the how" is one of the oldest good habits in software.

The file is written in TOML ("Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language"):

  • name = value sets a value;
  • text goes in double quotes;
  • lists go in square brackets;
  • a line like [coverage] starts a named group of settings, which TOML calls a table.

Python reads TOML with its built-in tomllib.

Alternatives considered

  • JSON doesn't allow comments and is fussy about commas.
  • YAML has surprising rules: the unquoted word no can turn into false.

TOML is what Python's own packaging uses (pyproject.toml), so it is the natural choice for a Python tool.

1title = "Dwarpal — Zero to Hero"

title = "Dwarpal — Zero to Hero" is the book's title, shown in the browser tab and the sidebar. The — survives because every file is read and written as UTF-8 (§0.2).

2subtitle = "Building a privacy-first AI age-assurance system, starting from absolutely nothing"

subtitle = … is a one-line description, printed in the footer.

3output = "zero_to_hero.html"

output = "zero_to_hero.html" is the name of the file build.py creates, next to build.py in docs/zero_to_hero/, as the project owner asked.

4abbreviations = "abbreviations.md"

abbreviations = "abbreviations.md" is the file of hover definitions, which is attached to every chapter and walkthrough note when it is converted.

5chapters = [
6  "chapters/00_front_matter.md",
7  "chapters/01_part0_basics.md",
8  "chapters/02_part1_problem.md",
9  "chapters/03_part2_ai.md",
10  "chapters/04_part3_thinking.md",
11  "chapters/05_part4_tools.md",
12  "chapters/06_part5_build.md",
13  "chapters/07_part5_phase1.md",
14  "chapters/08_part5_phase2.md",
15  "chapters/09_part5_phase3.md",
16  "chapters/90_how_this_book_is_built.md",
17  "chapters/98_ledger.md",
18  "chapters/99_glossary.md",
19]

chapters = [ … ] is the reading order of the book. Each line inside the brackets is one chapter file, and the order here is the order in the book. The numbers at the start of the file names only keep the folder tidy.

The list grows as the project does:

  • Phase 0 added Part 4 (the tools) and Part 5 (building it, file by file);
  • Phase 1 added 07_part5_phase1.md, the walking skeleton's chapter. Each phase gets its own chapter file, so no single file grows unmanageably long.

Try it yourself

Move the 99_glossary.md line to the top and run uv run tasks.py book: the glossary becomes the first chapter. Move it back afterwards.

Phase 3 added 09_part5_phase3.md: liveness and anti-spoofing (§5.3).

20
21[coverage]

[coverage] starts the group of settings for the coverage check — which project files must have a line-by-line explanation. In Python this group is read as config["coverage"].

22include = [
23  "**/*.py", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", "**/*.js", "**/*.mjs", "**/*.css", "**/*.html",
24  "**/*.toml", "**/*.yaml", "**/*.yml", "**/*.json", "**/*.sql", "**/*.sh", "**/*.ps1",
25  "**/*.txt", "**/Dockerfile", "**/Caddyfile", "**/.env.example",
26  "**/.gitignore", "**/.gitattributes", "**/.editorconfig", "**/.python-version", "**/*.mako",
27]

include = [ … ] lists glob patterns for files that count as code. In a glob, * means "any characters within one name", and ** means "any number of folders, including none". The patterns cover:

  • Python (.py);
  • TypeScript and JavaScript (.ts, .tsx, .js, .mjs);
  • styles (.css) and web pages (.html);
  • settings files (.toml, .yaml, .yml, .json);
  • database scripts (.sql) and shell scripts (.sh, .ps1);
  • text lists (.txt);
  • special files without extensions: Dockerfile, Caddyfile, .env.example;
  • four "dotfiles" that change how tools treat the whole project — .gitignore, .gitattributes, .editorconfig, .python-version (added in Phase 0);
  • Mako templates (.mako, added in Phase 1). Alembic uses one as the blueprint for every new database migration (§4.10). A file that shapes other code is code too, so it gets explained.

Markdown (.md) is deliberately not included: it is prose, not code.

28exclude = ["docs/zero_to_hero/zero_to_hero.html", "**/pnpm-lock.yaml", "**/package-lock.json", "**/uv.lock", "**/next-env.d.ts", "apps/web/public/mediapipe/**"]

exclude = [ … ] lists patterns that are removed even if they matched include:

  • the generated book itself — explaining the explainer's output would loop forever;
  • lockfiles (pnpm-lock.yaml, package-lock.json, uv.lock) — thousands of machine-written lines. §0.17 explains what they are instead;
  • next-env.d.ts — a file Next.js writes for itself into each web app, and which is never committed (added in Phase 1, see .gitignore).

apps/web/public/mediapipe/** (added in Phase 3) — MediaPipe's WebAssembly loaders, copied in before each build: tens of thousands of lines of someone else's generated code.

29prune = [
30  ".git", ".venv", "node_modules", "__pycache__", ".next", ".turbo", "dist",
31  ".datasets", ".runs", "mlruns", ".mypy_cache", ".ruff_cache", ".pytest_cache", ".hypothesis", ".snapshots", ".claude", "test-results", "playwright-report",
32]

prune = [ … ] lists folder names the scanner never enters, because they hold things we didn't write:

  • Git's own history (.git);
  • installed libraries (.venv, node_modules);
  • tool caches (__pycache__, .mypy_cache, .ruff_cache, .pytest_cache, and Hypothesis's .hypothesis);
  • build outputs (.next, .turbo, dist);
  • downloaded training data (.datasets);
  • training runs and experiment logs (.runs, mlruns);
  • the builder's own snapshots (.snapshots) — copies of code, which would otherwise be counted twice;
  • local AI-assistant settings (.claude), which are not part of the project and are never committed (see .gitignore);
  • the end-to-end tests' results (test-results, playwright-report), recreated on every run (added in Phase 1).

Careful — a loophole we closed

An earlier version also pruned folders called data and build. That was a hidden loophole: a real code folder named, say, ml/data/ would silently escape the check. Only names that are always generated or downloaded are pruned. That is also why the training data folder is deliberately called .datasets.

X.9.2 build.py — the book binder

docs/zero_to_hero/build.py413 lines · 100% explained

build.py is the book binder. It reads the settings, chapters, walkthroughs and template, and writes one finished HTML file. It also checks that every code line in the project has an explanation that is still up to date, and it keeps explanations attached to the right lines when code changes.

The file has four regions, top to bottom:

  1. Preparation (lines 1–42): a description, the tools it borrows (imports) and fixed settings (constants).
  2. Small helpers (lines 45–197): data containers, and short functions that each do one job. Most of them are pure — they only turn inputs into outputs, without touching files — which makes them easy to test (see tests/test_build.py, §5.0.7).
  3. The Book class (lines 200–343): the main machine. It renders walkthroughs, scans the project, builds the ledger and assembles the page.
  4. Commands (lines 346–401): the helper commands --new, --stamp and --reanchor, and main(), which decides what to do when you run the file.

Explain like I'm six

Think of a school project folder. build.py collects all the loose pages and checks that each one has a matching explanation. It puts a red sticker on any page that is out of date. Then it slides everything into a nice binder cover (the template) and adds a checklist page at the back (the ledger). And if someone adds new pages in the middle, it moves every sticky note to follow its page.

1"""Build the Zero-to-Hero book.
2
3Markdown chapters plus line-by-line walkthroughs of the project's source files
4are turned into ONE self-contained HTML file.
5
6    python build.py                  build the book
7    python build.py --strict         build, then fail if any source line is unexplained or stale
8    python build.py --new PATH       write a walkthrough skeleton for a source file
9    python build.py --stamp PATH     after reviewing a walkthrough, record PATH's fingerprint and a snapshot
10    python build.py --reanchor PATH  move a walkthrough's line numbers to follow edits made since its last snapshot
11"""

The docstring. Text between triple quotes (""") at the very top of a file is that file's docstring: a description for humans. Python stores it but does not run it. It explains the purpose in two sentences, then shows the five ways to run the program. PATH is a placeholder meaning "put a file path here".

12
13from __future__ import annotations

from __future__ import annotations makes Python treat every type hint in this file (labels like -> str or Note | None) as plain text that is never evaluated when the file loads. Python 3.14 already behaves this way by default. The line keeps the behaviour identical on Python 3.13, which the project uses, and costs nothing.

14
15import argparse

import argparse brings in Python's built-in argument parser. It reads the extra words typed after the program name on the command line (like --strict), checks them, and prints a help page for --help. It is used in main().

16import difflib

import difflib brings in Python's built-in tools for comparing sequences — the same idea as the "diff" view in code-review tools. It is used by line_mapping (line 148) to work out where lines moved after an edit.

17import hashlib

import hashlib brings in Python's collection of hash functions, including SHA-256, the "magic blender" that makes fingerprints (§X.5).

18import html

import html gives two small tools for HTML text:

  • html.escape turns characters that mean something in HTML (<, >, &, quotes) into safe codes, so text is shown rather than treated as tags;
  • html.unescape does the reverse.
19import os

import os gives tools for talking to the operating system. We use os.walk, which visits every folder and file under a starting folder.

20import re

import re gives regular expressions: a mini-language for describing text patterns. It is used for the @@ note markers, the !walk directives and the fingerprint line.

21import sys

import sys gives access to the running Python itself. We use sys.exit on the last line to hand an exit code back to whoever started the program: 0 for success, 1 for failure.

22import tomllib

import tomllib is Python's built-in reader for TOML files, used to read book.toml.

23from dataclasses import dataclass

from dataclasses import dataclass brings in one specific tool, the @dataclass decorator. from X import Y takes just Y out of module X.

24from datetime import UTC, datetime

from datetime import UTC, datetime brings in tools for dates and times. UTC is Coordinated Universal Time. We stamp the book with its build time in UTC, so the stamp means the same thing everywhere.

The very first version of this line imported timezone and wrote timezone.utc. The Ruff linter (§4.3) pointed out that modern Python offers the shorter alias UTC, so the line was updated.

25from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath:

  • Path represents a file or folder location as an object. It has useful abilities (.read_bytes(), .is_file(), .parent, joining with /) and handles Windows \ and Linux / correctly.
  • PurePosixPath is a path that always uses forward slashes and never touches the disk. We use it for pattern matching that must behave the same on every operating system.
26from typing import Any

from typing import Any imports the special type Any, meaning "a value of any kind". The settings read from book.toml mix text, lists and nested tables, so their type is "a dict whose keys are strings and whose values could be anything": dict[str, Any].

The type checker (mypy, §4.3) insisted on that precise label.

27
28import markdown

import markdown imports Python-Markdown, pinned in the project's pyproject.toml (§5.0.2). This is the first import that isn't built into Python, so it sits in its own group after a blank line. Standard library first, third-party second is a Python style rule that Ruff enforces.

29from pygments import highlight

from pygments import highlight imports the main function of Pygments. You give it source code, a lexer (which knows the language) and a formatter (which knows the output format), and it gives back highlighted text.

30from pygments.formatters import HtmlFormatter

from pygments.formatters import HtmlFormatter imports the formatter that produces HTML, such as <span class="k">def</span>.

31from pygments.lexers import TextLexer, get_lexer_for_filename

from pygments.lexers import TextLexer, get_lexer_for_filename — a lexer chops code into labelled pieces called tokens (this is a keyword, this is a string…).

  • get_lexer_for_filename picks the right lexer from a file name.
  • TextLexer is the fallback for files Pygments doesn't recognise.
32from pygments.util import ClassNotFound

from pygments.util import ClassNotFound imports the exception (error signal) Pygments raises when it has no lexer for a file name. We need its name so we can catch it on line 192.

33
34BOOK_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

BOOK_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent answers "where is this book folder?":

  • __file__ is the path of the file being run;
  • .resolve() makes it a full, absolute path;
  • .parent steps up to the folder containing it: …/docs/zero_to_hero.

Names in CAPITALS are constants: set once, never changed.

Why not just use the current folder?

You might run build.py from anywhere — the project root, the book folder, an automated test machine. Working out locations from __file__ makes the program find its files no matter where it was started.

35REPO_ROOT = BOOK_DIR.parents[1]

REPO_ROOT = BOOK_DIR.parents[1] — .parents is the chain of folders above a path: [0] is docs, and [1] is the project root. Every project-relative path, like docs/zero_to_hero/build.py, is measured from here.

36WALK_DIR = BOOK_DIR / "walkthroughs"

WALK_DIR = BOOK_DIR / "walkthroughs" — with Path objects, / means join paths, not divide. This is the folder holding every walkthrough file.

37SNAP_DIR = BOOK_DIR / ".snapshots"

SNAP_DIR = BOOK_DIR / ".snapshots" — the folder holding a snapshot (an exact copy) of each source file as it was when its walkthrough was last stamped. The name starts with a dot to mark it as a tool's private folder.
