It is deliberately excluded from coverage scans, linting and type checking (book.toml, pyproject.toml), because it contains copies of code, not code.

38NOTE_MARK = re.compile(r"^@@ *(\d+)(?: *- *(\d+))? *$")

NOTE_MARK = re.compile(r"^@@ *(\d+)(?: *- *(\d+))? *$") is the pattern that recognises a note marker line, such as @@ 12 or @@ 12-14. re.compile prepares the pattern once for fast reuse. The r makes a raw string, which keeps backslashes as typed.

Piece Means
^ the start of the line
@@ two literal @ signs
* zero or more spaces
(\d+) one or more digits, captured as group 1 (the start line)
(?: … )? an optional, uncaptured group containing…
*- *(\d+) …a dash with optional spaces, and more digits captured as group 2 (the end line)
*$ optional trailing spaces, then the end of the line 
39DIRECTIVE = re.compile(r"^!(walk|ledger)(?: +(\S+))? *$", re.MULTILINE)

DIRECTIVE = re.compile(…, re.MULTILINE) is the pattern for chapter directives such as !walk docs/zero_to_hero/build.py or !ledger:

  • (walk|ledger) captures either word (| means "or");
  • (?: +(\S+))? optionally captures a path made of non-space characters (\S+).

re.MULTILINE makes ^ and $ mean the start and end of each line, which matters because the whole chapter is searched at once.

40FINGERPRINT_LINE = re.compile(r"^fingerprint:.*$", re.MULTILINE)

FINGERPRINT_LINE finds the fingerprint: … line in a walkthrough's header, so --stamp can replace it. .* means "any characters, any number of them".

41EXTENSIONS = ["extra", "admonition", "sane_lists", "codehilite"]

EXTENSIONS lists the Python-Markdown extensions to switch on:

  • extra — tables, footnotes, abbreviations, definition lists, fenced code;
  • admonition — the !!! boxes;
  • sane_lists — keeps numbered and bulleted lists from merging;
  • codehilite — colours fenced code blocks with Pygments.
42EXT_CONFIG = {"codehilite": {"css_class": "hl", "guess_lang": False}}

EXT_CONFIG holds settings for those extensions, as a dict. For codehilite:

  • css_class: "hl" matches the colour rules in the template;
  • guess_lang: False means "don't guess the language of unlabelled code blocks" — wrong colours are worse than none.
43
44
45@dataclass
46class Note:
47    start: int
48    end: int
49    text: str

Note — a container for one explanation. @dataclass is a decorator: it writes the boring parts of the class for us, such as the code that builds a Note from three values. The three fields are:

  • start — first line number explained;
  • end — last line number;
  • text — the explanation, in Markdown.

Note(12, 14, "…") means "lines 12 to 14 are explained by this text".

50
51
52type Segment = tuple[int, int, Note | None]

type Segment = tuple[int, int, Note | None] is a type alias — a short name for a longer type. It uses the type statement added in Python 3.12. A segment is a stretch of lines: a start number, an end number, and either the Note explaining it or None if nothing does. The alias makes the function signatures below much easier to read.

53
54
55@dataclass(frozen=True)
56class Place:
57    first: int
58    last: int
59    edited: bool

Place — where one old line ended up in the new version. It has three fields:

  • first and last — the new line numbers that the old line now covers. Usually they are equal. When an edit turned one line into several, the old line's place stretches over all of them;
  • edited — whether the line's code changed, rather than just moved.

frozen=True makes every Place read-only once it is made. A Place is a fact about two versions of a file, and nothing should quietly change it later.

60
61
62@dataclass
63class Coverage:
64    path: str
65    lines: int
66    required: int
67    explained: int
68    stale: bool

Coverage — the score card for one file:

  • path — the file;
  • lines — total lines;
  • required — non-blank lines, which need explaining;
  • explained — how many required lines have an explanation;
  • stale — True if the code changed after it was explained.
69
70    @property
71    def percent(self) -> float:
72        return 100.0 if self.required == 0 else 100.0 * self.explained / self.required

percent is the share of required lines explained, out of 100. @property lets us read it like a field (cov.percent), although it is calculated fresh each time, so it can never be out of date.

The conditional expression A if condition else B guards against dividing by zero: a file with nothing to explain counts as 100 % explained.

73
74    @property
75    def complete(self) -> bool:
76        return self.explained == self.required and not self.stale

complete is True only when every required line is explained and the file hasn't changed since.

77
78
79def read_text(path: Path) -> str:
80    return path.read_bytes().decode("utf-8").replace("\r\n", "\n")

read_text — read any file safely:

  1. read_bytes() reads the raw bytes.
  2. .decode("utf-8") turns them into text using UTF-8 explicitly — this prevents the mojibake of §0.2.
  3. .replace("\r\n", "\n") converts Windows line endings to \n, so a file has the same fingerprint on every operating system.
81
82
83def write_text(path: Path, text: str) -> None:
84    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
85    path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")

write_text — write any file safely:

  • path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) first creates the folder the file goes in, and any missing folders above it, without complaining if they already exist.
  • It then writes the text as UTF-8 with Linux-style newlines (newline="\n"), so the file is byte-for-byte identical on Windows and Linux.

Every file this program writes goes through this one function, so those two promises hold everywhere.

86
87
88def fingerprint(text: str) -> str:
89    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

fingerprint — the magic blender:

  1. Encode the text as bytes.
  2. Blend it with SHA-256.
  3. Write the result as hexadecimal (hexdigest).
  4. Keep the first 16 characters ([:16] is a slice). That is still 2⁶⁴ possibilities.
90
91
92def walk_file_for(rel: str) -> Path:
93    return WALK_DIR / f"{rel}.md"

walk_file_for gives the walkthrough's location for a project file: the walkthroughs folder mirrors the project, with .md added (docs/zero_to_hero/build.py → walkthroughs/docs/zero_to_hero/build.py.md). f"{rel}.md" is an f-string: {rel} is replaced by the value of rel.

94
95
96def snapshot_for(rel: str) -> Path:
97    return SNAP_DIR / f"{rel}.snap"

snapshot_for gives the location of a project file's snapshot. It mirrors the project inside .snapshots, adding .snap to the name (tasks.py → .snapshots/tasks.py.snap).

Careful — why the .snap ending matters

The first design kept each copy's original name. Then the snapshot of .gitignore would itself be a file called .gitignore, and Git obeys .gitignore files in every folder. The snapshot of pyproject.toml might be mistaken for a real project by tools that search for one. Adding .snap makes every copy inert: no tool recognises it as anything special.

98
99
100def repo_relative(arg: str) -> str:
101    path = Path(arg) if Path(arg).is_absolute() else Path.cwd() / arg
102    return path.resolve().relative_to(REPO_ROOT).as_posix()

repo_relative turns whatever path the user typed into a project-relative one.

  • If the typed path is absolute, use it; otherwise glue it onto Path.cwd(), the terminal's current folder.
  • Then make it absolute (resolve), cut off the project root (relative_to), and write it with forward slashes (as_posix).
103
104
105def source_lines(text: str) -> list[str]:
106    lines = text.split("\n")
107    if lines[-1] == "":
108        lines.pop()
109    return lines

source_lines — split text into lines. split("\n") cuts at every newline. A tidy file ends with a newline, which leaves one empty string at the end — not a real line — so lines[-1] (the last item) is removed with .pop() when it is empty. Without this, every file would seem to have one extra line.

110
111
112def parse_walkthrough(text: str) -> tuple[dict[str, str], str, list[Note]]:

parse_walkthrough — read a walkthrough's text into its three parts. It returns a tuple of:

  1. a dict of header settings;
  2. the introduction text;
  3. a list of Notes.

It receives the text, not a file path, so it never touches the disk. That makes it a pure function that tests can feed with any text they like.

113    meta: dict[str, str] = {}

meta (short for metadata, "data about data") starts as an empty dict for the header values.

114    if text.startswith("---\n"):
115        header, _, text = text[4:].partition("\n---\n")

The header. If the text begins with three dashes, there is a header.

  • text[4:] skips those four characters (the dashes plus the newline).
  • .partition("\n---\n") splits the rest at the first closing dash line into three pieces: before, the separator itself, and after.
  • Tuple unpacking assigns the three pieces at once. _ is the conventional name for "a value we don't need". text becomes everything after the header.
116        for line in header.splitlines():
117            key, _, value = line.partition(":")
118            meta[key.strip()] = value.strip()

For each header line, split at the first : into key and value, trim the spaces from both (.strip()) and store them. So fingerprint: 3f9a… becomes meta["fingerprint"] == "3f9a…".

119    intro: list[str] = []
120    notes: list[Note] = []

Two empty lists to fill: intro for the introduction's lines, and notes for the Notes.

121    for line in text.split("\n"):

Walk through the body one line at a time. The for loop runs its indented block once per line.

122        mark = NOTE_MARK.match(line)

Try the marker pattern on this line. .match returns a match object for a marker, or None otherwise.

123        if mark:
124            start = int(mark[1])
125            notes.append(Note(start, int(mark[2] or start), ""))

If the line is a marker, start a new note.

  • mark[1] is the captured start number; int(...) turns "12" into 12.
  • mark[2] or start uses the end number if there is one, otherwise the start (or gives its left side if that is "truthy", else its right side).
126        elif notes:
127            notes[-1].text += line + "\n"

Otherwise, if a note has already started, this line belongs to the latest note (notes[-1]). += adds it, plus the newline that split removed.

128        else:
129            intro.append(line)

Otherwise — before the first marker — the line belongs to the introduction.

130    return meta, "\n".join(intro), notes

Return the three parts, gluing the introduction's lines back together with newlines.

131
132
133def is_explained(note: Note) -> bool:
134    body = note.text.strip()
135    return bool(body) and not body.startswith("TODO")

is_explained checks that a note's text is non-empty and doesn't start with TODO. This covers both the TODO skeletons from --new and the TODO(review) flags from --reanchor.

Why treat TODO as 'not explained'?

If placeholders counted, a freshly generated skeleton would show 100 % coverage, and the honesty check would be fooled by its own helper.

136
137
138def segments(notes: list[Note], total: int) -> tuple[list[Segment], list[str]]:

segments — chop a file into consecutive stretches, each covered by one note or by none. It returns two things: the list of Segments, and a list of problems found (bad notes).

In the first version of the book this was a method that wrote problems straight into the Book. Turning it into a separate function that returns its problems made it possible to test on its own.

139    result: list[Segment] = []
140    problems: list[str] = []
141    cursor = 1

result and problems start empty. cursor is a finger pointing at the first line not yet assigned to a stretch; it starts at line 1.

142    for note in sorted(notes, key=lambda n: n.start):

Visit the notes in order of their first line. sorted(...) returns a sorted copy. key=lambda n: n.start says what to sort by: a lambda is a tiny unnamed function, here "given a note n, give back n.start".

143        if note.start < cursor or note.end < note.start or note.end > total:
144            problems.append(f"note @@ {note.start}-{note.end} overlaps or is out of range")
145            continue

Reject impossible notes. A note is bad if it starts before the cursor (it overlaps the previous note), ends before it starts, or ends beyond the last line. Bad notes are recorded as problems and skipped with continue ("go straight to the next item"). Overlaps are forbidden so that each line has exactly one explanation and coverage can't be double-counted.

146        if note.start > cursor:
147            result.append((cursor, note.start - 1, None))

A gap before this note? The lines between the cursor and the note's start have no note. Record them as a stretch with None in the note position.

148        result.append((note.start, note.end, note))
149        cursor = note.end + 1

Record the note's own stretch, then move the cursor to just after it.

150    if cursor <= total:
151        result.append((cursor, total, None))

A gap at the end? If the cursor hasn't passed the last line, the tail of the file has no notes. Record it as one more stretch.

152    return result, problems

Return both lists. Together the stretches cover every line exactly once, in order.

153
154
155def line_mapping(old: list[str], new: list[str]) -> dict[int, Place]:

line_mapping — where did each old line go? It receives the lines of the old version (the snapshot) and of the new version. It returns a dict from each old line number to that line's Place in the new version.

156    mapping: dict[int, Place] = {}

Start with an empty dict. The annotation dict[int, Place] tells the type checker what it will hold.

157    for tag, i1, i2, j1, j2 in difflib.SequenceMatcher(a=old, b=new, autojunk=False).get_opcodes():

difflib.SequenceMatcher(a=old, b=new, autojunk=False) compares the two lists of lines. .get_opcodes() then describes the change as a list of operations that turn the old version into the new one. Each operation is five values:

  • tag — what happened: "equal" (these lines are unchanged), "replace" (these old lines became those new lines), "delete" (these old lines are gone) or "insert" (these new lines are brand new);
  • i1, i2 — where the operation starts and stops in the old list;
  • j1, j2 — the same in the new list.

Positions count from 0, and the stop position is not included — Python's usual half-open ranges, exactly like range(i1, i2).

Old lines New lines Operations
a, b, c a, B, c equal a · replace b → B · equal c
a, b, c new, a, c insert new · equal a · delete b · equal c

autojunk=False switches off a speed shortcut that ignores very common lines. In code, common lines such as blank lines and lone closing brackets matter.

158        if tag not in ("equal", "replace"):
159            continue

Deleted old lines have no new place, and inserted new lines have no old line to come from, so both kinds of operation are skipped (continue). A note whose lines were all deleted therefore finds no places, and is dropped later. New lines that nobody has explained yet show up in the book as not explained.

160        for k in range(i2 - i1):

For every old line in an equal or replace block — k counts 0, 1, 2… through the block…

161            first = j1 + min(k, j2 - j1 - 1)

…line it up with the new line in the same position of the new block. If the new block is shorter, min(…) stops at its last line, so the leftover old lines all point there.

162            last = j2 - 1 if k == i2 - i1 - 1 else first

The last old line of the block also takes any extra new lines: if the new block is longer, its last stretches to the block's final line (j2 - 1). Every other old line covers exactly one new line.

Explain like I'm six — two rows of chairs

Put the old row of chairs and the new row side by side, lined up from the left. Chair 1 faces chair 1, chair 2 faces chair 2, and so on. If the new row is longer, the last old chair looks after every leftover new chair. If it is shorter, the extra old chairs all face the last new one.

For an equal block both rows have the same length, so every line simply faces its twin.

163            mapping[i1 + k + 1] = Place(first + 1, last + 1, edited=tag == "replace")

Record the place. The + 1s convert difflib's positions, which count from 0, into line numbers, which count from 1. In edited=tag == "replace", the == compares, and its answer — True or False — is what gets stored: a line is edited exactly when it came from a replace block.

For example, with old lines a, b, c and new lines a, B1, B2, c, the mapping is: 1 → Place(1, 1, edited=False), 2 → Place(2, 3, edited=True), 3 → Place(4, 4, edited=False). tests/test_build.py checks exactly these values.

164    return mapping

Return the finished mapping.

165
166
167def reanchor_text(text: str, mapping: dict[int, Place]) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:

reanchor_text — move every note in a walkthrough to its lines' new places. It receives the walkthrough's text and the mapping. It returns the new text, plus a report of everything that needs a human's attention.

168    output: list[str] = []
169    report: list[str] = []
170    dropping = review = False

output collects the lines of the new walkthrough, and report the messages. Two on/off switches are written on one line (dropping = review = False sets both):

  • dropping — "skip the text of the current note, because its code is gone";
  • review — "the next line of text needs a TODO(review) label".
171    for line in text.split("\n"):

Go through the walkthrough line by line.

172        mark = NOTE_MARK.match(line)

Is this line a note marker?

173        if mark:

If it is…

174            start, end = int(mark[1]), int(mark[2] or mark[1])

…read its start and end line numbers. A single-line marker uses the start number for both.

175            places = [mapping[n] for n in range(start, end + 1) if n in mapping]

places collects the new places of the note's old lines. Lines with no place — deleted ones — are left out by if n in mapping.

176            dropping = not places
177            if dropping:
178                report.append(f"@@ {start}-{end}: its lines were deleted, so the note was dropped")
179                continue

No places at all means every line the note explained was deleted. Then the note is dropped: record a report message, and skip the marker (continue). The dropping switch makes the lines that follow — the note's text — be skipped too.

180            low, high = min(p.first for p in places), max(p.last for p in places)

The note's new range runs from the smallest first to the largest last among its places. The values are fed to min and max by generator expressions: p.first for p in places produces the numbers one by one, without building a list first.

181            review = high - low != end - start or any(p.edited for p in places)

The note needs review if either:

  • its size changed — lines were inserted inside it, or some of its lines were deleted. high - low is how far apart the new ends are, and end - start how far apart the old ones were, so comparing the two compares the sizes;
  • or any of its lines was edited (any(…) is true if at least one place says so).

A note whose lines only moved passes both tests: it follows them silently, and no human is needed.

182            if review:
183                report.append(f"@@ {start}-{end} -> {low}-{high}: code changed, marked TODO(review)")

If the note needs review, say so in the report, showing its old and new ranges.

184            output.append(f"@@ {low}" if low == high else f"@@ {low}-{high}")

Write the new marker: a single number if the note now covers one line, otherwise a range.

185        elif dropping:
186            continue

A text line while dropping is on belongs to a dropped note, so skip it.

187        elif review and line.strip():
188            output.append(line if line.startswith("TODO") else f"TODO(review) {line}")
189            review = False

The first non-blank text line after a marker that needs review gets the prefix TODO(review), which makes is_explained treat the note as unexplained. A line that already starts with TODO is left as it is, so running --reanchor twice can never produce a doubled prefix. Then the switch turns off, so only the first line is touched.

190        else:
191            output.append(line)

Every other line is copied unchanged.

192    return "\n".join(output), report

Return the rebuilt walkthrough text and the report.

193
194
195def highlight_lines(text: str, filename: str, count: int) -> list[str]:

highlight_lines — colour a file and return one HTML string per line.

196    try:
197        lexer = get_lexer_for_filename(filename, stripnl=False)
198    except ClassNotFound:
199        lexer = TextLexer(stripnl=False)

try / except. Ask Pygments for the lexer matching the file name. If it doesn't know the name, it raises ClassNotFound; we catch that and fall back to plain text.

stripnl=False is vital: by default Pygments drops blank lines at the start and end, which would shift every line number.

200    lines = highlight(text, lexer, HtmlFormatter(nowrap=True)).split("\n")

Highlight, then split. nowrap=True means "just the coloured spans, no surrounding box". Pygments closes and reopens its colour tags at every line break, so splitting at "\n" gives one valid HTML piece per line.

201    if len(lines) < count:
202        return [html.escape(line) for line in source_lines(text)]

Safety net. If highlighting produced fewer lines than the file has, don't trust it. Fall back to the plain lines, escaped so that < displays correctly. Wrong colours are acceptable; wrong line numbers are not.

203    return lines[:count]

Return exactly count lines. The slice drops the extra empty item left by the final newline.

204
205
206class Book:

class Book: — a class is a blueprint for an object that bundles data with behaviour. A Book remembers the settings, every file's score card and the problems found. Its methods do the work.

207    def __init__(self, config: dict[str, Any]) -> None:

__init__ runs when a Book is created: Book(config). self is the new object, and config is the dict read from book.toml — typed dict[str, Any] (see line 26).

208        self.config = config
209        self.coverage: dict[str, Coverage] = {}
210        self.problems: list[str] = []
211        self.abbreviations = read_text(BOOK_DIR / config["abbreviations"])
212        self.note_md = markdown.Markdown(extensions=EXTENSIONS, extension_configs=EXT_CONFIG)

The Book's memory:

  • config — the settings;
  • coverage — a dict from file path to its score card;
  • problems — a list of human-readable problem messages;
  • abbreviations — the hover definitions, read once;
  • note_md — one Markdown converter for walkthrough notes, created once and reused for hundreds of notes.
213
214    def note_html(self, text: str) -> str:
215        self.note_md.reset()
216        return self.note_md.convert(text + "\n\n" + self.abbreviations)

note_html — convert one note's Markdown to HTML. .reset() clears the converter's memory of the previous note so notes never leak into each other. The abbreviation definitions are attached after a blank line, then the note is converted.

217
218    def render_walkthrough(self, rel: str) -> str:

render_walkthrough — the heart of the book. It returns the HTML of one file's whole walkthrough, and records the file's score card.

219        source, walk = REPO_ROOT / rel, walk_file_for(rel)

Work out the source file's path and its walkthrough's path in one line (tuple unpacking).

220        if not source.is_file() or not walk.is_file():
221            self.problems.append(f"no source file or no walkthrough for {rel}")
222            return f'<p class="todo">Walkthrough for <code>{html.escape(rel)}</code> is missing.</p>'

Missing pieces. If either file is missing, record a problem and return a red warning instead of crashing. One missing explanation shouldn't stop the whole book from building, but it must be visible.

223        text = read_text(source)
224        lines = source_lines(text)

Read the source file and split it into lines.

225        meta, intro, notes = parse_walkthrough(read_text(walk))

Read the walkthrough file and parse it into its three parts.

226        code = highlight_lines(text, source.name, len(lines))

Highlight the source: one coloured HTML string per line.

227        required = {n for n, line in enumerate(lines, 1) if line.strip()}

Which lines need explaining? A set comprehension collects the numbers of non-blank lines. enumerate(lines, 1) counts from 1, because humans number lines from 1.

228        explained: set[int] = set()
229        rows: list[str] = []

explained will collect the numbers of lines that turn out to be explained (set() makes an empty set; {} would make a dict). rows will collect the HTML of each row.

230        parts, problems = segments(notes, len(lines))
231        self.problems += [f"{rel}: {p}" for p in problems]

Cut the file into stretches with segments (line 131). Any problems it found are added to the book's list, each prefixed with the file's path so the message says which walkthrough is broken. += on a list appends all the new items.

232        for start, end, note in parts:

Go through the stretches in order, unpacking each into start, end and note.

233            numbers = range(start, end + 1)

range(start, end + 1) gives the line numbers in this stretch. range stops before its second number, hence the + 1.

234            code_html = "\n".join(f'<span class="ln">{n}</span>{code[n - 1]}' for n in numbers)

The code side of the row: for each line number, a line-number label followed by that line's highlighted HTML, joined with newlines.

code[n - 1] uses n - 1 because Python lists count from 0 while line numbers count from 1 — the classic "off-by-one" trap.

235            if note and is_explained(note):
236                explained.update(numbers)
237                kind, side = "wrow", self.note_html(note.text)

Case 1 — a real explanation. Mark the lines as explained; the row gets the normal style, and the note is converted to HTML.

238            elif required.intersection(numbers):
239                kind, side = "wrow missing", '<p class="todo">Not explained yet.</p>'

Case 2 — no explanation, but there is code here. The row gets the missing style (a red bar) and a red "Not explained yet." message.

240            else:
241                kind, side = "wrow blank", ""

Case 3 — only blank lines. Nothing to explain: a compact blank row with no explanation box.

242            row = f'<div class="{kind}"><pre class="hl"><code>{code_html}</code></pre>'
243            rows.append(f'{row}<div class="wnote">{side}</div></div>')

Build the row's HTML in two steps — first the code box, then the note box and the closing tags — and add it to rows. Two short steps keep each line within the 120-character limit that Ruff checks.

244        stale = meta.get("fingerprint") != fingerprint(text)

Stale? The fingerprint recorded in the walkthrough's header must equal a fresh fingerprint of the code. A missing fingerprint (None) also counts as stale.

245        cov = Coverage(rel, len(lines), len(required), len(required & explained), stale)
246        self.coverage[rel] = cov

Record the score. required & explained is the intersection of the two sets: lines that are both required and explained. Blank lines inside a multi-line note don't inflate the count.

247        badge = '<span class="pill bad">code changed since explained</span>' if stale else ""

The red "code changed since explained" badge if stale, otherwise nothing.

248        head = (
249            f'<div class="whead"><code>{html.escape(rel)}</code>'
250            f"<span>{cov.lines} lines · {cov.percent:.0f}% explained</span>{badge}</div>"
251        )

The header bar: the file's path, its line count and its coverage. The parentheses let one string span several lines; Python glues adjacent strings together automatically. {cov.percent:.0f} formats the number with no decimal places.

252        intro_html = f'<div class="wintro">{self.note_html(intro)}</div>'

The file's introduction, converted from Markdown and wrapped in its own box.

253        return f'<section class="walk">{head}{intro_html}{"".join(rows)}</section>'

Assemble the walkthrough: a <section> holding the header bar, the introduction and every row.

254
255    def scan_sources(self) -> list[str]:

scan_sources — find every file in the project that must be explained.

256        rules = self.config["coverage"]
257        found: list[str] = []

rules is the [coverage] group from book.toml; found collects matching paths.

258        for folder, dirs, files in os.walk(REPO_ROOT):

os.walk(REPO_ROOT) visits the project root and every folder beneath it. For each folder it gives the folder's path, its sub-folder names and its file names.

259            dirs[:] = sorted(d for d in dirs if d not in rules["prune"])

Pruning. The list of sub-folders is replaced in place with a sorted copy that leaves out the names in prune.

dirs[:] = … changes the very list os.walk will use to decide where to go next. Plain dirs = … would make a new list that os.walk never sees. Sorting makes the ledger's order the same on every computer.

260            for name in sorted(files):

For each file name in this folder, in sorted order…

261                rel = PurePosixPath(Path(folder, name).relative_to(REPO_ROOT).as_posix())

…build its project-relative path with forward slashes, as a PurePosixPath.

262                wanted = any(rel.full_match(p) for p in rules["include"])

Does it match any include pattern? any(...) is True if at least one pattern matches. It stops at the first match.

263                if wanted and not any(rel.full_match(p) for p in rules["exclude"]):
264                    found.append(str(rel))

Keep it if it was wanted and matches no exclude pattern.

265        return found

Return the list of every file that must be explained.

266
267    def ledger_html(self) -> str:
268        rows: list[str] = []

ledger_html — build the coverage table at the back of the book. rows holds one table row per file.

269        for rel in self.scan_sources():

For every file the scan says must be explained…

270            has_walk = walk_file_for(rel).is_file()

…check whether it has a walkthrough file.

271            if rel not in self.coverage and has_walk:
272                self.render_walkthrough(rel)
273                self.problems.append(f"{rel}: its walkthrough is not placed in any chapter (add a !walk line)")

It has a walkthrough, but no chapter has shown it yet — render it anyway, so its coverage is counted, and record a problem: an explanation that exists but never appears in the book helps nobody.

Real world — a gap this closed

In Phase 1, 34 new walkthroughs were written before the chapter that shows them — and the strict check still passed, because it only asked whether each file was explained, not whether the explanation was shown. A check that passes while the reader sees nothing is a gap, so this line now makes it fail.

274            elif rel not in self.coverage:
275                lines = source_lines(read_text(REPO_ROOT / rel))
276                self.coverage[rel] = Coverage(rel, len(lines), sum(1 for x in lines if x.strip()), 0, False)
277                self.problems.append(f"{rel}: no walkthrough yet")

It has no walkthrough at all.

  • Count its lines anyway and record a score card with zero explained, so the totals honestly include it.
  • sum(1 for x in lines if x.strip()) adds 1 for every non-blank line.
  • Also record a problem.

Real world — a bug this fixed

The first version skipped files without walkthroughs when adding up totals. The very first build therefore announced "0/0 lines explained (100.0 %)" — a perfect score for doing nothing. A check that can report success when nothing was done is worse than no check.

278            cov = self.coverage[rel]

Fetch this file's score card. One of the branches above guarantees it exists.

279            label, tone = (
280                ("complete", "ok")
281                if cov.complete
282                else ("stale", "bad")
283                if cov.stale
284                else ("in progress", "warn")
285                if has_walk
286                else ("not explained", "bad")
287            )

Choose the status label and its colour with a chain of conditional expressions, read top to bottom:

  • complete → green;
  • otherwise stale → red;
  • otherwise has a walkthrough → amber "in progress";
  • otherwise → red "not explained".

Ruff's formatter spread the chain over several lines so each condition is easy to see.

288            rows.append(
289                f"<tr><td><code>{html.escape(rel)}</code></td><td>{cov.lines}</td>"
290                f"<td>{cov.explained}/{cov.required} ({cov.percent:.0f}%)</td>"
291                f'<td><span class="pill {tone}">{label}</span></td></tr>'
292            )

Add the table row: path, line count, explained/required with the percentage, and the coloured status pill.

293        head = "<tr><th>File</th><th>Lines</th><th>Explained (non-blank)</th><th>Status</th></tr>"
294        table = f'<div class="tw"><table><thead>{head}</thead><tbody>{"".join(rows)}</tbody></table></div>'

The heading row, then the whole table, wrapped in a box that scrolls sideways on narrow screens.

295        return f"<p><strong>Total:</strong> {self.totals()}</p>{table}"

Return a Total line followed by the table.

296
297    def totals(self) -> str:
298        required = sum(c.required for c in self.coverage.values())
299        explained = sum(c.explained for c in self.coverage.values())
300        percent = 100.0 if required == 0 else 100.0 * explained / required
301        return f"{len(self.coverage)} files · {explained:,}/{required:,} lines explained ({percent:.1f}%)"

totals — one line summarising the whole project's coverage. Add up the required and explained lines across every score card, work out the percentage (guarding against dividing by zero), and format the line. :, adds thousands separators and .1f shows one decimal place.

302
303    def build(self) -> str:
304        blocks: dict[str, tuple[str, str]] = {}

build — assemble the whole book. blocks remembers each directive found in the chapters: a placeholder name → (kind, argument).

305
306        def park(match: re.Match[str]) -> str:
307            key = f"ZTHBLOCK{len(blocks)}X"
308            blocks[key] = (match[1], match[2] or "")
309            return f"\n\n{key}\n\n"

park — a function inside a function. It is called for every directive found:

  1. invent a unique placeholder such as ZTHBLOCK3X;
  2. remember what the directive asked for;
  3. return the placeholder surrounded by blank lines, to replace the directive in the chapter.

Key idea — why park directives?

Walkthrough HTML must not go through the Markdown converter, which would mangle the code. So each directive is swapped for a harmless word, everything is converted, and then the real HTML is swapped back in (lines 311–312). The blank lines make Markdown wrap the placeholder in its own <p>…</p>, which is exactly what we search for.

310
311        chapters = [DIRECTIVE.sub(park, read_text(BOOK_DIR / c)) for c in self.config["chapters"]]

Read every chapter in the order book.toml gives, parking its directives. A list comprehension; DIRECTIVE.sub(park, text) replaces each directive with whatever park returns.

312        md = markdown.Markdown(
313            extensions=[*EXTENSIONS, "toc"], extension_configs={**EXT_CONFIG, "toc": {"toc_depth": "1-3"}}
314        )

The main Markdown converter, with our extensions plus toc. toc gives every heading an id you can link to, and records the headings for the sidebar.

  • [*EXTENSIONS, "toc"] builds a new list: everything in EXTENSIONS, then "toc". The * spreads a list's items.
  • {**EXT_CONFIG, …} does the same for dicts.
315        body = md.convert("\n\n".join(chapters) + "\n\n" + self.abbreviations)

Convert the whole book in one go, with the abbreviations attached once at the end. Converting everything together lets toc make every heading's id unique across all chapters.

316        walked = [arg for kind, arg in blocks.values() if kind == "walk"]
317        repeated = sorted({rel for rel in walked if walked.count(rel) > 1})
318        self.problems += [f"{rel}: its walkthrough is placed more than once" for rel in repeated]

Each walkthrough must be shown exactly once. walked lists the file named by every !walk directive, in order. repeated collects the files that appear more than once: the braces build a set, which keeps each file once, and sorted fixes the order. Each one becomes a problem. Showing the same file twice makes the book longer for no gain, and usually means a !walk line was meant to name a different file.

319        fragments = {k: self.render_walkthrough(arg) for k, (kind, arg) in blocks.items() if kind == "walk"}

Render every parked walkthrough — a dict comprehension keeping only walk blocks.

320        fragments |= {k: self.ledger_html() for k, (kind, _) in blocks.items() if kind == "ledger"}

Render the ledger last (|= merges entries into the dict), so every walkthrough shown in a chapter already has its score card.

321        for key, fragment in fragments.items():
322            body = body.replace(f"<p>{key}</p>", fragment)

Swap the real HTML back in for each <p>placeholder</p>.

323        body = body.replace("<table>", '<div class="tw"><table>').replace("</table>", "</table></div>")

Make wide tables scrollable on phones by wrapping each table in a tw box.

324        toc_tokens: list[dict[str, Any]] = getattr(md, "toc_tokens", [])

Get the list of headings for the sidebar. The toc extension attaches toc_tokens to the converter while the program runs, so the type checker — which reads the code beforehand — can't know it exists. getattr(md, "toc_tokens", []) reads the attribute by name, and gives an empty list if it is missing. The label list[dict[str, Any]] tells mypy what we expect to get.

325        return self.page(body, toc_tokens)

Hand the body and headings to page().

326
327    def page(self, body: str, toc_tokens: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> str:
328        links: list[str] = []

page — pour everything into the template. links collects one sidebar link per heading.

329
330        def visit(tokens: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> None:
331            for token in tokens:
332                name = html.escape(html.unescape(token["name"]))
333                links.append(f'<a class="h{token["level"]}" href="#{token["id"]}">{name}</a>')
334                visit(token["children"])

visit — turn the tree of headings into flat sidebar links. For each heading:

  1. make its name safe (unescape, then escape exactly once);
  2. add a link whose class (h1, h2, h3) lets the CSS indent it;
  3. call itself on the heading's children.

A function that calls itself is using recursion, the natural way to walk a tree.

335
336        visit(toc_tokens)

Start the walk from the top-level headings.

337        words = len(re.findall(r"\w+", re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", body)))

Count the words: replace every HTML tag with a space (re.sub), find every run of word characters (re.findall), and count them.

338        page = read_text(BOOK_DIR / "template.html")

Read the template.

339        values = {
340            "TITLE": html.escape(self.config["title"]),
341            "SUBTITLE": html.escape(self.config["subtitle"]),
342            "META": f"{words:,} words · {self.totals()}",
343            "BUILT": datetime.now(UTC).strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M UTC"),
344            "TOC": "\n".join(links),
345        }

The values for the template's blanks:

  • the escaped title and subtitle;
  • the word count and coverage totals;
  • the build time (strftime formats a date as text);
  • the sidebar links.
346        for key, value in values.items():
347            page = page.replace("{{" + key + "}}", value)

Fill the blanks: replace {{NAME}} with each value. The placeholder is built with + because inside an f-string, {{ means a single literal {, which would make an f-string version unreadable.

348        return page.replace("{{BODY}}", body)

Insert the body last — on purpose. The book contains text like {{TITLE}} (in the template's walkthrough, for example). If the body went in first, the loop above would wrongly replace those mentions too.

349
350    def report(self) -> str:
351        lines = [f"book: {self.totals()}".replace("·", "|")]
352        lines += [f"  problem: {p}" for p in self.problems]
353        return "\n".join(lines)

report — the summary printed in the terminal: the totals, then one indented line per problem. The · dot is swapped for | because some Windows terminals can't print it.

354
355
356def new_walkthrough(rel: str) -> int:
357    target = walk_file_for(rel)

new_walkthrough — the --new helper. Find where the file's walkthrough should go.

358    if target.exists():
359        print(f"{target} already exists")
360        return 1

Never overwrite. If a walkthrough already exists, refuse and return 1 (failure). One mistyped command must never destroy hours of written explanations.

361    text = read_text(REPO_ROOT / rel)

Read the source file.

362    marks = [f"@@ {n}\nTODO\n" for n, line in enumerate(source_lines(text), 1) if line.strip()]

One TODO note per non-blank line: a marker with the line number, then TODO. The author replaces each TODO, merging neighbouring lines into ranges where that reads better.

363    header = f"---\nfingerprint: {fingerprint(text)}\n---\nTODO: what this file is for.\n\n"

The header: the file's current fingerprint between dashes, and a TODO for the introduction.

364    write_text(target, header + "\n".join(marks))

Write the walkthrough: the header followed by all the notes.

365    write_text(snapshot_for(rel), text)

Save the first snapshot of the source, so --reanchor works from day one.

366    print(f"created {target}")
367    return 0

Report where the file was created, and return 0 (success).

368
369
370def stamp_walkthrough(rel: str) -> int:
371    target = walk_file_for(rel)
372    text = read_text(REPO_ROOT / rel)
373    write_text(target, FINGERPRINT_LINE.sub(f"fingerprint: {fingerprint(text)}", read_text(target), count=1))
374    write_text(snapshot_for(rel), text)
375    print(f"stamped {target}")
376    return 0

stamp_walkthrough — the --stamp helper, run after the explanations have been checked against the current code:

  1. find the walkthrough and read the current source;
  2. replace the walkthrough's fingerprint: line with a fresh one (count=1 changes only the first match);
  3. save a fresh snapshot;
  4. report and return success.

Stamping is deliberately manual: the builder can notice that code changed, but only a person can confirm the explanation still matches.

377
378
379def reanchor_walkthrough(rel: str) -> int:
380    snapshot, target = snapshot_for(rel), walk_file_for(rel)
381    if not snapshot.is_file() or not target.is_file():
382        print(f"{rel}: needs a walkthrough and a snapshot (made by --new or --stamp)")
383        return 1
384    current = read_text(REPO_ROOT / rel)
385    mapping = line_mapping(source_lines(read_text(snapshot)), source_lines(current))
386    text, report = reanchor_text(read_text(target), mapping)
387    write_text(target, text)
388    write_text(snapshot, current)
389    print("\n".join([f"re-anchored {target}", *report]))
390    return 0

reanchor_walkthrough — the --reanchor helper.

  1. Find the snapshot and the walkthrough. If either is missing, explain what's needed and return 1.
  2. Read the current source, and build the line mapping from the snapshot (the old version) to it.
  3. Rewrite the walkthrough with reanchor_text, and save it.
  4. Move the snapshot forward to the current source. From now on, the snapshot is the version that the walkthrough's line numbers refer to.
  5. Print the file name followed by every report line. [f"…", *report] builds one list from a first item plus all of report's items.

It never stamps: the fingerprint still belongs to the last approved version, so the strict check keeps failing until a person has reviewed the moved notes.

Real world — a bug this step fixed

The first version did not do step 4. Re-anchoring twice before a stamp then went wrong: the second run compared the stamped version with the newest one, and moved notes that had already been moved once. The builder's own tests now include exactly that case.

391
392
393def main() -> int:

main — what happens when you run build.py. It returns an exit code.

394    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Build the Zero-to-Hero book.")

Create the argument parser, with a description for the help text.

395    parser.add_argument("--strict", action="store_true", help="fail on unexplained, stale or missing walkthroughs")

--strict is an on/off switch (store_true).

396    parser.add_argument("--new", metavar="PATH", help="create a walkthrough skeleton for PATH")
397    parser.add_argument("--stamp", metavar="PATH", help="record PATH's fingerprint and snapshot in its walkthrough")
398    parser.add_argument("--reanchor", metavar="PATH", help="move PATH's notes to follow edits since its last snapshot")

--new, --stamp and --reanchor each take a path (shown as PATH in the help text).

399    args = parser.parse_args()

Read what was actually typed. Unknown options stop the program with a helpful message.

400    commands = {"new": new_walkthrough, "stamp": stamp_walkthrough, "reanchor": reanchor_walkthrough}

A dict from option name to the function that handles it. Functions are values in Python, so they can be stored in a dict like anything else.

401    for name, command in commands.items():
402        if getattr(args, name):
403            return command(repo_relative(getattr(args, name)))

Dispatch. For each helper command: if its option was given (getattr(args, name) reads the attribute whose name is in name), convert the path to project-relative form, run the function, and return its exit code. Nothing else runs.

The first version used three separate if blocks. The dict makes adding a fourth command a one-line change.

404    config = tomllib.loads(read_text(BOOK_DIR / "book.toml"))

Normal build. Read book.toml and parse it.

405    book = Book(config)

Create the Book.

406    write_text(BOOK_DIR / config["output"], book.build())

Build and save the page, at the path named by output in the settings.

407    print(book.report())

Print the report.

408    incomplete = any(not c.complete for c in book.coverage.values())

Is anything incomplete? True if at least one file isn't fully explained, or is stale.

409    return 1 if args.strict and (book.problems or incomplete) else 0

The exit code. In --strict mode any problem or incomplete file means failure (1); otherwise success (0). Robots such as CI read this number (§4.6).

410
411
412if __name__ == "__main__":
413    sys.exit(main())

The entry point. When a file is run directly, Python sets __name__ to "__main__"; when it is imported, __name__ is the module's name. So main() runs only when you run the file — the tests can import build without building the book.

X.9.3 template.html — the page shell

docs/zero_to_hero/template.html200 lines · 100% explained

template.html is the empty shell of the book's page. It contains everything except the content: the page structure (HTML), all the styling (CSS, inside <style>) and the small amount of behaviour (JavaScript, inside <script>). Where content belongs it has blanks written as a word in double curly braces — {{TITLE}}, {{TOC}}, {{BODY}} and so on. build.py fills them in (see its lines 255–264).

The book must work as one file, offline, with nothing downloaded from the internet, so everything is inline: no external stylesheets, scripts or fonts.

CSS in one minute. A CSS rule looks like selector { property: value; property: value; }:

  • the selector says which elements the rule applies to — h1 means every <h1>, .side every element with class="side", #q the element with id="q";
  • each property: value pair says how they should look.

When several rules apply to the same element, the more specific selector wins. Between equally specific rules, the one written later wins.

JavaScript in one minute. JavaScript is the browser's programming language. Here it does four small jobs:

  1. remember and switch the colour theme;
  2. filter the sidebar;
  3. highlight the section you're reading;
  4. draw the reading-progress bar.
1<!doctype html>

<!doctype html> — the first line of every modern web page. It tells the browser "this is modern HTML; use standard rules". Without it, browsers fall back to an old compatibility mode ("quirks mode") that lays pages out differently.

2<html lang="en">

<html lang="en"> — the start of the page. Everything else sits inside it. lang="en" declares the language as English, which helps screen readers pronounce words correctly and helps browsers offer translation.

3<head>

<head> — the page's "behind the scenes" section: settings, title and styles. Nothing in the head is shown directly in the page.

4<meta charset="utf-8">

<meta charset="utf-8"> — "this file's text is UTF-8". It must come early, before any text the browser might misread. Together with build.py writing UTF-8, this is what keeps —, द्वारपाल and 🧒 intact (§0.2).

5<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

<meta name="viewport" …> — makes phones show the page at its real width instead of pretending to be a wide desktop screen and shrinking everything. initial-scale=1 means "start at 100 % zoom".

6<title>{{TITLE}}</title>

<title>{{TITLE}}</title> — the text shown on the browser tab. {{TITLE}} is a blank that build.py fills with the title from book.toml.

7<style>

<style> — everything from here to </style> (line 138) is CSS.

8:root {

:root { — :root selects the top element of the page (<html>). Rules here act as the page's global settings. The { opens the list of settings.

9  color-scheme: light dark;

color-scheme: light dark; — tells the browser this page supports both light and dark modes. The browser then picks one based on the user's system setting. This also switches built-in parts (scrollbars, the search box) to matching colours.

10  --bg: light-dark(#ffffff, #0d1117);
11  --bg-2: light-dark(#f6f8fa, #161b22);
12  --bg-3: light-dark(#eaeef2, #21262d);
13  --text: light-dark(#1f2328, #e6edf3);
14  --text-2: light-dark(#59636e, #9198a1);
15  --text-3: light-dark(#818b98, #6e7681);
16  --border: light-dark(#d1d9e0, #30363d);
17  --accent: light-dark(#0969da, #4493f8);
18  --ok: light-dark(#1a7f37, #3fb950);
19  --warn: light-dark(#9a6700, #d29922);
20  --danger: light-dark(#cf222e, #f85149);
21  --purple: light-dark(#8250df, #ab7df8);

The colour palette, defined once. Names starting with two dashes (--bg, --text, …) are CSS custom properties, also called CSS variables: named values that other rules reuse as var(--bg). Changing a colour here changes it everywhere.

Each colour uses light-dark(A, B): "use A in light mode and B in dark mode". One line per colour covers both themes. The names describe roles, not colours:

Variable Role
--bg, --bg-2, --bg-3 page background, panels, slightly darker panels
--text, --text-2, --text-3 main text, secondary text, faint text
--border lines and box edges
--accent links and highlights (blue)
--ok, --warn, --danger, --purple green, amber and red status colours, and purple for the "kid" boxes

The colour values are written in hexadecimal: # then two digits each for red, green and blue (00–ff, i.e. 0–255). #ffffff is white; #0d1117 is a very dark blue-grey. These are GitHub's own interface colours, chosen to match the earlier AegisProxy book the project owner liked, and because they are tuned for readability.

Why light-dark() instead of writing two separate colour lists?

The older approach repeats the whole dark palette twice: once for "the system is in dark mode" and once for "the user clicked the dark button". Two copies inevitably drift apart. light-dark() (supported by all major browsers since 2024) needs each colour exactly once.

22  --sans: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;

--sans — the font for normal text: a font stack, a list of fonts in order of preference. system-ui means "the operating system's own interface font" (Segoe UI on Windows, San Francisco on Apple devices). If one font is missing, the browser tries the next. Using fonts already on the device means nothing has to be downloaded.

23  --mono: "Cascadia Code", ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas, monospace;

--mono — the font stack for code: monospaced fonts, where every character is the same width so code lines up. Cascadia Code ships with Windows Terminal; the others cover macOS and Linux.

24}

} — closes the :root rule.

25:root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
26:root[data-theme="dark"] { color-scheme: dark; }

The theme buttons' effect. When JavaScript sets data-theme="light" or "dark" on the page, these rules force that colour scheme. Every light-dark() above then follows it, regardless of the system setting. [data-theme="light"] is an attribute selector: it matches elements whose data-theme attribute has that value.

27*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; } — * means "every element", and ::before/::after are the invisible extra boxes CSS can attach to elements.

By default, an element's width doesn't include its padding and border, so a "300-pixel" box with padding ends up wider than 300 pixels — a classic source of layout confusion. border-box makes width mean total width. Almost every modern site starts with this line.

28body { margin: 0; background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); font: 16px/1.7 var(--sans); }

body { … } — the visible page:

  • margin: 0 removes the browser's default gap around the page;
  • the background and text colours come from the palette;
  • font: 16px/1.7 var(--sans) is shorthand for "16-pixel text, line spacing 1.7 times the text size, in the sans font".

The generous 1.7 line spacing makes long explanations easier to read.

29
30/* ---------- layout: sidebar + reading column ---------- */

/* … */ is a CSS comment — a note for humans that the browser ignores. Comments like this one divide the stylesheet into labelled sections.

31.shell { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 300px minmax(0, 1fr); min-height: 100vh; }

.shell — the two-column frame of the page. display: grid turns it into a grid; grid-template-columns defines two columns:

  • 300px for the sidebar;
  • minmax(0, 1fr) for the reading area. fr means "a fraction of the remaining space". The minmax(0, …) lets the column shrink below its content's natural width, so a wide code block scrolls inside its box instead of stretching the whole page sideways.

min-height: 100vh makes it at least as tall as the window. vh is a percentage of the viewport height.

32.side { position: sticky; top: 0; height: 100vh; overflow-y: auto; background: var(--bg-2);
33        border-right: 1px solid var(--border); padding: 18px 0 40px; }

.side — the sidebar:

  • position: sticky; top: 0 makes it stay pinned to the top of the window while the page scrolls;
  • height: 100vh with overflow-y: auto gives it its own scrollbar when the table of contents is taller than the window;
  • it has a panel-coloured background, a thin right border separating it from the content, and padding (inner space: 18 px at the top, 0 at the sides, 40 px at the bottom).
34.side-head { padding: 0 18px 12px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border); }

.side-head — the sidebar's top block (title and statistics): padding around it and a dividing line underneath.

35.side-head .name { font-weight: 700; font-size: 15px; }

.side-head .name — the book title in the sidebar. A space between two selectors means "inside": an element with class name inside .side-head. font-weight: 700 is bold.

36.side-head .meta { font: 11.5px/1.5 var(--mono); color: var(--text-3); margin-top: 4px; }

.side-head .meta — the small statistics line (word count, coverage): small monospaced text in the faint colour, with a little space above it.

37#q { width: calc(100% - 36px); margin: 12px 18px 8px; padding: 7px 10px; font-size: 13px;
38     border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }

#q — the sidebar's filter box (its id is q, for query). calc(100% - 36px) computes "full width minus 36 pixels", leaving room for the 18-pixel margins on each side. It has rounded corners (border-radius) and theme colours, so the box matches light and dark modes.

39.toc a { display: block; padding: 4px 18px; color: var(--text-2); text-decoration: none;
40         font-size: 13px; line-height: 1.4; border-left: 2px solid transparent; }

.toc a — the sidebar's links (a is the HTML anchor, i.e. link, element):

  • display: block makes each link a full-width line, so the whole line is clickable;
  • text-decoration: none removes underlines;
  • the transparent left border reserves space for the blue bar that marks the active section (line 45), so nothing shifts when it appears.
41.toc a:hover { color: var(--text); background: var(--bg-3); }

.toc a:hover — :hover is a pseudo-class meaning "while the mouse is over it". Hovered links get darker text and a light background.

42.toc a.h1 { font-weight: 650; color: var(--text); margin-top: 10px; }
43.toc a.h2 { padding-left: 30px; }
44.toc a.h3 { padding-left: 44px; font-size: 12.5px; color: var(--text-3); }

Indenting by heading level. build.py gives each link a class named after its heading's level:

  • h1 — parts: bold, with space above, so each part starts a visible group;
  • h2 — sections: indented 30 px;
  • h3 — sub-sections: indented 44 px, smaller and fainter.
45.toc a.active { color: var(--accent); border-left-color: var(--accent); background: var(--bg-3); }

.toc a.active — the link for the section you're currently reading: blue text, a blue left bar and a light background. JavaScript adds and removes the active class (lines 183–184).

46.toc a[hidden] { display: none; }

.toc a[hidden] { display: none; } — hides links that the filter has marked hidden.

Real world — a bug caught before it shipped

HTML's hidden attribute normally hides an element by itself. But line 39 says display: block for every sidebar link, and a page's own CSS beats the browser's built-in rules. So without this line, "hidden" links would stay visible and the filter would do nothing. This line restores hiding with a more specific selector. Mistakes like this are why every line deserves a careful look.

47main { padding: 48px 56px 160px; max-width: 1180px; min-width: 0; }

main — the reading column:

  • generous padding on each side (48 px top, 56 px sides, 160 px bottom, so the last line isn't stuck to the window edge);
  • max-width: 1180px, because lines of text longer than that are tiring to read;
  • min-width: 0, the same anti-stretching trick as on line 31.
48.topbar { position: fixed; top: 14px; right: 18px; display: flex; gap: 8px; z-index: 20; }

.topbar — the box holding the Top and Theme buttons. position: fixed pins it to the window itself — 14 px from the top, 18 px from the right — however far you scroll.

  • display: flex lines its children up in a row;
  • gap puts 8 px between them;
  • z-index: 20 stacks it above the page content, so text scrolls under the buttons rather than over them.
49.topbar button { border: 1px solid var(--border); background: var(--bg-2); color: var(--text-2);
50                 border-radius: 8px; padding: 6px 12px; font: 12.5px var(--sans); cursor: pointer; }

.topbar button — the buttons' look: a thin border, panel background, rounded corners, small text. cursor: pointer shows the hand-shaped pointer, signalling "clickable".

51.topbar button:hover { color: var(--text); }

On hover, the button's text darkens — a small sign that it reacts.

52#progress { position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto 0; height: 3px; background: var(--accent);
53            transform: scaleX(0); transform-origin: left; z-index: 30; }

#progress — the thin blue reading-progress bar at the very top of the window.

  • inset: 0 0 auto 0 pins its top, right and left edges to the window and leaves the bottom free, so it's a full-width strip 3 px tall.
  • transform: scaleX(0) shrinks it horizontally to nothing at first. JavaScript stretches it as you scroll (line 193).
  • transform-origin: left makes it grow from the left edge.
  • z-index: 30 keeps it above everything, including the buttons.
54
55/* ---------- typography ---------- */

Section comment: the rules that shape text.

56h1, h2, h3, h4 { line-height: 1.3; margin: 2em 0 .6em; letter-spacing: -.015em; scroll-margin-top: 24px; }

All headings, levels 1–4:

  • tight line spacing (1.3);
  • space above (2em — em means "times the current text size") and below (0.6em);
  • letters pulled very slightly closer (letter-spacing), which looks better at large sizes.

scroll-margin-top: 24px leaves a little space above a heading when you jump to it from the sidebar, so it doesn't sit flush against the window edge.

57h1 { font-size: 2.1em; padding-bottom: .3em; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border); }
58h2 { font-size: 1.5em; padding-bottom: .25em; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border); }

Part titles (h1) and section titles (h2): progressively smaller sizes, each with a thin underline drawn by border-bottom, like GitHub's documentation style.

59h3 { font-size: 1.2em; }
60h4 { font-size: 1.02em; color: var(--text-2); }

Smaller headings: h3 slightly larger than body text; h4 about body size, in the secondary colour.

61main > h1:first-child { margin-top: 0; }

main > h1:first-child — the very first heading of the page. > means "directly inside", and :first-child means "the first element in its parent". This removes its top margin, so the book doesn't start with an awkward gap.

62p, ul, ol, dl { margin: 0 0 1em; }

Paragraphs, lists and definition lists get no space above and 1em below — consistent rhythm between blocks.

63ul, ol { padding-left: 1.6em; }

Lists are indented 1.6em, which leaves room for bullets and numbers.

64li { margin: .3em 0; }

A little breathing room between list items.

65a { color: var(--accent); text-decoration: none; }
66a:hover { text-decoration: underline; }

Links: accent colour, no underline — except while hovered, so it's clear they're clickable.

67hr { border: 0; border-top: 1px solid var(--border); margin: 2.5em 0; }

hr — the horizontal divider line, restyled as a single thin border line with generous space around it.

68blockquote { margin: 0 0 1em; padding: .4em 1em; border-left: 4px solid var(--border); color: var(--text-2); }

blockquote — quoted text: a thick grey bar on the left and the secondary text colour.

69abbr[title] { text-decoration: underline dotted var(--text-3); cursor: help; }

abbr[title] — words with hover definitions (from abbreviations.md): a dotted underline, and cursor: help (a question-mark pointer) hinting "hover me for an explanation".

70dt { font-weight: 650; }
71dd { margin: 0 0 .8em 1.4em; }

Definition lists (used by the Glossary): the term (dt) in bold; its definition (dd) indented, with space below.

72
73/* ---------- code ---------- */

Section comment: code styling.

74code { font-family: var(--mono); font-size: .86em; background: var(--bg-3); padding: .15em .4em; border-radius: 6px;
75       font-variant-ligatures: none; }

code — short code inside a sentence, like build.py: monospaced, slightly smaller, on a tinted background with rounded corners, so it stands out from prose.

The second line, font-variant-ligatures: none, switches off ligatures. Some coding fonts, including Cascadia Code, merge certain character pairs into one symbol: -> is drawn as a single arrow →, and != as ≠. Experienced programmers like this, but a beginner reading → would hunt for an arrow key that doesn't exist. In this book, code must look exactly like what you would type.

code also applies inside code blocks (the pre code rule below only changes the background, padding and size), so this one setting covers every piece of code in the book.

76pre { background: var(--bg-2); border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 10px; padding: 14px 16px;
77      overflow-x: auto; margin: 0 0 1.2em; line-height: 1.55; font-size: 13px; }

pre — blocks of code. pre means pre-formatted: spaces and line breaks are kept exactly as written, which code needs.

  • Panel background, border, rounded corners and padding.
  • overflow-x: auto adds a sideways scrollbar for long lines instead of wrapping them; wrapped code is confusing.
  • Slightly taller line spacing and a 13 px font.
78pre code { background: none; padding: 0; font-size: inherit; }

pre code — code inside a code block shouldn't also get the inline-code background and padding from line 74, so this removes them. font-size: inherit takes the block's size instead of shrinking again.

79.hl .k, .hl .kn, .hl .kd, .hl .kr, .hl .kc, .hl .ow, .hl .o { color: light-dark(#cf222e, #ff7b72); }
80.hl .s, .hl .s1, .hl .s2, .hl .sd, .hl .sa, .hl .sb, .hl .sh, .hl .dl { color: light-dark(#0a3069, #a5d6ff); }
81.hl .c, .hl .c1, .hl .cm, .hl .ch, .hl .cs, .hl .cp { color: light-dark(#59636e, #8b949e); font-style: italic; }
82.hl .nf, .hl .fm, .hl .nd { color: light-dark(#8250df, #d2a8ff); }
83.hl .nc, .hl .nn { color: light-dark(#953800, #ffa657); }
84.hl .nb, .hl .bp, .hl .kt, .hl .na, .hl .se, .hl .si, .hl .sr, .hl .m, .hl .mi, .hl .mf, .hl .mh { color: light-dark(#0550ae, #79c0ff); }
85.hl .nt { color: light-dark(#116329, #7ee787); }

Syntax-highlighting colours. Pygments labels each piece of code with a short class name, and these rules colour the classes. Each uses light-dark() for both themes, with GitHub's code colours:

Classes Pygments meaning Colour
k kn kd kr kc ow o keywords (def, import, return, True), word operators (and, not), operators red
s s1 s2 sd sa sb sh dl strings of all kinds, and their quote marks dark blue / light blue
c c1 cm ch cs cp comments of all kinds grey italic
nf fm nd function names, special __methods__, decorators purple
nc nn class names, module names orange-brown
nb bp kt na se si sr m mi mf mh built-ins (len, self), types, attributes, escapes, numbers blue
nt HTML tag names green

Each selector starts with .hl (with a space), so only code inside highlighted boxes is coloured.

86
87/* ---------- tables ---------- */

Section comment: tables.

88.tw { overflow-x: auto; margin: 0 0 1.3em; border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 10px; }

.tw — the wrapper build.py puts around every table (its line 240). On narrow screens it scrolls sideways, and it gives the table a rounded border.

89table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; font-size: 14px; }

table — full width, with border-collapse: collapse so neighbouring cells share one border line instead of drawing two.

90th, td { padding: 8px 13px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border); text-align: left; vertical-align: top; }

th, td — header cells and data cells: padding, a line underneath, text aligned left and to the top. Top alignment matters when one cell has more lines than its neighbours.

91th { background: var(--bg-2); font-weight: 650; }

Header cells get a panel background and semi-bold text.

92tbody tr:last-child td { border-bottom: 0; }

The last row has no bottom line, because the wrapper's own border is already there. Without this, the bottom edge would look doubled.

93
94/* ---------- callout boxes ("!!! kid" etc. in the chapters) ---------- */

Section comment: the coloured callout boxes, written !!! kid "Title" in chapters.

95.admonition { --c: var(--text-3); --icon: "ℹ️"; border-left: 4px solid var(--c); border-radius: 0 10px 10px 0;
96              background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--c) 9%, transparent); padding: 12px 16px; margin: 0 0 1.2em; }

.admonition — the shared look of every box. It sets two local variables with defaults:

  • --c — the box's colour (default: faint grey);
  • --icon — its emoji (default: ℹ️).

The box has a thick left border in --c, rounded right corners, and a background made by color-mix(in srgb, var(--c) 9%, transparent) — "9 % of the box colour, the rest see-through". That gives a soft tint matching the border in both themes, with no extra colour definitions.

97.admonition > :last-child { margin-bottom: 0; }

Removes the bottom margin of the box's last element, so the space inside is even at top and bottom.

98.admonition-title { font-weight: 700; margin-bottom: .35em; }

.admonition-title — the box's title line: bold, with a little space below.

99.admonition-title::before { content: var(--icon) "  "; }

.admonition-title::before — a pseudo-element: content CSS inserts before the title text. content: var(--icon) " " inserts the box's emoji followed by two spaces. The icon therefore comes from CSS, so chapter authors never type it.

100.admonition.kid { --c: var(--purple); --icon: "🧒"; }
101.admonition.key { --c: var(--accent); --icon: "🔑"; }
102.admonition.why { --c: var(--ok); --icon: "🤔"; }
103.admonition.alt { --c: var(--text-3); --icon: "🔀"; }
104.admonition.warn { --c: var(--warn); --icon: "⚠️"; }
105.admonition.try { --c: var(--ok); --icon: "🧪"; }
106.admonition.word { --c: var(--accent); --icon: "📖"; }
107.admonition.real { --c: var(--warn); --icon: "🌍"; }
108.admonition.honest { --c: var(--danger); --icon: "🙋"; }

One line per box type, each setting only its colour and icon:

Box Colour Icon
kid purple 🧒
key blue 🔑
why green 🤔
alt grey 🔀
warn amber ⚠️
try green 🧪
word blue 📖
real amber 🌍
honest red 🙋

Because the shared look lives on lines 95–99, adding a new kind of box takes a single line.

109
110/* ---------- line-by-line walkthroughs ---------- */

Section comment: the line-by-line walkthroughs — the part you are looking at right now.

111.walk { border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 12px; margin: 0 0 2.2em; overflow: hidden; }

.walk — the frame around one file's walkthrough: a border with rounded corners, and space below. overflow: hidden clips the inner rows to the rounded corners, so square corners don't poke out.

112.whead { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap: 6px 14px; padding: 10px 16px;
113         background: var(--bg-3); font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-2); }

.whead — the header bar showing the file path, line count and coverage. display: flex lines the pieces up in a row, flex-wrap: wrap lets them flow onto a second line on narrow screens, and gap spaces them.

114.whead code { background: none; padding: 0; font-weight: 700; color: var(--text); }

.whead code — the file path in the header bar: no inline-code background (the whole bar is already tinted), bold, in the main text colour.

115.wintro { padding: 12px 16px 2px; }

.wintro — the file's introduction, with padding to line it up with the rows below.

116.wrow { display: grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 11fr) minmax(0, 9fr); border-top: 1px solid var(--border); }

.wrow — one row: code on the left, explanation on the right. It's a two-column grid in an 11 : 9 ratio, so the code gets slightly more room. minmax(0, …) again stops long lines from stretching the layout. Each row has a line above it.

117.wrow pre { margin: 0; border: 0; border-radius: 0; padding: 10px 12px; }

Inside a row, the code box loses its own margin, border and rounded corners — the row and frame provide those — and gets slightly tighter padding.

118.wnote { padding: 10px 16px; font-size: 14.5px; }

.wnote — the explanation side: padding, and text a little smaller than the main text so dense explanations stay compact.

119.wnote > :last-child { margin-bottom: 0; }

Removes the bottom margin of the last element in each explanation, so short notes don't end with a gap.

120.wrow.blank pre { padding-block: 0; }

.wrow.blank pre — rows containing only blank lines get no vertical padding. Two class names written together with no space (.wrow.blank) mean "an element that has both classes".

121.wrow.blank .wnote { display: none; }

.wrow.blank .wnote { display: none; } — rows that contain only blank lines have nothing to explain, so their (empty) explanation box is removed entirely. Without this, the narrow one-column layout showed an empty box with a dashed line under every blank line — visual noise that made the real explanations harder to follow.

122.wrow.missing { box-shadow: inset 4px 0 var(--danger); }

.wrow.missing — rows with unexplained code get a red bar down their left edge. box-shadow: inset 4px 0 var(--danger) draws a "shadow" 4 px wide inside the left edge, without changing the row's size.

123.ln { display: inline-block; min-width: 3ch; margin-right: 1.5ch; text-align: right; color: var(--text-3); user-select: none; }

.ln — the line numbers next to the code:

  • inline-block with a minimum width of three characters, right-aligned, so numbers line up whether they have one digit or three;
  • faint colour, so they don't compete with the code;
  • user-select: none stops them being copied when you select and copy code from the page.
124.todo { color: var(--danger); font-weight: 600; }

.todo — the red, bold "Not explained yet." message.

125.pill { display: inline-block; padding: 1px 9px; border-radius: 99px; font: 600 11.5px/1.7 var(--mono); white-space: nowrap; }

.pill — the small rounded labels ("complete", "stale"…). border-radius: 99px is larger than any pill's height, which makes the ends perfectly round. white-space: nowrap stops a two-word label such as "not explained" from breaking across two lines.

126.pill.ok { color: var(--ok); background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--ok) 13%, transparent); }
127.pill.warn { color: var(--warn); background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--warn) 14%, transparent); }
128.pill.bad { color: var(--danger); background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--danger) 12%, transparent); }

The pill colours: green for good, amber for in progress, red for problems. Each has a soft tinted background made with color-mix, as on line 96.

129footer { margin-top: 4em; color: var(--text-3); font: 12px var(--mono); }

footer — the small grey line at the very end showing when the book was built.

130
131@media (max-width: 1100px) { .wrow { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } .wnote { border-top: 1px dashed var(--border); } }

@media (max-width: 1100px) — a media query: rules that apply only when the condition is true, here "the window is 1100 px wide or less". On such screens, walkthrough rows switch to one column (code above, explanation below), with a dashed line between them. Side-by-side columns would be too narrow to read.

132@media (max-width: 900px) {
133  .shell { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
134  .side { position: static; height: auto; border-right: 0; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border); }
135  main { padding: 28px 16px 100px; }
136}

On screens 900 px wide or less (tablets and phones):

  • the page becomes a single column;
  • the sidebar stops being sticky, takes its natural height, and sits above the content with a line below it instead of beside it;
  • the side padding shrinks to 16 px, so text uses the small screen fully.
137@media print { .side, .topbar, #progress { display: none; } .shell { display: block; } }

When printing (@media print), the sidebar, buttons and progress bar are hidden and the grid is switched off, so paper gets just the content.

138</style>

</style> — the end of the CSS.

139</head>

</head> — the end of the behind-the-scenes section.

140<body>

<body> — the start of everything visible.

141<div id="progress"></div>

<div id="progress"></div> — the empty element that becomes the progress bar. A div is a general-purpose box with no meaning of its own; its look comes entirely from CSS (lines 52–53).

142<div class="topbar"><button id="top" type="button">Top</button><button id="theme" type="button">Theme</button></div>

The two buttons. type="button" says plainly that they don't submit any form. Each has an id so JavaScript can find it.

143<div class="shell">

<div class="shell"> — the two-column grid from line 31.

144  <aside class="side">

<aside class="side"> — the sidebar. <aside> is a semantic element: it tells browsers and screen readers "this is supporting content beside the main content", which a plain div would not.

145    <div class="side-head"><div class="name">{{TITLE}}</div><div class="meta">{{META}}</div></div>

The sidebar header. {{TITLE}} and {{META}} are filled by build.py with the title and the "words · files · coverage" statistics.

146    <input id="q" type="search" placeholder="Filter sections (Ctrl+K)" autocomplete="off" aria-label="Filter sections">

The filter box:

  • type="search" gives a search field (on many browsers, with a clear button);
  • placeholder is the grey hint text shown while it's empty;
  • autocomplete="off" stops the browser from suggesting old entries;
  • aria-label gives screen readers a name for the box, because it has no visible label. ARIA is a set of attributes that make pages accessible to people using assistive technology.
147    <nav class="toc">{{TOC}}</nav>

<nav class="toc">{{TOC}}</nav> — the table of contents. <nav> marks a navigation block for assistive technology. {{TOC}} becomes the list of links.

148  </aside>

</aside> — the sidebar ends.

149  <main>

<main> — the main content. A page should have exactly one <main>; screen readers offer a shortcut to jump straight to it.

150{{BODY}}

{{BODY}} — the entire book goes here: every chapter, walkthrough and table. It sits alone on its line at the far left so the inserted HTML isn't shifted by indentation. build.py fills it last, deliberately (see its line 264).

151    <footer>{{SUBTITLE}} · built {{BUILT}}</footer>

The footer, filled with the subtitle and the build time.

152  </main>
153</div>

Close <main>, then the shell grid.

154<script>

<script> — everything from here to </script> is JavaScript. It sits at the very end of the page, so when it runs, all the elements it looks for already exist.

155(() => {

(() => { — the start of an immediately invoked function. () => { … } defines a small unnamed function (an arrow function); wrapping it in parentheses and adding () at the end (line 197) runs it straight away. Every name created inside stays private to it and can't clash with anything else on the page.

156  const root = document.documentElement;

const root = document.documentElement; — const creates a name that won't be reassigned. document is the browser's object representing the whole page, and documentElement is its top element, <html> — the same element CSS calls :root.

157  const remember = (value) => { try { localStorage.setItem("z2h-theme", value); } catch {} };

remember — a tiny function that saves the chosen theme in localStorage, the browser's small per-site storage that survives closing the tab. It is wrapped in try { … } catch {} because storage can be unavailable — some private-browsing modes, or files opened in restricted viewers throw an error — and a failure to remember must never break the button itself.

158  try { const saved = localStorage.getItem("z2h-theme"); if (saved) root.dataset.theme = saved; } catch {}

On page load, restore the saved theme. Read "z2h-theme" from storage. If something was saved, set the page's data-theme attribute to it. root.dataset.theme is JavaScript's way of reading and writing a data-theme attribute. Again it is wrapped in try, for the same reason.
