159  document.getElementById("theme").addEventListener("click", () => {

When the Theme button is clicked… document.getElementById("theme") finds the button by its id. addEventListener("click", …) says "whenever it is clicked, run this function".

160    const dark = root.dataset.theme ? root.dataset.theme === "dark" : matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches;

…work out whether the page is dark right now. If a theme was chosen explicitly, it's dark if that choice is "dark". Otherwise, ask the system: matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches is true when the operating system is in dark mode. The ? : is JavaScript's conditional expression: condition ? if true : if false.

161    root.dataset.theme = dark ? "light" : "dark";

…switch to the opposite. Setting data-theme triggers the CSS on lines 25–26, and every colour flips instantly.

162    remember(root.dataset.theme);

…and remember the choice for next time.

163  });

}); — closes the click handler, then the addEventListener call.

164  document.getElementById("top").addEventListener("click", () => scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "smooth" }));

The Top button: when clicked, scroll the window to the top. behavior: "smooth" glides there instead of jumping.

165
166  const filter = document.getElementById("q");

filter — the search box, found by its id.

167  const links = [...document.querySelectorAll(".toc a")];

links — every link in the table of contents. querySelectorAll(".toc a") finds all elements matching a CSS selector. [... ] with three dots copies the results into a real array (JavaScript's list), which has more handy methods.

168  filter.addEventListener("input", () => {

Every time the filter's text changes (each typed or deleted character fires an "input" event)…

169    const wanted = filter.value.toLowerCase().trim();

…take the typed text, lower-cased and trimmed of spaces, so matching ignores capital letters.

170    for (const link of links) link.hidden = wanted !== "" && !link.textContent.toLowerCase().includes(wanted);

…and for each link, set hidden to true if something was typed and the link's text doesn't contain it. An empty box therefore shows every link. !== means "is not equal to"; ! means "not".

171  });

Closes the input handler.

172  addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {

Keyboard shortcuts: listen to every key pressed anywhere on the page. event describes the key press.

173    if ((event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey) && event.key.toLowerCase() === "k") { event.preventDefault(); filter.focus(); filter.select(); }

Ctrl + K (or Cmd + K on a Mac, the "meta" key) jumps to the filter box. preventDefault() stops the browser's own Ctrl + K action (in some browsers, focusing the address bar). focus() puts the cursor in the box, and select() highlights any old text so typing replaces it.

174    if (event.key === "Escape" && document.activeElement === filter) { filter.value = ""; filter.dispatchEvent(new Event("input")); filter.blur(); }

Escape while typing in the filter: clear it, announce the change (dispatchEvent(new Event("input")) makes the line-168 handler run, so all links reappear), and leave the box (blur).

175  });

Closes the keyboard handler.

176
177  const side = document.querySelector(".side");

side — the sidebar element, needed to scroll it on line 185.

178  const byId = new Map(links.map((link) => [decodeURIComponent(link.hash.slice(1)), link]));

byId — a Map (a dictionary) from a heading's id to its sidebar link. link.hash is the #part-0-absolute-basics part of the link's address; .slice(1) drops the #. decodeURIComponent turns any encoded characters (%20 and similar) back into normal text, so the key matches the heading's real id.

179  const spy = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {

The "section spy". An IntersectionObserver is a browser feature that tells you when watched elements enter or leave the visible area. It's far cheaper than checking positions on every scroll. The function given to it runs with a list of entries, one per watched heading that changed.

180    for (const entry of entries) {

For each change…

181      const link = entry.isIntersecting && byId.get(entry.target.id);

…if the heading has just become visible, look up its sidebar link. a && b gives b only if a is true; otherwise it gives false.

182      if (!link) continue;

If there's no link — the heading went out of view, or isn't listed in the sidebar — skip to the next entry.

183      links.forEach((other) => other.classList.remove("active"));

Remove the active class from every link…

184      link.classList.add("active");

…and add it to this one. The blue highlight from CSS line 45 moves to the section you're reading.

185      if (side.scrollHeight > side.clientHeight) side.scrollTo({ top: link.offsetTop - side.clientHeight / 3 });

Keep the active link in view. If the sidebar has its own scrollbar (its content is taller than its visible height), scroll it so the active link sits about a third of the way down. On phones the sidebar isn't scrollable, so nothing moves — which also stops the page from jumping back to the top.

186    }

Closes the loop.

187  }, { rootMargin: "0px 0px -75% 0px" });

Observer options. rootMargin: "0px 0px -75% 0px" shrinks the "visible area" to the top quarter of the window, so a heading counts as "current" once it reaches the upper part of the screen. That matches where your eyes are when you start a new section.

188  document.querySelectorAll("main :is(h1, h2, h3)[id]").forEach((heading) => spy.observe(heading));

Start watching every h1, h2 and h3 inside <main> that has an id. :is(h1, h2, h3) is CSS shorthand for "any of these".

189
190  const bar = document.getElementById("progress");

bar — the progress-bar element.

191  const onScroll = () => {

onScroll — a function, stored in a constant, that updates the bar.

192    const max = root.scrollHeight - innerHeight;

max — how far the page can scroll: the full height of the page (scrollHeight) minus the height of the window (innerHeight).

193    bar.style.transform = `scaleX(${max > 0 ? scrollY / max : 0})`;

Stretch the bar. scrollY / max is the fraction scrolled so far, from 0 at the top to 1 at the bottom; scaleX stretches the bar by that fraction. The text in back-ticks is a template literal: ${…} inside it inserts a value, like Python's f-strings. The max > 0 ? check avoids dividing by zero on a page too short to scroll.

194  };

Closes the onScroll function.

195  addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });

Run onScroll whenever the page scrolls. { passive: true } promises the browser that this function will never cancel the scroll, so the browser can scroll smoothly without waiting for it.

196  onScroll();

Run it once straight away, so the bar is right even before the first scroll — for example when the page is reloaded halfway down.

197})();

})(); — closes the immediately invoked function from line 153 and runs it.

198</script>

</script> — the end of the JavaScript.

199</body>
200</html>

</body> and </html> — the end of the visible content, and the end of the page.

The builder's own tests (tests/test_build.py) are walked through in §5.0.7, alongside the other Phase 0 files.

Coverage ledger

This table is generated by the program that builds the book, not typed by hand. Every time the book is built, the builder:

  1. walks through every folder of the project and lists every code and configuration file (ignoring folders full of downloaded libraries or generated files);
  2. for each file, finds its walkthrough and counts how many non-blank lines have an explanation;
  3. compares the file's current fingerprint with the fingerprint recorded when it was explained.

A file is complete only when every non-blank line is explained and the code has not changed since. Blank lines are not counted, because there is nothing on them to explain.

Some files are deliberately left out:

  • the generated book itself (zero_to_hero.html);
  • lockfiles (uv.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml), which are long machine-written lists of exact library versions. We explain what lockfiles are (§0.17) rather than explaining thousands of machine-written lines.

Glossary

Every technical word used in the book, in alphabetical order. The section in brackets is where the idea is first explained.

Age assurance
Any method of establishing someone's age with some level of confidence. The umbrella term for verification, estimation and inference. (§1.5)
Age estimation
Guessing age from a physical characteristic, usually the face. Fast and private, but it always carries some error. (§1.5)
Age inference
Deducing age from other facts, such as holding a credit card. (§1.5)
Age verification
Establishing age from an authoritative source, such as an ID document or a digital-ID app. (§1.5)
API
Application Programming Interface. A menu of requests one program offers to other programs. Each request it accepts is an endpoint. (§0.11)
Argument
A value handed to a function or a command. In python build.py --strict, --strict is an argument. (Part X)
Audit log
A permanent, ordered record of important events (who changed what, when). Ours is tamper-evident: each entry includes a fingerprint of the previous one. (§3.3)
Backend
The programs that run on servers, out of the user's sight. (§0.10)
Biometric data
Information about a person's body, such as their face. (§1.11)
Bit, byte
A bit is a single 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits, enough for a number from 0 to 255. (§0.1)
Buffer / challenge age
An extra margin above the legal age. For example, "pass only if the estimate is 25 or more, for a legal age of 18". (§1.8)
Certificate
A digital document, signed by a trusted organisation, proving a server's identity for HTTPS. (§0.9)
Client
A program that asks a server for something — for example, a web browser. (§0.7)
Clopper–Pearson bound
A method for working out, from a test result like "6 out of 600", the worst plausible true rate at a chosen confidence level. (§3.3)
Code / source code
The human-readable instructions of a program, written in a programming language. (§0.3)
Commit
A saved snapshot of a project in Git, with a message explaining the change. (§0.15)
Compiler
A program that translates a whole program into machine code before it runs. (§0.4)
Container
A running copy of a Docker image. (§0.14)
Coverage
In this book: the share of a file's non-blank lines that have an explanation. (Part X)
Database
A program that stores data permanently and answers questions about it quickly and safely. (§0.12)
Dataclass
A Python shortcut for defining a class that mainly holds data. (Part X)
Deploy
To copy a program onto a server and start it there. (§0.13)
Dictionary (dict)
A Python collection of labelled values, looked up by key: {"title": "Dwarpal"}. (Part X)
DNS
Domain Name System. The internet's phone book, turning names into IP addresses. (§0.6)
Docker / image / volume
Docker packs a program with everything it needs into an image. A volume is a folder that survives when containers are thrown away. (§0.14)
Domain
A human-friendly internet name, such as dwarpal.example. (§0.13)
Encoding
The agreement that maps characters to numbers. We always use UTF-8. (§0.2)
Endpoint
One specific request an API accepts, identified by a method and a path, such as POST /v1/verification-sessions. (§0.11)
Extension (file)
The letters after the last dot in a file name, such as .py, hinting at the kind of file. (§0.2)
Fail closed
When something goes wrong, the system chooses the safe answer ("retry" or "step-up"), never "pass". (§1.13)
False-adult rate
The share of children near the age limit whom the system wrongly lets through. Our most important safety number. (§1.7)
Fingerprint (hash)
A short code computed from a file's contents. Change one character and the fingerprint changes completely. (Part X)
Frontend
Everything that runs in the user's browser. (§0.10)
Function
A named, reusable block of code that takes inputs and gives back a result. (Part X)
Git, GitHub
Git records a project's history as commits. GitHub stores Git projects online. (§0.15)
GPU
Graphics Processing Unit. A chip that performs thousands of calculations at once — ideal for AI. (§0.1)
Hosting
Renting computers in a data centre to run your website. (§0.13)
HTML, CSS, JavaScript
The skeleton, the clothes and the muscles of a web page. (§0.10)
HTTP, HTTPS
The protocol browsers and servers use to talk. HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS encryption. (§0.8, §0.9)
Injection attack
Bypassing the camera completely, for example with software that pretends to be a camera. (§1.10)
Interpreter
A program that runs code by reading it line by line. (§0.4)
IP address, port
An IP address identifies a computer on a network (the building). A port identifies one program on it (the flat). (§0.6)
JSON
A plain-text format for structured data, with six kinds of value. (§0.11)
Library / package
Code written by someone else that you can reuse. (§0.17)
Licence
The legal rules for what you may do with someone else's code, model or data. (§0.16)
Liveness
Evidence that a real, live person is in front of the camera at that moment. (§1.10)
localhost
A name that always means "this same computer". (§0.6)
Lockfile
An automatically generated list of the exact version of every library a project uses. (§0.17)
Markdown
A simple way of writing formatted text with symbols like # for headings and ** for bold. This book is written in it. (Part X)
Method (HTTP)
The kind of action an HTTP request asks for: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE. (§0.8)
Model (AI)
A mathematical function with many adjustable numbers (parameters), tuned from examples so that it produces useful answers. (§1.6, Part 2)
Mojibake
Garbled text caused by reading a file with the wrong encoding. (§0.2)
Pinning
Recording the exact version of a library, so the project builds identically everywhere. (§0.17)
Pixel
One dot of a digital image, stored as red, green and blue numbers. (§0.1)
Presentation attack
Showing the camera something that isn't a live face: a photo, a screen, a mask. (§1.10)
Program
A set of instructions for a computer. (§0.3)
Protocol
An agreed set of rules for how messages are formatted and exchanged. (§0.8)
Proxy (attack)
An adult doing the age check on a child's behalf. (§1.10)
Regular expression (regex)
A tiny pattern language for finding text, such as "two @ signs followed by a number". (Part X)
Relying party
The website or app that relies on our age answer. (§3.3)
Request / response
One message from a client, and the server's reply. (§0.8)
Risk budget
The maximum share of dangerous mistakes a policy accepts, for example "at most 2 % of 13–17-year-olds may pass". (§3.3)
Server
A program (or the computer running it) that waits for requests and answers them. (§0.7)
Shell / terminal
The window and program where you type commands. (§0.5)
Signed token
A small digital message sealed with a private key, so anyone with the public key can check that it is genuine and unchanged. (§3.3)
Status code
The three-digit number at the start of an HTTP response: 2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. (§0.8)
Step-up
Moving to a stronger age-check method when the quick one is unsure. (§1.9)
Table (database)
Rows (things) and columns (their properties), like a spreadsheet. (§0.12)
Template
A file with blanks (here written like {{TITLE}}) that a program fills in. (Part X)
TLS
Transport Layer Security. The encryption behind HTTPS. (§0.9)
Transaction
A group of database changes that either all happen or none happen. (§0.12)
UTF-8
The universal text encoding, able to store every character in every language. (§0.2)
Version
A label like 3.11.1 (major.minor.patch) identifying one release of a library. (§0.17)
Virtual environment (venv)
A private folder holding a specific Python and specific libraries for one project, so projects don't interfere with each other. (Part X)
Walkthrough
In this book: a file that explains another file line by line. (Part X)
Waterfall
Trying the quickest, most private age check first, and moving to stronger methods only when needed. (§1.9)
Building a privacy-first AI age-assurance system, starting from absolutely nothing · built 2026-10-24 12:16 UTC
